options.why: Pyrazinamide decreases renal excretion of uric acid and can cause hyperuricemia and gout; adult reference ranges are roughly 2.5 to 7 mg/dL, varying by lab and sex.

options.text: Serum creatine kinase
options.why: Creatine kinase reflects muscle injury; the presentation is typical of gout from hyperuricemia.

takeaway: Pyrazinamide raises uric acid and can trigger gout; it is also hepatotoxic.

stem: During a monthly visit, a client taking ethambutol says, 'Lately red and green traffic lights look almost the same to me.' What should the nurse do?

options.text: Reassure the client that this is an expected, harmless effect.
options.why: Color vision change is a sign of potentially serious optic toxicity, not a harmless effect.

options.text: Recommend that the client wear sunglasses outdoors.
options.why: Sunglasses do not address drug-induced optic neuritis.

options.text: Advise the client to take the medication with food from now on.
options.why: Taking ethambutol with food may reduce GI upset but does not prevent or treat visual toxicity.

options.text: Instruct the client to hold the next dose and notify the provider promptly about possible optic neuritis.
options.why: Ethambutol can cause optic neuritis, often first seen as decreased red-green color discrimination or blurred vision; stopping the drug early usually allows recovery.

takeaway: Ethambutol requires baseline and regular vision checks (acuity and red-green color); report any visual change at once.

stem: A client who takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation, with a stable INR of 2.5, is starting rifampin as part of treatment for active tuberculosis. Which change should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: The INR is likely to fall, so INR will be checked more often and the warfarin dose will probably need to increase.
options.why: Rifampin is a strong inducer of the liver enzymes that metabolize warfarin, lowering its effect and the INR; when rifampin is later stopped, the INR can rise.

options.text: The INR is likely to rise, increasing the risk of bleeding.
options.why: Rifampin speeds warfarin metabolism, which lowers rather than raises the INR.

options.text: No change is expected because the drugs do not interact.
options.why: This is a major, well-documented interaction.

options.text: Warfarin must be stopped for the full course of TB treatment.
options.why: Anticoagulation is still needed; the dose is adjusted with closer INR monitoring.

takeaway: Rifampin induces liver enzymes and lowers levels of warfarin, hormonal contraceptives and many other drugs.

stem: The health department arranges directly observed therapy (DOT) for a client with active pulmonary tuberculosis. The client asks why someone needs to watch each dose. Which explanation by the nurse is best?

options.text: 'DOT is used only for people who have had problems with substance use.'
options.why: DOT is a standard adherence strategy for active TB, not a judgment about the client.

options.text: 'Taking every dose for the whole course prevents the TB from coming back and from becoming resistant to the medicines.'
options.why: Incomplete or irregular treatment leads to relapse and drug-resistant TB; DOT supports adherence and protects the client and community.

options.text: 'Someone needs to watch for an allergic reaction after each dose.'
options.why: Monitoring for adverse effects happens during DOT, but its main purpose is adherence.

options.text: 'Once you are no longer contagious after 2 weeks, you can stop the medicine.'
options.why: Treatment of active TB lasts months (commonly 6 months); becoming noninfectious does not mean the disease is cured.

takeaway: Directly observed therapy ensures adherence to the full TB regimen, preventing relapse and drug resistance.

stem: A hospitalized client with drug-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis is receiving standard four-drug therapy. Which finding best supports discontinuing airborne isolation?

options.text: The client has been afebrile for 24 hours.
options.why: Resolution of fever alone does not show that the client is no longer infectious.

options.text: One sputum smear collected on day 3 of therapy is negative.
options.why: A single negative smear this early is not sufficient; three consecutive negatives are required.

options.text: The client has received effective therapy for about 2 weeks, the cough has improved, and three consecutive sputum AFB smears are negative.
options.why: CDC criteria for ending isolation include adequate therapy for about 2 weeks, clinical improvement, and three consecutive negative sputum smears collected 8 to 24 hours apart, including one early-morning specimen.

options.text: A repeat chest x-ray shows an unchanged cavitary lesion.
options.why: Imaging does not determine infectiousness, and cavitary disease is associated with high bacterial loads.

takeaway: End TB airborne isolation only after about 2 weeks of effective therapy, clinical improvement and three consecutive negative sputum smears.

stem: A client in airborne isolation for suspected pulmonary tuberculosis must be transported to radiology. Which action by the nurse is correct?

options.text: Place a fit-tested N95 respirator on the client.
options.why: N95 respirators protect the wearer from inhaling particles; a surgical mask is used on the client for source control.

options.text: Transport the client without a mask as long as the staff wear N95 respirators.
options.why: An unmasked infectious client exposes everyone along the route.

options.text: Cancel the imaging until isolation is discontinued.
options.why: Medically necessary tests should not be delayed; precautions allow safe transport.

options.text: Place a surgical mask on the client for the transport.
options.why: A surgical mask on the client contains respiratory droplets at the source during transport; staff in the isolation room wear fit-tested N95 respirators.

takeaway: During transport, the client with airborne-spread TB wears a surgical mask; staff in the room wear N95 respirators.

stem: The nurse reads a tuberculin skin test 60 hours after placement on a client with HIV infection. The site shows 6 mm of induration and 15 mm of redness. How should the nurse interpret the result?

options.text: Positive, because induration of 5 mm or more is positive in a person with HIV.
options.why: For people with HIV and other high-risk groups, 5 mm of induration is the cutoff; the test was read within the 48 to 72 hour window.

options.text: Negative, because the induration is less than 10 mm.
options.why: The 10 mm cutoff applies to moderate-risk groups such as recent immigrants from high-prevalence countries and residents or employees of high-risk congregate settings, not to people with HIV.

options.text: Positive, because the redness is larger than 10 mm.
options.why: Only induration is measured; redness is not used to interpret the test.

options.text: Invalid, because the test must be read at exactly 24 hours.
options.why: Tuberculin skin tests are read 48 to 72 hours after placement.

takeaway: Measure induration, not redness, at 48 to 72 hours: 5 mm is positive for people with HIV or immunosuppression, 10 mm for moderate-risk groups, 15 mm for no risk factors.

stem: Ten minutes after an IV cefazolin infusion starts, a client reports throat tightness and has hives, wheezing and a BP of 82/48 mm Hg. The nurse stops the infusion and calls for help. Which medication should the nurse anticipate giving first?

options.text: Diphenhydramine 50 mg IV
options.why: Antihistamines relieve hives and itching but do not reverse hypotension or airway obstruction and should never delay epinephrine.

options.text: Epinephrine 0.5 mg (1 mg/mL) IM into the anterolateral thigh
options.why: Epinephrine is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis; it reverses bronchospasm, vasodilation and airway edema. The adult IM dose is 0.3 to 0.5 mg of the 1 mg/mL solution.

options.text: Methylprednisolone 125 mg IV
options.why: Corticosteroids have a slow onset and are not first-line for anaphylaxis.

options.text: Albuterol by nebulizer
options.why: Albuterol may help residual bronchospasm but does not treat shock or laryngeal edema.

takeaway: In anaphylaxis, give IM epinephrine first; antihistamines and corticosteroids are adjuncts only.

stem: A client who takes metoprolol for hypertension has anaphylaxis after a bee sting. After two doses of IM epinephrine and IV fluid boluses, the client remains hypotensive. Which medication is specifically indicated because of the client's beta-blocker therapy?

options.text: Diphenhydramine IV
options.why: Diphenhydramine is an adjunct for cutaneous symptoms and is not specific to beta-blocker–related resistance.

options.text: Famotidine IV
options.why: H2 blockers are adjuncts and do not overcome beta-blockade.

options.text: Glucagon IV
options.why: Beta-blockade can make anaphylaxis resistant to epinephrine; glucagon raises heart rate and contractility through a pathway that does not depend on beta receptors.

options.text: Methylprednisolone IV
options.why: Corticosteroids act slowly and do not reverse beta-blocker–related refractory hypotension.

takeaway: Clients on beta-blockers may not respond to epinephrine in anaphylaxis; glucagon is the specific rescue drug.

stem: The nurse teaches the parent of a 9-year-old with a peanut allergy how to use an epinephrine autoinjector. Which statement by the parent indicates understanding of what to do after giving the injection?

options.text: 'Once the shot is in, I'll have my child stand up and walk around so the medicine spreads faster.'
options.why: Standing or walking during anaphylaxis can cause a sudden, dangerous drop in blood pressure; the child should lie down with the legs raised (or sit up if breathing is difficult) while emergency help is on the way.

options.text: 'Next time the symptoms seem mild, I'll give diphenhydramine instead of the autoinjector.'
options.why: Antihistamines do not treat anaphylaxis; epinephrine should be given without delay when anaphylaxis is suspected.

options.text: 'If my child isn't better, I'll wait an hour before using the second autoinjector.'
options.why: A second dose may be given in about 5 to 15 minutes if symptoms persist or worsen; waiting an hour is dangerous.

options.text: 'I'll call 911 and have my child checked in the emergency department even if the symptoms improve.'
options.why: Epinephrine wears off in minutes and symptoms can recur (biphasic reaction), so the device instructions direct the family to get emergency medical care after every use.

takeaway: After an epinephrine autoinjector is used, always activate emergency services; a second dose may be needed within 5 to 15 minutes.

stem: A client with COPD and known chronic hypercapnia is admitted with an exacerbation. On oxygen at 4 L/min by nasal cannula, the SpO2 is 98%, and the client has become increasingly drowsy. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Reduce the oxygen flow to keep the SpO2 at 88% to 92% and notify the provider so an arterial blood gas can be obtained.
options.why: In clients at risk of hypercapnia, excessive oxygen can worsen CO2 retention; new drowsiness suggests rising PaCO2. Titrating to 88% to 92% and checking an ABG is the appropriate response.

options.text: Increase the oxygen to 6 L/min to prevent hypoxemia.
options.why: The client is already overoxygenated; more oxygen may worsen hypercapnia.

options.text: Change to a nonrebreather mask.
options.why: A nonrebreather delivers a high FiO2, which is not indicated with an SpO2 of 98% and may worsen CO2 retention.

options.text: Let the client sleep undisturbed, because rest reduces oxygen demand.
options.why: Increasing drowsiness in this setting may be CO2 narcosis and must be assessed, not ignored.

takeaway: For COPD with chronic hypercapnia, target SpO2 of 88% to 92%; new drowsiness on oxygen suggests rising PaCO2.

stem: A client using home oxygen by nasal cannula complains of dry, cracked nostrils. Which product should the nurse recommend?

options.text: Petroleum jelly applied to the nares
options.why: Petroleum-based products are flammable in an oxygen-enriched environment and can cause burns.

options.text: A water-based lubricant applied to the nares
options.why: Water-based lubricants soothe the nares and are not flammable, making them safe to use with oxygen.

options.text: A mentholated oil-based chest rub around the nose
options.why: Oil-based products near the oxygen source are a fire risk.

options.text: Removing the cannula for several hours each day to let the nose heal
options.why: Interrupting prescribed oxygen can cause hypoxemia; the dryness should be treated safely instead.

takeaway: With oxygen therapy, use water-based lubricants only; avoid petroleum or oil-based products near the face.

stem: A 4-year-old weighing 18 kg is prescribed prednisolone 1 mg/kg orally once daily for an asthma exacerbation. The available oral solution is 15 mg/5 mL. How many mL should the nurse give for each dose? (Round to the nearest tenth if needed.)

options.text: 3.6 mL
options.why: This results from dividing 18 by 5 instead of using the 15 mg per 5 mL concentration.

options.text: 1.2 mL
options.why: This results from dividing 18 mg by 15 mg and forgetting to multiply by the 5 mL volume.

options.text: 6 mL
options.why: Dose = 1 mg/kg × 18 kg = 18 mg. Volume = desired ÷ have × volume = 18 mg ÷ 15 mg × 5 mL = 6 mL.

options.text: 60 mL
options.why: This is a tenfold decimal error; the correct volume is 6 mL.

takeaway: Weight-based dose first (mg/kg × kg), then desired ÷ have × volume.

stem: A child with croup weighs 33 lb. The provider prescribes dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg orally as a single dose. The available oral solution is 1 mg/mL. How many mL should the nurse give? (1 kg = 2.2 lb; round to the nearest tenth if needed.)

options.why: This uses the weight in pounds (33 × 0.6) without converting to kilograms.

options.text: 0.9 mL
options.why: This is a tenfold decimal error.

options.text: 25 mL
options.why: This divides the weight in kilograms by the dose (15 ÷ 0.6) instead of multiplying.

options.text: 9 mL
options.why: 33 lb ÷ 2.2 = 15 kg. Dose = 0.6 mg/kg × 15 kg = 9 mg. Volume = 9 mg ÷ 1 mg × 1 mL = 9 mL.

takeaway: Convert pounds to kilograms (÷ 2.2) before any mg/kg calculation.

stem: A 6-year-old weighing 22 kg develops anaphylaxis on the pediatric unit. The provider prescribes epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg IM. The available solution is epinephrine 1 mg/mL. How many mL should the nurse draw up? (Round to the nearest hundredth.)

options.why: Dose = 0.01 mg/kg × 22 kg = 0.22 mg. Volume = 0.22 mg ÷ 1 mg × 1 mL = 0.22 mL, which is below the usual pediatric single-dose maximum of 0.3 mg.

options.text: 2.2 mL
options.why: This is a tenfold overdose (decimal error) that could cause severe hypertension and dysrhythmias.
This is a tenfold underdose (decimal error).

options.text: 0.3 mL
options.why: 0.3 mg is the usual maximum single IM dose for a prepubertal child, but the prescribed weight-based dose for 22 kg is 0.22 mg.

takeaway: IM epinephrine for anaphylaxis is 0.01 mg/kg of the 1 mg/mL solution (max 0.3 mg in a prepubertal child, 0.5 mg in an adult); double-check decimals.

stem: A client with asthma is newly prescribed propranolol for migraine prevention. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: Give the propranolol with albuterol to counteract any bronchospasm.
options.why: Propranolol directly antagonizes albuterol at beta2 receptors, so the rescue drug may not work.

options.text: Contact the provider, because a nonselective beta-blocker can trigger bronchospasm and block the effect of albuterol.
options.why: Propranolol blocks beta2 receptors in the airways, which can provoke severe bronchospasm in asthma and make beta2-agonist rescue less effective.

options.text: Teach the client to take propranolol at bedtime to avoid dizziness.
options.why: Timing does not address the main risk, which is bronchospasm.

options.text: Monitor only for hyperglycemia during therapy.
options.why: Beta-blockers can mask hypoglycemia symptoms, but the priority concern in asthma is bronchospasm.

takeaway: Nonselective beta-blockers such as propranolol are generally avoided in asthma because they can trigger bronchospasm and blunt albuterol.

stem: The parents of a 7-year-old who uses an inhaled corticosteroid daily for persistent asthma ask about long-term safety. Which statement by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: 'Inhaled steroids have no side effects because none of the drug is absorbed.'
options.why: Some drug is absorbed systemically; effects such as thrush, hoarseness and a slight reduction in growth velocity can occur.

options.text: 'Stop the inhaler during the summer so your child's growth can catch up.'
options.why: Stopping controller therapy risks exacerbations; changes should be made only by the provider.

options.text: 'Your child's height will be checked at each visit, because inhaled steroids can slightly slow growth; keeping asthma controlled is still the priority.'
options.why: Inhaled corticosteroids can cause a small reduction in growth velocity, so growth is monitored; the benefits of controlling persistent asthma outweigh this risk, and the lowest effective dose is used.

options.text: 'Your child will probably develop Cushing syndrome, so expect weight gain.'
options.why: Cushingoid effects are unlikely at usual inhaled doses.

takeaway: Children on inhaled corticosteroids need growth monitoring; use the lowest effective dose and do not stop therapy on your own.

stem: A client receiving continuous nebulized albuterol for a severe asthma exacerbation has these findings: heart rate 118/min, fine hand tremor, serum potassium 2.9 mEq/L and blood glucose 156 mg/dL. Which finding should the nurse report to the provider immediately?

options.text: Heart rate 118/min
options.why: Tachycardia is an expected effect of high-dose albuterol and of the exacerbation itself; it is monitored but is less urgent than severe hypokalemia.

options.text: Fine hand tremor
options.why: Tremor is a common, expected effect of beta2 agonists.

options.text: Blood glucose 156 mg/dL
options.why: Mild hyperglycemia is expected with beta2 agonists and corticosteroids and is less immediately dangerous than severe hypokalemia.

options.text: Serum potassium 2.9 mEq/L
options.why: High-dose beta2 agonists shift potassium into cells; a level of 2.9 mEq/L (normal 3.5 to 5 mEq/L) increases the risk of dangerous dysrhythmias and needs prompt treatment.

takeaway: High-dose or continuous albuterol can cause significant hypokalemia; monitor potassium and cardiac rhythm.

stem: A client has taken prednisone 30 mg orally daily for 6 weeks for a chronic inflammatory lung condition and asks about vaccines before international travel. Which vaccine should the nurse anticipate is contraindicated at this time?

options.text: Measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine
options.why: MMR is a live vaccine; prednisone 20 mg/day or more for 14 days or longer causes significant immunosuppression, and live vaccines should be delayed until at least 1 month after stopping.

options.text: Inactivated influenza vaccine by injection
options.why: Inactivated vaccines are safe for immunosuppressed clients, although the immune response may be reduced.

options.text: Tetanus, diphtheria and acellular pertussis (Tdap) vaccine
options.why: Tdap is not a live vaccine and can be given.

options.text: Hepatitis A vaccine
options.why: Hepatitis A vaccine is inactivated and can be given.

takeaway: High-dose systemic steroids (20 mg/day of prednisone or more for 14 days or longer) are a contraindication to live vaccines; inactivated vaccines may be given.

stem: A client starting varenicline has set a quit date. Which statement by the client indicates correct understanding?

options.text: 'I'll take both tablets together at bedtime on an empty stomach.'
options.why: Twice-daily doses are separated, and an empty stomach increases nausea.

options.text: 'I'll start the tablets 1 week before my quit date and take them after a meal with a full glass of water.'
options.why: Standard dosing begins 1 week before the quit date with a gradual increase; taking it after eating with water reduces nausea.

options.text: 'If I have a craving, I'll take an extra tablet.'
options.why: Extra doses increase adverse effects; cravings are managed with behavioral strategies and, if needed, provider-directed changes.

options.text: 'If I feel nauseated, it means I'm overdosing, so I'll stop the medicine.'
options.why: Nausea is a common adverse effect, not overdose; the client should report it, and the provider may adjust the dose.

takeaway: Varenicline: start about 1 week before the quit date, take after meals with water, and report nausea or mood changes.

stem: The nurse is teaching a client who has been prescribed albuterol by metered-dose inhaler. Which adverse effects should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Tremor
options.why: Correct. Beta2 stimulation of skeletal muscle commonly causes a fine tremor.

options.text: Bradycardia
options.why: Incorrect. Albuterol tends to increase, not decrease, the heart rate.

options.text: Nervousness or restlessness
options.why: Correct. CNS stimulation can cause nervousness and restlessness.

options.text: Oral thrush
options.why: Incorrect. Oral candidiasis is associated with inhaled corticosteroids, not albuterol.

options.text: Palpitations or a rapid heartbeat
options.why: Correct. Some beta1 stimulation and reflex responses cause tachycardia and palpitations.

takeaway: Albuterol commonly causes tremor, nervousness and tachycardia; frequent use also signals poor asthma control.

stem: A client taking oral theophylline is being monitored for toxicity. Which findings should the nurse recognize as possible signs of theophylline toxicity? Select all that apply.

options.text: Persistent vomiting
options.why: Correct. Nausea and vomiting are often the earliest signs of an excessive theophylline level.

options.text: Bradycardia
options.why: Incorrect. Theophylline toxicity causes tachycardia and tachydysrhythmias, not bradycardia.

options.text: Seizure
options.why: Correct. Seizures can occur at toxic levels, sometimes without earlier warning signs.

options.text: Ventricular dysrhythmias
options.why: Correct. Theophylline toxicity can cause serious ventricular dysrhythmias.

options.text: Slow, shallow respirations with pinpoint pupils
options.why: Incorrect. This pattern suggests opioid toxicity; theophylline is a stimulant.

options.text: Restlessness and insomnia
options.why: Correct. CNS stimulation causing restlessness, irritability and insomnia is an early sign of excess.

takeaway: Theophylline toxicity: GI upset first, then CNS stimulation, tachydysrhythmias and seizures; a commonly targeted level is 5 to 15 mcg/mL.

stem: A client with active tuberculosis is starting rifampin as part of a multidrug regimen. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: 'Your urine, sweat and tears may turn red-orange; this is harmless.'
options.why: Correct. Rifampin colors body fluids red-orange; clients should expect it.

options.text: 'Use a nonhormonal backup method of birth control during treatment.'
options.why: Correct. Rifampin induces liver enzymes and makes hormonal contraceptives less effective.

options.text: 'Avoid wearing soft contact lenses, because they can be permanently stained.'
options.why: Correct. Tears may permanently discolor soft contact lenses.

options.text: 'You can stop the medication once your cough goes away.'
options.why: Incorrect. The full course (usually at least 6 months for active TB) must be completed to prevent relapse and resistance.

options.text: 'Report yellowing of your skin or eyes, or dark urine.'
options.why: Correct. Rifampin can cause hepatotoxicity, especially combined with isoniazid and pyrazinamide.

options.text: 'Take each dose with an antacid to prevent stomach upset.'
options.why: Incorrect. Antacids can reduce rifampin absorption; it is best taken on an empty stomach, and doses should be separated from antacids.

takeaway: Rifampin: red-orange body fluids, stained soft lenses, reduced effect of hormonal contraceptives and many other drugs, and liver monitoring.

stem: A client is receiving isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for pulmonary tuberculosis. Which findings should the nurse instruct the client to report promptly? Select all that apply.

options.text: Blurred vision or difficulty telling red from green
options.why: Correct. These suggest ethambutol-related optic neuritis.

options.text: Orange-colored urine
options.why: Incorrect. Red-orange body fluids are an expected, harmless effect of rifampin.

options.text: Numbness or tingling in the feet
options.why: Correct. Peripheral neuropathy is an isoniazid adverse effect that needs evaluation.

options.text: Yellowing of the eyes and loss of appetite
options.why: Correct. These suggest hepatotoxicity, which can be caused by isoniazid, rifampin or pyrazinamide.

options.text: A hot, swollen, painful joint
options.why: Correct. Pyrazinamide raises uric acid and can cause acute gout.

options.text: Gradual weight gain of 1 kg over a month
options.why: Incorrect. Weight gain usually reflects recovery from TB-related weight loss, not a drug toxicity.

takeaway: First-line TB drug red flags: vision change (ethambutol), neuropathy (isoniazid), jaundice or anorexia (hepatotoxicity) and gout (pyrazinamide); orange fluids from rifampin are expected.

stem: The nurse is teaching a client who will use oxygen at home. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Do not allow anyone to smoke in the home, and post no-smoking signs.
options.why: Correct. Oxygen strongly supports combustion; smoking near oxygen can cause fires and facial burns.

options.text: Keep oxygen equipment away from open flames such as gas stoves and candles.
options.why: Correct. Any open flame near an oxygen source is a fire hazard.

options.text: Store oxygen cylinders upright and secured so they cannot fall.
options.why: Correct. A falling cylinder can damage the valve and become a dangerous projectile.

options.text: Use petroleum-based lip balm to prevent dry lips.
options.why: Incorrect. Petroleum-based products are flammable in oxygen-enriched air; water-based products are safe.

options.text: Turn up the flow rate on your own whenever you feel more short of breath.
options.why: Incorrect. Oxygen is a prescribed drug; changes require the provider, especially in clients at risk of CO2 retention.

options.text: Keep the oxygen concentrator in a closed closet to reduce noise.
options.why: Incorrect. Concentrators need open air space for ventilation; an enclosed space can cause overheating and oxygen buildup.

takeaway: Home oxygen safety: no smoking or open flames, water-based products only, secure cylinders upright, ventilate the concentrator, and do not change the flow without a prescription.

stem: A client asks the nurse about taking over-the-counter pseudoephedrine for nasal congestion. Which findings in the client's history should prompt the nurse to advise against using it without first consulting the provider? Select all that apply.

options.text: Uncontrolled hypertension
options.why: Correct. Pseudoephedrine is a sympathomimetic that raises blood pressure and heart rate.

options.text: Hyperthyroidism
options.why: Correct. Sympathomimetic effects add to the cardiovascular stimulation of hyperthyroidism.

options.text: Benign prostatic hyperplasia with difficulty urinating
options.why: Correct. Alpha-adrenergic stimulation of the bladder neck can worsen urinary retention.

options.text: Current use of phenelzine
options.why: Correct. Pseudoephedrine with an MAOI can cause a hypertensive crisis; the combination is contraindicated.

options.text: Osteoarthritis of the knees
options.why: Incorrect. Osteoarthritis is not affected by pseudoephedrine.

options.text: Iron-deficiency anemia
options.why: Incorrect. Iron-deficiency anemia is not a reason to avoid pseudoephedrine.

takeaway: Oral decongestants can raise BP and heart rate and worsen urinary retention; avoid with MAOIs and check with the provider in hypertension, heart disease, hyperthyroidism or prostatic hyperplasia.

stem: The nurse teaches a client who will take oral prednisone daily for several months. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Take the dose in the morning with food.
options.why: Correct. Morning dosing mimics the body's cortisol rhythm and causes less insomnia; food reduces GI irritation.

options.text: Expect to lose weight while taking this medication.
options.why: Incorrect. Corticosteroids typically increase appetite and cause weight gain and fluid retention.

options.text: Do not stop taking the medication suddenly.
options.why: Correct. Long-term use suppresses the adrenal glands; abrupt withdrawal can cause adrenal insufficiency.

options.text: Report fever, sore throat or other signs of infection.
options.why: Correct. Corticosteroids suppress immunity and can mask signs of infection.

options.text: Increase the salt in your diet.
options.why: Incorrect. Corticosteroids cause sodium and fluid retention; a lower-sodium diet is usually advised.

takeaway: Long-term prednisone: take in the morning with food, never stop abruptly, watch for infection, and expect weight gain and fluid retention.

stem: The parent of a 10-year-old taking montelukast for asthma asks which changes should be reported to the provider. Which findings indicate a possible neuropsychiatric adverse effect of montelukast? Select all that apply.

options.text: Frequent nightmares
options.why: Correct. Sleep disturbances, including abnormal dreams and nightmares, are among the neuropsychiatric events in the boxed warning.

options.text: Stuffy nose
options.why: Incorrect. Nasal congestion is not a neuropsychiatric effect.

options.text: New aggressive or irritable behavior
options.why: Correct. Agitation, aggression and irritability are reported neuropsychiatric events.

options.text: Talking about wanting to die
options.why: Correct. Suicidal thinking and behavior have been reported and require immediate evaluation.

options.text: Mild abdominal pain
options.why: Incorrect. Abdominal pain can occur but is not a neuropsychiatric effect.

takeaway: Montelukast has a boxed warning for neuropsychiatric events (sleep disturbances, agitation, depression, suicidal thoughts); families should report behavior changes.

stem: The nurse is teaching a client who has been prescribed varenicline for smoking cessation. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Take each dose after eating, with a full glass of water.
options.why: Correct. Taking varenicline after food with water reduces nausea, its most common adverse effect.

options.text: Drinking alcohol is safe because varenicline blocks its effects.
options.why: Incorrect. Varenicline may increase the intoxicating effects of alcohol; clients should limit alcohol until they know how they respond.

options.text: Nausea is common; report it if it continues or is severe.
options.why: Correct. Nausea is common, and the provider may adjust the dose if it persists.

options.text: Take an extra dose when cigarette cravings are strong.
options.why: Incorrect. Doses should not exceed the prescribed amount.

options.text: Report any changes in mood, behavior or thoughts of self-harm.
options.why: Correct. Neuropsychiatric changes have been reported with varenicline and smoking cessation and should be reported promptly.

takeaway: Varenicline: take after meals with water, expect possible nausea and vivid dreams, limit alcohol, and report mood or behavior changes.

stem: A 78-year-old client has been taking diphenhydramine every night for sleep. The nurse suspects anticholinergic adverse effects. Which findings support this suspicion? Select all that apply.

options.text: New confusion
options.why: Correct. Central anticholinergic effects cause confusion and delirium, especially in older adults.

options.text: Urinary retention
options.why: Correct. Anticholinergic effects reduce bladder contraction and can cause retention.

options.text: Diarrhea
options.why: Incorrect. Anticholinergic drugs slow GI motility and cause constipation, not diarrhea.

options.text: Dry mouth
options.why: Correct. Reduced salivary secretion is a classic anticholinergic effect.

options.text: Excessive salivation
options.why: Incorrect. Increased salivation is a cholinergic effect, the opposite of what diphenhydramine causes.

options.text: Constipation
options.why: Correct. Decreased GI motility leads to constipation.

takeaway: First-generation antihistamines are strongly anticholinergic: confusion, dry mouth, constipation and urinary retention; avoid them in older adults.

stem: The nurse is teaching a client to use an albuterol metered-dose inhaler without a spacer. In what order should the client perform the steps?

options.text: Breathe out fully, away from the mouthpiece.
options.why: Exhaling first empties the lungs so the following inhalation is deep enough to carry the drug into the airways.

options.text: Remove the cap and shake the inhaler.
options.why: The cap is removed and the canister shaken first to mix the drug and propellant so each puff has a consistent dose.

options.text: Hold the breath for about 10 seconds, then breathe out slowly.
options.why: Breath-holding is last; it lets the aerosol settle in the airways before exhaling.

options.text: Place the mouthpiece between the lips and form a tight seal.
options.why: The mouthpiece is positioned after exhaling so the puff goes straight into the airway.

options.text: Press down on the canister once while starting a slow, deep breath.
options.why: Pressing the canister at the start of a slow inhalation coordinates release with airflow.

takeaway: MDI: cap off and shake, exhale, seal, press while inhaling slowly, hold the breath about 10 seconds; wait about 1 minute before a second puff.

stem: A client is prescribed fluticasone-salmeterol by a disk-type dry powder inhaler. In what order should the client perform the steps?

options.text: Seal the lips around the mouthpiece and breathe in quickly and deeply.
options.why: After exhaling away from the device, a fast, deep inhalation pulls the powder into the lungs.

options.text: Rinse the mouth with water and spit it out.
options.why: Rinsing is last; it removes corticosteroid from the mouth and throat to prevent thrush and hoarseness.

options.text: Open the device and slide the lever to load the dose.
options.why: The dose is loaded first while the device is held level.

options.text: Hold the breath for about 10 seconds.
options.why: Breath-holding follows inhalation so the drug can deposit in the airways.

options.text: Breathe out fully, turned away from the mouthpiece.
options.why: Exhaling away from the device after loading prevents moisture from clumping the powder or blowing it out.

takeaway: Dry powder inhaler: load, exhale away from the device, inhale fast and deep, hold, then rinse if it contains a corticosteroid; do not shake it or exhale into it.

stem: The nurse is teaching a client with a severe insect-sting allergy how to use an epinephrine autoinjector. In what order should the client perform the steps?

options.text: Push the autoinjector firmly against the thigh until it clicks, and hold it in place for the time stated in the device instructions.
options.why: Firm pressure activates the device; holding it in place ensures the full dose is delivered.

options.text: Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department.
options.why: Emergency care is needed after any use because symptoms can recur when the epinephrine wears off.

options.text: Take the autoinjector out of its carrier case.
options.why: The device must be removed from its case before it can be readied.

options.text: Remove the device from the thigh and note the time of the injection.
options.why: Noting the time helps emergency staff and guides whether a second dose is needed.

options.text: Remove the safety release cap.
options.why: The safety cap is removed just before use so the device can fire.

options.text: Place the needle end against the outer thigh; it can go through clothing.
options.why: The anterolateral thigh is the recommended site, and the injection may be given through clothing.

takeaway: Autoinjector: out of the case, safety cap off, needle end on the outer thigh, push until it clicks and hold, note the time, then call 911.

stem: The nurse is administering ipratropium-albuterol by small-volume nebulizer to a client with COPD. In what order should the nurse perform these actions?

options.text: Instruct the client to breathe slowly and deeply through the mouthpiece until the mist stops.
options.why: Slow, deep breaths through the mouthpiece deliver the aerosol to the lower airways, continuing until the medication is gone.

options.text: Verify the prescription and identify the client with two identifiers.
options.why: Verifying the order and identity comes first to prevent medication errors.

options.text: Reassess breath sounds, heart rate and SpO2.
options.why: Reassessment after treatment measures effectiveness and adverse effects such as tachycardia.

options.text: Place the prescribed medication in the nebulizer cup.
options.why: The medication is added after baseline assessment and before the client starts treatment.

options.text: Assess baseline breath sounds, heart rate and SpO2.
options.why: A baseline is needed to judge the response to the bronchodilator.

options.text: Help the client sit upright and place the mouthpiece in the mouth.
options.why: Upright positioning improves lung expansion and aerosol deposition.

takeaway: Nebulizer: verify and identify, assess baseline, add the drug, position upright, slow deep breaths until the mist stops, then reassess.

stem: A client who had abdominal surgery yesterday has a prescription for hydromorphone 0.4 mg IV every 2 hours as needed for pain. When the nurse enters, the client rates pain 5/10 but keeps drifting off to sleep in the middle of answering questions and is easy to rouse. Respirations are 12/min and SpO2 is 94% on room air. The next dose is now available. What is the most appropriate nursing action?

options.text: Hold the hydromorphone dose, increase the frequency of sedation and respiratory checks, and contact the provider about reducing the opioid dose.
options.why: Falling asleep during conversation is a Pasero Opioid-Induced Sedation Scale (POSS) level 3, which is unacceptable sedation; the next opioid dose is held and the dose reduced, because sedation precedes opioid-induced respiratory depression.

options.text: Administer naloxone IV because the client is showing signs of opioid toxicity.
options.why: Naloxone is reserved for respiratory depression or a client who cannot be roused (POSS 4); this client is easy to rouse with a respiratory rate of 12/min, so reversal would cause unnecessary pain and is not indicated.

options.text: Give the hydromorphone now because the client still reports pain of 5/10.
options.why: Pain intensity alone does not justify more opioid when the client is excessively sedated; giving the dose adds to central nervous system depression and increases the risk of respiratory arrest.

options.text: Let the client sleep and recheck pain in 4 hours because rest promotes healing.
options.why: Sleep that interrupts conversation is not restful sleep but opioid sedation; leaving the client unmonitored for 4 hours misses the window in which respiratory depression typically develops.

takeaway: Sedation comes before respiratory depression. A client who drifts off mid-conversation (POSS 3) needs the opioid held or reduced and closer monitoring, not another dose.

stem: A client received naloxone IV for respiratory depression after an overdose of extended-release morphine. Twenty minutes later the client is alert with respirations of 16/min and asks to go home. Which statement by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: “Now that you are awake, the danger is over and you can be discharged.”
options.why: Being alert after naloxone does not mean the opioid is gone; when naloxone wears off, the remaining morphine can again depress breathing.

options.text: “We will give you a dose of morphine before you leave so you do not go into withdrawal.”
options.why: Giving more opioid after an overdose would increase the risk of recurrent respiratory depression and is not standard practice.

options.text: “You need to stay so we can keep checking your breathing, because the morphine may last longer than the naloxone.”
options.why: Naloxone acts for roughly 30 to 90 minutes, which is shorter than many opioids, especially extended-release products; re-sedation and recurrent respiratory depression can occur, so continued monitoring and possible repeat doses are needed.

options.text: “Your breathing is normal, so we only need to recheck it once before your discharge tomorrow.”
options.why: A single recheck the next day is far too infrequent; sedation and respirations must be monitored closely for several hours because of the risk of re-sedation.

takeaway: Naloxone often wears off before the opioid does. After reversal, monitor sedation and respirations closely for re-sedation and be ready to repeat the dose.

stem: A 70-year-old client who is opioid naive had knee surgery this morning and is receiving morphine. The client now rouses only with vigorous shaking, has respirations of 7/min and shallow, and has an SpO2 of 88%. After stimulating the client and applying oxygen, the nurse prepares naloxone 0.4 mg/mL. Which administration method is most appropriate?

options.text: Dilute the naloxone in 10 mL of normal saline and give small increments IV slowly, titrating to respiratory rate and arousal.
options.why: Postoperative opioid-induced respiratory depression is reversed by titrating dilute naloxone (for example, 0.02 to 0.04 mg at a time every 2 minutes) until breathing is adequate; this restores respiration without abruptly reversing all analgesia.

options.text: Give 2 mg undiluted by rapid IV push to make sure the client wakes up fully.
options.why: A large rapid bolus can precipitate severe pain, hypertension, tachycardia, pulmonary edema and dysrhythmias; the goal is adequate breathing, not full wakefulness.

options.text: Give the naloxone subcutaneously so that it is absorbed slowly over several hours.
options.why: Subcutaneous absorption is slow and unpredictable; with an IV line in place, the IV route gives the fastest, titratable reversal of respiratory depression.

options.text: Wait 30 minutes and recheck, because the morphine effect should peak and then decline.
options.why: A respiratory rate of 7/min with an SpO2 of 88% in a barely rousable client is an emergency; delaying reversal risks respiratory arrest.

takeaway: For postoperative opioid-induced respiratory depression, dilute naloxone and titrate small IV doses to adequate breathing, not to full alertness, to avoid abrupt loss of analgesia.

stem: A client with metastatic bone pain is starting scheduled oxycodone. Which instruction should the nurse include to prevent a common adverse effect?

options.text: “Your body will get used to the constipation within a week, so you will not need a laxative.”
options.why: Tolerance develops to opioid sedation and nausea, but not to constipation; it persists as long as the opioid is taken.

options.text: “Wait until you have gone 5 days without a bowel movement before taking anything.”
options.why: Waiting several days allows hard stool and possible impaction to develop; prevention should begin with the first opioid dose.

options.text: “Take a bulk-forming fiber supplement instead of a laxative, even if you are not drinking much.”
options.why: Bulk-forming fiber without adequate fluid can worsen opioid constipation and lead to obstruction; a stimulant laxative is preferred.

options.text: “Take the stimulant laxative senna every day for as long as you take oxycodone.”
options.why: Opioid-induced constipation is very common and does not lessen with time, so a scheduled stimulant laxative (often with a stool softener) is started together with the opioid.

takeaway: Clients do not develop tolerance to opioid constipation. Start a scheduled stimulant laxative, with or without a stool softener, together with the opioid.

stem: A 34-year-old client who takes no opioids at home had an appendectomy and reports incisional pain of 7/10. The provider prescribes a fentanyl 25 mcg/hour transdermal patch every 72 hours. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Apply the patch now so the client has continuous pain control after surgery.
options.why: Applying the patch to an opioid-naive client could cause life-threatening respiratory depression, and its slow onset would not treat acute pain promptly.

options.text: Question the prescription, because transdermal fentanyl is only for opioid-tolerant clients with persistent pain.
options.why: Fentanyl patches carry a boxed warning: they are contraindicated in opioid-naive clients and for acute or postoperative pain because of the risk of fatal respiratory depression; onset is also delayed 12 to 24 hours.

options.text: Apply the patch and tell the client the pain should be relieved within 30 minutes.
options.why: Transdermal fentanyl takes 12 to 24 hours to reach therapeutic levels, so this teaching is inaccurate and the patch is inappropriate here anyway.

options.text: Apply the patch to the abdomen near the incision for better local pain relief.
options.why: Transdermal fentanyl acts systemically, not locally, and should not be applied near a surgical wound; more importantly, it should not be used in this client.

takeaway: Transdermal fentanyl is only for opioid-tolerant clients with persistent pain. Question any order for an opioid-naive client or for acute postoperative pain.

stem: A client receiving methadone for chronic pain is also taking ondansetron and fluconazole. Which finding should the nurse report to the provider immediately?

options.text: QTc interval of 520 ms on the electrocardiogram
options.why: Methadone prolongs the QT interval, and ondansetron and fluconazole add to this effect; a QTc above 500 ms (normal is about 450 ms or less in men and 460 ms or less in women) greatly increases the risk of torsades de pointes.

options.text: Constricted pupils
options.why: Miosis is an expected effect of opioids and does not by itself indicate toxicity.

options.text: Hard stool passed with straining
options.why: Constipation is a common opioid effect that is managed with a bowel regimen; it is not an immediate safety threat.

options.text: Increased sweating during the day
options.why: Sweating is a frequent, bothersome methadone side effect but is not life-threatening.

takeaway: Methadone prolongs the QT interval. Watch for other QT-prolonging drugs and report a QTc above 500 ms promptly because of the risk of torsades de pointes.

stem: A nurse reviews new postoperative prescriptions for a 72-year-old opioid-naive client who weighs 60 kg. Which prescription should the nurse clarify before giving any dose?

options.text: Hydromorphone 10 mg IV every 3 hours as needed for severe pain
options.why: Hydromorphone is about five to seven times more potent than morphine; usual IV starting doses for an opioid-naive adult are about 0.2 to 1 mg, so 10 mg is a potentially fatal dose and a classic hydromorphone–morphine mix-up.

options.text: Morphine 2 mg IV every 2 hours as needed for severe pain
options.why: This is a conservative, appropriate IV morphine dose for an older opioid-naive adult.

options.text: Oxycodone 5 mg orally every 4 hours as needed for moderate pain
options.why: This is a usual starting oral dose of oxycodone for an opioid-naive adult.

options.text: Acetaminophen 650 mg orally every 6 hours
options.why: This totals 2,600 mg per day, well under the maximum daily dose, and is an appropriate opioid-sparing analgesic.

takeaway: Hydromorphone is several times more potent than morphine. A dose in the morphine range (for example, 10 mg IV) is a high-alert error that must be clarified.

stem: A client with chronic kidney disease (eGFR 22 mL/min/1.73 m²) has been receiving morphine every 4 hours for 3 days. The client has become increasingly drowsy and has new myoclonic jerking. Which explanation best accounts for these findings?

options.text: The client has developed tolerance and needs a higher dose of morphine.
options.why: Tolerance produces less effect, not increasing sedation; raising the dose would worsen the toxicity.

options.text: Active morphine metabolites are accumulating because the kidneys cannot excrete them.
options.why: Morphine-6-glucuronide (sedating) and morphine-3-glucuronide (neuroexcitatory, causing myoclonus) are cleared by the kidneys and accumulate when kidney function is poor, which is why morphine is avoided or reduced in significant kidney disease.

options.text: The client is experiencing opioid withdrawal.
options.why: Withdrawal causes agitation, yawning, rhinorrhea and diarrhea while opioid is stopped; this client is receiving regular doses and is drowsy.

options.text: Morphine is causing an allergic reaction affecting the nervous system.
options.why: True opioid allergy presents with urticaria, facial swelling or anaphylaxis, not sedation and myoclonus.

takeaway: Morphine's active metabolites accumulate in kidney impairment, causing sedation and myoclonus. Older adults and clients with reduced kidney function need lower doses or another opioid.

stem: A client in the emergency department with a migraine takes methadone daily for opioid use disorder. The provider prescribes butorphanol nasal spray. What is the nurse's priority concern?

options.text: Butorphanol will cause much stronger respiratory depression than methadone alone.
options.why: Mixed agonist-antagonists have a ceiling on respiratory depression; the main danger in an opioid-dependent client is precipitated withdrawal, not additive depression.

options.text: The nasal spray is likely to cause severe nasal bleeding.
options.why: Nasal irritation can occur but significant bleeding is not a typical concern and is not the priority.

options.text: Butorphanol may precipitate acute opioid withdrawal in a client who is physically dependent on opioids.
options.why: Butorphanol is a mixed agonist-antagonist; its mu-receptor antagonist activity can displace methadone and trigger abrupt withdrawal, so it should be avoided in opioid-dependent clients.

options.text: Butorphanol must not be used for headache because it has no analgesic effect.
options.why: Butorphanol does provide analgesia through kappa-receptor agonism and has been used for migraine; its problem here is the interaction with methadone.

takeaway: Mixed agonist-antagonists (butorphanol, nalbuphine) can precipitate withdrawal in clients who are physically dependent on full opioid agonists such as methadone.

stem: A client who had a total hip arthroplasty yesterday is scheduled for physical therapy at 10:00. The client has a prescription for oral oxycodone as needed for pain and reports pain of 4/10 at rest. At what time should the nurse give the oxycodone?

options.text: 10:00, when therapy begins
options.why: Giving the dose at the start of therapy means the drug is not yet effective during the most painful activity.

Oral oxycodone begins to work in about 10 to 30 minutes and peaks at about 30 to 60 minutes, so giving it 30 to 60 minutes before therapy provides peak relief during the session and supports participation.

options.text: After therapy, when the pain is at its worst
options.why: Treating pain only after it becomes severe is less effective than preventing it; pain is best managed before predictable painful activity.

options.text: 07:00, three hours before therapy
options.why: By 10:00 the drug will be past its peak and wearing off, so relief during therapy will be limited.

takeaway: Time oral analgesics so peak effect coincides with painful activity. For immediate-release oral opioids, give them about 30 to 60 minutes beforehand.

stem: A nurse teaches a client who is starting sublingual buprenorphine. Which statement by the client indicates the teaching was effective?

options.text: “I will put the tablet under my tongue and let it dissolve completely without chewing or swallowing it.”
options.why: Buprenorphine has poor oral bioavailability when swallowed; it must dissolve fully under the tongue to be absorbed, and the client should avoid eating or drinking until it has dissolved.

options.text: “I will swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water.”
options.why: Swallowed buprenorphine is largely destroyed by first-pass metabolism, so the dose would be ineffective.

options.text: “I will chew the tablet so it works faster.”
options.why: Chewing leads to swallowing much of the drug, reducing absorption; the tablet must dissolve under the tongue.

options.text: “I can drink my coffee while the tablet is dissolving.”
options.why: Eating or drinking while the tablet dissolves washes the drug into the stomach and lowers absorption.

takeaway: Sublingual buprenorphine must dissolve completely under the tongue; swallowing or chewing it greatly lowers absorption.

stem: A nurse finds the spouse of a client who is using an IV morphine PCA pump pressing the dose button while the client sleeps. What is the nurse's priority action?

options.text: Thank the spouse for helping keep the client comfortable during sleep.
options.why: Encouraging PCA by proxy bypasses the built-in safety mechanism and can lead to respiratory depression.

options.text: Tell the spouse that only the client may press the button, then assess the client's sedation level and respirations.
options.why: PCA is safe because a client who becomes sedated stops pressing the button; when others press it (PCA by proxy), this safeguard is lost and oversedation can occur, so the nurse stops the practice and checks the client.

options.text: Increase the lockout interval so that the spouse cannot give doses as often.
options.why: Changing pump settings requires a prescription and does not address the unsafe practice of someone other than the client pressing the button.

options.text: Remove the PCA pump and give morphine by intermittent IV push instead.
options.why: Stopping PCA is not necessary; education about who may press the button and assessment of the client are the appropriate first steps.

takeaway: Only the client should press the PCA button. Stop PCA by proxy right away and assess sedation and breathing.

stem: A client using an IV morphine PCA pump has the following settings: 1 mg per dose, 10-minute lockout, no basal rate. In the past hour the pump recorded 18 attempts and 6 doses delivered. The client is alert, rates pain 8/10, and has respirations of 18/min. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Tell the client to press the button more often to get more medication.
options.why: The pump is already delivering every dose the lockout allows; additional presses will not deliver more drug.

options.text: Report the findings to the provider and request a review of the PCA dose.
options.why: Six doses in an hour is the maximum possible with a 10-minute lockout; frequent unsuccessful attempts and severe pain in an alert client with normal breathing show the current dose is inadequate and needs adjustment.

options.text: Explain that the client is pressing the button too often and may be developing an addiction.
options.why: Frequent demands with uncontrolled pain reflect undertreated pain, not addiction; labeling the client this way is inaccurate and harmful.

options.text: Press the button for the client during the lockout period to deliver an extra dose.
options.why: The pump will not deliver during lockout, and nurses do not press the button for the client except under a specific authorized-agent protocol.

takeaway: Many attempts with maximum doses delivered and persistent pain in an alert client mean the PCA settings are inadequate. Report it so the dose can be adjusted.

stem: A client with osteoarthritis has taken ibuprofen 800 mg three times daily for several months. Which finding should the nurse report to the provider immediately?

options.text: Mild morning stiffness lasting 20 minutes
options.why: Brief morning stiffness is typical of osteoarthritis and is not an NSAID adverse effect needing urgent action.

options.text: Black, tarry stools for the past 2 days
options.why: Melena suggests upper gastrointestinal bleeding, a serious and potentially life-threatening complication of long-term NSAID use.

options.text: Occasional mild heartburn after meals
options.why: Mild dyspepsia is common with NSAIDs and should be monitored, but it is less urgent than signs of active bleeding.

options.text: Knee pain rated 3/10 after walking
options.why: Mild activity-related pain is consistent with osteoarthritis and does not indicate an adverse drug effect.

takeaway: Long-term NSAID use can cause gastrointestinal bleeding. Black, tarry stools or coffee-ground vomit need prompt reporting.

stem: A 79-year-old client with heart failure takes lisinopril and furosemide. The client begins taking naproxen 500 mg twice daily for shoulder pain. Which laboratory value should the nurse monitor most closely?

options.text: Serum amylase
options.why: Amylase is used to assess the pancreas and is not affected in a clinically important way by this drug combination.

options.text: Hemoglobin A1C
options.why: A1C reflects long-term blood glucose control and is unrelated to the main risk of this combination.

options.text: Thyroid-stimulating hormone
options.why: TSH evaluates thyroid function and is not affected by NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors or diuretics.

options.text: Serum creatinine
options.why: Combining an NSAID with an ACE inhibitor and a diuretic reduces kidney perfusion and can cause acute kidney injury; a rising creatinine (normal about 0.6 to 1.3 mg/dL) is the key warning sign.

takeaway: An NSAID plus an ACE inhibitor (or ARB) plus a diuretic can cause acute kidney injury, especially in older adults. Monitor creatinine and urine output.

stem: The parent of an 8-year-old with influenza asks whether aspirin can be given for the child's fever and body aches. Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: “Aspirin is safe if you give it with food to protect the stomach.”
options.why: Giving aspirin with food reduces stomach upset but does not reduce the risk of Reye syndrome.

options.text: “Use a low-dose baby aspirin, which is safe for children.”
options.why: Low-dose aspirin is still a salicylate and still carries the risk of Reye syndrome in a child with a viral infection.

options.text: “Aspirin is fine once the fever is above 102°F (38.9°C).”
options.why: The degree of fever does not change the risk; aspirin should be avoided in children and teenagers with viral illnesses.

options.text: “Do not give aspirin; it is linked to Reye syndrome in children with viral illnesses. Acetaminophen or ibuprofen can be used instead.”
options.why: Aspirin and other salicylates given to children and teenagers during viral illnesses such as influenza or chickenpox are associated with Reye syndrome, which causes acute encephalopathy and liver failure.

takeaway: Avoid aspirin and other salicylates in children and teenagers with viral illnesses because of Reye syndrome.

stem: Celecoxib is prescribed for a client with rheumatoid arthritis. Which item in the client's history should the nurse report to the provider before giving the first dose?

options.text: Rash after taking amoxicillin
options.why: Penicillin allergy does not cross-react with celecoxib and is not a contraindication.

options.text: Takes levothyroxine for hypothyroidism
options.why: Levothyroxine has no significant interaction with celecoxib.

options.text: Takes a daily calcium and vitamin D supplement
options.why: Calcium and vitamin D supplements do not interact meaningfully with celecoxib.

options.text: Hives after taking sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim
options.why: Celecoxib is contraindicated in clients who have had allergic-type reactions to sulfonamides, so this history must be reported before giving the drug.

takeaway: Celecoxib contains a sulfonamide group. Check for sulfonamide allergy and, like other NSAIDs, watch for cardiovascular, kidney and GI risks.

stem: A client with chronic low back pain is starting daily meloxicam. Which instruction about the drug's boxed warning should the nurse include?

options.text: “Expect your urine to turn reddish-orange while taking this drug.”
options.why: Meloxicam does not change urine color; this effect is associated with drugs such as rifampin or phenazopyridine.

options.text: “Seek emergency care right away for chest pain, shortness of breath, weakness on one side of your body, or slurred speech.”
options.why: NSAIDs carry a boxed warning for increased risk of heart attack and stroke, which can occur early in treatment and is higher with long-term use and existing heart disease.

options.text: “Stop the drug if you develop a dry cough.”
options.why: Dry cough is a typical adverse effect of ACE inhibitors, not NSAIDs.

options.text: “Take the drug only at bedtime because it causes drowsiness.”
options.why: Meloxicam is not notably sedating; the important warnings concern cardiovascular events and GI bleeding.

takeaway: NSAIDs (except low-dose aspirin) carry boxed warnings for heart attack, stroke and GI bleeding. Teach clients the warning signs that need emergency care.

stem: A 58-year-old client with knee osteoarthritis tells the nurse, “I take two 500-mg acetaminophen tablets every 4 hours around the clock because the pain never stops.” What should the nurse do?

options.text: Advise the client to take the tablets with food to prevent stomach upset.
options.why: Taking acetaminophen with food does not address the overdose risk; acetaminophen is not a major gastric irritant.

options.text: Suggest changing to an extended-release acetaminophen product at the same total daily amount.
options.why: Changing the formulation does not change the total of 6,000 mg per day, which remains hepatotoxic.

options.text: Reassure the client that acetaminophen is safe at any dose because it is sold over the counter.
options.why: Over-the-counter status does not make acetaminophen safe in excess; it is a leading cause of acute liver failure.

options.text: Explain that this amount exceeds the maximum safe daily dose and notify the provider.
options.why: Two 500-mg tablets every 4 hours is 1,000 mg × 6 doses = 6,000 mg per day, well above the 4,000-mg (4 g) maximum for adults, putting the client at risk of liver injury; the provider needs to know to evaluate the client and adjust the pain plan.

takeaway: Do the math on acetaminophen. Adults should not exceed 4 g per day (often less for older adults, heavy alcohol use or liver disease).

stem: A client discharged with hydrocodone-acetaminophen tablets asks about treating a cold at home. Which client statement indicates understanding of the teaching?

options.text: “Cold medicines never contain acetaminophen, so I can take any of them.”
options.why: Many multi-symptom cold and flu products contain acetaminophen; this belief could lead to overdose.

options.text: “I can take extra-strength acetaminophen with my pain pills, since they are different drugs.”
options.why: The prescription tablet already contains acetaminophen; adding more increases the total daily dose and the risk of liver injury.

options.text: “If a product says APAP, it means it is aspirin-free and safe to combine.”
options.why: APAP is an abbreviation for acetaminophen (N-acetyl-para-aminophenol), not a label for an aspirin-free safe product.

options.text: “I will check the ingredient list of any cold medicine for acetaminophen or APAP before I take it.”
options.why: Many combination opioid tablets and over-the-counter cold, flu and sleep products contain acetaminophen (sometimes listed as APAP), so reading labels prevents accidental overdose.

takeaway: Acetaminophen hides in combination opioids and OTC cold, flu and sleep products, sometimes labeled as APAP. Teach clients to read every label.

stem: A client is receiving the IV loading dose of acetylcysteine for acetaminophen overdose. Fifteen minutes into the infusion, the client develops flushing and hives on the chest and arms. Blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg, and there is no wheezing. What is the nurse's priority action?

options.text: Stop the infusion and notify the provider.
options.why: Anaphylactoid reactions (flushing, urticaria and, less often, bronchospasm or hypotension) occur most often during the IV loading dose; the infusion is stopped and the provider notified, and treatment with an antihistamine usually allows the infusion to be restarted, often at a slower rate.

options.text: Increase the infusion rate so the loading dose is finished sooner.
options.why: Reactions are related to the rate and concentration of the loading dose; increasing the rate would worsen the reaction.

options.text: Continue the infusion unchanged and document the expected finding.
options.why: Urticaria is a reaction that requires intervention; continuing without action could allow progression to bronchospasm or hypotension.

options.text: Administer naloxone IV.
options.why: Naloxone reverses opioids; it has no role in an acetylcysteine reaction or acetaminophen toxicity.

takeaway: IV acetylcysteine can cause anaphylactoid reactions, mostly during the loading dose. Stop the infusion and notify the provider; it is usually resumed after treatment because the antidote is essential.

stem: A client who began taking allopurinol 3 weeks ago for chronic gout calls the clinic and reports a new red rash on the trunk and a fever. What should the nurse instruct the client to do?

options.text: Continue allopurinol and apply hydrocortisone cream to the rash.
options.why: Continuing the drug after a rash appears risks progression to a life-threatening hypersensitivity reaction.

options.text: Take an extra dose of allopurinol, because the fever means a gout flare is starting.
options.why: Fever with rash points to a drug reaction, not gout; more allopurinol could worsen the reaction.

options.text: Take ibuprofen for the fever and call back if the rash lasts longer than 2 weeks.
options.why: Waiting 2 weeks could allow a severe cutaneous reaction to progress; the client needs prompt evaluation.

options.text: Stop taking allopurinol and come in to be evaluated today.
options.why: Allopurinol should be stopped at the first sign of rash because it can be an early sign of a severe hypersensitivity reaction such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome or DRESS, which usually appears within the first months of therapy.

takeaway: Stop allopurinol at the first sign of rash, especially with fever, because it may signal a severe hypersensitivity reaction.

stem: A nurse teaches a client with recurrent gout who is starting allopurinol. Which statement by the client indicates that the teaching was effective?

options.text: “I will drink plenty of fluids every day, enough to make at least 2 liters of urine.”
options.why: Generous fluid intake, with urine output of at least 2 liters a day, helps prevent uric acid and xanthine kidney stones while on allopurinol.

options.text: “I will take allopurinol only when my big toe starts to hurt.”
options.why: Allopurinol is a daily urate-lowering drug used for prevention; it does not relieve an acute attack.

options.text: “I will stop the allopurinol whenever I have a gout flare.”
options.why: Current guidance is to continue urate-lowering therapy during a flare; stopping and restarting causes urate swings that can provoke more attacks.

options.text: “This medicine should take away my joint pain within an hour.”
options.why: Allopurinol works gradually by lowering uric acid over weeks to months; it has no immediate analgesic effect.

takeaway: Allopurinol is daily prevention, not a rescue drug. Keep taking it during flares and drink enough fluid to produce at least 2 liters of urine a day.

stem: A client who takes colchicine 0.6 mg daily to prevent gout flares has a new prescription from an urgent care clinic. Which newly prescribed medication should the nurse question?

options.text: Acetaminophen
options.why: Acetaminophen does not interact meaningfully with colchicine and may be used for pain.

options.text: Lisinopril
options.why: Lisinopril does not affect colchicine metabolism or transport.

options.text: Cetirizine
options.why: Cetirizine has no clinically important interaction with colchicine.

options.text: Clarithromycin
options.why: Clarithromycin strongly inhibits CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein, which can raise colchicine to toxic, sometimes fatal, levels (GI symptoms, myopathy, bone marrow suppression); the combination is avoided or requires a major dose reduction.

takeaway: Colchicine toxicity can be fatal when it is combined with strong CYP3A4 or P-glycoprotein inhibitors such as clarithromycin, especially with kidney or liver impairment.

stem: A nurse teaches a client about colchicine 0.6-mg tablets for an acute gout flare. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: “I will take two tablets at the first sign of a flare and one more tablet an hour later.”
options.why: This matches the low-dose regimen (1.2 mg, then 0.6 mg after 1 hour), which works as well as high doses with far fewer GI effects.

options.text: “I will keep taking one tablet every hour until the pain goes away or I get diarrhea.”
options.why: This describes an outdated high-dose regimen that causes toxicity; the current low-dose regimen is 1.2 mg at the first sign of a flare followed by 0.6 mg one hour later (a maximum of 1.8 mg in that hour).

options.text: “I will avoid grapefruit juice while I am taking colchicine.”
options.why: Grapefruit juice inhibits CYP3A4 and can increase colchicine levels, so avoiding it is correct.

options.text: “I will call my provider if I have severe diarrhea, muscle weakness, or unusual bruising.”
options.why: These are signs of colchicine toxicity (GI toxicity, myopathy, bone marrow suppression) that should be reported.

takeaway: For a gout flare, colchicine is taken as 1.2 mg, then 0.6 mg one hour later. Taking it every hour until diarrhea occurs is outdated and toxic.

stem: A client with gout who could not tolerate allopurinol is prescribed febuxostat. Which medication on the client's list should the nurse report to the provider?

options.text: Azathioprine
options.why: Febuxostat is contraindicated with azathioprine and mercaptopurine because xanthine oxidase inhibition sharply increases their levels, causing severe bone marrow suppression.

options.text: Omeprazole
options.why: Omeprazole does not have a clinically significant interaction with febuxostat.

options.text: Amlodipine
options.why: Amlodipine does not interact meaningfully with febuxostat.

options.text: Docusate sodium
options.why: A stool softener has no interaction with febuxostat.

takeaway: Febuxostat (and allopurinol) block xanthine oxidase. Azathioprine and mercaptopurine then accumulate, so febuxostat is contraindicated with them.

stem: A nurse teaches a client who has been prescribed oral sumatriptan for migraine. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: “I will take a tablet as soon as I notice my migraine starting.”
options.why: Triptans work best when taken early in the headache phase.

options.text: “I will take one tablet every morning to keep migraines from starting.”
options.why: Sumatriptan is an abortive drug used to treat a migraine once it begins; it is not taken daily for prevention, and overuse can cause medication-overuse headache.

options.text: “If the headache comes back, I can take a second dose at least 2 hours after the first, without going over my daily limit.”
options.why: Oral sumatriptan may be repeated after 2 hours if needed, within the prescribed maximum daily dose.

options.text: “I will get help right away if I have chest pain that is severe or does not go away.”
options.why: Triptans constrict blood vessels and can rarely cause myocardial ischemia, so severe or persistent chest pain needs urgent evaluation.

takeaway: Triptans treat migraine attacks; they are not daily preventive drugs. Take them early and repeat only within the label limits.

stem: A client who has been taking ergotamine-caffeine tablets frequently for migraines calls the clinic. Which reported finding requires immediate evaluation?

options.text: Mild nausea after taking the tablets
options.why: Nausea is a common side effect of ergotamine and is not by itself dangerous.

options.text: Cold, pale, numb fingers and toes with aching leg muscles
options.why: These are signs of ergotism, peripheral ischemia from ergot-induced vasoconstriction, which can lead to gangrene; the drug should be stopped and the client evaluated right away.

options.text: Feeling jittery after a dose
options.why: Mild jitteriness is expected from the caffeine component and is not an emergency.

options.text: Headache relief within an hour of the dose
options.why: This is the intended therapeutic effect.

takeaway: Overuse of ergotamine can cause ergotism, with cold, numb, pale extremities and muscle pain. Stop the drug and seek urgent evaluation.

stem: Cyclobenzaprine is prescribed for a client with an acute low back strain. Which finding in the client's history should the nurse report before giving the drug?

options.text: Takes acetaminophen as needed for pain
options.why: Acetaminophen can be used safely with cyclobenzaprine and is often part of a multimodal plan.

options.text: Seasonal allergic rhinitis
options.why: Seasonal allergies are not a contraindication to cyclobenzaprine.

options.text: Myocardial infarction 3 weeks ago
options.why: Cyclobenzaprine is structurally related to tricyclic antidepressants and is contraindicated during the acute recovery phase of myocardial infarction and in clients with dysrhythmias, heart block or heart failure.

options.text: Works as a schoolteacher
options.why: Occupation is relevant to teaching about drowsiness but is not a contraindication.

takeaway: Cyclobenzaprine acts like a tricyclic. Avoid it after a recent MI and in clients with dysrhythmias, heart block, heart failure, hyperthyroidism or MAOI use.

stem: A client with spinal cord injury has an implanted intrathecal baclofen pump and missed the scheduled refill appointment. The client now has severe itching, markedly increased muscle spasticity, a temperature of 101.8°F (38.8°C), and new confusion. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give acetaminophen for the fever and recheck the temperature in 1 hour.
options.why: Treating the fever alone delays recognition of a life-threatening withdrawal syndrome.

options.text: Notify the provider immediately of possible baclofen withdrawal.
options.why: Abrupt interruption of intrathecal baclofen causes high fever, altered mental status, rebound spasticity and pruritus, which can progress to rhabdomyolysis, multiple organ failure and death; it requires emergency treatment and restoration of baclofen.

options.text: Apply warm packs to the spastic muscles and reposition the client.
options.why: Comfort measures do not address the cause, which is loss of baclofen delivery.

options.text: Reassure the client that spasticity often fluctuates in spinal cord injury.
options.why: Fever, confusion and severe rebound spasticity together are not a normal fluctuation and must be reported urgently.

takeaway: Intrathecal baclofen withdrawal (fever, altered mental status, rebound spasticity, itching) is a medical emergency. Report it immediately.

stem: A client with multiple sclerosis is starting oral baclofen for spasticity. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: “I will avoid drinking alcohol while taking baclofen.”
options.why: Alcohol adds to baclofen's central nervous system depression, so avoiding it is correct.

options.text: “I will get up slowly and be careful when I first start the medicine.”
options.why: Drowsiness, dizziness and weakness are common at first, so caution helps prevent falls.

options.text: “If the medicine makes me too sleepy, I will just stop taking it.”
options.why: Stopping baclofen abruptly can cause withdrawal with hallucinations, seizures and rebound spasticity; the dose must be tapered under provider direction.

options.text: “I will not drive until I know how the medicine affects me.”
options.why: Because of sedation, avoiding driving until the effect is known is appropriate.

takeaway: Never stop baclofen abruptly. Withdrawal can cause hallucinations, seizures and rebound spasticity, so the dose is tapered.

stem: A client who takes oxycodone 10 mg every 6 hours for cancer pain is started on gabapentin for neuropathic pain. Which nursing action is the priority after the first doses?

options.text: Check serum potassium every morning.
options.why: Gabapentin does not affect potassium, and potassium monitoring is not part of this drug combination.

options.text: Measure blood glucose before each dose.
options.why: Gabapentin does not cause clinically important changes in blood glucose.

options.text: Monitor sedation level and respiratory rate closely.
options.why: Gabapentinoids taken with opioids increase the risk of serious respiratory depression and oversedation, an FDA warning that applies especially to older adults and clients with lung disease.

options.text: Assess for pinpoint pupils as the main sign of toxicity.
options.why: Miosis is expected with opioids and is not a reliable sign of dangerous toxicity; sedation and respiratory status are the key assessments.

takeaway: Gabapentin or pregabalin added to an opioid increases the risk of respiratory depression. Monitor sedation and respirations closely, especially at first.

stem: A client who began taking pregabalin for diabetic peripheral neuropathy 1 week ago calls the clinic. Which reported symptom requires immediate action?

options.text: Mild dizziness when standing up
options.why: Dizziness is a common, expected side effect that is managed with caution and slow position changes.

options.text: Dry mouth
options.why: Dry mouth is a common, minor side effect of pregabalin.

options.text: Gaining 2 lb (0.9 kg) over the week
options.why: Modest weight gain and mild peripheral edema can occur with pregabalin; they are monitored but are not emergencies.

options.text: Swelling of the lips and tongue
options.why: Pregabalin can cause swelling of the face, mouth and throat that may compromise the airway; the client should stop the drug and seek emergency care.

takeaway: Pregabalin can cause serious allergic-type swelling. Swelling of the face, lips or tongue needs emergency care; dizziness and sleepiness are common and expected.

stem: A client who takes duloxetine for diabetic neuropathic pain was prescribed tramadol 2 days ago for a knee injury. Which finding should the nurse report immediately?

options.text: Temperature of 102.6°F (39.2°C), agitation, tremor, and muscle twitching
