options.why: Duloxetine (an SNRI) and tramadol both increase serotonin; hyperthermia, agitation, tremor and myoclonus or hyperreflexia indicate serotonin syndrome, which can be fatal.

options.text: Mild nausea after taking duloxetine
options.why: Nausea is a common duloxetine side effect, especially early in therapy, and is not an emergency.

options.text: Dry mouth
options.why: Dry mouth is a common, minor side effect of both drugs.

options.text: Slight drowsiness in the evening
options.why: Mild drowsiness is expected with tramadol and does not suggest serotonin syndrome.

takeaway: SNRIs or SSRIs combined with tramadol (or other serotonergic drugs) can cause serotonin syndrome: hyperthermia, agitation, tremor, clonus and hyperreflexia.

stem: A client with chronic low back pain asks the nurse what can be done besides medication. Which recommendation is most appropriate?

options.text: Stay on bed rest until the pain is completely gone.
options.why: Prolonged bed rest leads to deconditioning and slower recovery; staying active is recommended.

options.text: Wear a lumbar brace at all times, including during sleep.
options.why: Continuous bracing weakens core muscles and is not supported for chronic low back pain.

options.text: Take part in a regular exercise program such as yoga or tai chi.
options.why: Exercise-based therapies such as yoga and tai chi, along with mindfulness and cognitive behavioral approaches, are recommended first-line nonpharmacologic treatments for chronic low back pain.

options.text: Avoid any activity that causes even mild discomfort.
options.why: Avoiding all activity promotes fear-avoidance and disability; gradual, guided activity is encouraged.

takeaway: For chronic low back pain, stay active. Exercise, yoga, tai chi and mind-body therapies come before medication, and bed rest is avoided.

stem: A client with diabetic peripheral neuropathy wants to use a warm pack for an aching shoulder. Which instruction is most important?

options.text: “Check the pack's temperature on skin with normal feeling, place a cloth between the pack and your skin, and limit use to about 20 minutes.”
options.why: Reduced sensation means the client may not feel a burn developing; testing temperature on skin with normal sensation, using a barrier and limiting the time prevent thermal injury.

options.text: “Use the highest setting, since your nerves will not feel the heat well.”
options.why: Higher heat greatly increases the risk of burns in a client who cannot sense excessive temperature.

options.text: “Fall asleep with the heating pad on the low setting to keep the muscles relaxed overnight.”
options.why: Prolonged heat application, even on low, can cause burns, especially when the client is asleep and has reduced sensation.

options.text: “Place the warm pack directly on your skin so the heat penetrates better.”
options.why: Direct contact without a barrier increases the risk of burns.

takeaway: Heat is a useful comfort measure, but clients with reduced sensation need a barrier, a time limit (about 20 minutes) and a temperature check on skin with normal feeling.

stem: A nurse is assessing pain in a 5-year-old who had a tonsillectomy this morning. The child is awake and talking. Which pain assessment tool is most appropriate?

options.text: 0-to-10 numeric rating scale
options.why: Numeric scales require an understanding of numbers and proportion and are generally used for children about 8 years and older.

options.text: FLACC (Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability) scale
options.why: FLACC is a behavioral scale for infants, toddlers and children who cannot self-report; a verbal 5-year-old should be asked to self-report.

options.text: Wong-Baker FACES Pain Rating Scale
options.why: The FACES scale is validated for children about 3 years and older who can point to the face that matches how they feel, so it is appropriate for a verbal preschooler.

options.text: CRIES neonatal pain scale
options.why: CRIES is designed for postoperative pain in neonates, not preschool children.

takeaway: Match the pain tool to the child's development: FLACC for preverbal children, FACES for about age 3 and up, and numeric scales for about age 8 and up.

stem: A nurse is preparing to perform a heel stick on a 2-day-old newborn. Which intervention is most effective for reducing procedural pain?

options.text: Give oral acetaminophen immediately before the heel stick.
options.why: Acetaminophen has not been shown to reduce the pain of heel lance in newborns and is not used for this purpose.

options.text: Apply a topical lidocaine-prilocaine cream to the heel right before the stick.
options.why: Topical anesthetic cream needs about an hour to work and has not been shown to reduce heel lance pain; applying it right before the procedure has no effect.

options.text: Give oral sucrose solution on a pacifier about 2 minutes before the heel stick.
options.why: Oral sucrose with non-nutritive sucking given about 2 minutes before a brief painful procedure is an evidence-based way to reduce newborn pain; skin-to-skin contact, swaddling and breastfeeding also help.

options.text: Wait until the newborn is in deep sleep so the newborn will not feel the stick.
options.why: Newborns feel pain whether asleep or awake; waking a sleeping infant with a painful procedure does not prevent pain.

takeaway: For brief newborn procedures, use oral sucrose with a pacifier, skin-to-skin contact, swaddling or breastfeeding. Newborns feel pain even when asleep.

stem: A client 2 days after a laminectomy is laughing with visitors and tells the nurse, “My back pain is 8 out of 10.” The client has a prescription for an as-needed analgesic and is alert with normal respirations. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Accept the client's rating, give the prescribed analgesic, and reassess its effect.
options.why: Pain is what the client says it is; self-report is the most reliable indicator, and behaviors such as laughing or distraction do not rule out severe pain.

options.text: Withhold the analgesic because the client's behavior does not match the rating.
options.why: Clients cope with pain in many ways, including humor and distraction; withholding analgesia based on behavior leads to undertreated pain.

options.text: Ask the visitors to leave so the client will report a more accurate rating.
options.why: This implies the client's report is unreliable and isolates the client without addressing the pain.

options.text: Document that the client appears to be exaggerating the pain.
options.why: This judgment is biased and unsupported; the nurse should document the client's own rating and the response to treatment.

takeaway: Self-report is the gold standard for pain. Behaviors such as laughing, sleeping or normal vital signs do not disprove a client's pain rating.

stem: A nurse reviews prescriptions for an 84-year-old client with reduced kidney function who has hip fracture pain. Which prescription should the nurse question?

options.text: Acetaminophen 650 mg orally every 6 hours
options.why: Scheduled acetaminophen within the daily maximum is a recommended first-line analgesic for older adults.

options.text: Oxycodone 2.5 mg orally every 4 hours as needed
options.why: A low starting dose of oxycodone is appropriate for an older adult with moderate to severe pain, with monitoring.

options.text: Senna 8.6 mg orally at bedtime
options.why: A stimulant laxative is appropriate to prevent opioid-induced constipation.

options.text: Meperidine 50 mg IM every 4 hours as needed
options.why: Meperidine is on the Beers Criteria list of drugs to avoid in older adults; its metabolite normeperidine accumulates, especially with reduced kidney function, causing tremors, delirium and seizures, and it is a poor analgesic.

takeaway: Avoid meperidine, especially in older adults and in kidney impairment, because normeperidine accumulates and can cause seizures.

stem: A client has received ketorolac 15 mg IV every 6 hours for 4 days after abdominal surgery. A new prescription continues IV ketorolac for 3 more days. Which action by the nurse is appropriate?

options.text: Give the drug as prescribed, since the IV route avoids stomach irritation.
options.why: NSAID GI toxicity is systemic, from prostaglandin inhibition, so the IV route does not prevent GI bleeding.

options.text: Change to oral ketorolac to continue the 3-day course.
options.why: Oral ketorolac counts toward the same 5-day total limit, and the nurse cannot change the route without a prescription.

options.text: Contact the provider, because the total course of ketorolac should not exceed 5 days.
options.why: Ketorolac (IV, IM and oral combined) is limited to 5 days because the risk of GI bleeding and acute kidney injury rises with longer use; 7 days total exceeds this limit.

options.text: Give the drug and monitor only the client's pain rating.
options.why: Even within the limit, ketorolac requires monitoring of kidney function, bleeding and GI symptoms; here the duration itself must be clarified.

takeaway: Ketorolac is limited to 5 days in total by all routes combined because of GI bleeding and kidney injury risk.

stem: A client is discharged with extended-release oxycodone tablets. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: “I will swallow the tablet whole, one tablet at a time.”
options.why: Extended-release tablets must be swallowed whole to keep the controlled release.

options.text: “I will store the tablets in a locked place away from visitors and children.”
options.why: Secure storage prevents accidental ingestion and misuse.

options.text: “If the tablet is hard to swallow, I will crush it and mix it with applesauce.”
options.why: Crushing, chewing or dissolving extended-release opioids releases the whole dose at once (dose dumping) and can cause a fatal overdose.

options.text: “I will not drink alcohol while I am taking this medicine.”
options.why: Alcohol adds to opioid sedation and respiratory depression and should be avoided.

takeaway: Never crush, chew or split extended-release opioids. Dose dumping can be fatal.

stem: Thirty minutes after receiving morphine 4 mg IV for the first time, a postoperative client asks to walk to the bathroom. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Tell the client to walk alone to promote independence.
options.why: Walking unassisted soon after the first IV opioid dose puts the client at risk of falling from dizziness or orthostatic hypotension.

options.text: Insert an indwelling urinary catheter so the client does not need to get up.
options.why: Catheterization requires a prescription, increases infection risk and is not needed to manage this situation.

options.text: Give a PRN antiemetic before the client stands up.
options.why: An antiemetic does not prevent orthostatic hypotension and is not indicated without nausea.

options.text: Have the client sit on the side of the bed for a few minutes, then assist the client to walk.
options.why: Opioids can cause orthostatic hypotension and dizziness; dangling first and assisting the client help prevent a fall.

takeaway: After opioid doses, especially the first, change position slowly and assist with ambulation to prevent falls from orthostatic hypotension and dizziness.

stem: A prescription reads hydromorphone 0.6 mg IV push now for pain. The vial contains hydromorphone 2 mg/mL. How many mL should the nurse draw up? (Round to the nearest tenth.)

options.why: This misplaces the decimal point; 0.6 ÷ 2 equals 0.3, not 0.03, so this would be one-tenth of the dose.

options.text: 0.3 mL
options.why: Correct calculation: desired ÷ have × volume = 0.6 mg ÷ 2 mg × 1 mL = 0.3 mL.

options.text: 1.2 mL
options.why: This multiplies the dose by the concentration (0.6 × 2) instead of dividing, giving four times the correct volume.

options.text: 3.3 mL
options.why: This inverts the formula (2 ÷ 0.6) and would deliver more than ten times the prescribed dose.

takeaway: Desired ÷ have × volume. For high-alert opioids, double-check the decimal point and have the dose independently verified when policy requires it.

stem: A child who weighs 18 kg has a prescription for ibuprofen 10 mg/kg orally every 6 hours as needed for pain. The suspension available is 100 mg/5 mL. How many mL should the nurse give per dose? (Round to the nearest tenth.)

options.text: 3.6 mL
options.why: This divides 180 by 50 instead of by 20 mg/mL; the suspension contains 100 mg per 5 mL, which is 20 mg/mL.

options.text: 18 mL
options.why: This doubles the correct volume and would deliver 360 mg, twice the prescribed dose.

options.text: 9 mL
options.why: Correct calculation: 10 mg/kg × 18 kg = 180 mg; 180 mg ÷ 100 mg × 5 mL = 9 mL.

options.text: 4.5 mL
options.why: This gives only 90 mg, half the prescribed dose of 180 mg.

takeaway: Weight-based pediatric doses take two steps: mg/kg × kg = mg, then mg ÷ concentration = mL. Check the result against the maximum single dose.

stem: A child who weighs 33 lb has a prescription for morphine 0.05 mg/kg IV every 3 hours as needed for postoperative pain. The vial contains morphine 2 mg/mL. How many mL should the nurse give? (Round to the nearest hundredth.)

options.why: Correct calculation: 33 lb ÷ 2.2 = 15 kg; 0.05 mg/kg × 15 kg = 0.75 mg; 0.75 mg ÷ 2 mg/mL = 0.375 mL, which rounds to 0.38 mL.
This is the dose in mg (0.75 mg) entered as mL without dividing by the 2 mg/mL concentration, giving twice the prescribed dose.
This uses pounds instead of kilograms (0.05 × 33 = 1.65 mg ÷ 2 = 0.83 mL), more than twice the correct dose.

options.text: 1.5 mL
options.why: This multiplies 0.75 mg by the concentration instead of dividing, giving four times the correct volume.

takeaway: Convert pounds to kilograms (÷ 2.2) before calculating a mg/kg dose; using pounds overdoses a child more than twofold.

stem: A nurse is identifying postoperative clients at increased risk for opioid-induced respiratory depression. Which client factors increase this risk? Select all that apply.

options.text: Obstructive sleep apnea
options.why: Correct. Clients with sleep apnea already have airway obstruction during sleep, and opioids further blunt arousal and respiratory drive.

options.text: No opioid use before surgery
options.why: Correct. Opioid-naive clients have not developed tolerance to respiratory depression and are at higher risk, especially in the first 24 hours.

options.text: Takes lorazepam at bedtime
options.why: Correct. Benzodiazepines add to opioid central nervous system and respiratory depression.

options.text: Age 78 years
options.why: Correct. Older adults have reduced drug clearance and greater sensitivity to opioid sedation.

options.text: Has taken a stable dose of opioid for chronic pain for 2 years
options.why: Incorrect. Long-term opioid use produces tolerance to respiratory depression, so this is not a risk factor compared with opioid-naive clients (although dose increases still need monitoring).

options.text: Pain rated 8/10
options.why: Incorrect. Pain stimulates respiration; severe pain itself is not a risk factor for respiratory depression, although it does require careful dose titration.

takeaway: High risk for opioid respiratory depression: opioid-naive, older age, sleep apnea or obesity, lung disease, and other sedatives such as benzodiazepines or gabapentinoids.

stem: A nurse is teaching a client who is starting naproxen for osteoarthritis. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Take each dose with food or milk.
options.why: Correct. Taking NSAIDs with food reduces gastric irritation.

options.text: Take the tablets on an empty stomach so they work faster.
options.why: Incorrect. Taking NSAIDs on an empty stomach increases GI irritation and the risk of ulcers.

options.text: Report black stools or vomit that looks like coffee grounds.
options.why: Correct. These are signs of GI bleeding, a serious NSAID adverse effect.

options.text: Do not take over-the-counter ibuprofen along with naproxen.
options.why: Correct. Combining NSAIDs adds GI, kidney and cardiovascular risk without added benefit.

options.text: Swelling of the ankles and weight gain are harmless and can be ignored.
options.why: Incorrect. NSAIDs cause sodium and fluid retention, which can worsen hypertension or heart failure; edema and weight gain should be reported.

takeaway: NSAID teaching: take with food, use only one NSAID at a time, and report GI bleeding, edema, weight gain and cardiovascular warning signs.

stem: A client is taking prescribed acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours. The nurse teaches the client to avoid duplicating acetaminophen. Which products contain acetaminophen? Select all that apply.

options.text: Oxycodone-acetaminophen (Percocet)
options.why: Correct. This combination opioid contains acetaminophen in every tablet.

options.text: NyQuil Cold & Flu
options.why: Correct. This nighttime multi-symptom product contains acetaminophen along with dextromethorphan and doxylamine.

options.text: Naproxen sodium (Aleve)
options.why: Incorrect. Naproxen is an NSAID and contains no acetaminophen.

options.text: Excedrin Migraine
options.why: Correct. This product combines acetaminophen, aspirin and caffeine.

options.text: Ibuprofen (Advil)
options.why: Incorrect. Ibuprofen is an NSAID and does not contain acetaminophen.

options.text: Tylenol PM
options.why: Correct. This sleep product contains acetaminophen and diphenhydramine.

takeaway: Acetaminophen is found in many combination opioids, cold and flu remedies, migraine products and 'PM' sleep aids. Teach clients to count every source toward the daily limit.

stem: A client is receiving a continuous peripheral nerve block infusion of ropivacaine after shoulder surgery. Which findings should the nurse recognize as early signs of local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST)? Select all that apply.

options.text: Numbness around the mouth
options.why: Correct. Circumoral numbness is a classic early central nervous system sign of LAST.

options.text: Metallic taste
options.why: Correct. A metallic taste is an early neurologic warning sign of rising local anesthetic levels.

options.text: Pinpoint pupils
options.why: Incorrect. Miosis is associated with opioids, not local anesthetic toxicity.

options.text: Ringing in the ears
options.why: Correct. Tinnitus is an early sign of local anesthetic toxicity that may progress to seizures and cardiac dysrhythmias.

options.text: Numbness of the operative arm
options.why: Incorrect. Numbness in the blocked extremity is the intended effect of a peripheral nerve block.

takeaway: Early LAST signs include circumoral numbness, metallic taste, tinnitus, dizziness and agitation; it can progress to seizures and cardiac arrest. Stop the infusion and get help.

stem: A nurse is teaching a client with chronic cancer pain who uses transdermal fentanyl. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Avoid heating pads, electric blankets, hot tubs and saunas.
options.why: Correct. Heat increases blood flow to the skin and fentanyl absorption, which can cause an overdose.

options.text: Replace the patch every 24 hours.
options.why: Incorrect. Most fentanyl patches are changed every 72 hours; changing every 24 hours could cause overdose.

options.text: Fold a used patch in half with the sticky sides together before disposal.
options.why: Correct. Used patches still contain fentanyl; folding them and disposing of them as directed (such as flushing, per FDA guidance) prevents accidental exposure.

options.text: Call the provider if you develop a fever.
options.why: Correct. Fever raises skin temperature and can increase fentanyl absorption.

options.text: Cut the patch in half on days when your pain is less.
options.why: Incorrect. Cutting a fentanyl patch damages the controlled release and can cause a rapid, dangerous dose.

options.text: Store patches where children and pets cannot reach them.
options.why: Correct. Even one patch can cause fatal respiratory depression in a child or pet.

takeaway: Fentanyl patch safety: no heat, report fever, never cut, change on schedule (usually every 72 hours), and store and discard so children and pets cannot be exposed.

stem: A nurse uses the PAINAD scale to assess pain in a client with advanced dementia who cannot give a self-report. Which observations suggest the client is in pain? Select all that apply.

options.text: Grimacing
options.why: Correct. Facial grimacing is a key behavioral indicator of pain in nonverbal clients.

options.text: Moaning when repositioned
options.why: Correct. Negative vocalizations such as moaning or groaning indicate possible pain.

options.text: Absence of crying, so the client has no pain
options.why: Incorrect. Lack of crying does not mean lack of pain; clients with dementia often show pain in other ways.

options.text: Clenched fists and rigid body posture
options.why: Correct. Rigid or tense body language and clenched fists are PAINAD indicators of pain.

options.text: Heart rate of 92/min as the main proof of pain
options.why: Incorrect. Vital signs are unreliable indicators of pain and should not be used alone to confirm or rule it out.

takeaway: In nonverbal clients, look at behavior (face, vocalizations, body language, breathing, consolability). Vital signs are not reliable pain indicators.

stem: A nurse is planning nonpharmacologic pain relief for a client 1 day after an open abdominal surgery. Which interventions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Teach the client to splint the incision with a pillow when coughing.
options.why: Correct. Splinting supports the incision and lessens pain during coughing and deep breathing.

options.text: Use nonpharmacologic methods in place of prescribed analgesics.
options.why: Incorrect. Nonpharmacologic methods add to, but do not replace, analgesics for moderate to severe postoperative pain.

options.text: Offer music or guided imagery the client enjoys.
options.why: Correct. Distraction and relaxation techniques reduce pain perception and anxiety.

options.text: Keep the client flat and still to avoid stretching the incision.
options.why: Incorrect. Immobility increases the risk of complications such as pneumonia and thrombosis; early ambulation with pain control is encouraged.

options.text: Reposition the client and support the body with pillows.
options.why: Correct. Regular repositioning with support reduces muscle tension and pressure discomfort.

options.text: Apply a heating pad directly to the incision.
options.why: Incorrect. Heat on a fresh incision can increase swelling and bleeding and risks burns; cold may be used if prescribed.

takeaway: Nonpharmacologic measures (splinting, positioning, distraction, relaxation) complement analgesics; they do not replace them.

stem: Sumatriptan is prescribed for a client's migraines. Which findings in the client's history should the nurse report to the provider before the first dose? Select all that apply.

options.text: Coronary artery disease with stable angina
options.why: Correct. Triptans cause vasoconstriction and are contraindicated in ischemic heart disease.

options.text: Blood pressure of 176/104 mm Hg at today's visit
options.why: Correct. Uncontrolled hypertension is a contraindication because triptans can raise blood pressure further.

options.text: Takes levothyroxine for hypothyroidism
options.why: Incorrect. Levothyroxine does not interact with sumatriptan and hypothyroidism is not a contraindication.

options.text: Took ergotamine 8 hours ago
options.why: Correct. Triptans must not be used within 24 hours of an ergot drug because of additive vasoconstriction.

options.text: Takes phenelzine for depression
options.why: Correct. MAO-A inhibitors increase sumatriptan levels; sumatriptan is contraindicated with or within 2 weeks of an MAO inhibitor.

takeaway: Triptan contraindications include ischemic heart or cerebrovascular disease, uncontrolled hypertension, an ergot drug within 24 hours, and MAO inhibitors (for sumatriptan).

stem: A client who takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation asks which over-the-counter products are safe for minor aches and an upset stomach. Which products should the nurse advise the client to avoid unless the provider approves? Select all that apply.

options.text: Aspirin
options.why: Correct. Aspirin inhibits platelet function and greatly increases bleeding risk when combined with an anticoagulant.

options.text: Acetaminophen
options.why: Incorrect. Acetaminophen at recommended doses does not affect platelets and is the preferred OTC analgesic for clients taking anticoagulants.

options.text: Naproxen
options.why: Correct. NSAIDs impair platelet function and irritate the GI lining, increasing the risk of serious bleeding with apixaban.

options.text: Bismuth subsalicylate
options.why: Correct. This product contains a salicylate related to aspirin and its label advises asking a provider before use with anticoagulants.

options.text: Docusate sodium
options.why: Incorrect. A stool softener does not affect bleeding or apixaban levels.

options.text: Loratadine
options.why: Incorrect. Loratadine does not affect platelet function or apixaban.

takeaway: Clients on anticoagulants should avoid aspirin, other salicylates and NSAIDs unless prescribed. Acetaminophen is the usual OTC choice.

stem: A nurse is teaching a client who is starting gabapentin for postherpetic neuralgia. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Get up slowly and take care to prevent falls.
options.why: Correct. Dizziness and drowsiness are common, especially when starting or increasing the dose.

options.text: Avoid alcohol.
options.why: Correct. Alcohol adds to gabapentin's central nervous system depression.

options.text: Take aluminum-magnesium antacids at the same time as gabapentin.
options.why: Incorrect. These antacids lower gabapentin absorption; gabapentin should be taken at least 2 hours after them.

options.text: Do not stop the drug suddenly; the provider will taper it.
options.why: Correct. Abrupt discontinuation can cause withdrawal symptoms and, in clients with seizure disorders, seizures.

options.text: Report new or worsening depression or thoughts of self-harm.
options.why: Correct. Antiepileptic drugs, including gabapentin, carry a warning about suicidal thoughts and behavior.

options.text: If you miss a dose, take a double dose next time.
options.why: Incorrect. Doubling doses increases sedation and dizziness; the client should take the missed dose when remembered unless the next dose is soon.

takeaway: Gabapentin teaching: fall precautions, no alcohol, separate it from antacids, taper rather than stop suddenly, and report mood changes.

stem: A nurse is replacing a client's transdermal fentanyl patch. Place the steps in the correct order.

options.text: Clean a new, intact, hairless site on the upper body with clear water and let it dry.
options.why: Step 3. Soap, lotion or alcohol can irritate the skin or change absorption, so only water is used, and a new site reduces irritation.

options.text: Document the date, time, and site of the new patch.
options.why: Step 5. Recording the application allows accurate timing of the next change and site rotation.

options.text: Perform hand hygiene and put on gloves.
options.why: Step 1. Gloves protect the nurse from absorbing fentanyl through the skin, so they go on first.

options.text: Apply the new patch and press firmly with the palm for about 30 seconds.
options.why: Step 4. Firm pressure ensures full contact, especially around the edges, for consistent absorption.

options.text: Remove the old patch, fold the sticky sides together, and dispose of it according to policy.
options.why: Step 2. Removing the old patch before applying the new one prevents a double dose, and folding it prevents accidental exposure.

takeaway: Fentanyl patch change: gloves, remove and fold the old patch, clean the new site with water only, press the new patch for 30 seconds, then document.

stem: A nurse is giving morphine 2 mg by IV push through a peripheral IV line to a postoperative client. Place the nurse's actions in the correct order.

options.text: Flush the line with saline at the same slow rate.
options.why: Step 4. Flushing at the same rate delivers the drug remaining in the tubing without giving it as a rapid bolus.

options.text: Assess the client's pain, sedation level, and respiratory rate.
options.why: Step 1. Baseline assessment confirms that the dose is needed and safe to give.

options.text: Reassess sedation and respirations about 15 to 30 minutes later.
options.why: Step 5. IV morphine peaks in about 20 minutes, so reassessment then captures its peak effect and any oversedation.

options.text: Flush the IV line with normal saline to confirm patency.
options.why: Step 2. Confirming patency before injecting prevents giving the drug into an infiltrated line.

options.text: Inject the morphine slowly over 4 to 5 minutes.
options.why: Step 3. Slow injection reduces the risk of hypotension and sudden respiratory depression.

takeaway: IV push opioid: assess, flush for patency, inject slowly, flush at the same rate, then reassess at the drug's peak.

stem: A nurse is assessing pain in a client with severe dementia who cannot reliably answer questions. Place the steps of the pain assessment hierarchy for nonverbal clients in the correct order.

options.text: Try an analgesic and watch for a change in pain behaviors.
options.why: Step 5. An analgesic trial is the final step; a reduction in pain behaviors after treatment confirms that pain was likely the cause.

options.text: Observe pain behaviors using a validated tool.
options.why: Step 3. Behaviors such as grimacing, moaning or guarding provide evidence of pain when self-report is not possible.

options.text: Attempt to obtain a self-report, even a simple yes or no or a pointed answer.
options.why: Step 1. Self-report is always attempted first because it is the most reliable indicator, and many cognitively impaired clients can give a simple answer.

options.text: Ask family members or caregivers who know the client well about changes in behavior.
options.why: Step 4. Surrogates can describe the client's usual behavior and recognize changes that may signal pain.

options.text: Search for potential causes of pain, such as recent surgery, fractures, or pressure injuries.
options.why: Step 2. If a painful condition or procedure is present, pain should be assumed present.

takeaway: Hierarchy for nonverbal clients: self-report, causes of pain, behaviors, surrogate report, then an analgesic trial.

stem: A nurse is teaching a client how to use lidocaine 5% topical patches prescribed for postherpetic neuralgia. Place the steps in the correct order.

options.text: Cut the patch to fit the painful area, if needed, before removing the release liner.
options.why: Step 2. Patches may be cut to size, and cutting before removing the liner keeps the adhesive manageable.

options.text: Remove the patch after 12 hours.
options.why: Step 4. Lidocaine 5% patches are worn for up to 12 hours in a 24-hour period.

options.text: Inspect the painful area to make sure the skin is intact.
options.why: Step 1. Lidocaine patches are applied only to intact skin, because broken skin increases absorption and the risk of toxicity.

options.text: Leave the skin uncovered for 12 hours before applying the next patch.
options.why: Step 5. A 12-hour patch-free period limits systemic absorption and skin irritation.

options.text: Remove the release liner and apply the patch to the most painful area.
options.why: Step 3. The patch is then placed directly over the area of neuropathic pain.

takeaway: Lidocaine 5% patches: intact skin only, cut before removing the liner, wear up to 12 hours, then 12 hours off.

stem: A client with community-acquired pneumonia has a documented history of throat swelling and low blood pressure after taking amoxicillin 5 years ago. The new prescription is amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg orally every 12 hours. What is the nurse's best action?

options.text: Give the first dose and observe the client closely for 30 minutes.
options.why: Amoxicillin-clavulanate contains amoxicillin, the exact drug that caused a prior anaphylactic reaction; observation does not make giving it safe.

options.text: Withhold the medication and contact the prescriber for an alternative antibiotic.
options.why: Throat swelling and hypotension describe anaphylaxis. Giving the same penicillin again risks a life-threatening reaction, so the nurse holds the dose and clarifies the order.

options.text: Give diphenhydramine 30 minutes before the first dose.
options.why: Antihistamine premedication does not prevent an IgE-mediated anaphylactic reaction and can mask early warning signs.

options.text: Give the dose with food to lower the risk of a reaction.
options.why: Food reduces gastrointestinal upset from amoxicillin-clavulanate; it has no effect on allergic reactions.

takeaway: Always compare a new prescription with the client's allergy history. A penicillin combination product (such as amoxicillin-clavulanate or piperacillin-tazobactam) is still a penicillin.

stem: Ten minutes into the first IV infusion of piperacillin-tazobactam, Mr. Haddad, 58, says his throat feels tight. He has audible wheezing, hives across his chest, BP 82/50 mm Hg and HR 124/min. The nurse has stopped the infusion and called for help. Which medication should the nurse prepare to give first?

options.text: Diphenhydramine 50 mg IV
options.why: Antihistamines relieve itching and hives but do not reverse airway swelling, bronchospasm or hypotension; they are adjuncts only.

options.text: Methylprednisolone 125 mg IV
options.why: Corticosteroids take hours to work and do not treat the acute airway and circulatory compromise of anaphylaxis.

options.text: Epinephrine 0.5 mg (1 mg/mL) IM in the anterolateral thigh
options.why: Epinephrine is the first-line drug for anaphylaxis: alpha effects raise blood pressure and reduce airway edema, and beta effects relieve bronchospasm. The adult IM dose is 0.3 to 0.5 mg of the 1 mg/mL concentration.

options.text: Albuterol 2.5 mg by nebulizer
options.why: Albuterol may help bronchospasm but does not treat upper-airway swelling or hypotension, so it is not the first drug.

takeaway: In anaphylaxis, stop the trigger and give IM epinephrine first. Antihistamines, steroids and bronchodilators are add-ons, never substitutes.

stem: The nurse prepares penicillin G benzathine 2.4 million units for a client with primary syphilis. Which action is essential when giving this medication?

options.text: Dilute it in 50 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride and infuse over 30 minutes.
options.why: Penicillin G benzathine is a thick suspension that must never be given IV; inadvertent IV administration has caused cardiorespiratory arrest and death.

options.text: Inject it subcutaneously into the abdomen to slow absorption.
options.why: The drug is labeled for deep IM use only; subcutaneous injection causes pain and tissue injury and is not an approved route.

options.text: Give the full dose as one injection into the deltoid muscle.
options.why: 2.4 million units is about 4 mL, too much for the deltoid. It is given into a large muscle and is often split into two injections.

options.text: Inject it deep IM into a large muscle, such as the ventrogluteal site, and never intravenously.
options.why: Deep IM injection into a large muscle is the only approved route. The label carries a boxed warning against IV administration because of the risk of cardiorespiratory arrest.

takeaway: Penicillin G benzathine is deep IM only, into a large muscle. Never give it IV.

stem: Vancomycin 1.5 g IV every 12 hours is prescribed for a client with MRSA bacteremia. To lower the risk of vancomycin infusion reaction, what is the minimum time over which the nurse should infuse each dose?

options.text: 150 minutes
options.why: Vancomycin should be infused no faster than 10 mg/min (or over at least 60 minutes, whichever is longer). 1,500 mg ÷ 10 mg/min = 150 minutes.

options.text: 30 minutes
options.why: Infusing 1.5 g over 30 minutes is a rate of 50 mg/min, far faster than recommended, and greatly raises the risk of flushing, itching and hypotension.

options.text: 60 minutes
options.why: Sixty minutes is the minimum only for doses of 600 mg or less. For 1.5 g, a 60-minute infusion would run at 25 mg/min, far faster than the 10 mg/min limit.

options.text: 90 minutes
options.why: Ninety minutes would run at about 17 mg/min, still faster than the 10 mg/min maximum.

takeaway: Infuse vancomycin at no more than 10 mg/min (at least 60 minutes). Larger doses need longer infusions.

stem: A client receives vancomycin every 12 hours, and the next dose is due at 2100. The prescriber orders a trough level. When should the nurse arrange for the blood sample to be drawn?

options.text: 30 minutes after the 2100 infusion is finished
options.why: A sample drawn shortly after the infusion reflects a level near the peak, not the trough.

options.text: Within 30 minutes before the 2100 dose
options.why: A trough is the lowest concentration and is drawn just before the next dose (usually within 30 minutes). Many facilities now use AUC-based dosing with timed levels; the nurse follows the protocol.

options.text: As soon as the 2100 infusion is started
options.why: Once the infusion starts, the serum level begins to rise, so the result would not be a true trough.

options.text: At any time during the shift, as long as the time is recorded
options.why: Vancomycin levels are only interpretable when drawn at the correct time in relation to the dose.

takeaway: Draw a trough immediately before the next dose. Hold the dose until the sample is drawn, and follow the facility's vancomycin protocol.

stem: Ms. Okafor, 66, has received IV vancomycin and IV piperacillin-tazobactam for 4 days for an infected diabetic foot ulcer. Which finding should the nurse report to the prescriber immediately?

options.text: WBC 10,800/mm³, down from 16,000/mm³ on admission
options.why: A falling WBC count suggests that the infection is responding to treatment; it is an expected, favorable trend.

options.text: Fingerstick blood glucose of 168 mg/dL before lunch
options.why: Mild hyperglycemia is common during infection in a client with diabetes. It needs follow-up but is not as urgent as a rising creatinine.

options.text: Serum creatinine 1.8 mg/dL, up from a baseline of 0.9 mg/dL
options.why: Creatinine has doubled (normal about 0.6–1.2 mg/dL), indicating acute kidney injury. Vancomycin is nephrotoxic, and adding piperacillin-tazobactam increases the risk. The prescriber may need to adjust or change therapy.

options.text: Mild nausea after breakfast
options.why: Mild nausea is a common, minor effect of antibiotics and does not need immediate reporting.

takeaway: Monitor creatinine and urine output during vancomycin therapy, especially with other nephrotoxic drugs. A rising creatinine is reported promptly.

stem: A client is receiving vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV every 12 hours for osteomyelitis. Which assessments should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Serum creatinine and urine output
options.why: Correct. Vancomycin can cause nephrotoxicity, so kidney function is monitored throughout therapy.

options.text: Client reports of ringing in the ears or hearing changes
options.why: Correct. Ototoxicity is a known, though less common, adverse effect, especially with high levels or other ototoxic drugs.

options.text: Flushing, itching or rash on the face, neck and upper body during the infusion
options.why: Correct. These signs suggest vancomycin infusion reaction, which is managed by stopping or slowing the infusion.

options.text: Serum vancomycin levels at the times set by protocol
options.why: Correct. Levels (trough or AUC-based) guide dosing to balance effectiveness against toxicity.

options.text: Daily INR
options.why: Incorrect. Vancomycin does not affect clotting factors; INR is not routinely needed.

options.text: Serum amylase
options.why: Incorrect. Pancreatitis is not a recognized adverse effect of vancomycin that requires routine monitoring.

takeaway: Vancomycin monitoring centers on the kidneys, hearing, the infusion rate and drug levels.

stem: A client is receiving gentamicin IV every 8 hours (traditional dosing), and both a peak and a trough level are ordered around the next dose. Place the nurse's actions in the correct order.

options.text: Draw the peak level.
options.why: This is last: the peak is drawn 30 minutes after a 30-minute infusion ends, when the serum level is highest.

options.text: Start the gentamicin infusion.
options.why: Second: the dose is started only after the trough sample has been drawn.

options.text: Draw the trough level within 30 minutes before the dose.
options.why: First: the trough shows the lowest level and must be drawn before the new dose enters the bloodstream.

options.text: Let the 30-minute infusion finish, then wait 30 minutes.
options.why: Third: this waiting period allows the drug to distribute so the next sample reflects the true peak.

takeaway: Aminoglycoside levels: trough just before the dose, then the dose, then the peak 30 minutes after a 30-minute infusion ends.

stem: Gentamicin 120 mg IV every 8 hours is prescribed, to be infused over 30 minutes. The nurse starts the infusion at 0900. At what time should the peak level be drawn?

options.why: At 0900 the infusion has just begun; a sample taken then would reflect the trough, not the peak.
At 0930 the infusion has just ended and the drug is still distributing, so the level would be falsely high.
Fifteen minutes after the infusion ends is too early; the standard timing is 30 minutes after the end of a 30-minute infusion.
The infusion ends at 0930, and the peak is drawn 30 minutes after it ends: 0930 + 30 minutes = 1000.

takeaway: For a 30-minute aminoglycoside infusion, draw the peak 30 minutes after the infusion ends.

stem: A client receiving tobramycin IV every 8 hours has a trough level of 3.1 mcg/mL, drawn before the 1400 dose. The laboratory lists the desired trough as less than 2 mcg/mL. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Hold the 1400 dose and notify the prescriber of the result.
options.why: A high trough means the drug is not being cleared between doses, which increases the risk of nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity. The nurse holds the dose and gets new orders.

options.text: Give the dose as scheduled and recheck the trough tomorrow.
options.why: Giving another dose when the trough is already high adds to the accumulation and raises the risk of toxicity.

options.text: Give half of the scheduled dose.
options.why: Changing the dose is outside the nurse's scope without a new prescription.

options.text: Give the dose and encourage the client to drink more fluids.
options.why: Fluids support the kidneys but do not make it safe to give a dose when the trough is already above target.

takeaway: If an aminoglycoside trough is above target, hold the dose and notify the prescriber. The dose or interval usually needs to change.

stem: A client receiving IV gentamicin for Pseudomonas pneumonia has several new prescriptions. Which medication requires the closest monitoring because it adds to gentamicin's risk of ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity?

options.text: Pantoprazole 40 mg IV daily
options.why: Pantoprazole does not increase the risk of aminoglycoside ototoxicity or nephrotoxicity.

options.text: Furosemide 40 mg IV every 12 hours
options.why: Loop diuretics are ototoxic, and the volume loss they cause can concentrate aminoglycosides and harm the kidneys. The nurse monitors hearing, creatinine, urine output and drug levels closely.

options.text: Enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously daily
options.why: Enoxaparin raises the risk of bleeding but does not add to aminoglycoside toxicity. Its dose may need adjustment if kidney function declines.

options.text: Acetaminophen 650 mg orally every 6 hours as needed
options.why: Acetaminophen at this dose is not ototoxic or nephrotoxic and does not interact with gentamicin.

takeaway: Loop diuretics with aminoglycosides increase the risk of hearing loss and kidney injury. Monitor hearing, creatinine and levels closely.

stem: Mr. Delgado, 74, takes prednisone 10 mg daily for polymyalgia rheumatica. He started levofloxacin 3 days ago for pneumonia and now reports sudden pain and swelling just above his right heel. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Apply a heating pad and encourage him to keep walking.
options.why: Heat and walking could worsen a damaged Achilles tendon and increase the risk of rupture.

options.text: Give ibuprofen and reassess the pain in 1 hour.
options.why: An analgesic may hide symptoms without dealing with the cause, which is suspected fluoroquinolone tendinitis.

options.text: Hold the next levofloxacin dose, have him rest the leg and notify the prescriber.
options.why: Fluoroquinolones carry a boxed warning for tendinitis and tendon rupture, and the risk is higher in adults over 60 and in clients taking corticosteroids. The drug should be stopped and the tendon rested.

options.text: Teach him calf-stretching exercises to relieve the tightness.
options.why: Stretching puts stress on an inflamed tendon and could cause it to rupture.

takeaway: Tendon pain during fluoroquinolone therapy: hold the drug, rest the limb and report it. The risk is higher with age over 60 and with corticosteroids.

stem: The nurse teaches a client about oral ciprofloxacin for a complicated urinary tract infection. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I'll drink plenty of fluids while I'm taking this."
options.why: Good hydration is recommended with ciprofloxacin to help prevent crystalluria.

options.text: "I'll call my provider if I get pain in my ankles or heels."
options.why: This is correct: tendon pain can signal fluoroquinolone tendinitis and should be reported.

options.text: "I'll take my tablet at least 2 hours before my antacid."
options.why: This is correct: ciprofloxacin is taken at least 2 hours before or 6 hours after antacids and calcium, iron, magnesium or zinc products.

options.text: "I'll take my tablet with my calcium supplement and a glass of calcium-fortified orange juice."
options.why: This needs correcting. Calcium binds ciprofloxacin in the gut and reduces absorption. The dose must be separated from calcium supplements, and the label advises against taking it with dairy products or calcium-fortified juice alone (without a meal).

takeaway: Separate fluoroquinolones from calcium, magnesium, aluminum, iron and zinc products: take the antibiotic 2 hours before or 6 hours after them.

stem: The nurse reviews four new antibiotic prescriptions. Which prescription should the nurse question before giving the medication?

options.text: Nitrofurantoin for a 30-year-old with uncomplicated cystitis and normal kidney function
options.why: Nitrofurantoin is a first-line choice for uncomplicated cystitis in a client with normal kidney function.

options.text: Levofloxacin for a 52-year-old with myasthenia gravis
options.why: Fluoroquinolones carry a boxed warning: they can worsen muscle weakness in myasthenia gravis and have caused respiratory failure. They should be avoided in clients with a known history of the disease.

options.text: Cephalexin for a 45-year-old with seasonal allergic rhinitis
options.why: Seasonal allergies are not a contraindication to cephalosporins.

options.text: Azithromycin for a 40-year-old with a normal ECG and normal electrolytes
options.why: With a normal QTc and normal electrolytes, there is no specific reason to question azithromycin.

takeaway: Check the history before giving a fluoroquinolone: it can worsen myasthenia gravis, and it carries other risks such as tendon rupture and QT prolongation.

stem: The nurse reviews the history of a client who has been prescribed levofloxacin. Which findings increase the client's risk of a serious adverse reaction to this drug? Select all that apply.

options.text: Age 78 years
options.why: Correct. Adults over 60 have a higher risk of fluoroquinolone-associated tendinitis and tendon rupture.

options.text: Takes prednisone 5 mg daily
options.why: Correct. Corticosteroid use further increases the risk of tendon rupture with fluoroquinolones.

options.text: Hypothyroidism controlled with levothyroxine
options.why: Incorrect. Treated hypothyroidism is not a recognized risk factor for serious fluoroquinolone reactions.

options.text: History of myasthenia gravis
options.why: Correct. Fluoroquinolones can worsen myasthenic weakness, including respiratory muscle weakness (boxed warning).

options.text: Lactose intolerance
options.why: Incorrect. Lactose intolerance does not affect fluoroquinolone safety.

options.text: Appendectomy 20 years ago
options.why: Incorrect. A remote abdominal surgery has no bearing on fluoroquinolone risk.

takeaway: Major fluoroquinolone risk flags: age over 60, corticosteroids, organ transplant, myasthenia gravis and QT-prolonging conditions or drugs.

stem: A 70-year-old client receiving IV azithromycin for community-acquired pneumonia also takes citalopram for depression. Which finding should the nurse report immediately?

options.text: QTc of 528 ms on today's ECG, up from 440 ms at admission
options.why: Azithromycin and citalopram both prolong the QT interval. A QTc above 500 ms (normal is below about 450 ms in men and 460 ms in women) greatly increases the risk of torsades de pointes and must be reported at once.

options.text: Two loose stools since yesterday
options.why: Mild diarrhea is a common effect of macrolides. It should be monitored but is not as urgent as a dangerously long QTc.

options.text: Mild nausea after the morning dose
options.why: Nausea is a common, minor effect of macrolides.

options.text: Slight discomfort at the IV site during the infusion
options.why: IV azithromycin can cause discomfort at the infusion site. This is minor and is managed by checking the site and following the dilution and rate instructions.

takeaway: Macrolides can prolong the QT interval, especially when given with other QT-prolonging drugs. Report a QTc above 500 ms or a large increase from baseline.

stem: Which client's prescription for oral tetracycline should the nurse question?

options.text: A 45-year-old with rosacea
options.why: Tetracyclines are commonly used for inflammatory rosacea in nonpregnant adults.

options.text: A 50-year-old receiving bismuth quadruple therapy for Helicobacter pylori
options.why: Tetracycline is a standard part of bismuth quadruple therapy for H. pylori.

options.text: A 22-year-old man with moderate inflammatory acne
options.why: Tetracyclines are appropriate for moderate inflammatory acne in nonpregnant adults.

options.text: A 24-year-old with acne who is 14 weeks pregnant
options.why: Tetracyclines are avoided in pregnancy, especially after the first trimester, because they deposit in developing teeth and bone, causing permanent tooth discoloration and impaired bone growth.

takeaway: Avoid tetracyclines in pregnancy and in children under 8 years (short courses of doxycycline are an exception), because they stain developing teeth and affect bone growth.

stem: The nurse is teaching a client who has been prescribed oral doxycycline for Lyme disease. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Take each dose with a full glass of water and stay upright for at least 30 minutes.
options.why: Correct. This helps prevent the tablet from lodging in the esophagus and causing esophageal irritation or ulceration.

options.text: Use sunscreen and protective clothing, and avoid tanning beds.
options.why: Correct. Tetracyclines cause photosensitivity, so severe sunburn can occur with ordinary sun exposure.

options.text: Take the dose together with an antacid to prevent stomach upset.
options.why: Incorrect. Antacids containing aluminum, calcium or magnesium bind doxycycline and reduce its absorption.

options.text: Tell your provider if you are pregnant or could become pregnant.
options.why: Correct. Tetracyclines are generally avoided in pregnancy because of their effects on fetal teeth and bone.

options.text: Take your iron supplement at the same time as the doxycycline.
options.why: Incorrect. Iron binds tetracyclines and reduces absorption, so the doses should be separated.

takeaway: Doxycycline teaching: full glass of water and stay upright, protect from the sun, separate from antacids and iron, and report pregnancy.

stem: The nurse teaches a client who has been prescribed sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim for a urinary tract infection. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I'll cut back on water so I don't have to get up at night to urinate."
options.why: This needs correcting. Sulfonamides can crystallize in concentrated urine. Clients should drink plenty of fluids to keep urine dilute and prevent crystalluria.

options.text: "I'll take every dose until the prescription is finished."
options.why: This is correct: completing the course helps prevent relapse and resistance.

options.text: "I'll wear sunscreen when I go outside."
options.why: This is correct: sulfonamides can cause photosensitivity.

options.text: "I'll call right away if I get a rash or sores in my mouth."
options.why: This is correct: a rash or mucosal sores can be early signs of a severe skin reaction such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

takeaway: Sulfonamides: drink plenty of fluids, protect from the sun, finish the course and report any rash or mouth sores right away.

stem: On day 9 of sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim therapy, Ms. Nguyen, 34, reports fever, burning eyes and painful mouth sores. She has a dusky red rash with small blisters spreading across her trunk. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Apply hydrocortisone cream to the rash.
options.why: Topical steroids do not treat a severe systemic drug reaction and would delay the essential step of stopping the drug.

options.text: Give diphenhydramine and continue the antibiotic.
options.why: Continuing the suspected cause allows a potentially fatal reaction to progress.

options.text: Hold the next dose and notify the provider immediately.
options.why: Fever, mucosal involvement and a blistering, dusky rash suggest Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Stopping the drug at once is the most important factor in outcome, and urgent evaluation is needed.

options.text: Encourage saltwater mouth rinses and reassess tomorrow.
options.why: Supportive mouth care may help later, but waiting to act on a possible Stevens-Johnson syndrome is unsafe.

takeaway: A blistering rash with fever and mucosal sores during sulfonamide therapy suggests Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Stop the drug and report it immediately.

stem: An 81-year-old client with chronic kidney disease takes lisinopril daily and has been taking sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim for 5 days. Which laboratory result is the priority to report?

options.text: Sodium 137 mEq/L
options.why: This is within the normal range of 135–145 mEq/L.

options.text: Potassium 6.2 mEq/L
options.why: This is above the normal range of 3.5–5 mEq/L. Trimethoprim blocks potassium excretion in the kidney, much like amiloride, and with an ACE inhibitor, chronic kidney disease and older age it can cause dangerous hyperkalemia and dysrhythmias.

options.text: Fasting glucose 112 mg/dL
options.why: This is slightly above the normal fasting range of 70–99 mg/dL, but it is not an urgent problem.

options.text: WBC 9,200/mm³
options.why: This is within the normal range of about 5,000–10,000/mm³ and suggests that the infection is controlled.

takeaway: Trimethoprim can raise potassium. Watch for hyperkalemia in older adults, clients with kidney disease and clients taking ACE inhibitors, ARBs or potassium-sparing diuretics.

stem: The nurse is teaching a client who has been prescribed oral metronidazole for bacterial vaginosis. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Report numbness, tingling or burning in your hands or feet.
options.why: Correct. Metronidazole can cause peripheral neuropathy, especially with longer or repeated courses; new numbness or tingling is reported so the provider can decide whether to stop the drug.

options.text: A metallic taste in your mouth is a common side effect.
options.why: Correct. A metallic or bitter taste is common and expected.

options.text: Your urine may turn dark or reddish-brown.
options.why: Correct. Metronidazole can darken the urine, which is harmless.

options.text: Douche after each dose to help clear the infection.
options.why: Incorrect. Douching disrupts the normal vaginal flora and is associated with a higher risk of bacterial vaginosis; it does not help treatment.

options.text: You may stop the medication once your symptoms go away.
options.why: Incorrect. Stopping early increases the risk of relapse; the full course should be completed.

takeaway: Metronidazole: a metallic taste and dark urine are expected, numbness or tingling is reported, the full course is completed and douching is avoided.

stem: Mr. Brooks, 62, has taken oral clindamycin for 6 days for a dental abscess. He now reports five watery stools in 24 hours, lower abdominal cramping and a temperature of 100.6 °F (38.1 °C). Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Give loperamide to slow the diarrhea.
options.why: Antimotility drugs are avoided in suspected C. difficile infection because they can keep the toxin in the colon and raise the risk of toxic megacolon.

options.text: Encourage a high-fiber diet to firm up the stools.
options.why: Dietary fiber does not treat C. difficile infection and delays appropriate evaluation.

options.text: Tell him that diarrhea is an expected side effect and to keep taking the medicine.
options.why: Watery diarrhea with fever and cramping after clindamycin is not a minor side effect. It suggests C. difficile infection, which needs testing.

options.text: Notify the provider, anticipate a stool test for C. difficile and start contact precautions.
options.why: Clindamycin is strongly linked to C. difficile infection. Three or more unformed stools in 24 hours with fever and cramping call for testing, contact precautions and review of the antibiotic.

takeaway: New watery diarrhea during or after antibiotics (especially clindamycin) suggests C. difficile. Test, isolate, avoid antimotility drugs and report it.

stem: A client with Clostridioides difficile infection is discharged. Which instruction should the nurse give environmental services for cleaning the room?

options.text: Use an EPA-registered sporicidal disinfectant, such as a bleach-based product.
options.why: C. difficile forms spores that resist many routine disinfectants. Sporicidal agents, such as chlorine-based products, are needed to kill them on surfaces.

options.text: Wipe surfaces with alcohol-based wipes.
options.why: Alcohol does not kill C. difficile spores.

options.text: Use the standard quaternary ammonium cleaner used in other rooms.
options.why: Most quaternary ammonium products are not sporicidal and will not reliably remove C. difficile spores.

options.text: Do routine cleaning only, because the client's diarrhea had stopped before discharge.
options.why: Spores survive on surfaces for months whether or not the client still has symptoms, so enhanced cleaning is still needed.

takeaway: C. difficile spores need soap-and-water hand washing and sporicidal (for example, bleach-based) environmental cleaning. Alcohol does not kill them.

stem: The nurse is caring for a client with C. difficile infection. Which infection-control measures are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Wash hands with soap and water after removing gloves.
options.why: Correct. Scrubbing with soap and running water physically removes spores, which alcohol-based rubs do not kill.

options.text: Put on a gown and gloves when entering the room.
options.why: Correct. Contact precautions require a gown and gloves for all room entries.

options.text: Use a dedicated stethoscope and blood pressure cuff for this client.
options.why: Correct. Dedicated equipment prevents spores from being carried to other clients.

options.text: Use alcohol-based hand rub alone when leaving the room.
options.why: Incorrect. Alcohol-based rubs do not kill C. difficile spores.

options.text: Wear a fit-tested N95 respirator during care.
options.why: Incorrect. C. difficile is spread by contact, not through the air; a respirator is not required.

options.text: Place the client in a private room or with another client who has C. difficile.
options.why: Correct. A private room or cohorting reduces spread to other clients.

takeaway: C. difficile: contact precautions, a private room, dedicated equipment and soap-and-water hand hygiene.

stem: A client with confirmed, nonsevere Clostridioides difficile infection has a new prescription: vancomycin 125 mg IV every 6 hours for 10 days. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give the medication as prescribed.
options.why: IV vancomycin is not effective for C. difficile infection because very little of it reaches the colon. Giving it as written would leave the infection untreated.

options.text: Obtain a vancomycin trough level before the fourth dose.
options.why: Trough monitoring applies to systemic IV therapy, but the real problem is that the route is wrong for this infection.

options.text: Contact the prescriber to clarify the route, because oral vancomycin is used for C. difficile.
options.why: Oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily (or fidaxomicin) treats C. difficile because it stays in the gut and reaches high concentrations in the colon. The IV route does not, so the order must be clarified.

options.text: Infuse each dose over at least 60 minutes to prevent infusion reaction.
options.why: The infusion rate does not matter, because the IV route is wrong for C. difficile infection.

takeaway: C. difficile is treated with oral vancomycin (or fidaxomicin). IV vancomycin does not reach the colon.

stem: The nurse teaches a client who has been prescribed nitrofurantoin for acute cystitis. Which statement by the client indicates understanding?

options.text: "I should take each capsule on an empty stomach."
options.why: Nitrofurantoin is taken with food, which improves absorption and reduces nausea.

options.text: "My urine may turn dark yellow or brown, and that is harmless."
options.why: Nitrofurantoin commonly darkens the urine to rust-yellow or brown. This is expected and not a sign of harm.

options.text: "I can stop taking it as soon as the burning goes away."
options.why: Symptoms often improve before the infection is cleared. The full course should be completed.

options.text: "This medicine may turn my tears and sweat orange."
options.why: Orange discoloration of body fluids is caused by rifampin, not nitrofurantoin.

takeaway: Nitrofurantoin: take with food, expect brown urine and finish the course.

stem: Mrs. Lindqvist, 78, has taken nitrofurantoin nightly for 6 months to prevent recurrent urinary tract infections. She reports a new dry cough and shortness of breath when walking, and the nurse hears fine crackles in both lung bases. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Reassure her that the cough is probably from seasonal allergies.
options.why: Attributing new respiratory symptoms to allergies could delay recognition of a serious drug reaction.

options.text: Encourage her to increase her fluid intake.
options.why: Fluids do not address the possibility of drug-induced lung injury.

options.text: Report the findings promptly, because nitrofurantoin can cause pulmonary reactions.
options.why: Long-term nitrofurantoin can cause chronic pulmonary reactions, such as interstitial pneumonitis or fibrosis, especially in older adults. The drug may need to be stopped, so the findings must be reported promptly.

options.text: Suggest an over-the-counter cough suppressant at bedtime.
options.why: Suppressing the cough hides an important symptom and does not treat the cause.

takeaway: New cough, dyspnea or crackles in a client on long-term nitrofurantoin may be a pulmonary reaction. Report it promptly.

stem: A client who takes sertraline for depression is started on IV linezolid for a VRE wound infection. Which findings should the nurse recognize as possible signs of serotonin syndrome? Select all that apply.

options.text: Agitation and restlessness
options.why: Correct. Changes in mental status, such as agitation, anxiety or confusion, are common in serotonin syndrome.

options.text: Temperature of 102.4 °F (39.1 °C)
options.why: Correct. Hyperthermia reflects autonomic instability and increased muscle activity.

options.text: Hyperreflexia with clonus in the ankles
options.why: Correct. Neuromuscular hyperactivity, especially clonus and hyperreflexia, is a key feature.

options.text: Heavy sweating
options.why: Correct. Diaphoresis is a sign of autonomic overactivity.

options.text: Bradycardia and lethargy
options.why: Incorrect. Serotonin syndrome usually causes tachycardia and agitation, not bradycardia and sedation.

options.text: Flaccid muscles with absent reflexes
options.why: Incorrect. Serotonin syndrome causes increased muscle tone and reflexes, not flaccidity.

takeaway: Linezolid is a weak MAO inhibitor. With SSRIs, watch for agitation, fever, sweating, tachycardia, hyperreflexia and clonus.

stem: A client being discharged on oral linezolid is choosing meals from a menu. Which selection indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: Grilled chicken breast with rice and green beans
options.why: Fresh poultry, rice and vegetables are low in tyramine and safe to eat with linezolid.

options.text: Scrambled eggs with whole-wheat toast
options.why: Fresh eggs and bread are low in tyramine.

options.text: Baked fresh salmon with a garden salad
options.why: Fresh fish and fresh vegetables are low in tyramine.

options.text: An aged cheddar and salami sandwich with a draft (tap) beer
options.why: Aged cheese, cured meats and tap beer are high in tyramine. Because linezolid inhibits monoamine oxidase, large amounts of tyramine can cause a sudden rise in blood pressure.

takeaway: Linezolid inhibits MAO. Teach the client to limit high-tyramine foods (aged cheese, cured meats, tap beer, soy sauce) and to report severe headache.

stem: A client whose INR has been stable at 2.4 on warfarin is started on oral fluconazole for esophageal candidiasis. What is the priority nursing consideration?

options.text: Expect the INR to fall, and anticipate an increase in the warfarin dose.
options.why: Fluconazole raises warfarin levels rather than lowering them, so the INR is expected to rise, not fall.

options.text: Teach the client to eat more leafy green vegetables to balance the medications.
options.why: Changing vitamin K intake makes anticoagulation less predictable and does not deal with the drug interaction.

options.text: Monitor the INR closely and watch for bleeding, because fluconazole increases warfarin's effect.
options.why: Fluconazole inhibits CYP2C9, the main enzyme that breaks down warfarin. This can raise the INR sharply and cause bleeding, so closer INR checks and bleeding assessment are needed.

options.text: Give fluconazole 2 hours apart from warfarin to avoid the interaction.
options.why: This interaction occurs in the liver, not in the gut, so separating the doses does not prevent it.

takeaway: Azole antifungals (such as fluconazole) increase warfarin's effect. Monitor the INR closely and watch for bleeding.

stem: The nurse teaches a client who has been prescribed nystatin oral suspension for oral candidiasis. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I'll swallow each dose right away so it can work from my stomach."
options.why: This needs correcting. Nystatin works topically and is hardly absorbed, so it must stay in contact with the mouth: swish and hold it as long as possible before swallowing.

options.text: "I'll take my dentures out before each dose."
options.why: This is correct: removing dentures lets the drug reach all the mucosa, and the dentures can harbor Candida.

options.text: "I'll swish it around my mouth for as long as I can before I swallow."
options.why: This is correct: longer contact with the oral mucosa improves the effect.

options.text: "I'll keep taking it for 2 days after my mouth looks normal."
options.why: This is correct: the label advises continuing for at least 48 hours after symptoms resolve to prevent relapse.

takeaway: Nystatin suspension is a topical treatment: remove dentures, then swish and hold it in the mouth as long as possible before swallowing.

stem: A client with cryptococcal meningitis is prescribed conventional amphotericin B deoxycholate IV. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Give acetaminophen and diphenhydramine before the infusion as prescribed.
options.why: Correct. Premedication reduces the fever, chills and rigors that commonly occur during infusion.

options.text: Monitor serum potassium and magnesium levels.
options.why: Correct. Amphotericin B causes kidney wasting of potassium and magnesium, which can lead to dysrhythmias.

options.text: Dilute the dose in 0.9% sodium chloride.
options.why: Incorrect. Amphotericin B deoxycholate precipitates in saline. It is diluted in 5% dextrose in water (D5W), and the line is flushed with D5W.

options.text: Monitor serum creatinine and urine output.
options.why: Correct. Nephrotoxicity is the main dose-limiting toxicity.

options.text: Infuse the dose over 15 minutes to limit the duration of the reaction.
options.why: Incorrect. Rapid infusion increases the risk of severe reactions and dysrhythmias. Conventional amphotericin B is usually infused over 2 to 6 hours.

takeaway: Amphotericin B: premedicate, mix in D5W, infuse slowly and monitor creatinine, potassium and magnesium.

stem: A client with herpes simplex encephalitis is to start acyclovir 10 mg/kg IV every 8 hours. Which nursing action is most important to prevent a serious adverse effect?

options.text: Give each dose by IV push over 2 minutes so it reaches the brain quickly.
options.why: Rapid IV push increases the risk of crystals forming in the kidney tubules and of local tissue injury. Acyclovir is never given by bolus.

options.text: Infuse each dose over at least 1 hour and keep the client well hydrated.
options.why: Acyclovir can crystallize in the renal tubules and cause acute kidney injury. Infusing over at least 1 hour with adequate hydration and urine output reduces this risk.

options.text: Restrict fluids to prevent cerebral edema.
options.why: Fluid restriction concentrates the urine and increases the risk of crystal nephropathy.

options.text: Refrigerate the diluted solution until it is time to give it.
options.why: Refrigerating diluted acyclovir can cause it to precipitate. The label advises against refrigeration.

takeaway: IV acyclovir: infuse over at least 1 hour, keep the client well hydrated and monitor creatinine and urine output.

stem: A healthy 35-year-old developed influenza symptoms yesterday and is prescribed oseltamivir 75 mg orally twice daily for 5 days. Which statement by the client indicates understanding?

options.text: "Now that I'm on this medicine, I won't need my yearly flu shot."
options.why: Oseltamivir is not a substitute for annual influenza vaccination.

options.text: "I can stop taking it once my fever goes away."
options.why: The full 5-day course should be completed.

options.text: "It works best because I'm starting it within 2 days of when I got sick."
options.why: In outpatients, oseltamivir is most effective when started within 48 hours of symptom onset, when it can shorten the illness.

options.text: "I can go back to work tomorrow even if I still have a fever."
options.why: Oseltamivir does not make the client immediately noncontagious. People should stay home until they have been fever-free for at least 24 hours without antipyretics.

takeaway: Oseltamivir works best when started within 48 hours of flu symptoms. It does not replace the annual vaccine.

stem: A client with HIV takes bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide once daily. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I take it at the same time every day, with or without food."
options.why: This is correct: consistent daily dosing keeps drug levels steady and prevents resistance.

options.text: "If my viral load stays undetectable, I won't pass HIV to a partner through sex."
options.why: This is correct: a durably undetectable viral load means effectively no sexual transmission (undetectable = untransmittable).

options.text: "I'll check with my provider before starting any antacid or supplement."
options.why: This is correct: antacids and supplements containing aluminum, magnesium, calcium or iron can bind integrase inhibitors, so timing must be planned.

options.text: "Once my viral load is undetectable, I can stop taking my pills."
options.why: This needs correcting. Antiretroviral therapy suppresses HIV but does not cure it. Stopping it lets the virus rebound and can lead to resistance and transmission.

takeaway: Antiretroviral therapy is lifelong. An undetectable viral load depends on taking it every day without stopping.

stem: A client is starting daily oral HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) with emtricitabine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate. Which statements by the nurse are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: "You need a negative HIV test before starting, and you'll be tested again about every 3 months."
options.why: Correct. PrEP alone is not a complete HIV treatment, so taking it with undiagnosed HIV can lead to resistance. Regular testing is required.

options.text: "Your kidney function will be checked while you take this medicine."
options.why: Correct. Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate can affect the kidneys, so creatinine clearance is monitored.

options.text: "Taking it every day gives you the best protection."
options.why: Correct. The effectiveness of daily oral PrEP depends closely on adherence.

options.text: "You won't need condoms anymore, because this protects you from all sexually transmitted infections."
options.why: Incorrect. PrEP prevents HIV only. Condoms still reduce the risk of gonorrhea, chlamydia, syphilis and other infections.

options.text: "You can stop taking it after 30 days, once you're protected."
options.why: Incorrect. Protection lasts only while the drug is taken consistently, for as long as the client is at risk.

takeaway: PrEP requires a negative HIV test first, testing every 3 months, kidney monitoring and daily adherence. It does not prevent other STIs.

stem: While disposing of a used needle, a nurse sustains a needlestick injury after giving an injection to a client who has HIV. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Wash the puncture site with soap and water.
options.why: Immediate first aid is to wash the wound with soap and water. Next, the nurse reports the exposure right away so that post-exposure prophylaxis can be started, ideally within hours and no later than 72 hours.

options.text: Squeeze the wound to make it bleed, then soak it in bleach.
options.why: Squeezing the wound and applying caustic agents such as bleach are not recommended and can damage the tissue.

options.text: Wait for the client's latest viral load before deciding on treatment.
options.why: Post-exposure prophylaxis should not be delayed while waiting for source results. The sooner it starts, the better it works.

options.text: Finish the shift and then complete an incident report.
options.why: Waiting until the end of the shift delays evaluation and post-exposure prophylaxis, which works best when started as soon as possible.

takeaway: After a needlestick: wash with soap and water, then report immediately. HIV PEP works best when started within hours (no later than 72 hours).

stem: A client with chronic hepatitis B takes entecavir daily. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I take it on an empty stomach, at least 2 hours after a meal."
options.why: This is correct: entecavir is taken on an empty stomach, at least 2 hours after a meal and 2 hours before the next one.

options.text: "I can stop the medicine once my liver tests are back to normal."
options.why: This needs correcting. Stopping hepatitis B antivirals can cause a severe, sometimes fatal flare of hepatitis (boxed warning). They should be stopped only under close medical supervision.

options.text: "I'll keep my appointments for liver blood tests."
options.why: This is correct: regular liver function and viral load tests check the response to treatment.

options.text: "My partner should be tested and vaccinated for hepatitis B."
options.why: This is correct: susceptible sexual and household contacts should be tested and vaccinated.

takeaway: Never stop hepatitis B antivirals on your own. Stopping can trigger a severe flare of hepatitis.

stem: A client is scheduled to start sofosbuvir/velpatasvir for chronic hepatitis C. Before the first dose, which test result should the nurse confirm is in the record?

options.text: Hepatitis A IgM antibody
options.why: IgM anti-HAV detects acute hepatitis A. It is not a required safety screen before hepatitis C treatment.

options.text: Fasting lipid panel
options.why: A lipid panel is not required before starting hepatitis C direct-acting antivirals.

options.text: Hepatitis B surface antigen and core antibody
options.why: Direct-acting antivirals for hepatitis C carry a boxed warning about hepatitis B reactivation, which can cause fulminant hepatitis. Every client is screened for current or past hepatitis B infection before starting treatment.

options.text: Tuberculin skin test
options.why: TB screening is required before some immunosuppressive therapies, but not before hepatitis C antivirals.

takeaway: Screen for hepatitis B (HBsAg and anti-HBc) before starting hepatitis C antivirals, because hepatitis B can reactivate.

stem: The nurse is screening adults at an immunization clinic. Which clients should NOT receive the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine today? Select all that apply.

options.text: A 26-year-old who is 10 weeks pregnant
options.why: Correct. MMR is a live vaccine and is contraindicated in pregnancy. It is given after delivery, and pregnancy should be avoided for 4 weeks after vaccination.

options.text: A 40-year-old receiving chemotherapy for leukemia
options.why: Correct. Live vaccines are contraindicated in severe immunosuppression, such as during chemotherapy.

options.text: A 33-year-old with HIV whose CD4 count is 150 cells/mm³
options.why: Correct. MMR is contraindicated in HIV with severe immunosuppression (CD4 count below 200 cells/mm³ in adults).

options.text: A breastfeeding mother of a 3-month-old
options.why: Incorrect. Breastfeeding is not a contraindication to MMR.

options.text: A client who lives with a pregnant woman
options.why: Incorrect. Vaccinated people do not transmit MMR vaccine viruses in a way that endangers household contacts; vaccinating them is recommended.

options.text: A client with a mild cold and a temperature of 99.1 °F (37.3 °C)
