options.why: Incorrect. A mild illness, with or without a low-grade temperature, is not a reason to delay vaccination.

takeaway: Live vaccines (such as MMR and varicella) are contraindicated in pregnancy and in severe immunosuppression. A mild illness, breastfeeding and a pregnant household member are not contraindications.

stem: A 40-year-old client who gets hives after eating eggs asks for an influenza vaccine. Which action by the nurse is appropriate?

options.text: Explain that people with egg allergy cannot receive any influenza vaccine.
options.why: This is false. People with egg allergy can safely receive influenza vaccine.

options.text: Give an egg-free recombinant vaccine only, and observe the client for 30 minutes.
options.why: Current CDC/ACIP guidance does not limit people with egg allergy to egg-free products or require a longer observation period.

options.text: Refer the client to an allergist for the vaccine to be given in a medical setting.
options.why: Since the 2023–2024 season, ACIP no longer recommends extra precautions for egg allergy alone, including special settings.

options.text: Give any age-appropriate influenza vaccine with the same precautions as for any vaccine.
options.why: ACIP recommends that people with egg allergy receive any licensed, age-appropriate influenza vaccine. No additional safety measures are needed beyond those for any vaccine.

takeaway: Egg allergy alone is not a reason to withhold or change influenza vaccine. Use any age-appropriate vaccine with standard precautions.

stem: Several infants are due for oral rotavirus vaccine. For which infant should the nurse withhold the vaccine and consult the provider?

options.text: A 4-month-old who had intussusception at 3 months of age
options.why: A history of intussusception is a contraindication to rotavirus vaccine, because the vaccine carries a small risk of intussusception.

options.text: A 2-month-old with a runny nose and no fever
options.why: A mild illness without fever is not a reason to delay vaccination.

options.text: A 2-month-old who was born at 36 weeks of gestation
options.why: Preterm infants are vaccinated according to chronological age, using the same schedule.

options.text: A 4-month-old whose mother is pregnant
options.why: A pregnant household member is not a contraindication to rotavirus vaccine. Good hand hygiene after diaper changes is advised.

takeaway: Rotavirus vaccine is contraindicated after a history of intussusception or with severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID).

stem: A 13-month-old received the MMR vaccine today, but the varicella vaccine was not in stock. The parent asks when the child can receive the varicella vaccine. What is the earliest correct time?

options.text: 7 days from today
options.why: Seven days is too soon. When two live injectable vaccines are not given on the same day, the immune response to the first can interfere with the second.

options.text: At least 28 days from today
options.why: Live injectable vaccines that are not given on the same day must be separated by at least 28 days (4 weeks), or the second dose may not work as well.

options.text: At least 3 months from today
options.why: Three months is longer than required; the minimum interval is 28 days.

options.text: At least 6 months from today
options.why: Six months is unnecessarily long and would leave the child unprotected for longer.

takeaway: Give live injectable vaccines on the same day, or separate them by at least 28 days.

stem: A client at 22 weeks of gestation received Tdap during her previous pregnancy 2 years ago. She asks whether she needs it again. Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "No. Tdap protects you for 10 years, so you don't need another dose."
options.why: Tdap is recommended in every pregnancy, whatever the timing of earlier doses, so that antibodies pass to the newborn.

options.text: "Yes. You should receive it today, at 22 weeks."
options.why: The recommended window is 27 to 36 weeks, which gives the best antibody transfer to the fetus.

options.text: "Yes. It's recommended in every pregnancy, ideally between 27 and 36 weeks."
options.why: CDC recommends one dose of Tdap in each pregnancy, preferably in the early part of weeks 27 to 36, to protect the newborn from pertussis.

options.text: "You should wait and receive it right after delivery."
options.why: Postpartum vaccination does not provide antibodies to the newborn during the highest-risk first months of life.

takeaway: Give Tdap in every pregnancy, at 27 to 36 weeks, to protect the newborn from pertussis.

stem: A 62-year-old client asks about the recombinant zoster (shingles) vaccine. Which statement by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "Because it's a live vaccine, you can't get it if your immune system is weak."
options.why: Recombinant zoster vaccine is not live. It is recommended for immunocompromised adults aged 19 years and older.

options.text: "One dose protects you for life."
options.why: The vaccine is a 2-dose series.

options.text: "You don't need it if you had chickenpox as a child."
options.why: A history of chickenpox is the reason shingles can occur, since the virus stays dormant. Adults aged 50 and older are vaccinated regardless.

options.text: "It's two doses, given 2 to 6 months apart, and you can get it even if you've had shingles before."
options.why: Recombinant zoster vaccine is recommended for adults aged 50 and older as 2 doses, 2 to 6 months apart, including people who have already had shingles.

takeaway: Recombinant zoster vaccine: not live, 2 doses 2 to 6 months apart, for adults 50 and older (and immunocompromised adults 19 and older).

stem: A 15-month-old has just received the varicella vaccine. Which instruction is most important for the nurse to give the parent?

options.text: "Avoid giving aspirin or other salicylate products, such as bismuth subsalicylate, for 6 weeks."
options.why: The varicella vaccine label advises avoiding salicylates for 6 weeks after vaccination because of the risk of Reye syndrome, which has been linked to aspirin use during wild-type varicella.

options.text: "Keep your child home from childcare for 2 weeks."
options.why: Children do not need to be excluded after vaccination. Spread of the vaccine virus is rare and occurs only if a rash develops.

options.text: "Give ibuprofen before each meal for the next 3 days."
options.why: Routine scheduled analgesics are not needed. Fever reducers are given only for discomfort or fever, and never aspirin.

options.text: "Apply a warm compress to the injection site for 24 hours."
options.why: Cool compresses are generally used for injection-site soreness. This is not the most important safety teaching.

takeaway: After varicella vaccination, avoid salicylates (aspirin, bismuth subsalicylate) for 6 weeks because of the risk of Reye syndrome.

stem: A college student admitted with meningococcal meningitis is placed on droplet precautions. IV ceftriaxone was started at 1000 today. When may droplet precautions be discontinued?

options.text: When the cerebrospinal fluid culture comes back negative
options.why: Repeat cultures are not the criterion. Precautions are based on the length of effective therapy.

options.text: After 24 hours of effective antibiotic therapy
options.why: CDC recommends droplet precautions for Neisseria meningitidis until the client has received 24 hours of effective antibiotic therapy.

options.text: After the full course of antibiotics is completed
options.why: Continuing precautions for the whole course is unnecessary, because transmission risk falls sharply after 24 hours of effective therapy.

options.text: When the client has been fever-free for 12 hours
options.why: Fever is not the criterion for ending meningococcal droplet precautions.

takeaway: Meningococcal disease: droplet precautions until 24 hours of effective antibiotic therapy have been given.

stem: The nurse is assigning rooms on a medical unit. Which clients require droplet precautions? Select all that apply.

options.text: A client with confirmed influenza A
options.why: Correct. Influenza spreads by large respiratory droplets, so droplet precautions are required.

options.text: A client with Neisseria meningitidis meningitis who started antibiotics 6 hours ago
options.why: Correct. Droplet precautions continue until 24 hours of effective therapy have been given.

options.text: A client with mumps
options.why: Correct. Mumps spreads by respiratory droplets and saliva; droplet precautions are used.

options.text: A client with measles (rubeola)
options.why: Incorrect. Measles is airborne and requires an airborne infection isolation room and a fit-tested N95 respirator.

options.text: A client with suspected pulmonary tuberculosis
options.why: Incorrect. Tuberculosis is airborne and requires airborne precautions.

options.text: A client with an MRSA-infected leg wound
options.why: Incorrect. MRSA requires contact precautions, not droplet precautions.

takeaway: Droplet precautions: influenza, meningococcal disease, mumps and pertussis. Airborne precautions: measles, varicella and TB.

stem: The emergency department has one airborne infection isolation room available. Which client should the charge nurse place in this room?

options.text: A client with MRSA cellulitis of the forearm
options.why: MRSA is spread by contact and needs contact precautions, not a negative-pressure room.

options.text: A client with confirmed influenza A
options.why: Influenza needs droplet precautions. A standard private room is enough.

options.text: A client with a productive cough, night sweats and a cavitary lesion on chest x-ray
options.why: These findings suggest pulmonary tuberculosis, which is airborne and needs a negative-pressure airborne infection isolation room.

options.text: A client with C. difficile diarrhea
options.why: C. difficile needs contact precautions and soap-and-water hand hygiene, not airborne isolation.

takeaway: Save airborne infection isolation rooms for airborne diseases: TB, measles, varicella and disseminated zoster.

stem: The nurse is about to enter the room of a client on contact and droplet precautions. Place the steps for putting on PPE in the order recommended by the CDC.

options.text: Put on gloves, extending them over the gown cuffs.
options.why: Last: gloves go on last so they cover the gown cuffs and stay clean for client contact.

options.text: Perform hand hygiene.
options.why: First: clean hands before touching clean PPE.

options.text: Put on a surgical mask.
options.why: Third: the mask goes on after the gown and is secured before the eye protection.

options.text: Put on the gown and tie it at the neck and waist.
options.why: Second: the gown goes on first among the PPE items.

options.text: Put on goggles or a face shield.
options.why: Fourth: eye protection goes on after the mask so it fits over it.

takeaway: Donning: hand hygiene, gown, mask or respirator, eye protection, gloves.

stem: The nurse is leaving the room of a client on contact and droplet precautions and is wearing a gown, surgical mask, goggles and gloves. Place the steps for removing PPE in the order recommended by the CDC.

options.text: Remove the gown, pulling it away from the body and rolling it inside out.
options.why: Third: the gown is removed after the eye protection, touching only the inside.

options.text: Remove the gloves.
options.why: First: gloves are the most contaminated item and are removed first.

options.text: Remove the goggles by the earpieces or headband.
options.why: Second: eye protection is removed by the clean back parts after the gloves are off.

options.text: Remove the mask by the ties or ear loops without touching the front.
options.why: Fourth: the mask is removed last, touching only the ties or loops.

options.text: Perform hand hygiene.
options.why: Last: hand hygiene after removing all PPE removes any contamination picked up along the way.

takeaway: Doffing (CDC sequence): gloves, eye protection, gown, mask or respirator, then hand hygiene.

stem: A client in the emergency department meets criteria for sepsis, with a serum lactate of 3.8 mmol/L. One IV line is in place, and a second is being inserted. Prescriptions include blood cultures x2, cefepime 2 g IV over 30 minutes, vancomycin 1.75 g IV over 3 hours and a repeat lactate. Place the nurse's actions in order.

options.text: Start the vancomycin infusion.
options.why: Third: vancomycin takes hours to infuse, so starting it after the short cefepime infusion avoids delaying the broad-spectrum beta-lactam.

options.text: Obtain two sets of blood cultures from separate sites.
options.why: First: cultures are drawn before antibiotics when this causes no significant delay, so the organism can be identified.

options.text: Recheck the serum lactate level.
options.why: Last: the Surviving Sepsis bundle calls for remeasuring lactate (usually within 2 to 4 hours) when the first level is above 2 mmol/L, to assess the response to treatment.

options.text: Infuse cefepime.
options.why: Second: the broad-spectrum beta-lactam infuses quickly, so all antibiotics are started as soon as possible, ideally within 1 hour of recognizing sepsis.

takeaway: Sepsis: cultures first if they cause no delay, antibiotics within the hour (the fastest broad-spectrum agent first), then remeasure an elevated lactate.

stem: Mr. Asante, 69, has suspected septic shock from pneumonia: BP 84/46 mm Hg, HR 122/min and lactate 4.6 mmol/L. Two attempts to draw blood cultures have failed, and phlebotomy cannot arrive for 90 minutes. Piperacillin-tazobactam is at the bedside, and a 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus is infusing. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Hold the antibiotic until phlebotomy obtains the blood cultures.
options.why: A 90-minute delay in antibiotics during septic shock increases mortality. Cultures should not substantially delay antibiotics.

options.text: Draw the blood cultures from the IV line that is infusing the crystalloid.
options.why: Samples drawn from a line with fluids running are diluted and contaminated, and the results would be unreliable.

options.text: Continue the fluid bolus only, and start antibiotics after the blood pressure improves.
options.why: Fluids and antibiotics are both time-critical. Antibiotics should start within 1 hour of recognizing septic shock, not after the blood pressure improves.

options.text: Give the piperacillin-tazobactam now, notify the provider and obtain cultures as soon as possible.
options.why: Surviving Sepsis guidance is to draw cultures before antibiotics only when this does not substantially delay treatment. In septic shock, antibiotics are given within 1 hour, so the nurse gives the dose and obtains cultures as soon as possible.

takeaway: Draw cultures before antibiotics only when doing so causes no significant delay. In septic shock, antibiotics within 1 hour come first.

stem: A client with suspected pyelonephritis has these prescriptions: urinalysis with urine culture, ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily, and acetaminophen 650 mg orally as needed for fever. IV access is in place. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Collect the urine specimen for culture.
options.why: Specimens for culture are collected before the first antibiotic dose when this can be done quickly, so that antibiotics do not sterilize the sample and hide the causative organism.

options.text: Give the ceftriaxone.
options.why: Antibiotics are a priority, but collecting a urine culture takes only minutes. Giving ceftriaxone first could make the culture falsely negative.

options.text: Give the acetaminophen.
options.why: Treating fever is a comfort measure and is less important than getting an accurate culture and starting antibiotics.

options.text: Document the client's pain level.
options.why: Documentation can follow; it does not affect the accuracy of the culture or how soon antibiotics start.

takeaway: Collect cultures before the first antibiotic dose, as long as doing so does not significantly delay treatment.

stem: Vancomycin 750 mg in 250 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride is prescribed to infuse over 90 minutes. At what rate should the nurse set the infusion pump? (Round to the nearest whole number.)

options.text: 125 mL/hr
options.why: 125 mL/hr would deliver 250 mL over 2 hours, not 90 minutes.

options.text: 167 mL/hr
options.why: Volume ÷ time in hours = 250 mL ÷ 1.5 hr = 166.7, rounded to 167 mL/hr. This delivers 750 mg over 90 minutes, about 8.3 mg/min, which meets the label limits of no more than 10 mg/min and at least 60 minutes.

options.text: 278 mL/hr
options.why: This comes from dividing 250 by 0.9 (treating 90 minutes as 0.9 hours), which is a conversion error.

options.text: 250 mL/hr
options.why: 250 mL/hr would deliver the dose over 60 minutes, not the prescribed 90 minutes.

takeaway: mL/hr = total volume ÷ hours. Convert minutes to hours by dividing by 60 (90 minutes = 1.5 hours).

stem: An 18-kg child with acute otitis media is prescribed high-dose amoxicillin 90 mg/kg/day orally, divided every 12 hours. The available suspension is 400 mg/5 mL. How many mL should the nurse give per dose? (Round to the nearest tenth.)

options.why: This is the total daily volume (1,620 mg ÷ 400 × 5 = 20.25 mL). The daily dose is divided into two doses.

options.text: 5.1 mL
options.why: This volume equals about 405 mg, roughly half of the correct dose. It results from dividing the daily dose by 4 instead of 2.
90 mg/kg/day × 18 kg = 1,620 mg/day ÷ 2 doses = 810 mg per dose. 810 mg ÷ 400 mg × 5 mL = 10.125 mL, rounded to 10.1 mL.

options.text: 6.8 mL
options.why: This is the result if the daily dose is divided every 8 hours (540 mg per dose), but the prescription is every 12 hours.

takeaway: For weight-based pediatric doses: mg/kg/day × kg ÷ number of doses, then desired ÷ have × volume.

stem: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM is prescribed for a client with uncomplicated gonorrhea. The nurse reconstitutes a 1-g vial with 2.1 mL of 1% lidocaine, as directed on the label, giving a concentration of 350 mg/mL. How many mL should the nurse give? (Round to the nearest tenth.)

options.text: 0.7 mL
options.why: 0.7 mL contains about 245 mg, roughly half of the prescribed dose.

options.text: 1 mL
options.why: 1 mL contains 350 mg, which is less than the prescribed 500 mg.

options.text: 2.1 mL
options.why: 2.1 mL is the volume of diluent, not the dose. It would deliver about the whole 1-g vial.

options.text: 1.4 mL
options.why: Desired ÷ have × volume = 500 mg ÷ 350 mg × 1 mL = 1.43 mL, rounded to 1.4 mL. Ceftriaxone reconstituted with lidocaine is for IM use only and must never be given IV.

takeaway: Use the concentration after reconstitution (mg/mL) from the label: desired ÷ concentration = mL to give.

stem: A 10-day-old neonate with suspected sepsis is receiving a continuous IV infusion of calcium gluconate for hypocalcemia. Which antibiotic prescription should the nurse question?

options.text: Ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IV
options.why: Ceftriaxone is contraindicated in neonates (28 days old or younger) who need calcium-containing IV solutions, because fatal ceftriaxone-calcium precipitates have formed in the lungs and kidneys. It can also displace bilirubin.

options.text: Ampicillin 50 mg/kg IV
options.why: Ampicillin is a standard part of empiric therapy for neonatal sepsis and is compatible with this situation.

options.text: Gentamicin 4 mg/kg IV
options.why: Gentamicin is commonly paired with ampicillin for neonatal sepsis, with drug-level monitoring.

options.text: Acyclovir 20 mg/kg IV
options.why: Acyclovir is often added when neonatal herpes simplex virus is suspected. It is not contraindicated with calcium.

takeaway: Do not give ceftriaxone to neonates (28 days old or younger) who are receiving calcium-containing IV solutions, because it can form fatal precipitates.

stem: A 7-year-old with streptococcal pharyngitis took the first dose of amoxicillin at 0800 today. The parent asks when the child can go back to school. What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "Your child can go back this afternoon, since treatment has started."
options.why: A few hours of antibiotics are not enough to make the child noncontagious.

options.text: "Your child can return after at least 12 hours of antibiotics, once there's no fever."
options.why: CDC advises that children with strep throat can return to school once they no longer have a fever and have taken antibiotics for at least 12 hours.

options.text: "Your child needs to stay home for 5 days."
options.why: A fixed 5-day exclusion is not required for strep pharyngitis that is being treated.

options.text: "Your child must stay home until all 10 days of the antibiotic are finished."
options.why: The full course is needed to prevent complications, but the child is no longer contagious long before the course ends.

takeaway: Children with strep throat may return to school after at least 12 hours of antibiotics, once they are fever-free.

stem: Rosa Delgado, 58, has taken lisinopril 20 mg daily for 4 months. She reports a dry, tickling cough that keeps her awake at night. Her lungs are clear and she has no fever. Which change does the nurse anticipate the provider will make?

options.text: Add dextromethorphan and continue lisinopril at the same dose
options.why: Cough suppressants do not address the cause; the bradykinin-related cough usually continues as long as the ACE inhibitor is taken.

options.text: Switch lisinopril to losartan
options.why: An ARB blocks the angiotensin II receptor without inhibiting the breakdown of bradykinin, so it controls blood pressure with a much lower rate of cough.

options.text: Double the lisinopril dose and take it at bedtime
options.why: A higher dose would not help and may worsen the cough; timing does not prevent this adverse effect.

options.text: Order a chest x-ray to rule out pneumonia before any change
options.why: With clear lungs and no fever, the classic dry ACE-inhibitor cough is the likely cause; delaying the medication change is unnecessary.

takeaway: A persistent dry cough is a common ACE-inhibitor adverse effect caused by bradykinin buildup; switching to an ARB usually resolves it.

stem: Two years after starting enalapril, a client arrives at the clinic with swelling of the lips and tongue that began 1 hour ago. The client's voice sounds muffled. What is the nurse's priority action?

options.text: Give oral diphenhydramine and observe for 30 minutes
options.why: ACE-inhibitor swelling of the face and airway is driven by bradykinin, not histamine, so antihistamines often have little effect, and an oral drug is unsafe with a swelling tongue.

options.text: Reassure the client that this reaction cannot be from enalapril because it was started 2 years ago
options.why: This bradykinin-mediated swelling from an ACE inhibitor can appear at any time, even after years of uneventful use.

options.text: Apply ice packs to the lips and schedule a follow-up visit
options.why: Local comfort measures ignore the risk of airway obstruction; this is an emergency, not a routine follow-up.

options.text: Assess airway patency and activate emergency response for possible airway compromise
options.why: A muffled voice suggests the swelling is spreading toward the airway; airway assessment and emergency help come first, and enalapril must be stopped permanently.

takeaway: Bradykinin-mediated facial and airway swelling from an ACE inhibitor can occur any time during therapy; tongue swelling or voice change is an airway emergency, and the drug class is never restarted.

stem: The nurse teaches Mr. Okafor, who has started lisinopril for hypertension, about his diet. Which statement indicates the teaching was effective?

options.text: "I'll season my food with herbs and lemon and avoid salt substitutes unless my provider approves them."
options.why: Herbs and citrus lower sodium intake safely, and avoiding potassium-containing salt substitutes prevents hyperkalemia with an ACE inhibitor.

options.text: "I'll use a potassium-based salt substitute instead of table salt."
options.why: Most salt substitutes contain potassium chloride; combined with an ACE inhibitor, which reduces potassium excretion, they can cause hyperkalemia.

options.text: "I should eat two extra bananas a day to replace the potassium this pill removes."
options.why: ACE inhibitors tend to raise, not lower, serum potassium; extra potassium is not needed and could be harmful.

options.text: "I can stop taking lisinopril on days when I eat a low-salt diet."
options.why: Antihypertensives are taken daily regardless of diet; skipping doses leads to uncontrolled blood pressure.

takeaway: ACE inhibitors and ARBs raise serum potassium; teach clients to avoid potassium salt substitutes and supplements unless prescribed.

stem: A 31-year-old client with chronic hypertension takes lisinopril 10 mg daily. She tells the nurse she and her partner plan to start trying to become pregnant next month. What is the nurse's best action?

options.text: Tell her to continue lisinopril until her first prenatal visit
options.why: ACE inhibitors carry a boxed warning for fetal toxicity; waiting until a prenatal visit could expose the fetus during early pregnancy before the drug is changed.

options.text: Notify the provider so her antihypertensive can be changed before she tries to conceive
options.why: Drugs acting on the renin-angiotensin system can injure the developing fetal kidneys and cause death; switching to a pregnancy-compatible agent such as labetalol or nifedipine before conception is safest.

options.text: Advise her to stop all blood pressure medication now
options.why: Stopping treatment abruptly leaves chronic hypertension uncontrolled, which is itself dangerous for the client and a future pregnancy.

options.text: Explain that lisinopril is safe in pregnancy because it is an older medication
options.why: The age of a drug does not determine its safety; ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy.

takeaway: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are fetotoxic; clients planning pregnancy need a switch to a pregnancy-compatible antihypertensive, and the drug is stopped as soon as pregnancy is detected.

stem: A client with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is being switched from enalapril to sacubitril/valsartan. The last dose of enalapril was taken on Monday at 0900. What is the earliest time the nurse may give the first dose of sacubitril/valsartan?

options.text: Monday at 2100
options.why: Only 12 hours have passed; giving the drug this soon greatly increases the risk of life-threatening facial and airway swelling.

options.text: Tuesday at 0900
options.why: Only 24 hours have passed, which is short of the required washout period.

options.text: Tuesday at 2100
options.why: This is 36 hours after the last enalapril dose, the minimum washout required by the drug's labeling to lower the risk of life-threatening facial and airway swelling (Monday 0900 + 36 hours = Tuesday 2100).

options.text: Thursday at 0900
options.why: A 72-hour wait is longer than necessary and delays beneficial heart failure therapy.

takeaway: Sacubitril/valsartan must not be given within 36 hours of an ACE inhibitor; combining neprilysin inhibition with ACE inhibition raises the risk of life-threatening bradykinin-mediated swelling of the face and airway.

stem: A client with heart failure started sacubitril/valsartan 1 week ago. Which findings should the nurse monitor for as adverse effects of this medication? Select all that apply.

options.text: Dizziness when standing with a drop in blood pressure
options.why: Correct. Hypotension is the most common adverse effect, especially in clients who are also taking diuretics.

options.text: Serum potassium above 5 mEq/L
options.why: Correct. The valsartan component reduces aldosterone effect and can cause hyperkalemia (normal potassium 3.5–5 mEq/L).

options.text: Rising serum creatinine
options.why: Correct. Blocking angiotensin II can reduce glomerular filtration, so renal function is monitored.

options.text: Swelling of the face, lips or tongue
options.why: Correct. Bradykinin-mediated swelling of the face and airway can occur, and the risk is higher in clients with a previous episode of this reaction or recent ACE-inhibitor use.

options.text: Low blood glucose with tremor
options.why: Incorrect. Hypoglycemia is not an expected adverse effect of sacubitril/valsartan.

options.text: Ringing in the ears
options.why: Incorrect. Ototoxicity is associated with loop diuretics and aminoglycosides, not with this drug.

takeaway: Monitor clients on sacubitril/valsartan for hypotension, hyperkalemia, worsening renal function and facial or airway swelling.

stem: The nurse is preparing 0900 medications for four clients. Which medication should the nurse hold and discuss with the provider before giving?

options.text: Metoprolol succinate for a client with an apical pulse of 66/min and BP 124/78 mm Hg
options.why: These values are within commonly used parameters, so the dose can be given.

options.text: Lisinopril for a client with a serum potassium of 4.5 mEq/L and BP 138/84 mm Hg
options.why: Potassium is normal (3.5–5 mEq/L) and blood pressure supports giving the dose.

options.text: Carvedilol for a client with an apical pulse of 47/min who reports feeling lightheaded
options.why: Symptomatic bradycardia below 50/min is a reason to hold a beta blocker and notify the provider, because the drug would slow the heart further.

options.text: Furosemide for a client with a serum potassium of 4 mEq/L and crackles in both lung bases
options.why: Potassium is normal and crackles show ongoing fluid overload, which the diuretic is meant to treat.

takeaway: Hold a beta blocker for marked or symptomatic bradycardia or hypotension and notify the provider.

stem: Kenji, 44, has type 1 diabetes and was started on propranolol for migraine prevention. Which statement shows he understands how this drug affects his diabetes management?

options.text: "I'll check my blood glucose if I start sweating or feel confused, because my heart may not race when my sugar is low."
options.why: Beta blockers blunt adrenergic warning signs such as tachycardia, palpitations and tremor, while sweating is usually preserved; checking glucose with any suspicious symptom is the correct plan.

options.text: "Propranolol will make my low blood sugars easier to notice."
options.why: Beta blockers mask, rather than heighten, many of the warning signs of hypoglycemia.

options.text: "I can stop checking my glucose at night because propranolol protects me from lows."
options.why: Propranolol does not prevent hypoglycemia and can delay recovery from it, so monitoring remains essential.

options.text: "If my heart rate is normal, I know my blood sugar is normal too."
options.why: A normal heart rate does not exclude hypoglycemia in a client taking a beta blocker.

takeaway: Beta blockers mask tachycardia and tremor from hypoglycemia (sweating is usually preserved); clients with diabetes should check glucose with any suspicious symptom.

stem: Which prescription should the nurse question before administering?

options.text: Amlodipine 5 mg daily for a client with hypertension and Raynaud phenomenon
options.why: Calcium channel blockers dilate arteries and are often used for Raynaud phenomenon, so this is appropriate.

options.text: Lisinopril 10 mg daily for a client with hypertension and type 2 diabetes
options.why: ACE inhibitors are a preferred choice in diabetes because they help protect the kidneys.

options.text: Metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily for a client with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
options.why: Metoprolol succinate is an evidence-based beta blocker for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.

options.text: Propranolol 40 mg twice daily for a client with moderate persistent asthma
options.why: Propranolol is a nonselective beta blocker that blocks beta-2 receptors in the bronchi and can trigger severe bronchospasm in a client with asthma.

takeaway: Nonselective beta blockers such as propranolol can cause bronchospasm and should be avoided in clients with asthma.

stem: The nurse teaches a client with angina who is starting metoprolol tartrate. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I'll check my pulse and call if it stays below the number you gave me."
options.why: Monitoring heart rate is appropriate because bradycardia is an expected risk.

options.text: "If I run out, it's fine to skip a few days until I pick up my refill."
options.why: Stopping a beta blocker abruptly can cause rebound tachycardia, worsening angina and even myocardial infarction; this statement needs correction.

options.text: "I'll get up slowly from bed because I might feel dizzy."
options.why: Rising slowly reduces orthostatic dizziness and falls, which shows understanding.

options.text: "I'll take it with or right after a meal at the same times each day."
options.why: Metoprolol tartrate is commonly taken with or immediately after meals at consistent times, which shows understanding.

takeaway: Beta blockers must not be stopped suddenly; abrupt withdrawal can precipitate angina, dysrhythmias or myocardial infarction.

stem: A client who started amlodipine 10 mg daily 3 weeks ago has bilateral ankle swelling. Lungs are clear, weight is unchanged, and there is no shortness of breath. Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "This is a common effect of amlodipine caused by widening of small arteries; I'll let your provider know so the dose can be reviewed."
options.why: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers dilate arterioles and raise capillary pressure, causing dose-related ankle edema; with no signs of heart failure, reporting it for dose review is appropriate.

options.text: "These are signs of heart failure, so you need to go to the emergency department now."
options.why: Clear lungs, stable weight and no dyspnea do not suggest heart failure; this response causes unnecessary alarm.

options.text: "Stop the amlodipine today and restart it when the swelling goes away."
options.why: The client should not stop an antihypertensive without provider direction.

options.text: "Take an extra water pill from a family member to remove the fluid."
options.why: Taking someone else's medication is unsafe, and diuretics are often ineffective for calcium channel blocker edema because it is not caused by fluid overload.

takeaway: Peripheral edema from amlodipine is caused by arteriolar dilation, is dose related and responds poorly to diuretics; report it so the provider can adjust therapy.

stem: The nurse is teaching a client who is starting nifedipine extended-release for hypertension. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice.
options.why: Correct. Grapefruit inhibits CYP3A4 in the gut, raising nifedipine levels and the risk of hypotension.

options.text: Swallow the tablet whole without crushing or chewing it.
options.why: Correct. Crushing an extended-release tablet releases the whole dose at once and can cause sudden hypotension.

options.text: Change position slowly, especially when getting out of bed.
options.why: Correct. Vasodilation can cause orthostatic dizziness.

options.text: You may see an empty tablet shell in your stool; this is expected.
options.why: Correct. Some extended-release forms leave an insoluble shell after the drug has been released.

options.text: Take a double dose if you miss a day.
options.why: Incorrect. Doubling the dose can cause marked hypotension; a missed dose should be handled as the provider or pharmacist directs, without doubling.

options.text: Drink a glass of grapefruit juice each morning to improve absorption.
options.why: Incorrect. Grapefruit increases drug levels unpredictably and should be avoided.

takeaway: Teach clients on nifedipine ER to avoid grapefruit, swallow tablets whole, rise slowly and expect a possible tablet shell in the stool.

stem: A client with atrial fibrillation and a ventricular rate of 132/min has a history of heart failure with an ejection fraction of 25%. BP is 108/70 mm Hg, and crackles are heard in both lung bases. The provider prescribes IV diltiazem. What is the nurse's best action?

options.text: Give the diltiazem as prescribed and recheck the heart rate in 15 minutes
options.why: Giving the drug without clarifying ignores a significant contraindication in this client.

options.text: Question the prescription because diltiazem can worsen heart failure in a client with a reduced ejection fraction
options.why: Nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers depress myocardial contractility and are not recommended in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction; the provider may choose another rate-control drug.

options.text: Hold the drug until the blood pressure falls below 100/60 mm Hg
options.why: A lower blood pressure would make diltiazem even more hazardous; this reasoning is backward.

options.text: Ask the client to bear down to slow the heart rate before giving diltiazem
options.why: A vagal maneuver does not address the safety concern, and the issue is the drug choice in reduced ejection fraction.

takeaway: Diltiazem and verapamil reduce contractility and should be avoided in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.

stem: A client with heart failure receives furosemide 40 mg IV twice daily. Which findings should the nurse report to the provider? Select all that apply.

options.text: Serum potassium 3 mEq/L
options.why: Correct. Hypokalemia (normal 3.5–5 mEq/L) is a common loop-diuretic effect and increases the risk of dysrhythmias.

options.text: New report of ringing in the ears
options.why: Correct. Tinnitus can signal ototoxicity, particularly with high doses or rapid IV administration.

options.text: BP drops from 118/72 to 92/56 mm Hg on standing, with dizziness
options.why: Correct. Symptomatic orthostatic hypotension suggests volume depletion from overdiuresis.

options.text: Leg cramps and generalized muscle weakness
options.why: Correct. These symptoms may reflect hypokalemia or hypomagnesemia.

options.text: Urine output of 900 mL in the 3 hours after the dose
options.why: Incorrect. Brisk diuresis after a loop diuretic is the intended effect.

options.text: Weight 0.6 kg lower than yesterday with fewer crackles
options.why: Incorrect. This indicates effective fluid removal in heart failure.

takeaway: With loop diuretics, report hypokalemia, tinnitus, symptomatic hypotension and cramps; brisk diuresis and weight loss show the drug is working.

stem: A client has taken hydrochlorothiazide for 6 months. Which laboratory change does the nurse recognize as an expected effect of this medication?

options.text: Increase in serum potassium
options.why: Thiazides increase potassium loss in the urine and tend to cause hypokalemia, not hyperkalemia.

options.text: Decrease in serum uric acid
options.why: Thiazides reduce uric acid excretion, raising serum uric acid and the risk of gout.

options.text: Mild increase in serum calcium
options.why: Thiazides reduce urinary calcium excretion, so serum calcium may rise slightly (normal about 8.5–10.5 mg/dL).

options.text: Decrease in blood glucose
options.why: Thiazides can raise blood glucose, especially at higher doses.

takeaway: Thiazides lower potassium, sodium and magnesium but raise calcium, uric acid and glucose.

stem: A client with heart failure takes spironolactone 25 mg and lisinopril 20 mg daily. This morning's serum potassium is 5.8 mEq/L. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give both medications and encourage a low-potassium diet
options.why: Giving drugs that both raise potassium when it is already elevated could worsen hyperkalemia and cause dysrhythmias.

options.text: Give the spironolactone but hold the lisinopril
options.why: Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic and is the more direct contributor; giving it would worsen hyperkalemia.

options.text: Give the lisinopril with a glass of orange juice
options.why: Orange juice adds potassium, and this does nothing to address the elevated level.

options.text: Hold the spironolactone, place the client on a cardiac monitor per protocol, and notify the provider
options.why: Potassium of 5.8 mEq/L exceeds the normal range (3.5–5 mEq/L); both drugs raise potassium, so the nurse withholds the potassium-sparing diuretic, monitors for ECG changes and obtains prescriptions, including direction about the lisinopril.

takeaway: Spironolactone plus an ACE inhibitor or ARB raises the risk of hyperkalemia. Report potassium above 5 mEq/L, and expect the potassium-sparing diuretic to be held or reduced when potassium reaches 5.5 mEq/L or higher.

stem: An 81-year-old client with chronic kidney disease takes digoxin 0.125 mg daily. Which finding is often the earliest indication of digoxin toxicity?

options.text: Loss of appetite and nausea
options.why: Anorexia and nausea are common early signs of digoxin toxicity, especially in older adults with reduced renal clearance.

options.text: Hair loss
options.why: Alopecia is not associated with digoxin toxicity.

options.text: Increased urine output
options.why: Digoxin toxicity does not cause diuresis; reduced renal function actually allows the drug to accumulate.

options.text: Elevated blood pressure
options.why: Hypertension is not a typical sign of digoxin toxicity.

takeaway: GI symptoms such as anorexia and nausea are often the first signs of digoxin toxicity, and visual changes and dysrhythmias follow; renal impairment increases the risk.

stem: The nurse is preparing to give a scheduled oral dose of digoxin to a hospitalized adult. Place the steps in the order the nurse should perform them.

options.text: Give the medication
options.why: The dose is given only after the assessment data support it.

options.text: Review the most recent serum potassium and digoxin levels
options.why: Lab data are checked first because hypokalemia or an elevated level would change the plan before the nurse reaches the bedside.

options.text: Compare the apical rate with the hold parameter (commonly below 60/min in adults)
options.why: The nurse decides whether to give or hold the dose based on the measured rate.

options.text: Document the apical pulse and administration
options.why: Documentation follows administration and includes the apical rate.

options.text: Auscultate the apical pulse for 1 full minute
options.why: A full minute of apical counting detects irregularities and bradycardia that a short count or radial pulse may miss.

takeaway: Before giving digoxin: check potassium and drug level, count the apical pulse for a full minute, compare with hold parameters, give, then document.

stem: A client took extra digoxin tablets by mistake. The serum digoxin level is 3.4 ng/mL, potassium is 5.9 mEq/L, and the monitor shows a heart rate of 40/min with frequent ventricular ectopy. Which medication should the nurse prepare to administer?

options.text: Digoxin immune fab
options.why: Digoxin immune fab binds digoxin and is indicated for life-threatening toxicity, including dangerous dysrhythmias and potassium above 5 mEq/L in acute toxicity (therapeutic digoxin about 0.5–2 ng/mL).

options.text: Potassium chloride IV
options.why: The client is already hyperkalemic; added potassium could cause a fatal dysrhythmia.

options.text: Protamine sulfate
options.why: Protamine reverses heparin and has no effect on digoxin.

options.text: Phytonadione (vitamin K)
options.why: Vitamin K reverses warfarin, not digoxin.

takeaway: Digoxin immune fab is the antidote for life-threatening digoxin toxicity, such as dangerous dysrhythmias or hyperkalemia in acute overdose.

stem: The nurse reviews the record of a client who takes digoxin. Which findings increase this client's risk for digoxin toxicity? Select all that apply.

options.text: Serum potassium 3.1 mEq/L
options.why: Correct. Hypokalemia increases digoxin binding at the myocardial sodium-potassium pump and promotes toxicity (normal 3.5–5 mEq/L).

options.text: Serum creatinine 2.3 mg/dL
options.why: Correct. Digoxin is cleared mainly by the kidneys; renal impairment causes accumulation (normal creatinine about 0.6–1.3 mg/dL).

options.text: Amiodarone started 1 week ago
options.why: Correct. Amiodarone raises serum digoxin levels, so the digoxin dose is usually reduced.

options.text: Serum magnesium 1.2 mg/dL
options.why: Correct. Hypomagnesemia increases myocardial sensitivity to digoxin (normal about 1.7–2.2 mg/dL).

options.text: Serum potassium 4.4 mEq/L
options.why: Incorrect. This potassium is within the normal range and does not add risk.

options.text: Acetaminophen as needed for arthritis pain
options.why: Incorrect. Acetaminophen does not meaningfully affect digoxin levels.

takeaway: Hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, renal impairment and interacting drugs such as amiodarone increase the risk of digoxin toxicity.

stem: Marcus, 62, arrives at the emergency department with substernal chest pressure. BP is 132/80 mm Hg. While the nurse prepares sublingual nitroglycerin, he says he took sildenafil about 10 hours ago. What is the nurse's best action?

options.text: Give the nitroglycerin and recheck blood pressure in 5 minutes
options.why: Nitrates taken within 24 hours of sildenafil can cause severe, refractory hypotension, so the drug should not be given routinely.

options.text: Give half the usual nitroglycerin dose
options.why: There is no safe reduced dose; the interaction comes from combined increases in cyclic GMP, which causes profound vasodilation.

options.text: Withhold the nitroglycerin and notify the provider of the sildenafil use
options.why: Nitrates are contraindicated within 24 hours of sildenafil (48 hours for tadalafil); the provider needs this information to choose other anti-ischemic therapy.

options.text: Withhold the nitroglycerin and wait 2 hours before giving it
options.why: Two hours is far too short; the contraindication lasts about 24 hours after sildenafil.

takeaway: Nitrates are contraindicated within 24 hours of sildenafil or vardenafil and 48 hours of tadalafil because the combination can cause severe hypotension.

stem: The nurse is teaching a client with stable angina how to use sublingual nitroglycerin 0.4 mg tablets at home. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Sit or lie down before taking a tablet.
options.why: Correct. Nitroglycerin can cause sudden hypotension and dizziness; sitting reduces the risk of falls.

options.text: Call 911 if the chest pain is not better or is worse 5 minutes after the first tablet.
options.why: Correct. AHA guidance is to call emergency services at that point rather than waiting until all doses are used, because the pain may be a heart attack.

options.text: Keep the tablets in their original dark glass bottle with the cap tightly closed.
options.why: Correct. Light, heat, moisture and air reduce potency.

options.text: A headache is common; acetaminophen may help.
options.why: Correct. Vasodilation of meningeal vessels often causes headache, which usually lessens with continued use.

options.text: Swallow the tablet with a full glass of water.
options.why: Incorrect. The tablet must dissolve under the tongue; swallowing it greatly reduces its effect because of first-pass metabolism.

options.text: Take one tablet every minute until the pain is gone.
options.why: Incorrect. Doses are taken 5 minutes apart, with no more than 3 doses in 15 minutes.

takeaway: Sublingual nitroglycerin: sit down, dissolve under the tongue, call 911 if pain is not better 5 minutes after the first dose, and store in the original glass bottle.

stem: A client is prescribed a transdermal nitroglycerin patch for angina prevention. Which statement indicates the client understands how to use the patch?

options.text: "I'll leave the patch on all the time and change it every 24 hours so I'm always protected."
options.why: Continuous use leads to nitrate tolerance, so the drug becomes less effective.

options.text: "I'll put the new patch on the same spot each day so I don't forget where it is."
options.why: Sites should be rotated to prevent skin irritation.

options.text: "I'll cut the patch in half if I get a headache."
options.why: Cutting a patch alters drug delivery unless the product is specifically designed for it; headaches should be reported and managed as directed.

options.text: "I'll put the patch on in the morning and take it off at bedtime so I have a patch-free time each night."
options.why: A daily patch-free interval of about 10–12 hours prevents nitrate tolerance; wearing it 12–14 hours during the day matches the usual regimen.

takeaway: Nitroglycerin patches are usually worn 12–14 hours and removed for a 10–12 hour nitrate-free interval to prevent tolerance; rotate sites.

stem: A client with pulmonary embolism is receiving a weight-based heparin infusion monitored with anti-factor Xa levels. The facility's therapeutic range is 0.3–0.7 units/mL. The 6-hour anti-Xa level is 0.18 units/mL, and there are no signs of bleeding. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Stop the infusion and notify the provider
options.why: Stopping heparin when the level is below range would leave the client unprotected against clot extension.

options.text: Administer protamine sulfate
options.why: Protamine reverses heparin and is used for excessive anticoagulation with bleeding, not for a subtherapeutic level.

options.text: Adjust the infusion according to the facility's heparin nomogram and recheck the level when directed
options.why: The level is below the therapeutic range; the nomogram typically calls for a bolus and/or rate increase with a repeat level at a set interval.

options.text: Continue at the current rate and recheck the level tomorrow
options.why: Leaving a subtherapeutic level unchanged for a day increases the risk of clot propagation.

takeaway: Heparin infusions are titrated by a nomogram to keep aPTT or anti-Xa levels (often 0.3–0.7 units/mL) in range; subtherapeutic levels are corrected promptly.

stem: On day 7 of an IV heparin infusion, a client's platelet count has fallen from 236,000/mm³ to 92,000/mm³, and the left leg is newly swollen and painful. What does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Changing the heparin infusion to enoxaparin injections
options.why: Low-molecular-weight heparin cross-reacts with heparin-induced antibodies and is avoided in suspected heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT).

options.text: Transfusing platelets to correct the low count
options.why: Platelet transfusion is generally avoided in HIT because it may fuel further thrombosis; the problem is clotting, not bleeding.

options.text: Stopping all heparin, including flushes, and starting a non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban
options.why: A drop of more than 50% after 5–10 days with new thrombosis suggests HIT; every heparin source is removed and a non-heparin anticoagulant is started because the risk of clotting is high (normal platelets about 150,000–400,000/mm³).

options.text: Continuing heparin and repeating the platelet count in 24 hours
options.why: Continuing heparin in suspected HIT risks limb- and life-threatening thrombosis.

takeaway: Suspect HIT when platelets fall by more than 50% 5–10 days into heparin therapy; stop all heparin (including flushes and LMWH) and start a non-heparin anticoagulant.

stem: The nurse is teaching a client to self-inject enoxaparin from a prefilled syringe. Which instructions are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Do not push out the air bubble before injecting.
options.why: Correct. The air bubble in the prefilled syringe helps clear the medication from the needle and prevents loss of drug.

options.text: Inject into the abdomen at least 2 inches (5 cm) from the navel, alternating left and right sides.
options.why: Correct. The abdominal wall is the recommended site, and rotation reduces bruising.

options.text: Gently pinch a fold of skin and hold it during the injection, inserting the full needle length.
options.why: Correct. The full needle is inserted at a 90-degree angle into the skin fold, which is held throughout the injection.

options.text: Pull back on the plunger to check for blood before injecting.
options.why: Incorrect. Aspiration is not done with enoxaparin; it increases tissue trauma and bruising.

options.text: Rub the site firmly afterward to help absorption.
options.why: Incorrect. Rubbing increases bruising and hematoma formation.

options.text: Report black stools, nosebleeds that do not stop or unusual bruising.
options.why: Correct. These can be signs of bleeding, the main adverse effect of enoxaparin, and should be reported promptly.

takeaway: Enoxaparin: keep the air bubble, inject into an abdominal skin fold at least 2 inches from the navel, hold the fold, do not aspirate or rub, and report signs of bleeding.

stem: A client taking warfarin 5 mg daily for atrial fibrillation has an INR of 5.2. There is no bleeding, and vital signs are stable. What is the nurse's best action?

options.text: Hold the warfarin dose and notify the provider
options.why: An INR of 5.2 is above the usual target of 2–3 for atrial fibrillation; withholding the dose and obtaining direction (which may include low-dose oral vitamin K) is appropriate.

options.text: Give the warfarin dose and recheck the INR next week
options.why: Giving the dose would push the INR higher and increase bleeding risk.

options.text: Prepare to give vitamin K 10 mg IV now
options.why: High-dose IV vitamin K is reserved for serious or life-threatening bleeding; this client is not bleeding.

options.text: Prepare to give protamine sulfate
options.why: Protamine reverses heparin, not warfarin.

takeaway: For an elevated INR without bleeding, hold warfarin and notify the provider; IV vitamin K and factor replacement are reserved for significant bleeding.

stem: Amina, who has taken warfarin for 1 year with a stable INR, tells the nurse she plans to start drinking a large spinach-and-kale smoothie every morning as part of a new diet. What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "You must avoid all green vegetables while taking warfarin."
options.why: Strict avoidance is unnecessary and limits a healthy diet; consistency of vitamin K intake is the goal.

options.text: "That's a healthy change, so there's no need to tell anyone about it."
options.why: A sudden large increase in vitamin K will lower the INR, so the provider must be informed.

options.text: "Tell your provider about this change so your INR can be checked and your dose adjusted if needed, and then keep your vitamin K intake consistent."
options.why: A sudden increase in vitamin K counteracts warfarin; with closer INR monitoring and a steady intake, the dose can be matched to her new diet.

options.text: "Take an extra warfarin tablet on the days you drink the smoothie."
options.why: Self-adjusting the dose is unsafe and can cause unpredictable INR swings.

takeaway: Warfarin clients do not need to avoid vitamin K foods; they need a consistent intake and should report major diet changes so the INR can be monitored.

stem: A client taking warfarin falls at home and is diagnosed with an intracranial hemorrhage. The INR is 3.6. Which treatment does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Protamine sulfate IV
options.why: Protamine reverses heparin and has no meaningful effect on warfarin.

options.text: Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate plus vitamin K by slow IV infusion
options.why: Four-factor PCC replaces factors II, VII, IX and X within minutes, and IV vitamin K sustains the reversal as the PCC wears off; this is the recommended approach for life-threatening warfarin-associated bleeding.

options.text: Idarucizumab IV
options.why: Idarucizumab is specific to dabigatran and does not reverse warfarin.

options.text: Holding the next warfarin dose only
options.why: Holding a dose takes days to lower the INR, which is far too slow for an intracranial bleed.

takeaway: Life-threatening warfarin bleeding is treated with four-factor PCC plus IV vitamin K; holding the dose alone is too slow.

stem: A client who takes dabigatran is admitted with a massive gastrointestinal bleed and needs emergency surgery. Which reversal agent does the nurse expect to prepare?

options.text: Phytonadione
options.why: Vitamin K reverses warfarin by restoring vitamin K-dependent factors; it does not reverse a direct thrombin inhibitor.

options.text: Desmopressin
options.why: Desmopressin is used in some platelet-function and von Willebrand disorders, not to reverse dabigatran.

options.text: Protamine sulfate
options.why: Protamine neutralizes heparin and does not bind dabigatran.

options.text: Idarucizumab
options.why: Idarucizumab is a monoclonal antibody fragment that binds dabigatran and reverses its anticoagulant effect within minutes.

takeaway: Idarucizumab is the specific reversal agent for dabigatran.

stem: The nurse is teaching a client newly prescribed apixaban for atrial fibrillation. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I'll need weekly INR blood tests to adjust my dose."
options.why: Apixaban does not require routine INR monitoring; the INR does not reliably reflect its effect, so this statement needs correction.

options.text: "I won't stop this medicine on my own, even before a procedure, without talking to my provider."
options.why: Stopping a direct oral anticoagulant early raises the risk of stroke, so this shows understanding.

options.text: "I'll tell my dentist that I take a blood thinner."
options.why: Informing all providers allows safe planning for procedures.

options.text: "I'll call if I see black stools or blood in my urine."
options.why: Recognizing and reporting bleeding is appropriate.

takeaway: Direct oral anticoagulants such as apixaban do not need routine INR checks, but they must not be stopped without provider guidance.

stem: A client who received a coronary stent 2 months ago takes clopidogrel and low-dose aspirin. The client asks whether it is safe to buy over-the-counter omeprazole for heartburn. What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "Check with your provider first; omeprazole can make clopidogrel less effective, and a different stomach medicine may be recommended."
options.why: Omeprazole and esomeprazole inhibit CYP2C19, the enzyme that converts clopidogrel to its active form; the label advises avoiding them, and another agent such as pantoprazole may be chosen.

options.text: "Yes, omeprazole will protect your stomach from the aspirin, so start it today."
options.why: Although stomach protection is reasonable, omeprazole specifically is the concern because it can reduce clopidogrel's effect.

options.text: "Stop the clopidogrel while you take omeprazole."
options.why: Stopping clopidogrel after a recent stent risks stent thrombosis and myocardial infarction.

options.text: "Take omeprazole with the clopidogrel so they are absorbed together."
options.why: Taking them together does not prevent the enzyme interaction.

takeaway: Omeprazole and esomeprazole reduce activation of clopidogrel through CYP2C19; clients should check with the provider before starting them.

stem: A client who had a drug-eluting coronary stent placed 3 months ago says, "My dentist told me to stop clopidogrel for a week before my tooth extraction." What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "That's standard, so stop it 7 days before the extraction."
options.why: Stopping dual antiplatelet therapy early after a drug-eluting stent can cause stent thrombosis, which is often fatal.

options.text: "Stop the aspirin instead and keep taking the clopidogrel."
options.why: The client should not change either antiplatelet without guidance from the cardiologist.

options.text: "Please don't stop it until your cardiologist and dentist have talked; stopping it this soon after a stent can cause a clot in the stent."
options.why: The cardiologist must weigh stent-thrombosis risk against bleeding risk; many dental extractions can be done safely with local measures while antiplatelets continue.

options.text: "You can stop it, but take an extra aspirin each day to make up for it."
options.why: Extra aspirin does not replace clopidogrel's protection and increases bleeding risk.

takeaway: Early interruption of antiplatelet therapy after a coronary stent risks stent thrombosis; any interruption must be coordinated with the cardiologist.

stem: A client with atrial fibrillation is discharged on rivaroxaban 20 mg once daily. Which statement indicates the client understands how to take this medication?

options.text: "I'll take it on an empty stomach first thing in the morning."
options.why: The 15 mg and 20 mg rivaroxaban doses need food for adequate absorption; taking them fasting lowers drug exposure.

options.text: "I'll take it with my evening meal every day."
options.why: For atrial fibrillation, the labeling directs rivaroxaban 20 mg to be taken once daily with the evening meal to ensure full absorption.

options.text: "I'll need to avoid green leafy vegetables."
options.why: Vitamin K intake does not affect rivaroxaban, which does not act through vitamin K-dependent synthesis.

options.text: "If I miss a dose, I'll take two tablets the next evening."
options.why: Doubling the next dose of a once-daily regimen increases bleeding risk; a missed dose is taken the same day as soon as remembered.

takeaway: Rivaroxaban 15 mg and 20 mg tablets should be taken with food (for atrial fibrillation, with the evening meal); vitamin K intake does not matter.

stem: A client with an acute ischemic stroke is being evaluated for IV alteplase. Which findings are contraindications the nurse should report before the drug is given? Select all that apply.

options.text: History of a hemorrhagic stroke 2 years ago
options.why: Correct. Any prior intracranial hemorrhage is a contraindication to thrombolytic therapy.

options.text: Black, tarry stools for the past 2 days
options.why: Correct. Active internal (gastrointestinal) bleeding is a contraindication.

options.text: Blood pressure persistently 198/116 mm Hg despite antihypertensive treatment
options.why: Correct. Blood pressure must be lowered below 185/110 mm Hg before alteplase can be given safely.

options.text: Age 74 years
options.why: Incorrect. Older age alone is not a contraindication to alteplase for stroke.

options.text: Takes atorvastatin daily
options.why: Incorrect. Statin therapy does not increase bleeding risk with thrombolytics.

options.text: Platelet count 64,000/mm³
options.why: Correct. A platelet count below 100,000/mm³ is a contraindication (normal about 150,000–400,000/mm³).

takeaway: Before thrombolytics, screen for prior intracranial hemorrhage, active bleeding, uncontrolled blood pressure above 185/110 mm Hg and platelets below 100,000/mm³.

stem: A client is receiving an IV infusion of alteplase. Which actions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Avoid intramuscular injections.
options.why: Correct. IM injections can cause large hematomas during and after thrombolytic therapy.

options.text: Apply pressure to venipuncture sites for longer than usual.
options.why: Correct. Prolonged pressure is needed because clotting is impaired.

options.text: Perform frequent neurologic checks and blood pressure measurements.
options.why: Correct. Frequent checks detect intracranial hemorrhage and hypertension, which raises bleeding risk.

options.text: Insert a nasogastric tube routinely to monitor for bleeding.
options.why: Incorrect. Invasive tubes are avoided during and shortly after thrombolysis unless essential, because insertion can cause bleeding.

options.text: Use an electric razor for shaving.
options.why: Correct. An electric razor reduces the risk of cuts.

options.text: Obtain arterial blood gases every hour.
options.why: Incorrect. Arterial punctures are avoided because they can cause bleeding that is hard to control.

takeaway: During thrombolytic therapy, avoid punctures and invasive procedures, hold pressure longer, use an electric razor and monitor closely for bleeding.

stem: Thirty minutes into an IV alteplase infusion for an ischemic stroke, the client reports a sudden severe headache, vomits, and becomes harder to arouse. Place the nurse's actions in order of priority.

options.text: Notify the provider or stroke team of the change
options.why: The team is notified promptly with current data so they can direct reversal therapy.

options.text: Prepare the client for an emergent non-contrast head CT
options.why: Imaging confirms or rules out intracranial hemorrhage once the infusion is stopped and the team is involved.

options.text: Stop the alteplase infusion
options.why: The drug is stopped first because these signs suggest intracranial hemorrhage, and continuing it would worsen bleeding.

options.text: Assess airway, vital signs and neurologic status
options.why: After the infusion is stopped, the nurse checks airway protection (vomiting, decreasing alertness) and gathers data to report.

takeaway: A sudden headache, vomiting or neurologic decline during thrombolysis means stopping the infusion first, then assessing, notifying the team and obtaining an emergent CT.

stem: A client has taken amiodarone for 5 months for atrial fibrillation. The client reports a new dry cough and shortness of breath when climbing stairs. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Advise the client to use an over-the-counter cough syrup
options.why: Treating the symptom may delay recognition of a serious drug toxicity.

options.text: Explain that this is an expected, harmless effect of amiodarone
options.why: Pulmonary symptoms are not harmless; they may signal amiodarone pulmonary toxicity, which can be fatal.

options.text: Tell the client to double the dose to control the heart rhythm
options.why: Increasing the dose would worsen toxicity and is not indicated.

options.text: Report the findings to the provider promptly, anticipating a chest x-ray and pulmonary function evaluation
options.why: New cough and dyspnea can signal amiodarone pulmonary toxicity (pneumonitis or fibrosis); prompt evaluation and possible drug discontinuation are needed.

takeaway: New dyspnea or cough in a client taking amiodarone suggests pulmonary toxicity and must be reported promptly.

stem: A client is starting long-term oral amiodarone. Which monitoring and teaching should the nurse plan? Select all that apply.

options.text: Thyroid function tests
options.why: Correct. Amiodarone contains iodine and can cause hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism.

options.text: Liver function tests
options.why: Correct. Amiodarone can cause hepatotoxicity.

options.text: Baseline and follow-up chest x-ray and pulmonary function evaluation
options.why: Correct. Pulmonary toxicity is one of the most serious adverse effects.

options.text: Regular eye examinations
options.why: Correct. Corneal microdeposits and, rarely, optic neuropathy can occur.

options.text: Daily intake of grapefruit juice to boost absorption
options.why: Incorrect. Grapefruit juice raises amiodarone levels and should be avoided.

options.text: Exposing skin to sunlight to prevent skin discoloration
options.why: Incorrect. Amiodarone causes photosensitivity and a blue-gray skin discoloration; sun protection, not sun exposure, is taught.

takeaway: Amiodarone requires monitoring of thyroid, liver, lung and eye function, sun protection and avoidance of grapefruit juice.

stem: The nurse is preparing to give adenosine 6 mg IV to a hemodynamically stable client with supraventricular tachycardia. Place the steps in the correct order.

options.text: Immediately follow with a rapid 20 mL normal saline flush
options.why: A rapid flush pushes the drug into the central circulation before its very short half-life (under 10 seconds) ends.

options.text: Confirm continuous ECG monitoring with a rhythm strip recording
options.why: The rhythm response, including the expected brief pause, must be captured, and emergency equipment should be ready.

options.text: Push the adenosine rapidly over 1 to 2 seconds
options.why: Adenosine is metabolized within seconds, so it must be given as a rapid push.

options.text: Attach the adenosine syringe and a saline flush syringe to the injection port closest to the client
options.why: Using the port nearest the client (in a large proximal vein, such as the antecubital) shortens the distance the drug travels.

options.text: Observe the monitor for conversion and a brief period of asystole
options.why: A transient pause is expected before sinus rhythm returns; the nurse evaluates the response.

takeaway: Give adenosine as a rapid IV push at the port closest to the client, followed immediately by a rapid 20 mL saline flush, with continuous ECG recording.

stem: Immediately after receiving adenosine 6 mg IV, a client says, "My chest feels tight, and I feel flushed." The monitor shows a 4-second pause followed by sinus rhythm at 84/min. What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: Reassure the client that these effects are expected and brief, and continue monitoring the rhythm
options.why: Flushing, chest pressure, a sense of doom and a brief pause are expected because adenosine transiently blocks the AV node; the effects resolve quickly because of its short half-life.

options.text: Begin chest compressions
options.why: A brief pause followed by an organized, perfusing rhythm is not cardiac arrest; compressions are not indicated.

options.text: Administer atropine for the pause
options.why: Atropine is not needed for the expected transient pause after adenosine.

options.text: Give a second dose of 12 mg to prevent recurrence
options.why: A repeat dose is given only if the tachycardia persists; the rhythm has already converted.

takeaway: Transient asystole, flushing and chest pressure are expected after adenosine and resolve within seconds.

stem: A client who takes atorvastatin 80 mg daily reports diffuse muscle aches and weakness and says his urine has turned the color of cola. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Tell the client to increase physical activity to relieve the stiffness
options.why: Exercise can worsen muscle injury if rhabdomyolysis is developing.

options.text: Instruct the client to hold atorvastatin and notify the provider for an evaluation, including creatine kinase
options.why: Muscle pain with dark urine suggests statin-induced rhabdomyolysis; the drug is held and CK and renal function are checked urgently.

options.text: Suggest taking the dose in the morning instead of at night
options.why: Changing dose timing does not address possible muscle breakdown.

options.text: Advise an over-the-counter pain reliever and recheck in 1 month
options.why: Delaying evaluation risks acute kidney injury from myoglobin.

takeaway: Unexplained muscle pain or weakness with dark urine in a client on a statin suggests rhabdomyolysis: hold the drug and check CK and renal function.

stem: The nurse is teaching a client who is starting simvastatin. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I'll report any unexplained muscle pain or weakness."
options.why: This is correct; muscle symptoms can signal myopathy.

options.text: "I'll take it in the evening."
options.why: Simvastatin has a short half-life and is traditionally taken in the evening, when cholesterol synthesis peaks.

options.text: "I'll keep following my low-fat diet and walking program."
options.why: Lifestyle measures remain part of lipid management.

options.text: "I'll drink grapefruit juice with my pill each night."
options.why: Grapefruit inhibits CYP3A4 and can greatly raise simvastatin levels, increasing the risk of myopathy; this statement needs correction.

takeaway: Simvastatin and lovastatin interact with grapefruit through CYP3A4; teach clients to avoid grapefruit and report muscle symptoms.

stem: A client in septic shock is receiving norepinephrine through a peripheral IV in the forearm while a central line is being arranged. The nurse finds the skin around the site cool, pale and hard. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Stop the norepinephrine infusion at that site.
options.why: Correct. Stopping the infusion limits further drug from leaking into tissue.

options.text: Notify the provider immediately.
options.why: Correct. The provider must direct antidote therapy and replacement access.

options.text: Prepare phentolamine for subcutaneous infiltration of the area.
options.why: Correct. Phentolamine, an alpha-adrenergic blocker, reverses local vasoconstriction and helps prevent tissue necrosis.

options.text: Apply an ice pack to the site.
options.why: Incorrect. Cold causes further vasoconstriction and worsens ischemia from a vasopressor extravasation.

options.text: Slow the infusion rate at the same site and continue monitoring.
options.why: Incorrect. Any further infusion into infiltrated tissue increases the risk of necrosis.

options.text: Restart the vasopressor promptly through a new, patent site to maintain blood pressure.
options.why: Correct. A client in shock depends on the vasopressor, so infusion must resume quickly through another site.

takeaway: For vasopressor extravasation: stop the infusion at that site, notify the provider, infiltrate phentolamine and restart the vasopressor promptly through another site.

stem: The IV site of a client receiving a dopamine infusion becomes pale and cold, and the infusion has been stopped. Which medication should the nurse anticipate to prevent tissue necrosis?

options.text: Naloxone
options.why: Naloxone reverses opioids and has no role in vasopressor extravasation.

options.text: Hyaluronidase
options.why: Hyaluronidase is used for some non-vasoactive extravasations but does not reverse alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction.

options.text: Phentolamine
options.why: Phentolamine blocks alpha-adrenergic receptors, reversing the intense local vasoconstriction caused by extravasated dopamine or norepinephrine; it is infiltrated into the affected area as soon as possible.

options.text: Protamine sulfate
options.why: Protamine reverses heparin and is unrelated to extravasation.

takeaway: Phentolamine, infiltrated subcutaneously, is the antidote for extravasation of alpha-adrenergic vasopressors such as dopamine and norepinephrine.

stem: A client with a hypertensive emergency received IV labetalol 20 mg 10 minutes ago. The client now asks to walk to the bathroom. What is the nurse's best action?

options.text: Help the client walk to the bathroom because blood pressure is still elevated
options.why: Even with elevated pressure, IV labetalol can cause marked orthostatic hypotension; walking before testing tolerance risks syncope and falls.

options.text: Encourage independent walking to promote circulation
options.why: Independent ambulation is unsafe immediately after IV labetalol.

options.text: Give a second dose so the client can walk sooner
options.why: Additional doses are given based on blood pressure response, not to allow ambulation, and would increase orthostatic risk.

options.text: Provide a bedpan or bedside urinal and keep the client lying down until tolerance of an upright position is checked
options.why: Labeling advises keeping the client supine during and immediately after IV labetalol and confirming the client can tolerate an upright position before ambulating.

takeaway: After IV labetalol, keep the client supine and check orthostatic tolerance before allowing ambulation.

stem: A client with long-standing hypertension arrives at the emergency department with a BP of 214/122 mm Hg, headache, sweating and anxiety. The client says, "I ran out of my clonidine 0.3 mg twice a day two days ago." How should the nurse interpret these findings?

options.text: Expected blood pressure variation that needs no specific treatment
options.why: A blood pressure of 214/122 mm Hg with symptoms is not normal variation and needs prompt treatment.

options.text: Rebound hypertension from abrupt clonidine withdrawal
options.why: Stopping clonidine suddenly causes a surge of sympathetic activity, producing severe hypertension, tachycardia, sweating and anxiety; clonidine is tapered rather than stopped abruptly.

options.text: An allergic reaction to clonidine
options.why: An allergic reaction would cause rash, urticaria or facial swelling, not a hypertensive surge after stopping the drug.

options.text: Clonidine toxicity
options.why: Toxicity causes hypotension, bradycardia and sedation, the opposite of these findings.

takeaway: Abrupt withdrawal of clonidine can cause rebound hypertensive crisis; teach clients never to run out of it and to taper only as directed.

stem: Luis, 67, has heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and no diabetes. He is started on empagliflozin. Which statement indicates he understood the teaching?

options.text: "I'll keep my genital area clean and dry and report itching, redness or discharge."
options.why: SGLT2 inhibitors increase urinary glucose, which raises the risk of genital yeast infections; good hygiene and early reporting are appropriate.

options.text: "This medicine is only for diabetes, so my provider must have made a mistake."
options.why: SGLT2 inhibitors such as empagliflozin and dapagliflozin reduce heart failure hospitalization and death, even in clients without diabetes.

options.text: "I should limit my fluids to 500 mL a day while taking this."
options.why: Severe fluid restriction with an SGLT2 inhibitor, which causes mild diuresis, could lead to dehydration.

options.text: "I'll keep taking it even if I'm vomiting and can't eat for several days."
options.why: During acute illness with poor intake, SGLT2 inhibitors are usually held (sick-day rules) to reduce the risk of dehydration and ketoacidosis.

takeaway: SGLT2 inhibitors benefit heart failure even without diabetes; teach genital hygiene, hydration and sick-day rules.

stem: A client with type 2 diabetes who takes dapagliflozin is 2 days postoperative after bowel surgery and has eaten little. The client reports nausea and abdominal pain. Results: blood glucose 188 mg/dL, pH 7.21, bicarbonate 11 mEq/L and serum ketones positive. How should the nurse interpret these findings?

options.text: Expected postoperative stress response
options.why: Stress may raise glucose, but it does not explain a metabolic acidosis with positive ketones.

options.text: Respiratory acidosis from shallow breathing after surgery
options.why: Respiratory acidosis involves a raised PaCO2, not a low bicarbonate with ketones.

options.text: Euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis associated with the SGLT2 inhibitor
options.why: SGLT2 inhibitors can cause ketoacidosis with only mildly elevated glucose, especially with surgery and reduced intake; pH below 7.35 and bicarbonate below 22 mEq/L with ketones confirm metabolic acidosis (normal pH 7.35–7.45, bicarbonate 22–26 mEq/L).

options.text: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
options.why: HHS involves very high glucose (often above 600 mg/dL) with little or no ketosis.

takeaway: SGLT2 inhibitors can cause euglycemic DKA; suspect it with nausea, abdominal pain and acidosis even when glucose is below 250 mg/dL, and hold the drug before surgery as directed.
