stem: A client with heart failure takes lisinopril 10 mg and spironolactone 25 mg daily. The serum potassium is 5.1 mEq/L. Which new prescription should the nurse question?

options.text: Furosemide 20 mg PO daily
options.why: A loop diuretic increases potassium excretion and is commonly combined with these drugs in heart failure.

options.text: Potassium chloride 20 mEq PO daily
options.why: With potassium already above normal (3.5–5 mEq/L) and two potassium-retaining drugs, a supplement could cause dangerous hyperkalemia.

options.text: Daily weight before breakfast
options.why: Daily weights are a standard heart failure monitoring measure.

options.text: Carvedilol 3.125 mg PO twice daily
options.why: Low-dose carvedilol is guideline-directed therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and does not raise potassium significantly.

takeaway: Question potassium supplements for clients taking ACE inhibitors, ARBs or potassium-sparing diuretics, especially when potassium is already high.

stem: A client who weighs 82 kg has a deep vein thrombosis. After the bolus, the prescription is a heparin infusion at 18 units/kg/hr. The bag contains heparin 25,000 units in 500 mL of D5W. At what rate should the nurse set the pump? (Round to the nearest tenth.)

options.text: 14.8 mL/hr
options.why: This rate assumes a concentration of 100 units/mL (25,000 units in 250 mL); this bag is 50 units/mL.

options.text: 18 mL/hr
options.why: This confuses the dose in units/kg/hr with the pump rate in mL/hr.

options.text: 295.2 mL/hr
options.why: This divides by 5 instead of 50 units/mL, a tenfold error that would cause a massive overdose.

options.text: 29.5 mL/hr
options.why: Dose: 18 units/kg/hr × 82 kg = 1,476 units/hr. Concentration: 25,000 units ÷ 500 mL = 50 units/mL. Rate: 1,476 ÷ 50 = 29.52, rounded to 29.5 mL/hr.

takeaway: For weight-based heparin: units/kg/hr × kg = units/hr, then divide by the concentration (units/mL) to get mL/hr.

stem: A 70-kg client is receiving heparin at 18 units/kg/hr from a bag containing 25,000 units in 250 mL. The aPTT is below range, and the nomogram directs the nurse to increase the infusion by 2 units/kg/hr. What is the new pump rate?

options.text: 14 mL/hr
options.why: New dose: 18 + 2 = 20 units/kg/hr × 70 kg = 1,400 units/hr. Concentration: 25,000 units ÷ 250 mL = 100 units/mL. Rate: 1,400 ÷ 100 = 14 mL/hr.

options.text: 12.6 mL/hr
options.why: This is the current rate (18 units/kg/hr × 70 kg = 1,260 units/hr ÷ 100 units/mL), before the increase.

options.text: 1.4 mL/hr
options.why: This is a decimal error that would deliver only one-tenth of the needed dose.

options.text: 140 mL/hr
options.why: This tenfold error would deliver 14,000 units/hr and cause a dangerous overdose.

takeaway: When a nomogram changes a heparin dose in units/kg/hr, recalculate units/hr from the client's weight and divide by the bag concentration.

stem: A client who weighs 76 kg is prescribed dopamine at 5 mcg/kg/min. The premixed bag contains dopamine 400 mg in 250 mL of D5W. At what rate should the nurse set the pump? (Round to the nearest tenth.)

options.text: 0.2 mL/hr
options.why: This omits the conversion from minutes to hours (380 mcg/min ÷ 1,600 mcg/mL = 0.24 mL/min, not mL/hr).

options.text: 14.3 mL/hr
options.why: Dose: 5 mcg/kg/min × 76 kg = 380 mcg/min × 60 = 22,800 mcg/hr. Concentration: 400 mg = 400,000 mcg ÷ 250 mL = 1,600 mcg/mL. Rate: 22,800 ÷ 1,600 = 14.25, rounded to 14.3 mL/hr.

options.text: 28.5 mL/hr
options.why: This uses 800 mcg/mL (the 200 mg in 250 mL premix), which is not the bag supplied.

options.text: 142.5 mL/hr
options.why: This tenfold error would deliver a dangerously high dopamine dose.

takeaway: mcg/kg/min drips: mcg/kg/min × kg × 60 = mcg/hr; divide by the bag concentration in mcg/mL to get mL/hr.

stem: A client who weighs 90 kg is receiving dobutamine from a premixed bag of 500 mg in 250 mL of D5W. The pump is running at 18 mL/hr. What dose is the client receiving in mcg/kg/min? (Round to the nearest tenth.)

options.text: 3.3 mcg/kg/min
options.why: This uses a concentration of 1,000 mcg/mL (250 mg in 250 mL), not the 2,000 mcg/mL in this bag.

options.text: 13.3 mcg/kg/min
options.why: This doubles the actual concentration, using 4,000 mcg/mL.

options.text: 6.7 mcg/kg/min
options.why: Concentration: 500 mg = 500,000 mcg ÷ 250 mL = 2,000 mcg/mL. 18 mL/hr × 2,000 = 36,000 mcg/hr ÷ 60 = 600 mcg/min ÷ 90 kg = 6.67, rounded to 6.7 mcg/kg/min.

options.text: 400 mcg/kg/min
options.why: This is mcg/kg/hr (36,000 ÷ 90); the conversion from hours to minutes was omitted.

takeaway: To check a running drip: mL/hr × mcg/mL = mcg/hr; divide by 60 and by weight to get mcg/kg/min.

stem: A client is receiving IV furosemide for fluid overload and IV gentamicin for pneumonia. Which finding is the priority to report to the provider?

options.text: Urine output of 250 mL in the past 2 hours
options.why: Brisk urine output is the expected effect of furosemide.

options.text: Mild thirst
options.why: Mild thirst can accompany diuresis and is not the priority concern.

options.text: A new report of ringing in the ears and muffled hearing
options.why: Loop diuretics and aminoglycosides are both ototoxic, and together they increase the risk of permanent hearing loss; new tinnitus needs prompt reporting.

options.text: A 0.4 kg decrease in weight since yesterday
options.why: A small weight decrease reflects the intended removal of fluid.

takeaway: Loop diuretics and aminoglycosides have additive ototoxicity; report tinnitus or hearing changes promptly.

stem: After receiving report, which client should the nurse assess first?

options.text: A client on warfarin for atrial fibrillation with an INR of 2.4
options.why: An INR of 2.4 is within the typical therapeutic range of 2–3.

options.text: A client on digoxin with a serum level of 0.9 ng/mL and an apical pulse of 72/min
options.why: The level is therapeutic (about 0.5–2 ng/mL, with lower targets in heart failure) and the heart rate is acceptable.

options.text: A client on metoprolol with a heart rate of 62/min and BP of 118/70 mm Hg
options.why: These values are expected with beta blockade and do not indicate instability.

options.text: A client on a heparin infusion who has passed a black, tarry stool and has a heart rate of 118/min
options.why: Melena with tachycardia suggests active gastrointestinal bleeding and early hypovolemia in an anticoagulated client; this client is unstable and needs immediate assessment.

takeaway: Prioritize anticoagulated clients with signs of active bleeding and hemodynamic change over clients with expected or therapeutic values.

stem: The nurse is caring for clients on a cardiac unit with an assistive personnel (AP). Which task can the nurse delegate to the AP?

options.text: Weigh a client receiving furosemide each morning before breakfast using the same scale
options.why: Measuring and reporting daily weights is a standard, routine task within the AP's scope; the nurse interprets the results.

options.text: Count the apical pulse and decide whether to give the client's digoxin
options.why: Deciding whether to give a medication requires nursing judgment and cannot be delegated.

options.text: Teach a client how to self-inject enoxaparin
options.why: Teaching is a registered nurse responsibility.

options.text: Evaluate whether a client's chest pain was relieved by sublingual nitroglycerin
options.why: Evaluating response to medication is an assessment that the nurse must perform.

takeaway: Routine measurements such as daily weights can be delegated to AP; assessment, teaching, evaluation and medication decisions cannot.

stem: Four clients on a telemetry unit have the following updates. Which client should the nurse see first?

options.text: A client on enoxaparin with a small bruise at an abdominal injection site
options.why: Minor bruising at enoxaparin sites is common and not urgent.

options.text: A client on an IV nitroglycerin infusion whose BP is now 84/50 mm Hg and who reports dizziness
options.why: Symptomatic hypotension during a nitroglycerin infusion requires immediate action, such as reducing or stopping the infusion per protocol, to restore perfusion.

options.text: A client on atorvastatin asking what time of day to take the next dose
options.why: This is a teaching need that can wait.

options.text: A client on furosemide with a potassium of 3.7 mEq/L who is asking for the urinal
options.why: Potassium is normal (3.5–5 mEq/L), and toileting can be handled by other staff or after the urgent client.

takeaway: Symptomatic hypotension during a vasodilator infusion is an urgent priority over stable clients with routine needs.

stem: A new prescription reads, "Digoxin 125 mg PO daily." The client's previous home dose was 0.125 mg daily. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give 0.125 mg because that is obviously what the prescriber meant
options.why: Nurses should not interpret or change an unclear prescription on their own; the dose must be verified with the prescriber.

options.text: Hold the medication and wait for the prescriber's next rounds
options.why: Delaying without communicating leaves the client without needed therapy; the prescriber should be contacted now.

options.text: Give 125 mg as written because the prescriber is responsible for the order
options.why: The nurse is accountable for giving a safe dose; 125 mg of digoxin would be lethal.

options.text: Contact the prescriber to clarify the dose before giving the medication
options.why: 125 mg is a 1,000-fold error (125 mcg = 0.125 mg); the prescription must be clarified, and the event is reported per facility policy.

takeaway: Clarify any prescription with an implausible dose directly with the prescriber; do not guess the intended dose.

stem: A hospitalized client with known angina reports new chest pain. Sublingual nitroglycerin 0.4 mg every 5 minutes, up to 3 doses, is prescribed. Place the nurse's actions in order.

options.text: Give a second tablet if the pain persists and systolic BP is still at least 90 mm Hg
options.why: A repeat dose is given only after reassessment shows ongoing pain and adequate blood pressure.

options.text: Reassess pain and blood pressure 5 minutes later
options.why: Reassessment at 5 minutes determines the response and whether another dose is safe.

options.text: Assess the pain rating and check that systolic BP is at least 90 mm Hg
options.why: Baseline pain and blood pressure confirm that the nitrate can be given safely, because it can cause hypotension.

options.text: Place one 0.4 mg tablet under the client's tongue to dissolve
options.why: The tablet is given only after baseline data confirm it is safe.

takeaway: Sublingual nitroglycerin: assess pain and BP, give one tablet, reassess in 5 minutes, then repeat only if pain persists and BP is adequate.

stem: At 0730 the nurse prepares to give insulin lispro 6 units subcutaneously to a client with type 1 diabetes. The client's breakfast tray has not yet arrived on the unit. Which action is best?

options.text: Give the injection now so the insulin is working when breakfast arrives.
options.why: Lispro starts to act in about 15 minutes; if the tray is delayed the client may become hypoglycemic before eating.

options.text: Hold the dose and give it at bedtime instead.
options.why: Rapid-acting insulin covers the carbohydrate in a meal; moving it to bedtime would leave breakfast uncovered and risk nighttime hypoglycemia.

options.text: Confirm that the tray is available and give the dose within 15 minutes before the client eats.
options.why: Lispro has an onset of about 15 minutes and peaks in about 1 hour, so it is given within 15 minutes before a meal (or right after starting) to match the rise in glucose.

options.text: Change the dose to insulin glargine so meal timing does not matter.
options.why: The nurse cannot substitute insulins; glargine is a basal insulin and does not cover meals.

takeaway: Rapid-acting insulin (lispro, aspart, glulisine) acts in about 15 minutes; give it only when food is in hand.

stem: A client who takes insulin glargine 20 units at bedtime and insulin aspart with meals asks whether both insulins can be drawn into one syringe at dinner to avoid two injections. Which response by the nurse is correct?

options.text: "Glargine must not be mixed with any other insulin, so you need two separate injections."
options.why: Mixing glargine with another insulin changes its acidic formulation and its long, peakless action, so it is always given alone.

options.text: "Yes, draw up the aspart first and then the glargine."
options.why: The clear-before-cloudy rule applies to regular insulin and NPH; glargine is clear but cannot be mixed at all.

options.text: "Yes, as long as you inject the mixture within 5 minutes."
options.why: No time limit makes the mixture safe; glargine is never combined with another insulin.

options.text: "Only if you shake the syringe well before injecting."
options.why: Shaking does not make glargine compatible and can damage insulin proteins.

takeaway: Glargine, detemir and degludec are not mixed with other insulins in a syringe.

stem: A client receives regular insulin 8 units subcutaneously at 0700. The nurse should be most alert for signs of hypoglycemia during which time period?

options.why: Regular insulin begins to act in about 30 to 60 minutes, so this is before its onset.
This window matches the peak of NPH (intermediate-acting) insulin, not regular insulin.

options.text: Equal risk at all times, because regular insulin has no peak
options.why: A peakless profile describes long-acting insulins such as glargine; regular insulin has a definite peak.
Regular (short-acting) insulin peaks about 2 to 4 hours after subcutaneous injection, so hypoglycemia is most likely from about 0900 to 1100.

takeaway: Regular insulin: onset 30 to 60 minutes, peak 2 to 4 hours, duration about 5 to 8 hours.

stem: A client in diabetic ketoacidosis has a prescription for a continuous IV insulin infusion. Which insulin should the nurse obtain from the pharmacy for the infusion bag?

options.text: Insulin glargine
options.why: Glargine is a long-acting insulin made for subcutaneous use only; it must never be given IV.

options.text: Regular insulin
options.why: Regular (short-acting) human insulin is the standard insulin for continuous IV infusion in DKA and other hospital insulin drips.

options.text: NPH insulin
options.why: NPH is a cloudy suspension and must never be given IV.

options.text: Insulin detemir
options.why: Detemir is a long-acting basal insulin for subcutaneous use only.

takeaway: Regular insulin is the standard IV insulin; cloudy (NPH) and long-acting insulins are never given IV.

stem: The nurse is preparing regular insulin 6 units and NPH insulin 14 units in one syringe. Place the steps in the correct order.

options.text: Inject 6 units of air into the regular insulin vial.
options.why: Air goes into the clear (regular) vial second, just before that dose is withdrawn, so the needle never enters NPH before regular is drawn.

options.text: Withdraw 14 units of NPH insulin, for a total of 20 units in the syringe.
options.why: NPH is drawn last so the clear regular insulin is not contaminated with the cloudy suspension.

options.text: Gently roll the NPH vial between the palms to resuspend it.
options.why: NPH is a suspension; rolling (not shaking) mixes it evenly and is done first.

options.text: Withdraw 6 units of regular insulin.
options.why: Clear before cloudy: regular insulin is drawn into the syringe before NPH.

options.text: Inject 14 units of air into the NPH vial without letting the needle touch the insulin.
options.why: Air goes into the NPH vial first while the syringe is still empty, so no regular insulin can be pushed into the NPH vial.

takeaway: Air into cloudy, air into clear, draw clear, then draw cloudy: regular (clear) is always drawn before NPH (cloudy).

stem: The nurse is teaching a client how to store insulin at home. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep unopened insulin in the refrigerator until the expiration date.
options.why: Correct. Unopened insulin is stored refrigerated at 36 to 46 °F (2 to 8 °C) to keep it potent until the printed expiration date.

options.text: Store extra vials in the freezer so they last longer.
options.why: Incorrect. Freezing damages insulin; insulin that has been frozen must be discarded.

options.text: An in-use vial or pen may be kept at room temperature, away from heat and direct sunlight.
options.why: Correct. In-use insulin can stay at room temperature (up to about 86 °F / 30 °C), which also makes injections more comfortable.

options.text: Discard an opened vial or pen after the number of days listed by the manufacturer, even if insulin remains.
options.why: Correct. Opened insulin loses potency and sterility over time; many products are discarded 28 days after opening, but the limit varies by product.

options.text: Leave the insulin pen in the car's glove compartment so it is always handy.
options.why: Incorrect. Cars can become very hot or freezing, which degrades insulin.

options.text: Shake the NPH vial hard before drawing up a dose.
options.why: Incorrect. NPH is gently rolled; vigorous shaking causes bubbles and inaccurate doses.

takeaway: Refrigerate unopened insulin, never freeze it, keep in-use insulin at room temperature, and discard it after the labeled number of days.

stem: A client with type 1 diabetes has had unpredictable glucose readings for 2 months despite taking every insulin dose. The nurse notes a soft, raised, rubbery area on the left side of the abdomen, and the client says, "I always inject there because it doesn't hurt." What is the nurse's best action?

options.text: Tell the client to switch all injections to the arm, which absorbs insulin fastest.
options.why: The abdomen, not the arm, generally absorbs insulin fastest; the real problem is the damaged tissue, not the region chosen.

options.text: Teach the client to avoid the raised area and to rotate injection points systematically within the abdomen.
options.why: The raised area is lipohypertrophy from repeated injections in one spot; insulin absorbs erratically from it. Rotating sites, at least 1 inch apart, prevents it and steadies glucose levels.

options.text: Recommend increasing each insulin dose by 10% until readings are stable.
options.why: Dose changes are the prescriber's decision, and injecting outside the damaged tissue may suddenly increase absorption and cause hypoglycemia.

options.text: Apply a warm compress to the area before each injection to improve absorption.
options.why: Heat changes absorption unpredictably and does not correct lipohypertrophy.

takeaway: Lipohypertrophy from injecting in the same spot causes erratic insulin absorption; rotate sites and avoid the lumpy areas.

stem: A client's prescription reads: insulin lispro correction scale before meals — glucose 151 to 200 mg/dL: 2 units; 201 to 250: 4 units; 251 to 300: 6 units; 301 to 350: 8 units; above 350: 10 units and notify the health care provider. The client's glucose before lunch is 362 mg/dL. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give 8 units of insulin lispro and recheck glucose before dinner.
options.why: 8 units is for 301 to 350 mg/dL; 362 mg/dL falls in the highest range.

options.text: Hold the insulin and call the provider for a new prescription.
options.why: The scale already gives a dose for this range; holding insulin leaves severe hyperglycemia untreated.

options.text: Give 10 units of insulin lispro and notify the health care provider.
options.why: A glucose of 362 mg/dL falls in the "above 350" range, which calls for 10 units AND notifying the provider so the overall regimen can be reviewed.

options.text: Give 10 units of insulin glargine now.
options.why: Glargine is a basal insulin and is not used for correction doses.

takeaway: Read correction scales exactly as written, including any "notify the provider" instruction tied to a range.

stem: A client with type 2 diabetes who takes insulin says, "I feel shaky and sweaty." The client is alert and able to swallow, and the fingerstick glucose is 58 mg/dL. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Give 4 oz (120 mL) of fruit juice and recheck glucose in 15 minutes.
options.why: For a conscious client with glucose below 70 mg/dL, give 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate (about 4 oz of juice or regular soda) and recheck in 15 minutes (the rule of 15).

options.text: Give a peanut butter sandwich and a glass of milk.
options.why: Fat and protein slow absorption; a mixed snack is given after the glucose has come back up, not as the first treatment.

options.text: Give glucagon 1 mg intramuscularly.
options.why: Glucagon is for a client who cannot safely swallow; this client is alert and can take oral carbohydrate.

options.text: Withhold treatment and recheck glucose in 30 minutes to confirm the result.
options.why: A glucose of 58 mg/dL with symptoms needs treatment now; waiting risks loss of consciousness or seizure.

takeaway: Rule of 15: 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck in 15 minutes, repeat if glucose is still below 70 mg/dL.

stem: A client with diabetes who is awake and able to swallow reports feeling shaky and confused. Lunch will be served in 2 hours. Place the nurse's actions in the correct order.

options.text: Give a snack that contains protein and complex carbohydrate.
options.why: Once glucose is above 70 mg/dL, a snack is given because the next meal is more than an hour away; this keeps glucose from dropping again.

options.text: Check the fingerstick blood glucose.
options.why: Confirming hypoglycemia is the first step when a meter is readily available.

options.text: Recheck the blood glucose 15 minutes after the carbohydrate.
options.why: Fast-acting carbohydrate needs about 15 minutes to raise glucose; rechecking shows whether treatment worked.

options.text: Give 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate, such as 4 glucose tablets.
options.why: After glucose is confirmed below 70 mg/dL, 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate is given.

options.text: Repeat 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate if glucose is still below 70 mg/dL.
options.why: The 15 g dose is repeated until glucose is at least 70 mg/dL.

takeaway: Check, treat with 15 g, recheck in 15 minutes, repeat if needed, then give a snack or meal to keep glucose up.

stem: The nurse is teaching the spouse of a client with type 1 diabetes how to use glucagon if the client is found unresponsive at home. Which instruction is most important for the nurse to include?

options.text: Give the client orange juice by mouth before giving the glucagon.
options.why: Nothing is given by mouth to an unresponsive person because of the risk of aspiration.

options.text: Give a second dose of glucagon right away if the client does not wake in 2 minutes.
options.why: Glucagon takes about 10 to 15 minutes to work; product labels allow a repeat dose after about 15 minutes, while emergency help is on the way.

options.text: Turn the client onto the side after giving the glucagon.
options.why: Glucagon often causes nausea and vomiting; placing the client on the side protects the airway from aspiration.

options.text: Expect the client to stay drowsy for several hours and let the client sleep.
options.why: The client should wake within about 15 minutes; once awake and able to swallow, the client needs carbohydrate to prevent hypoglycemia from returning.

takeaway: After glucagon, turn the client onto the side (vomiting is common), and give carbohydrate once the client is awake and can swallow.

stem: A hospitalized client with diabetes is found unresponsive and diaphoretic. The fingerstick glucose is 36 mg/dL, and the client has a patent peripheral IV line. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Place glucose gel inside the client's cheek.
options.why: Oral glucose is unsafe for an unresponsive client because of aspiration risk.

options.text: Give dextrose 50% IV per the hypoglycemia protocol.
options.why: With IV access available, IV dextrose raises glucose within minutes and is the fastest treatment for severe hypoglycemia.

options.text: Draw a venous glucose sample to confirm the reading before treating.
options.why: Treatment must not wait for a lab confirmation in an unresponsive client; delay risks brain injury.

options.text: Start the client's scheduled IV insulin infusion at a lower rate.
options.why: Any insulin would worsen severe hypoglycemia; insulin is stopped, not reduced.

takeaway: Severe hypoglycemia with IV access: give IV dextrose per protocol; glucagon is used when there is no IV.

stem: A client with type 2 diabetes takes insulin glargine, insulin lispro and metoprolol. Which sign is most likely to remain a reliable warning of hypoglycemia for this client?

options.text: Tachycardia
options.why: Beta-blockers blunt the rise in heart rate that epinephrine usually causes during hypoglycemia.

options.text: Tremor
options.why: Shakiness is a beta-adrenergic response and is reduced by beta-blockers.

options.text: Palpitations
options.why: Palpitations come from beta-adrenergic stimulation, which metoprolol blocks.

options.text: Sweating
options.why: Sweating during hypoglycemia is driven mainly by cholinergic sympathetic nerves, so beta-blockers do not mask it.

takeaway: Beta-blockers mask tremor, tachycardia and palpitations of hypoglycemia, but sweating still occurs; teach frequent glucose checks.

stem: A client with diabetic ketoacidosis has received a 1-liter bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride. Results: glucose 512 mg/dL, pH 7.12, bicarbonate 9 mEq/L, potassium 2.9 mEq/L. The provider has prescribed an IV insulin infusion and IV potassium chloride. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Start the insulin infusion now and give the potassium afterward.
options.why: Insulin drives potassium into cells; starting it with potassium already 2.9 mEq/L can cause fatal dysrhythmias and respiratory muscle weakness.

options.text: Give IV push potassium chloride, then start the insulin infusion.
options.why: Potassium chloride is never given IV push; it can cause cardiac arrest.

options.text: Start the potassium infusion and hold the insulin until the provider confirms potassium has risen to the protocol threshold.
options.why: Potassium is replaced first and insulin is held until potassium reaches the protocol threshold (3.5 mEq/L in the 2024 ADA-led consensus; some older protocols use 3.3 mEq/L; normal 3.5 to 5 mEq/L), because insulin would push the level even lower.

options.text: Give IV sodium bicarbonate to correct the acidosis before any other treatment.
options.why: Bicarbonate is not routine in DKA at this pH and also drives potassium into cells, worsening hypokalemia.

takeaway: In DKA, fluids come first, and insulin is held until potassium is replaced to a safe level.

stem: A client in diabetic ketoacidosis has been on an IV insulin infusion for 6 hours. Glucose has fallen from 480 to 238 mg/dL, but bicarbonate is 13 mEq/L and the anion gap is 19 mEq/L. Which prescription should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Stop the insulin infusion because glucose is close to target.
options.why: Stopping insulin while the anion gap is open lets ketoacidosis continue; DKA resolves only when ketones clear, not when glucose falls.

options.text: Add dextrose to the IV fluids and continue the insulin infusion.
options.why: When glucose drops to about 250 mg/dL in DKA, dextrose is added so insulin can continue clearing ketones without causing hypoglycemia; bicarbonate is still low (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L) and the gap open (normal about 8 to 12 mEq/L).

options.text: Switch the client to subcutaneous correction-scale insulin only.
options.why: Correction-scale insulin cannot clear ketosis while the gap is open, and transition requires basal insulin with an overlap.

options.text: Increase the insulin infusion rate to lower glucose faster.
options.why: Lowering glucose faster raises the risk of hypoglycemia and cerebral edema; the problem is ketosis, not glucose.

takeaway: In DKA, add dextrose when glucose nears 250 mg/dL and keep insulin running until the anion gap closes.

stem: A client recovering from DKA is now eating, with pH 7.34, bicarbonate 20 mEq/L and a closed anion gap. The provider prescribes insulin glargine 18 units subcutaneously now and discontinuation of the IV insulin infusion. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Stop the IV infusion first, then give the glargine 1 hour later.
options.why: Any gap without insulin is dangerous because IV regular insulin wears off within minutes, and ketoacidosis can return quickly.

options.text: Give the glargine and stop the IV insulin infusion at the same moment.
options.why: Glargine takes 1 to 2 hours to begin acting, so stopping the drip at once leaves the client without insulin.

options.text: Give the glargine and continue the IV insulin infusion for 1 to 2 hours before stopping it.
options.why: Basal subcutaneous insulin is given 1 to 2 hours before the IV infusion stops so its action overlaps the very short action of IV insulin, preventing rebound hyperglycemia and DKA.

options.text: Hold the glargine until the next morning because the client is still on IV insulin.
options.why: Waiting delays basal coverage; the overlap should start now so the infusion can be safely stopped.

takeaway: When switching from IV to subcutaneous insulin, overlap: give basal insulin 1 to 2 hours before stopping the drip.

stem: A 79-year-old client with type 2 diabetes and heart failure is admitted with confusion. Glucose is 940 mg/dL, serum osmolality 362 mOsm/kg, serum ketones negative, and pH 7.37. Which nursing action is the priority?

options.text: Start isotonic IV fluids as prescribed and assess lung sounds and oxygen saturation often.
options.why: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state causes severe dehydration, so fluid replacement is the first treatment; heart failure means the nurse must watch closely for crackles and fluid overload. Normal serum osmolality is about 275 to 295 mOsm/kg.

options.text: Restrict fluids to 1,500 mL/day because of the heart failure.
options.why: The client is profoundly volume depleted; restricting fluid would worsen shock and kidney injury.

options.text: Give an IV bolus of regular insulin before any fluids.
options.why: Insulin before fluid shifts water into cells and can cause circulatory collapse; fluids come first.

options.text: Give sodium bicarbonate to treat ketoacidosis.
options.why: This client has no ketoacidosis (pH and ketones are normal); bicarbonate is not indicated.

takeaway: HHS: huge fluid deficit without ketosis. Replace fluids first, then insulin, and watch older or cardiac clients for overload.

stem: A client with DKA had a potassium of 5.4 mEq/L on admission. After 4 hours of IV fluids and an insulin infusion, the potassium is 3.4 mEq/L. Which interpretation by the nurse is correct?

options.text: The kidneys have stopped excreting potassium, so the next value will be high.
options.why: The level is falling, not rising; urine output usually improves with fluids, which adds to potassium loss.

options.text: Insulin is moving potassium back into the cells, and the client needs potassium replacement.
options.why: Acidosis and lack of insulin shift potassium out of cells, hiding a total-body deficit. Insulin and fluids move it back in, so the serum level falls (normal 3.5 to 5 mEq/L) and replacement is added to the IV fluids.

options.text: This is a lab error, because potassium cannot change that quickly.
options.why: Large shifts within hours are expected in DKA treatment; the value should be acted on, not dismissed.

options.text: The insulin infusion should be stopped until potassium returns to 5 mEq/L.
options.why: Insulin is still needed to clear ketones; the usual response is to add potassium to the fluids, with insulin held only if potassium falls below the protocol threshold.

takeaway: In DKA, the admission potassium may be normal or high, but total-body potassium is low; expect it to fall with insulin.

stem: The nurse is teaching sick-day rules to a client with type 1 diabetes who uses basal and mealtime insulin. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep taking your basal insulin even if you are not eating.
options.why: Correct. Illness raises stress hormones and glucose; stopping basal insulin can trigger DKA in type 1 diabetes.

options.text: Check your blood glucose about every 3 to 4 hours while you are sick.
options.why: Correct. Glucose can change quickly during illness, so it is checked more often than usual.

options.text: Check urine or blood ketones if your glucose is above 240 mg/dL.
options.why: Correct. Ketone testing at this level detects early DKA in type 1 diabetes.

options.text: Skip all insulin on days you cannot eat solid food.
options.why: Incorrect. Basal insulin is always needed; mealtime doses may be adjusted, but stopping all insulin risks DKA.

options.text: If you cannot eat solid food, drink liquids that contain carbohydrate, such as juice or broth with crackers.
options.why: Correct. Carbohydrate-containing liquids provide energy and prevent hypoglycemia while insulin is continued.

options.text: Call your provider if you cannot keep fluids down or your ketones are moderate or large.
options.why: Correct. Ongoing vomiting or rising ketones signal developing DKA that needs prompt care.

takeaway: Sick days: never stop basal insulin, check glucose and ketones often, keep up fluids and carbohydrate, and call early for vomiting or ketones.

stem: A client with type 2 diabetes who takes metformin 1,000 mg twice daily is scheduled for a CT scan with IV iodinated contrast tomorrow. The client's eGFR is 41 mL/min/1.73 m². Which action should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Give the metformin with extra water before the scan to protect the kidneys.
options.why: Fluids may help, but continuing metformin around contrast in reduced kidney function raises the risk of lactic acidosis.

options.text: Cancel the CT scan because metformin is a contraindication to contrast.
options.why: Metformin is not a reason to cancel imaging; it is temporarily held instead.

options.text: Switch metformin to the extended-release form for 2 days.
options.why: Changing the formulation does not reduce the risk of lactic acidosis.

options.text: Hold metformin at the time of the scan and restart it only after kidney function is rechecked about 48 hours later.
options.why: Labeling advises stopping metformin at or before iodinated contrast when eGFR is 30 to 60, then rechecking eGFR in 48 hours and restarting if kidney function is stable.

takeaway: Hold metformin for iodinated contrast in clients with reduced kidney function, and restart after eGFR is rechecked at about 48 hours.

stem: A client started metformin 3 months ago. Which finding should the nurse report to the provider immediately?

options.text: Mild diarrhea that began the first week and is now improving
options.why: GI upset is the most common side effect, is usually short-lived, and is reduced by taking metformin with meals.

options.text: Unusual muscle aches, rapid breathing and increasing drowsiness
options.why: This combination suggests lactic acidosis, a rare but potentially fatal adverse effect of metformin that needs emergency evaluation (normal lactate is below about 2 mmol/L).

options.text: A metallic taste in the mouth
options.why: A metallic taste is a known, harmless side effect of metformin.

options.text: A fasting glucose of 126 mg/dL
options.why: This shows the drug is working toward goals; it is not an urgent finding.

takeaway: Report muscle pain, rapid breathing, unusual sleepiness or abdominal pain on metformin: these suggest lactic acidosis.

stem: The nurse is teaching a client who is newly prescribed metformin. Which statements by the nurse are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: "Take metformin with meals to lessen stomach upset."
options.why: Correct. Taking it with food reduces nausea and diarrhea, which are most common when therapy starts.

options.text: "Limit alcohol, because it raises the risk of a serious side effect called lactic acidosis."
options.why: Correct. Alcohol affects lactate metabolism and increases the risk of lactic acidosis with metformin.

options.text: "Metformin used alone often causes severe low blood sugar, so eat a snack every 2 hours."
options.why: Incorrect. Metformin lowers glucose output by the liver and rarely causes hypoglycemia when used alone.

options.text: "Your vitamin B12 level may be checked periodically while you take this drug."
options.why: Correct. Long-term metformin can lower vitamin B12 absorption and cause deficiency and neuropathy.

options.text: "Tell staff you take metformin before any test that uses contrast dye."
options.why: Correct. Metformin may need to be held around iodinated contrast to prevent lactic acidosis.

options.text: "Stop the drug if you have any diarrhea during the first week."
options.why: Incorrect. Mild GI upset early in therapy is expected and usually fades; the client should not stop without talking with the provider.

takeaway: Metformin: take with meals, limit alcohol, rarely causes hypoglycemia alone, can lower B12, and is held for contrast in at-risk clients.

stem: The nurse is reviewing four clients with type 2 diabetes. Which client is at highest risk for hypoglycemia?

options.text: A 54-year-old taking metformin who walks 30 minutes daily
options.why: Metformin alone rarely causes hypoglycemia.

options.text: A 61-year-old taking sitagliptin who eats regular meals
options.why: DPP-4 inhibitors have a low risk of hypoglycemia when used without insulin or a sulfonylurea.

options.text: An 83-year-old with an eGFR of 27 mL/min/1.73 m² who takes glyburide and has been skipping meals
options.why: Sulfonylureas stimulate insulin release regardless of glucose level; glyburide has active metabolites cleared by the kidneys, so older age, kidney impairment and skipped meals together create the highest risk.

options.text: A 47-year-old taking weekly dulaglutide who reports nausea
options.why: GLP-1 receptor agonists release insulin only when glucose is elevated, so hypoglycemia is uncommon when they are used alone.

takeaway: Sulfonylureas (especially glyburide) cause hypoglycemia; risk is greatest in older adults, kidney impairment and missed meals.

stem: A client with type 2 diabetes who takes empagliflozin and metformin comes to the clinic with 2 days of nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and fatigue after a stomach virus. Fingerstick glucose is 182 mg/dL and respirations are 26/min and deep. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Reassure the client that glucose is near target and encourage clear liquids at home.
options.why: A near-normal glucose does not rule out ketoacidosis in a client taking an SGLT2 inhibitor; sending the client home could miss a life-threatening condition.

options.text: Recommend the client take an extra dose of metformin to bring glucose down.
options.why: Glucose is not the problem, and metformin during dehydration and acidosis raises the risk of lactic acidosis.

options.text: Teach the client to take empagliflozin with food to reduce nausea.
options.why: This treats the symptom as a minor side effect and misses the danger.

options.text: Notify the provider promptly and anticipate testing for ketones and arterial blood gases.
options.why: SGLT2 inhibitors can cause euglycemic DKA (ketoacidosis with glucose below about 250 mg/dL), especially with illness, vomiting or reduced intake; deep, rapid breathing suggests metabolic acidosis.

takeaway: SGLT2 inhibitors (-gliflozins) can cause DKA with near-normal glucose; check ketones in any ill client taking one.

stem: The nurse is teaching a client who is starting dapagliflozin for type 2 diabetes. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep the genital area clean and dry, and report itching or unusual discharge.
options.why: Correct. Glucose in the urine promotes genital yeast infections, a common adverse effect of SGLT2 inhibitors.

options.text: Report pain, tenderness or swelling of the genital or perineal area with fever right away.
options.why: Correct. These can signal Fournier gangrene (necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum), a rare but serious adverse effect.

options.text: Expect to urinate more often, and drink enough fluids to avoid dehydration.
options.why: Correct. The drug causes osmotic diuresis, which can lead to volume depletion and dizziness.

options.text: Tell the surgeon about this medicine, because it is usually stopped a few days before planned surgery.
options.why: Correct. Labeling advises stopping dapagliflozin at least 3 days before scheduled surgery to lower the risk of ketoacidosis.

options.text: A urine dipstick that is positive for glucose means the drug is not working.
options.why: Incorrect. Glucose in the urine is how the drug works; it blocks glucose reabsorption in the kidney.

options.text: Take an extra dose on days when you eat a large meal.
options.why: Incorrect. SGLT2 inhibitors are taken once daily and are not adjusted for meals.

takeaway: SGLT2 inhibitors: genital infections, dehydration, rare Fournier gangrene and euglycemic DKA; hold before planned surgery.

stem: A client with type 2 diabetes is prescribed weekly semaglutide injections. Which finding in the client's history should the nurse report to the provider before the first dose?

options.text: A sister was treated for medullary thyroid carcinoma.
options.why: GLP-1 receptor agonists carry a boxed warning for thyroid C-cell tumors; a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN 2 is a contraindication.

options.text: The client had a cholecystectomy 10 years ago.
options.why: Gallbladder disease is a caution with GLP-1 agonists, but a gallbladder already removed is not a contraindication.

options.text: The client takes metformin 1,000 mg twice daily.
options.why: Semaglutide is commonly combined with metformin.

options.text: The client's BMI is 34 kg/m².
options.why: Obesity is not a contraindication; GLP-1 agonists also promote weight loss.

takeaway: GLP-1 agonists are contraindicated with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN 2.

stem: A client who started liraglutide 6 weeks ago calls the clinic. Which report requires the nurse to tell the client to stop the drug and seek care right away?

options.text: Mild nausea after meals that is slowly improving
options.why: Nausea is the most common side effect and usually lessens over weeks; it is not a reason for emergency care.

options.text: Feeling full sooner at meals and a 2-kg weight loss
options.why: Early fullness and weight loss are expected effects of slowed gastric emptying.

options.text: Severe, constant upper abdominal pain that spreads to the back, with vomiting
options.why: These are classic signs of acute pancreatitis, a serious adverse effect of GLP-1 receptor agonists; the drug is stopped and the client is evaluated urgently.

options.text: Redness at the injection site that faded within a day
options.why: Brief local reactions are minor and do not require stopping the drug.

takeaway: On a GLP-1 agonist, severe abdominal pain radiating to the back means possible pancreatitis: stop the drug and seek care.

stem: A client is scheduled for an upper endoscopy with sedation. During the preprocedure interview, which information is most important for the nurse to communicate to the anesthesia team?

options.text: The client takes a daily multivitamin.
options.why: A multivitamin has no meaningful effect on sedation or airway safety.

options.text: The client had a flu vaccine 2 weeks ago.
options.why: Recent vaccination does not affect sedation risk.

options.text: The client takes acetaminophen as needed for knee pain.
options.why: Occasional acetaminophen does not change procedural risk.

options.text: The client injects semaglutide once weekly for weight loss.
options.why: GLP-1 receptor agonists slow gastric emptying, so food may remain in the stomach despite fasting, which raises the risk of aspiration under sedation; the team decides how to manage it.

takeaway: GLP-1 agonists delay gastric emptying; always flag them before sedation or anesthesia because of aspiration risk.

stem: A client with type 2 diabetes is starting sitagliptin. Which statement by the client indicates the teaching was effective?

options.text: "This medicine rarely causes low blood sugar by itself, but it can if I also take a sulfonylurea or insulin."
options.why: DPP-4 inhibitors increase insulin release only when glucose is high, so hypoglycemia is uncommon unless combined with drugs that cause it.

options.text: "I need to inject this into my abdomen once a week."
options.why: Sitagliptin is an oral tablet taken once daily.

options.text: "I can stop it once my A1C is normal."
options.why: Diabetes medicines are continued unless the provider changes therapy; a normal A1C shows the regimen is working.

options.text: "Joint pain and stomach pain are normal with this drug, so I don't need to report them."
options.why: Severe joint pain and persistent severe abdominal pain (possible pancreatitis) are reported adverse effects of DPP-4 inhibitors.

takeaway: DPP-4 inhibitors (-gliptins): oral, daily, low hypoglycemia risk alone; report severe abdominal or joint pain.

stem: The nurse is teaching a client about taking levothyroxine. Which instructions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Take it with a full glass of water 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast.
options.why: Correct. Food reduces absorption, so it is taken on an empty stomach at the same time each day.

options.text: Take it with your calcium carbonate supplement so you remember both.
options.why: Incorrect. Calcium binds levothyroxine; separate them by at least 4 hours.

options.text: Take iron supplements at least 4 hours apart from levothyroxine.
options.why: Correct. Iron also binds levothyroxine and decreases its absorption.

options.text: Report a racing heart, chest pain, tremor or trouble sleeping.
options.why: Correct. These suggest too much thyroid hormone (iatrogenic hyperthyroidism).

options.text: Stop taking the medicine once your energy returns to normal.
options.why: Incorrect. Hypothyroidism usually needs lifelong replacement; feeling well means the dose is working.

options.text: Expect blood tests of TSH to check whether the dose is right.
options.why: Correct. TSH is checked about 6 to 8 weeks after a dose change to guide adjustment.

takeaway: Levothyroxine: empty stomach with water, same time daily, 4 hours from calcium or iron, lifelong, adjusted by TSH.

stem: A 77-year-old client with coronary artery disease starts levothyroxine 25 mcg daily for hypothyroidism. Which finding should the nurse report to the provider immediately?

options.text: Continued fatigue after 5 days of therapy
options.why: Thyroid replacement takes weeks to relieve symptoms, so fatigue after a few days is expected.

options.text: New chest pain when walking to the bathroom
options.why: Thyroid hormone increases heart rate and myocardial oxygen demand; new angina in an older client with heart disease suggests the dose is too much for the heart and must be reported.

options.text: Dry skin and mild constipation
options.why: These are symptoms of hypothyroidism that improve slowly as hormone levels rise.

options.text: Weight loss of 0.5 kg in the first week
options.why: Slight weight loss is expected as fluid and metabolism improve with treatment.

takeaway: Older adults and clients with heart disease start levothyroxine low and slow; report chest pain or palpitations at once.

stem: A client is prescribed levothyroxine 0.075 mg by mouth daily. The pharmacy supplies levothyroxine 25-mcg tablets. How many tablets should the nurse give?

options.text: 1 tablet
options.why: This assumes the tablet strength matches the dose; 25 mcg is only one-third of 75 mcg.

options.text: One-third of a tablet
options.why: This divides the tablet strength by the dose (25 ÷ 75) instead of the dose by the tablet strength.

options.text: 3 tablets
options.why: Convert first: 0.075 mg × 1,000 = 75 mcg. Desired ÷ have = 75 mcg ÷ 25 mcg = 3 tablets.

options.text: 30 tablets
options.why: This comes from a decimal error, treating the dose as 0.75 mg (750 mcg).

takeaway: Convert mg to mcg (× 1,000) before calculating; 0.075 mg = 75 mcg.

stem: A client who has taken methimazole for Graves disease for 6 weeks calls the clinic reporting a sore throat and a temperature of 101.6 °F (38.7 °C). What should the nurse instruct the client to do?

options.text: Hold the methimazole and come in today for a complete blood count with differential.
options.why: Fever and sore throat can signal agranulocytosis, a rare but life-threatening adverse effect of thionamides; the drug is held until the white cell count (normal neutrophils about 1,500 to 8,000/mm³) is checked.

options.text: Continue the methimazole and gargle with warm salt water.
options.why: Treating this as a simple sore throat could miss agranulocytosis and overwhelming infection.

options.text: Double the next methimazole dose to control the infection.
options.why: Methimazole does not treat infection, and a higher dose could worsen bone marrow suppression.

options.text: Take acetaminophen and call back if the fever lasts more than a week.
options.why: Waiting a week is unsafe; the client needs an urgent blood count.

takeaway: Fever or sore throat on methimazole or PTU: stop the drug and check a CBC for agranulocytosis.

stem: A client who is 7 weeks pregnant has newly diagnosed Graves disease that needs drug treatment. Which plan should the nurse expect?

options.text: Methimazole throughout the pregnancy
options.why: Methimazole is linked to birth defects when used in the first trimester, so it is avoided during early pregnancy.

options.text: Radioactive iodine therapy as soon as possible
options.why: Radioactive iodine is contraindicated in pregnancy because it destroys the fetal thyroid.

options.text: Levothyroxine alone to block thyroid hormone production
options.why: Levothyroxine replaces thyroid hormone; it does not treat hyperthyroidism.

options.text: Propylthiouracil during the first trimester, with a possible switch to methimazole afterward
options.why: PTU is preferred in the first trimester because methimazole can cause birth defects; because PTU can cause severe liver injury, many clients switch to methimazole after the first trimester.

takeaway: Hyperthyroidism in pregnancy: PTU in the first trimester (methimazole is teratogenic), then often methimazole (PTU is hepatotoxic).

stem: A client is taking propylthiouracil (PTU). Which findings should the nurse teach the client to report promptly? Select all that apply.

options.text: Yellowing of the skin or eyes
options.why: Correct. Jaundice may signal severe liver injury, a boxed warning for PTU.

options.text: Dark urine and pain in the right upper abdomen
options.why: Correct. These are also signs of drug-induced liver injury.

options.text: Fever with a sore throat or mouth sores
options.why: Correct. These suggest agranulocytosis and need an urgent blood count.

options.text: Heart rate gradually slowing from 112 to 86/min over several weeks
options.why: Incorrect. A slower heart rate shows hyperthyroidism is coming under control; it is an expected effect.

options.text: Easy bruising or unusual bleeding
options.why: Correct. Thionamides can suppress the bone marrow, including platelets.

options.text: Feeling less bothered by heat than before
options.why: Incorrect. Better heat tolerance is a sign the drug is working.

takeaway: PTU: report jaundice, dark urine, abdominal pain (liver injury) and fever, sore throat or bleeding (marrow suppression).

stem: A client in thyroid storm has a temperature of 104.4 °F (40.2 °C), heart rate 158/min and agitation. Which prescription should the nurse question?

options.text: Aspirin 650 mg by mouth for fever
options.why: Salicylates displace thyroid hormone from its binding proteins and raise free T4 and T3, which can worsen thyroid storm; acetaminophen and cooling measures are used instead.

options.text: Propranolol by mouth every 4 hours
options.why: Beta-blockers control the tachycardia, tremor and agitation caused by excess thyroid hormone.

options.text: Propylthiouracil by mouth now
options.why: PTU blocks new hormone synthesis and the conversion of T4 to T3, so it is a first-line drug in thyroid storm.

options.text: Hydrocortisone IV every 8 hours
options.why: Glucocorticoids reduce T4-to-T3 conversion and treat possible relative adrenal insufficiency in thyroid storm.

takeaway: In thyroid storm, treat fever with acetaminophen and cooling, never aspirin, which raises free thyroid hormone.

stem: A client with hyperthyroidism is going home after an oral dose of radioactive iodine (I-131). Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Sleep alone for the number of nights the nuclear medicine team specifies.
options.why: Correct. Keeping distance from others for the specified time limits their radiation exposure.

options.text: Avoid close contact with infants, young children and anyone who is pregnant for the specified time.
options.why: Correct. Children and fetuses are most sensitive to radiation.

options.text: Flush the toilet twice after each use and wash hands well.
options.why: Correct. Most of the radioactive iodine leaves the body in urine; extra flushing and handwashing reduce contamination.

options.text: Breastfeeding can continue as long as you pump and discard milk for 1 day.
options.why: Incorrect. Radioactive iodine concentrates in breast milk; breastfeeding must stop for this child, and the client follows the team's guidance about future feeding.

options.text: Use separate utensils and do not prepare food for others during the precaution period.
options.why: Correct. Saliva contains radioactive iodine, so sharing utensils and food can expose others.

options.text: Expect to be hypothyroid for life immediately after this dose.
options.why: Incorrect. Thyroid hormone levels fall over weeks to months; many clients do eventually need levothyroxine, so follow-up blood tests are needed.

takeaway: After radioactive iodine: distance (especially from children and pregnant people), sleep alone, double flush, no shared utensils, no breastfeeding.

stem: A client with long-standing untreated hypothyroidism is admitted with myxedema coma: temperature 93.6 °F (34.2 °C), BP 82/50 mm Hg, sodium 126 mEq/L, glucose 61 mg/dL. Adrenal function has not yet been tested. Which action should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Applying a heating blanket at the highest setting to raise temperature quickly
options.why: Rapid active warming causes vasodilation and can trigger cardiovascular collapse; passive rewarming with blankets is used.

options.text: Giving levothyroxine tablets through a nasogastric tube as the only treatment
options.why: Gut absorption is unreliable in myxedema coma, so levothyroxine is given IV, and steroid coverage is also needed.

options.text: Infusing 0.45% sodium chloride rapidly to correct hypotension
options.why: Hypotonic fluid would worsen the low sodium (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L).

options.text: Giving IV hydrocortisone before or with the first IV levothyroxine dose
options.why: Coexisting adrenal insufficiency is possible; thyroid hormone speeds cortisol use and can precipitate adrenal crisis, so stress-dose hydrocortisone is given until adrenal insufficiency is ruled out.

takeaway: Myxedema coma: IV levothyroxine plus IV hydrocortisone, passive rewarming, airway support and careful correction of sodium and glucose.

stem: A client with type 2 diabetes started prednisone 40 mg every morning for a COPD flare. Over 2 days, fasting glucose has been 108 to 118 mg/dL, while glucose at 1600 has been 274 to 296 mg/dL. Which interpretation should guide the nurse's plan?

options.text: The prednisone is not causing the hyperglycemia, because fasting glucose is normal.
options.why: Normal fasting values are typical with once-daily morning steroids; the effect wears off overnight.

options.text: The pattern is typical of morning glucocorticoid dosing, and insulin coverage should target afternoon and evening glucose.
options.why: A morning dose of prednisone raises glucose most in the afternoon and evening; regimens often add morning NPH or more mealtime insulin, then reduce it as the steroid is tapered.

options.text: Bedtime long-acting insulin should be increased to lower the afternoon readings.
options.why: Raising overnight basal insulin would mainly lower fasting glucose, which is already normal, and could cause nighttime hypoglycemia.

options.text: The prednisone should be stopped today to control the glucose.
options.why: The steroid is treating the COPD flare; hyperglycemia is managed with insulin, not by stopping needed therapy.

takeaway: Morning glucocorticoids cause afternoon and evening hyperglycemia; match insulin to that pattern and reduce it as the dose tapers.

stem: A client has taken prednisone 30 mg daily for 5 weeks for an autoimmune condition, and a tapering schedule has been prescribed. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "Since my symptoms are gone, I can stop the prednisone tomorrow."
options.why: Weeks of glucocorticoid therapy suppress the body's own cortisol production; stopping abruptly can cause adrenal insufficiency or crisis, so the taper must be followed.

options.text: "I'll take my dose in the morning with breakfast."
options.why: Morning dosing with food mimics the natural cortisol rhythm and reduces stomach upset.

options.text: "I should check my blood sugar if I feel very thirsty or urinate a lot."
options.why: Glucocorticoids raise blood glucose, so these symptoms are worth checking.

options.text: "I'll avoid people who are sick while I'm on this medicine."
options.why: Glucocorticoids suppress immunity, so reducing exposure to infection is appropriate.

takeaway: Never stop glucocorticoids abruptly after more than a few weeks of use; follow the taper.

stem: A client with primary adrenal insufficiency takes hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone daily. The nurse reviews what to do during illness. Which statement by the client indicates understanding?

options.text: "If I get the flu, I'll skip my hydrocortisone until I can eat normally again."
options.why: Missing glucocorticoid during illness is the classic trigger of adrenal crisis.

options.text: "I'll stop the fludrocortisone if I start running a fever."
options.why: Fludrocortisone is continued; illness does not mean it should be stopped.

options.text: "I only need extra hydrocortisone if I need surgery."
options.why: Fever, infection, vomiting and injury also increase cortisol needs, not just surgery.

options.text: "If I have a fever, I'll double or triple my hydrocortisone, and if I'm vomiting I'll use my emergency injection and get care."
options.why: Stress dosing during febrile illness and an injectable hydrocortisone kit for vomiting are the core sick-day rules that prevent adrenal crisis.

takeaway: Adrenal insufficiency sick-day rules: increase hydrocortisone (often 2 to 3 times) for fever, injection plus emergency care if vomiting.

stem: A client with Addison disease had the fludrocortisone dose increased 2 weeks ago. Which finding suggests the dose is now too high?

options.text: Weight gain of 2.5 kg in a week, ankle edema and BP 164/96 mm Hg
options.why: Fludrocortisone is a mineralocorticoid that retains sodium and water; weight gain, edema and hypertension indicate excess, often with low potassium.

options.text: Dizziness when standing and a craving for salty food
options.why: These suggest too little mineralocorticoid (volume depletion and sodium loss).

options.text: Serum potassium of 5.6 mEq/L
options.why: High potassium suggests too little mineralocorticoid effect; excess causes low potassium (normal 3.5 to 5 mEq/L).

options.text: Darkening of the skin creases and gums
options.why: Hyperpigmentation reflects high ACTH from inadequate glucocorticoid replacement, not fludrocortisone excess.

takeaway: Too much fludrocortisone: weight gain, edema, hypertension, low potassium. Too little: orthostatic dizziness, salt craving, high potassium.

stem: A client is being evaluated for Cushing syndrome. Which findings should the nurse expect? Select all that apply.

options.text: Fasting glucose of 168 mg/dL
options.why: Correct. Excess cortisol increases gluconeogenesis and insulin resistance, causing hyperglycemia.

options.text: Blood pressure of 158/98 mm Hg
options.why: Correct. Cortisol excess causes sodium and water retention and hypertension.

options.text: Serum potassium of 3.1 mEq/L
options.why: Correct. Excess cortisol has mineralocorticoid effects that cause potassium loss (normal 3.5 to 5 mEq/L).

options.text: Wide purple striae on the abdomen and easy bruising
options.why: Correct. Cortisol thins the skin and weakens connective tissue.

options.text: Blood pressure of 86/54 mm Hg
options.why: Incorrect. Hypotension is typical of adrenal insufficiency, not cortisol excess.

options.text: Serum potassium of 5.9 mEq/L
options.why: Incorrect. Hyperkalemia is seen with Addison disease (aldosterone deficiency), not Cushing syndrome.

takeaway: Cushing: high glucose, high BP, low potassium, purple striae, fragile skin. Addison is the mirror image.

stem: On the first day after removal of a cortisol-secreting adrenal adenoma, a client has BP 84/50 mm Hg, heart rate 120/min, glucose 63 mg/dL, nausea and severe weakness. The client's bleeding and drain output are minimal. Which prescription should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Increase the IV fluid rate and prepare to return the client to surgery
options.why: Fluids help, but minimal drain output and the lab pattern point to adrenal insufficiency rather than hemorrhage.

options.text: IV hydrocortisone
options.why: Long-term cortisol excess from the tumor suppressed the other adrenal gland; after removal the client cannot make enough cortisol, so hypotension and hypoglycemia need IV glucocorticoid replacement.

options.text: Subcutaneous insulin correction for the stress response
options.why: The client is hypoglycemic; insulin would be dangerous.

options.text: Oral spironolactone
options.why: A diuretic would worsen the hypotension and has no role here.

takeaway: After removing a cortisol-secreting tumor, the remaining adrenal is suppressed; watch for adrenal insufficiency and expect glucocorticoid replacement.

stem: A client with central diabetes insipidus started desmopressin. Which finding best indicates the medication is effective?

options.text: Serum sodium rising from 146 to 152 mEq/L
options.why: Rising sodium means continued free-water loss; the drug is not yet working (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L).

options.text: Urine specific gravity of 1.002
options.why: Very dilute urine is the hallmark of untreated diabetes insipidus.

options.text: Increased thirst and drinking 6 L/day
options.why: Polydipsia reflects ongoing water loss.

options.text: Urine output falling from 7 L/day to 2.2 L/day with urine specific gravity of 1.014
options.why: Desmopressin replaces ADH, so the kidneys reabsorb water; less urine that is more concentrated (normal specific gravity about 1.005 to 1.030) shows a therapeutic effect.

takeaway: Desmopressin works when urine output drops and urine specific gravity rises.

stem: A client taking desmopressin for diabetes insipidus reports a headache, nausea and confusion, and has gained 2 kg in 3 days. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Hold the next desmopressin dose and notify the provider for a stat serum sodium.
options.why: These findings suggest water intoxication and hyponatremia, the most serious adverse effect of desmopressin; the drug is held and sodium is checked urgently.

options.text: Encourage the client to drink more water for the headache.
options.why: More free water would worsen dilutional hyponatremia.

options.text: Give the next dose early, because these are signs of diabetes insipidus returning.
options.why: Diabetes insipidus causes weight loss and dehydration, not weight gain; another dose would worsen water retention.

options.text: Give acetaminophen and reassess in 4 hours.
options.why: Treating only the headache misses possible hyponatremia that can progress to seizures.

takeaway: Desmopressin can cause water retention and hyponatremia: watch for headache, nausea, confusion and weight gain.

stem: A client with SIADH after a head injury has a serum sodium of 123 mEq/L and concentrated urine. Which actions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Restrict fluid intake to the amount prescribed.
options.why: Correct. Fluid restriction is first-line treatment because excess ADH causes water retention.

options.text: Weigh the client daily on the same scale.
options.why: Correct. Daily weight tracks water retention and response to treatment.

options.text: Encourage at least 3 L of fluid daily.
options.why: Incorrect. Extra water would worsen dilutional hyponatremia.

options.text: Institute seizure precautions.
options.why: Correct. Low sodium (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L) causes cerebral edema and can lead to seizures.

options.text: Infuse 0.45% sodium chloride to maintain IV access.
options.why: Incorrect. Hypotonic fluid adds free water and lowers sodium further.

options.text: Monitor serum sodium and neurologic status closely.
options.why: Correct. Sodium must be corrected slowly while the nurse watches for worsening confusion or overly rapid correction.

takeaway: SIADH = too much water: restrict fluid, weigh daily, monitor sodium, seizure precautions, avoid hypotonic fluids.

stem: A hospitalized client with SIADH started tolvaptan. Serum sodium was 118 mEq/L before the first dose and is 131 mEq/L 18 hours later. The client is alert. What is the nurse's priority action?

options.text: Continue the current dose because the sodium is now close to normal.
options.why: The concern is the rate of rise, not the current value.

options.text: Restrict the client's fluids to 1 L/day to keep the sodium rising.
options.why: Fluid restriction is avoided during the first 24 hours of tolvaptan because it adds to the risk of overly rapid correction.

options.text: Hold the next dose and notify the provider immediately about the rapid rise in sodium.
options.why: A rise of 13 mEq/L in 18 hours exceeds safe limits (generally no more than 8 to 10 mEq/L in 24 hours for high-risk clients, and never more than 12); overly rapid correction can cause osmotic demyelination syndrome.

options.text: Give a 0.9% sodium chloride bolus to support the sodium level.
options.why: Additional sodium would push the correction even faster.

takeaway: With tolvaptan or any hyponatremia treatment, the danger is correcting too fast; report rises above the prescribed limit right away.

stem: A 12-year-old receiving daily somatropin (growth hormone) injections has a new limp and pain in the right knee. What is the nurse's best action?

options.text: Reassure the parent that growing pains are expected with growth hormone.
options.why: Dismissing a new limp could miss a serious complication.

options.text: Report the finding to the provider promptly for evaluation of the hip.
options.why: Growth hormone increases the risk of slipped capital femoral epiphysis, which often presents as knee or hip pain with a limp and needs prompt evaluation.

options.text: Increase the dose to support faster bone growth.
options.why: The nurse does not change doses, and more growth hormone would not help a possible slipped epiphysis.

options.text: Apply heat and encourage more running to loosen the joint.
options.why: Activity on a slipped epiphysis can worsen displacement.

takeaway: Children on growth hormone: report a limp or hip or knee pain (slipped capital femoral epiphysis), severe headaches or vision changes.

stem: A client is recovering after a transsphenoidal pituitary tumor resection. Which finding should the nurse report to the surgeon immediately?

options.text: Mild nasal stuffiness from the packing
options.why: Nasal congestion from packing is expected after this surgery.

options.text: Pain at the incision rated 3 out of 10
options.why: Mild pain is expected and is treated per the plan.

options.text: Mouth breathing because of nasal packing
options.why: With nasal packing, mouth breathing is expected; oral care keeps the mouth moist.

options.text: A constant clear, watery drip down the back of the throat
options.why: Persistent clear postnasal drainage suggests a cerebrospinal fluid leak, which raises the risk of meningitis; drainage that tests positive for glucose supports CSF.

takeaway: After transsphenoidal surgery, report clear nasal or postnasal drainage (possible CSF leak), and teach the client to avoid coughing, sneezing, blowing the nose and bending.

stem: A client with osteoporosis is prescribed immediate-release risedronate 35 mg once weekly. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Take the tablet first thing in the morning with 6 to 8 oz of plain water.
options.why: Correct. Food, coffee, juice and minerals sharply reduce absorption of oral bisphosphonates.

options.text: Stay sitting or standing upright for at least 30 minutes after the dose.
options.why: Correct. Staying upright keeps the tablet from irritating the esophagus.

options.text: Wait at least 30 minutes before eating or taking other medicines.
options.why: Correct. This allows absorption before food or other drugs interfere.

options.text: Take it with your calcium supplement to strengthen bones.
options.why: Incorrect. Calcium blocks absorption; take calcium later in the day.

options.text: Chew the tablet to help it dissolve faster.
options.why: Incorrect. The tablet is swallowed whole; chewing can cause mouth and throat ulcers.

options.text: Report new jaw pain or thigh or groin pain.
options.why: Correct. These may signal osteonecrosis of the jaw or an atypical femur fracture, rare but serious adverse effects.

takeaway: Oral bisphosphonates: morning, plain water, empty stomach, upright 30 minutes, nothing else for 30 minutes.

stem: A client with osteoporosis and chronic kidney disease is due for a denosumab injection. Which laboratory result should the nurse review before giving the dose?

options.text: Serum calcium
options.why: Denosumab can cause hypocalcemia, especially with kidney disease; low calcium (normal about 8.5 to 10.5 mg/dL) must be corrected before the dose.

options.text: Serum potassium
options.why: Potassium is not affected by denosumab.

options.text: Hemoglobin A1C
options.why: Glucose control has no bearing on denosumab safety.

options.text: Thyroid-stimulating hormone
options.why: TSH does not affect whether denosumab can be given safely.

takeaway: Check calcium before every denosumab dose; it is given every 6 months and should not be stopped without a follow-up plan, because of rebound fractures.

stem: Oral alendronate is prescribed for four clients with osteoporosis. For which client should the nurse question the prescription?

options.text: A 68-year-old woman with a hip T-score of −2.8
options.why: A T-score of −2.5 or lower confirms osteoporosis, which is the indication for the drug.

options.text: A 72-year-old man taking long-term prednisone for polymyalgia rheumatica
options.why: Glucocorticoid-induced bone loss is an indication for bisphosphonate therapy.

options.text: A 70-year-old woman with an esophageal stricture who has trouble swallowing pills
options.why: Esophageal abnormalities that delay emptying, such as stricture or achalasia, are contraindications because the tablet can lodge and cause severe esophagitis or ulcers.

options.text: A 65-year-old woman who takes calcium and vitamin D daily
options.why: Calcium and vitamin D are recommended with bisphosphonates, taken at a different time.

takeaway: Oral bisphosphonates are contraindicated with esophageal stricture or achalasia, inability to stay upright 30 minutes, and uncorrected hypocalcemia.

stem: A client with type 1 diabetes is NPO after midnight for surgery tomorrow. The admission prescription reads "Hold all insulin while NPO." The client usually takes insulin glargine 22 units at bedtime. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Hold the glargine as prescribed and check glucose in the morning.
options.why: A client with type 1 diabetes makes no insulin; with no basal insulin, ketoacidosis can develop within hours even without food.

options.text: Contact the provider to clarify the prescription, because a client with type 1 diabetes needs basal insulin even while NPO.
options.why: Basal insulin prevents ketosis and is continued (often at a reduced dose) before surgery; a blanket hold is unsafe and must be clarified.

options.text: Give the client's usual mealtime lispro at bedtime instead of the glargine.
options.why: Rapid-acting insulin without food causes hypoglycemia and does not provide basal coverage.

options.text: Give 4 oz of juice at bedtime so the full insulin dose can be given.
options.why: The client is NPO; giving juice violates the preoperative prescription and does not address the unsafe order.

takeaway: Type 1 diabetes always needs basal insulin, even when NPO; clarify any prescription to hold it entirely.

stem: A client in DKA weighs 176 lb. The prescription is regular insulin 0.1 units/kg/hour IV. The pharmacy sends regular insulin 100 units in 100 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride. At what rate in mL/hour should the nurse set the pump?

options.text: 0.8 mL/hour
options.why: This is off by a factor of 10; each mL contains 1 unit, so 8 units needs 8 mL.

options.text: 8 mL/hour
options.why: Convert weight: 176 lb ÷ 2.2 = 80 kg. Dose: 80 kg × 0.1 units/kg/hour = 8 units/hour. Concentration: 100 units ÷ 100 mL = 1 unit/mL. Rate: 8 units/hour ÷ 1 unit/mL = 8 mL/hour.

options.text: 17.6 mL/hour
options.why: This uses the weight in pounds (176 × 0.1) instead of converting to kilograms.

options.text: 80 mL/hour
options.why: This uses the weight in kilograms as the dose, dropping the 0.1 units/kg factor.

takeaway: Convert pounds to kilograms (÷ 2.2) before weight-based dosing, then divide the dose by the concentration.

stem: A client's IV insulin infusion contains regular insulin 50 units in 250 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride and is running at 15 mL/hour. How many units of insulin per hour is the client receiving?

options.text: 0.3 units/hour
options.why: This divides the rate by the units in the bag (15 ÷ 50) and ignores the bag volume.

options.text: 1.5 units/hour
options.why: This uses a concentration of 0.1 unit/mL, as if the bag held 500 mL.

options.text: 3 units/hour
options.why: Concentration: 50 units ÷ 250 mL = 0.2 units/mL. Dose: 0.2 units/mL × 15 mL/hour = 3 units/hour.

options.text: 7.5 units/hour
options.why: This uses a concentration of 0.5 units/mL, as if the bag held 100 mL.

takeaway: Units per hour = (units in bag ÷ mL in bag) × mL/hour.

stem: A client with type 1 diabetes plans to start jogging 3 mornings a week. Which statement by the client indicates the teaching was effective?

options.text: "I'll check my glucose before I run and carry glucose tablets with me."
options.why: Exercise increases glucose uptake and insulin sensitivity, so checking before activity and carrying fast-acting carbohydrate prevents and treats hypoglycemia.

options.text: "I'll inject my morning insulin into my thigh right before I run."
options.why: Exercising the injected limb speeds insulin absorption and raises the risk of hypoglycemia; the abdomen is preferred before running.

options.text: "If my glucose is over 300 mg/dL and I have ketones, I'll run to bring it down."
options.why: Exercise with ketosis can worsen hyperglycemia and ketoacidosis; the client should not exercise until ketones clear.

options.text: "Once I'm active, I won't need to worry about low glucose later in the day."
options.why: Hypoglycemia can occur hours after exercise, including overnight, as muscles restore glycogen.

takeaway: Before exercise on insulin: check glucose, carry fast-acting carbohydrate, avoid injecting the working limb, skip exercise with ketones.

stem: The nurse is teaching foot care to a client with diabetes and peripheral neuropathy. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I'll check my feet every day, using a mirror for the bottoms."
options.why: Daily inspection finds small injuries the client cannot feel because of neuropathy.

options.text: "I'll wear shoes or slippers, even inside the house."
options.why: Going barefoot risks unnoticed cuts and burns.

options.text: "I'll dry well between my toes after washing."
options.why: Moisture between the toes promotes fungal infection and skin breakdown.

options.text: "I'll soak my feet in hot water every night to help the circulation."
options.why: Soaking dries and macerates the skin, and reduced sensation means the client can be burned without feeling it; water temperature is checked with the hand or elbow and feet are washed, not soaked.

takeaway: Diabetic foot care: inspect daily, never go barefoot, dry between toes, check water temperature by hand, avoid soaking.

stem: A client is admitted with diabetic ketoacidosis. Initial potassium is 4.1 mEq/L. Place the treatment steps in the order the nurse should expect them to occur.

options.text: Add dextrose to the IV fluids when glucose falls to about 250 mg/dL.
options.why: Dextrose lets the insulin infusion continue clearing ketones without causing hypoglycemia.

options.text: Give subcutaneous basal insulin once the anion gap has closed and the client can eat.
options.why: Basal insulin is started before the drip is stopped so coverage overlaps.

options.text: Start an IV bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride.
options.why: Restoring circulating volume is the first treatment; it also lowers glucose and improves kidney perfusion.

options.text: Stop the IV insulin infusion 1 to 2 hours after the basal dose.
options.why: The overlap prevents a gap in insulin and rebound ketoacidosis.

options.text: Start the IV regular insulin infusion, with potassium added to fluids as needed.
options.why: Insulin is started after fluids are running and potassium is confirmed safe (here 4.1 mEq/L).

options.text: Confirm the potassium result is above the protocol threshold.
options.why: Insulin lowers potassium, so the level is confirmed before the infusion starts.

takeaway: DKA sequence: fluids, check potassium, insulin drip, add dextrose at about 250 mg/dL, basal insulin when the gap closes, then stop the drip 1 to 2 hours later.

stem: The nurse is teaching a client to use a prefilled insulin pen. Place the steps in the correct order.

options.text: Dial the prescribed dose.
options.why: The dose is selected after priming so the primed units are not counted as part of the dose.

options.text: Insert the needle into the skin and press the button until the dose window reads zero.
options.why: The full dose is delivered once the dose counter returns to zero.

options.text: Attach a new pen needle.
options.why: A new needle for each injection reduces infection risk, pain and needle blockage.
