options.text: Hold the needle in the skin for the count recommended by the manufacturer, then remove it.
options.why: Holding it in place (often about 6 to 10 seconds) prevents insulin from leaking back out.

options.text: Do a safety test by dispensing 2 units into the air and confirming insulin appears at the needle tip.
options.why: Priming removes air and confirms the pen and needle are working, so the full dose is delivered.

takeaway: Insulin pen: new needle, prime 2 units, dial dose, inject, hold for the labeled count, remove and dispose of the needle.

stem: Mariana, a 38-year-old client who smokes about one pack of cigarettes a day, asks the nurse to help her start a combined estrogen-progestin oral contraceptive. Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "A low-estrogen combined pill is safe for you as long as you take it at the same time every day."
options.why: Even low-dose estrogen pills are not recommended for people 35 or older who smoke; the dose does not remove the risk of heart attack and stroke.

options.text: "Because you are over 35 and smoke, a combined pill increases your risk of heart attack and stroke, so let's talk with your provider about progestin-only or nonhormonal options."
options.why: Correct. Smoking at age 35 or older is a contraindication to estrogen-containing contraception (CDC Medical Eligibility Criteria category 4 at 15 or more cigarettes a day), so the nurse should explain the risk and point her toward safer methods such as an IUD, implant, progestin-only pill or barrier methods.

options.text: "The combined pill is fine for you as long as your blood pressure is normal at today's visit."
options.why: A normal blood pressure does not cancel the arterial thrombosis risk that comes with estrogen use in smokers 35 and older.

options.text: "You can start the combined pill after you have stopped smoking for 1 week."
options.why: There is no 1-week rule; recent quitters still carry risk, and the decision about estrogen belongs with the provider after a full risk assessment.

takeaway: Estrogen-containing contraception is avoided in clients 35 or older who smoke because of the risk of myocardial infarction and stroke; offer progestin-only, IUD or barrier methods.

stem: A client taking a 28-day monophasic combined oral contraceptive (21 active pills, 7 placebo) calls on the morning of day 11 of her pack. She forgot her active pills on days 9 and 10 and has not had intercourse since finishing her last pack. Which instruction by the nurse is correct?

options.text: "Take both missed pills and today's pill right now, then continue the pack as usual."
options.why: Current CDC guidance is to take only the most recent missed pill as soon as possible and discard the other missed pill; taking three pills at once adds nausea without added protection.

options.text: "Throw away this pack and start a new pack tomorrow."
options.why: Restarting a pack is not needed for pills missed in the second week and wastes active pills; the client should simply resume the current pack.

options.text: "Take one missed pill now, take today's pill at the usual time, finish the pack, and use condoms or avoid sex until you have taken active pills for 7 days in a row."
options.why: Correct. When 2 or more consecutive active pills are missed, CDC recommends taking the most recent missed pill as soon as possible, continuing the rest of the pack at the usual time (even two in one day), and using backup contraception until 7 consecutive days of active pills have been taken.

options.text: "Because the pills were missed in the second week, you are still protected and do not need a backup method."
options.why: Missing 2 or more consecutive active pills at any point in the cycle reduces protection; backup contraception for 7 days is recommended.

takeaway: Two or more consecutive missed active pills: take the most recent missed pill now, continue the pack, and use backup for 7 days; if missed in the last week of active pills, skip the placebo week.

stem: A client who takes a combined oral contraceptive is starting rifampin for latent tuberculosis infection. Which instruction should the nurse include in the teaching?

options.text: "Rifampin can make your birth control pill less effective, so use another reliable method, such as condoms or an IUD, while you take rifampin and for as long afterward as your provider advises."
options.why: Correct. Rifampin strongly induces liver enzymes that metabolize estrogen and progestin, lowering hormone levels and contraceptive effectiveness; an alternative or additional method is needed during treatment and for a period after it stops.

options.text: "Take your pill at bedtime instead of in the morning so the two drugs do not interact."
options.why: Changing the time of day does not prevent enzyme induction, which lasts for the whole course of rifampin.

options.text: "Take two contraceptive pills each day while you are on rifampin."
options.why: Doubling the dose is not a recommended or reliable way to overcome enzyme induction and increases adverse effects.

options.text: "There is no interaction, but rifampin may turn your urine orange."
options.why: The orange discoloration of body fluids is true, but there is a clinically important interaction that can cause contraceptive failure.

takeaway: Rifampin (an enzyme inducer) lowers hormonal contraceptive levels; clients need a nonhormonal or IUD method during therapy and for a period afterward.

stem: The nurse teaches a client who has started norethindrone 0.35 mg daily (a progestin-only pill). Which statement by the client indicates that teaching was effective?

options.text: "I will take a pill for 21 days and then have a week off so I can have a period."
options.why: Progestin-only pills are taken every day continuously with no pill-free week; a break reduces protection.

options.text: "Because this pill contains a small amount of estrogen, I need to watch for leg pain."
options.why: Norethindrone-only pills contain no estrogen, which is why they are an option for clients who cannot take estrogen.

options.text: "If I miss a pill, I can wait and restart at the beginning of my next period."
options.why: Waiting leaves the client unprotected; she should take the pill as soon as she remembers and use backup contraception.

options.text: "I need to take it at the same time every day, and if I am more than 3 hours late, I should use condoms for the next 2 days."
options.why: Correct. Norethindrone progestin-only pills have a narrow window; a pill taken more than 3 hours late counts as missed, and backup contraception is advised for 2 days (48 hours).

takeaway: Norethindrone progestin-only pills are taken continuously at the same time daily; more than 3 hours late means backup for 48 hours.

stem: The nurse teaches a client about injectable medroxyprogesterone acetate for contraception. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I should get enough calcium and vitamin D and do weight-bearing exercise while I use this method."
options.why: This statement is correct. Depot medroxyprogesterone can reduce bone mineral density, so calcium, vitamin D and weight-bearing exercise are encouraged.

options.text: "I can come in for my shot whenever I remember, about twice a year."
options.why: This statement needs correction. The injection is repeated every 3 months (13 weeks); twice-yearly dosing would leave the client unprotected for months at a time.

options.text: "My periods may become irregular or stop altogether."
options.why: This statement is correct. Irregular bleeding and, with continued use, amenorrhea are common and expected effects.

options.text: "It may take several months or longer to get pregnant after I stop the shots."
options.why: This statement is correct. Return of fertility after depot medroxyprogesterone is often delayed, with a median of about 10 months after the last injection.

takeaway: Depot medroxyprogesterone is given every 3 months (13 weeks); teach about bone density, irregular bleeding and delayed return of fertility.

stem: The nurse is counseling a client who had unprotected intercourse 30 hours ago and asks about emergency contraception. Which statements by the nurse are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: "Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg works best when you take it as soon as possible after unprotected sex."
options.why: Correct. Levonorgestrel emergency contraception is most effective the sooner it is taken; it is labeled for use within 72 hours.

options.text: "You can buy levonorgestrel emergency contraception over the counter without a prescription."
options.why: Correct. Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg is available over the counter in the United States without an age restriction or prescription.

options.text: "Emergency contraception will end a pregnancy that has already implanted."
options.why: Incorrect. Emergency contraception works mainly by delaying ovulation; it does not interrupt an established pregnancy.

options.text: "A copper IUD placed within 5 days of unprotected sex is the most effective form of emergency contraception."
options.why: Correct. The copper IUD is the most effective emergency contraceptive and also provides ongoing contraception.

options.text: "After you take emergency contraception, you are protected for the rest of this cycle."
options.why: Incorrect. Emergency contraception does not protect against later acts of intercourse; the client should use or start a regular method and use condoms.

options.text: "Take a pregnancy test if your period is more than a week late."
options.why: Correct. A period delayed by more than 7 days after emergency contraception warrants a pregnancy test.

takeaway: Emergency contraception should be taken as soon as possible; the copper IUD is most effective, it does not end an established pregnancy, and it does not protect against later intercourse.

stem: The nurse reviews the health histories of clients who request a combined estrogen-progestin oral contraceptive. Which findings should the nurse report to the provider as contraindications to this method? Select all that apply.

options.text: Deep vein thrombosis 2 years ago
options.why: Correct. A history of venous thromboembolism is a contraindication because estrogen increases clotting risk.

options.text: Migraine headaches with visual aura
options.why: Correct. Migraine with aura carries an increased risk of ischemic stroke with estrogen and is a contraindication.

options.text: Painful menstrual cramps since adolescence
options.why: Incorrect. Primary dysmenorrhea is not a contraindication; combined pills often reduce menstrual pain.

options.text: Blood pressure of 168/102 mmHg on two readings
options.why: Correct. Hypertension at or above 160/100 mmHg is a contraindication to estrogen-containing contraception.

options.text: Moderate facial acne
options.why: Incorrect. Acne is not a contraindication; some combined pills are used to improve acne.

options.text: Age 36 years and has never smoked
options.why: Incorrect. Age over 35 alone, in a nonsmoker without other risks, is not a contraindication.

takeaway: Contraindications to estrogen-containing contraception include prior VTE, migraine with aura, BP 160/100 or higher, smoking at 35 or older and estrogen-sensitive cancers.

stem: A 54-year-old client with severe hot flashes is prescribed oral conjugated estrogens 0.625 mg daily. Her history shows no hysterectomy, and no other new medications were prescribed. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: Teach the client to take the tablet at bedtime to reduce night sweats.
options.why: Timing of the dose does not address the main safety problem with this prescription.

options.text: Confirm that the client had a mammogram within the past year and give the first dose.
options.why: Screening is appropriate, but giving the dose ignores the risk of unopposed estrogen in a client with a uterus.

options.text: Contact the provider to clarify whether a progestogen should be added because the client has a uterus.
options.why: Correct. Estrogen given without a progestogen to a client with an intact uterus causes endometrial hyperplasia and raises the risk of endometrial cancer, so a progestogen (or a combined product) is standard.

options.text: Tell the client the dose will probably be doubled because low doses rarely relieve hot flashes.
options.why: Current practice uses the lowest effective dose; there is no reason to anticipate doubling it.

takeaway: A client with a uterus who takes systemic estrogen needs a progestogen to protect the endometrium; question unopposed estrogen.

stem: A client started combined estrogen-progestin menopausal hormone therapy 1 month ago. Which report from the client requires the nurse's immediate follow-up?

options.text: Pain, warmth and swelling in the left calf
options.why: Correct. Unilateral calf pain and swelling suggest deep vein thrombosis, a serious risk of estrogen therapy that needs urgent evaluation.

options.text: Mild breast tenderness
options.why: Breast tenderness is a common, usually temporary adverse effect early in hormone therapy.

options.text: Some abdominal bloating
options.why: Bloating is a common, minor adverse effect that often improves with time.

options.text: Mild nausea after taking the tablet
options.why: Mild nausea is common and may improve by taking the dose with food.

takeaway: Teach clients on estrogen therapy to report signs of clots (calf pain/swelling, chest pain, dyspnea, neurologic changes) immediately.

stem: A client is diagnosed with trichomoniasis and prescribed metronidazole 500 mg orally twice daily for 7 days. Which statement by the client indicates that teaching was effective?

options.text: "I can stop taking the pills once the discharge goes away."
options.why: Stopping early risks treatment failure; the full 7-day course is needed even if symptoms resolve.

options.text: "My partner has no symptoms, so he does not need to be treated."
options.why: Most infected partners, especially men, have no symptoms; untreated partners commonly reinfect the client.

options.text: "After this treatment, I will be immune, so I will not need condoms."
options.why: Trichomoniasis does not produce immunity; reinfection is common, and condoms reduce the risk.

options.text: "My partner needs to be treated too, and we should not have sex until we have both finished treatment and have no symptoms."
options.why: Correct. Sex partners need treatment, and the couple should abstain until both have completed treatment and symptoms have resolved to prevent reinfection.

takeaway: Treat sex partners of clients with trichomoniasis and abstain until both are treated and symptom-free; women are retested in about 3 months because reinfection is common.

stem: A client at 20 weeks' gestation tests positive for chlamydia. The provider's prescription reads doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: Contact the provider to question the prescription, because azithromycin is the recommended treatment during pregnancy.
options.why: Correct. Doxycycline is avoided in the second and third trimesters because it can discolor fetal teeth and affect bone; CDC recommends azithromycin 1 g orally as a single dose for chlamydia in pregnancy.

options.text: Give the first dose with a full glass of water and teach the client to stay upright for 30 minutes.
options.why: This is correct technique for doxycycline, but the drug should not be given to this pregnant client.

options.text: Teach the client that her partner needs treatment only if he develops symptoms.
options.why: Partners should be evaluated and treated regardless of symptoms, because chlamydia is often asymptomatic.

options.text: Tell the client that no repeat testing is needed after she finishes treatment.
options.why: In pregnancy, a test of cure about 4 weeks after treatment and retesting within 3 months are recommended.

takeaway: Chlamydia in pregnancy is treated with azithromycin 1 g orally once; doxycycline is avoided in the second and third trimesters, and a test of cure is done about 4 weeks later.

stem: A nonpregnant 70-kg client is diagnosed with uncomplicated cervical gonorrhea, and chlamydia has not been ruled out. Which items should the nurse anticipate in the plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM as a single dose
options.why: Correct. CDC recommends a single 500-mg IM dose of ceftriaxone for uncomplicated gonorrhea in clients under 150 kg.

options.text: Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days
options.why: Correct. When chlamydial infection has not been excluded, doxycycline is added for a nonpregnant client.

options.text: Instructions to avoid sex for 7 days after treatment and until partners are treated
options.why: Correct. Abstaining prevents reinfection and further transmission.

options.text: Referral of sex partners from the past 60 days for evaluation and treatment
options.why: Correct. Partners from the 60 days before symptoms or diagnosis should be evaluated and treated.

options.text: Oral penicillin as an equally effective alternative
options.why: Incorrect. Gonorrhea is widely resistant to penicillin, and it is not a recommended treatment.

options.text: Routine test of cure 1 week after treatment for this cervical infection
options.why: Incorrect. A test of cure is recommended for pharyngeal gonorrhea; for urogenital infection, retesting is advised about 3 months after treatment.

takeaway: Uncomplicated gonorrhea: ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once, add doxycycline if chlamydia is not excluded, treat partners, abstain 7 days and retest at 3 months.

stem: Five hours after receiving benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM for secondary syphilis, a client reports chills, muscle aches and headache. Temperature is 101 °F (38.3 °C), blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, and lungs are clear with no hives or swelling. Which interpretation by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: The client is having anaphylaxis to penicillin and needs epinephrine.
options.why: Anaphylaxis typically presents within minutes with hypotension, wheezing, hives or swelling of the face and throat, none of which are present.

options.text: The treatment has failed, and a second dose of penicillin is needed today.
options.why: Fever after the first dose does not indicate treatment failure; response is judged later by falling nontreponemal titers.

options.text: This is likely a Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction, which is usually self-limited and treated with antipyretics and rest.
options.why: Correct. The Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction is an acute febrile reaction with headache and myalgia within 24 hours of starting syphilis treatment; it is managed supportively and is not a penicillin allergy.

options.text: This is serum sickness, and penicillin should be listed as an allergy.
options.why: Serum sickness develops days to weeks after exposure, with rash, joint pain and fever; this timing and picture fit a Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction.

takeaway: Fever, chills, headache and myalgia within 24 hours of starting syphilis treatment is usually a self-limited Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction, not penicillin allergy.

stem: A client at 16 weeks' gestation is diagnosed with syphilis. She reports a past anaphylactic reaction to penicillin. Which treatment plan should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 14 days
options.why: Doxycycline is avoided in pregnancy and does not reliably treat fetal infection.

options.text: Penicillin desensitization in a monitored setting, followed by benzathine penicillin G
options.why: Correct. Penicillin is the only treatment known to prevent congenital syphilis, so pregnant clients with penicillin allergy are desensitized and then treated with penicillin.

options.text: Azithromycin 2 g orally as a single dose
options.why: Azithromycin is not recommended for syphilis because of resistance and does not adequately treat the fetus.

options.text: Ceftriaxone daily for 10 days instead of penicillin
options.why: Alternatives such as ceftriaxone have not been shown to prevent congenital syphilis and are not recommended in pregnancy.

takeaway: Pregnant clients with syphilis and penicillin allergy are desensitized and treated with penicillin, the only proven way to prevent congenital syphilis.

stem: The nurse is preparing to give benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units to an adult client with primary syphilis. Which action is correct?

options.text: Dilute the suspension in 50 mL of normal saline and infuse it IV over 30 minutes.
options.why: Benzathine penicillin is a thick suspension; IV administration has caused cardiac arrest and death.

options.text: Give the dose IV push slowly over 5 minutes.
options.why: Any IV administration of benzathine penicillin G is dangerous and contraindicated.

options.text: Give the dose subcutaneously in the abdomen.
options.why: The suspension must reach a large muscle; subcutaneous injection is painful and does not provide the intended depot effect.

options.text: Inject it deep IM into a large muscle such as the ventrogluteal site and never give it IV.
options.why: Correct. Benzathine penicillin G is given only by deep IM injection into a large muscle; the label carries a warning against IV use because it can be fatal.

takeaway: Benzathine penicillin G is for deep IM injection only; never give it IV.

stem: The parent of a 10-year-old boy asks the nurse when his son should get the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine. Which response by the nurse is correct?

options.text: "Only after he becomes sexually active, because that is when the risk begins."
options.why: The vaccine works best when given before any exposure to HPV, so it is not delayed until sexual activity.

options.text: "The vaccine is recommended only for girls."
options.why: HPV vaccination is recommended for all adolescents, regardless of sex, to prevent HPV-related cancers and genital warts.

options.text: "It is routinely given at 11 to 12 years of age, and it can be started as early as age 9."
options.why: Correct. CDC recommends routine HPV vaccination at age 11 to 12, and the series may be started at age 9.

options.text: "It is given at age 18, when he can consent for himself."
options.why: Waiting until 18 delays protection and is not the routine schedule.

takeaway: HPV vaccine is routinely given at age 11 to 12 (can start at 9) to all adolescents, before exposure to the virus.

stem: The nurse teaches a pregnant client with iron-deficiency anemia about ferrous sulfate. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I'll take my iron pill with my morning glass of milk."
options.why: This statement needs correction. Calcium in milk, as well as antacids and tea, reduces iron absorption; iron is best taken apart from these.

options.text: "I'll take my iron pill with a glass of orange juice."
options.why: This statement is correct. Vitamin C increases iron absorption.

options.text: "My stools may turn dark green or black."
options.why: This statement is correct. Dark stools are an expected, harmless effect of oral iron.

options.text: "I'll eat more fiber and drink more fluids to help with constipation."
options.why: This statement is correct. Constipation is common with iron, and fiber and fluids help prevent it.

takeaway: Take oral iron with vitamin C, not with milk, antacids or tea; dark stools and constipation are expected.

stem: A client whose previous pregnancy was affected by a neural tube defect tells the nurse she would like to become pregnant again. Which recommendation should the nurse anticipate the provider will make?

options.text: Continue the 0.4 mg of folic acid in a standard prenatal vitamin, which is enough for everyone.
options.why: 0.4 mg is the dose for people at average risk; a prior affected pregnancy raises the risk and calls for a higher dose.

options.text: Take folic acid 4 mg daily, starting before conception and continuing through the first 12 weeks of pregnancy.
options.why: Correct. For a client with a previous pregnancy affected by a neural tube defect, a 4-mg daily dose is recommended, beginning at least 1 month (ACOG suggests 3 months) before conception and continuing through the first trimester.

options.text: Start folic acid as soon as a pregnancy test is positive.
options.why: The neural tube closes by about 4 weeks after conception, often before pregnancy is recognized, so supplementation must start before conception.

options.text: Rely on foods rich in folate instead of supplements.
options.why: Diet alone does not reliably provide the protective dose for a high-risk client.

takeaway: After a pregnancy affected by a neural tube defect, folic acid 4 mg daily is started before conception and continued through the first trimester.

stem: A pregnant client who has a 3-year-old child at home has started a prenatal vitamin that contains iron. Which instruction by the nurse is most important for the child's safety?

options.text: "Child-resistant caps make it safe to keep the bottle on the kitchen counter."
options.why: Child-resistant caps slow children down but do not make bottles childproof; storage out of reach is still required.

options.text: "Your child can have a gummy vitamin from your bottle as a treat."
options.why: Adult prenatal vitamins contain much more iron than children need, and treating vitamins like candy encourages ingestion.

options.text: "If your child swallows some pills, give syrup of ipecac to cause vomiting."
options.why: Syrup of ipecac is no longer recommended; the parent should call Poison Control or 911.

options.text: "Keep the vitamins locked up and out of reach, and call Poison Control right away if your child swallows any."
options.why: Correct. Iron is a leading cause of serious poisoning in young children; safe storage and immediately calling Poison Control (1-800-222-1222) are essential.

takeaway: Iron-containing vitamins are dangerous to young children; store them locked and out of reach and call Poison Control immediately after any ingestion.

stem: A client with preeclampsia with severe features is receiving magnesium sulfate at 2 g/hour. Which finding requires the nurse's immediate action?

options.text: The client says she feels warm and flushed.
options.why: Warmth and flushing are common, expected effects of magnesium sulfate.

options.text: Patellar reflexes are 2+ bilaterally.
options.why: 2+ reflexes are normal and suggest that magnesium is not at a toxic level.

options.text: Urine output totals 80 mL over the past 4 hours.
options.why: Correct. 80 mL over 4 hours is 20 mL/hour, below the minimum of 30 mL/hour. Magnesium is excreted by the kidneys, so oliguria can quickly lead to magnesium toxicity; the provider needs to know now.

options.text: The respiratory rate is 16/min.
options.why: A respiratory rate of 16/min is normal; a rate below 12/min would signal toxicity.

takeaway: During magnesium sulfate therapy, urine output below 30 mL/hour raises the risk of toxicity because magnesium is cleared by the kidneys.

stem: A client receiving magnesium sulfate for preeclampsia is difficult to arouse, has a respiratory rate of 9/min and absent patellar reflexes. Place the nurse's actions in order of priority.

options.text: Give calcium gluconate IV slowly as prescribed
options.why: Calcium gluconate (typically 1 g, 10 mL of a 10% solution) reverses magnesium effects at the neuromuscular junction once the provider prescribes it.

options.text: Stop the magnesium sulfate infusion
options.why: Stopping the source of toxicity comes first, because every minute of infusion raises the magnesium level further.

options.text: Notify the provider or call the rapid response team
options.why: After the infusion is stopped and breathing is supported, the nurse calls for help and obtains the antidote prescription.

options.text: Assess airway and breathing and support ventilation with oxygen
options.why: With a respiratory rate of 9/min, airway and breathing are the next priority after stopping the drug.

options.text: Draw a serum magnesium level and continue monitoring reflexes, respirations and fetal heart rate
options.why: Ongoing assessment and lab confirmation follow the emergency interventions.

takeaway: For magnesium toxicity: stop the infusion, support breathing, call for help, give calcium gluconate, then keep monitoring.

stem: A client with preeclampsia is prescribed a magnesium sulfate maintenance infusion of 2 g/hour. The premixed bag contains magnesium sulfate 40 g in 1,000 mL. At what rate in mL/hour should the nurse set the infusion pump? (Round to the nearest whole number.)

options.text: 50 mL/hour
options.why: Correct. Desired ÷ have × volume = 2 g ÷ 40 g × 1,000 mL = 50 mL/hour. (Concentration is 0.04 g/mL; 2 ÷ 0.04 = 50.)

options.text: 20 mL/hour
options.why: This rate would deliver only 0.8 g/hour (20 × 0.04 g/mL), less than half the prescribed dose.

options.text: 25 mL/hour
options.why: This rate would deliver 1 g/hour (25 × 0.04 g/mL), half the prescribed dose.

options.text: 80 mL/hour
options.why: This rate would deliver 3.2 g/hour (80 × 0.04 g/mL), an overdose that could cause toxicity.

takeaway: Magnesium sulfate 40 g/1,000 mL = 0.04 g/mL; 2 g/hour = 50 mL/hour. Always run magnesium on a pump.

stem: A client is prescribed magnesium sulfate 2 g/hour. During the bedside check, the nurse finds a bag labeled magnesium sulfate 20 g in 500 mL infusing on the pump at 75 mL/hour. How many grams per hour is the client receiving?

options.text: 1.5 g/hour
options.why: This would result from mistakenly using 0.02 g/mL; the concentration is 20 g ÷ 500 mL = 0.04 g/mL.

options.text: 3 g/hour
options.why: Correct. 20 g ÷ 500 mL = 0.04 g/mL; 0.04 g/mL × 75 mL/hour = 3 g/hour. This is 1.5 times the prescribed dose; the correct rate is 2 g ÷ 0.04 g/mL = 50 mL/hour, so the nurse should correct the rate per protocol, assess for toxicity and notify the provider.

options.text: 3.75 g/hour
options.why: This miscalculation multiplies 75 mL by 0.05 g/mL; the actual concentration is 0.04 g/mL.

options.text: 2 g/hour
options.why: The client would receive 2 g/hour only at 50 mL/hour; at 75 mL/hour the dose is higher.

takeaway: Check high-alert infusions at the bedside by calculating dose from concentration × rate: 0.04 g/mL × 75 mL/hour = 3 g/hour.

stem: An oxytocin infusion is prepared as 30 units in 500 mL of lactated Ringer's solution. The prescription is to infuse oxytocin at 6 milliunits/minute. At what rate in mL/hour should the nurse set the pump?

options.text: 3 mL/hour
options.why: This rate would deliver only 3 milliunits/minute (3 mL/hour × 60 milliunits/mL ÷ 60 minutes).

options.text: 12 mL/hour
options.why: This rate would deliver 12 milliunits/minute, twice the prescribed dose.

options.text: 0.1 mL/hour
options.why: This answer results from converting minutes to hours incorrectly and would deliver almost no drug.

options.text: 6 mL/hour
options.why: Correct. 30 units = 30,000 milliunits ÷ 500 mL = 60 milliunits/mL. 6 milliunits/minute × 60 minutes = 360 milliunits/hour ÷ 60 milliunits/mL = 6 mL/hour.

takeaway: With oxytocin 30 units/500 mL (60 milliunits/mL), the rate in mL/hour equals the dose in milliunits/minute.

stem: A client has received an oxytocin infusion for 18 hours for induction of labor. She now reports a headache and nausea, appears confused, and her urine output has decreased. Which laboratory result should the nurse check first?

options.text: Serum magnesium
options.why: The client is not receiving magnesium sulfate, so magnesium toxicity is not the likely cause.

options.text: Serum sodium
options.why: Correct. Oxytocin has an antidiuretic effect, and prolonged high-dose infusion can cause water intoxication with dilutional hyponatremia, producing headache, nausea, confusion and decreased urine output that can progress to seizures.

options.text: Platelet count
options.why: Platelets matter for bleeding and HELLP syndrome, but these symptoms point to fluid and sodium imbalance from oxytocin.

options.text: Serum glucose
options.why: Glucose abnormalities can cause confusion, but the combination with decreased urine output after prolonged oxytocin points to water intoxication.

takeaway: Prolonged oxytocin can cause water intoxication (hyponatremia): watch for headache, confusion, nausea and decreased urine output and check serum sodium.

stem: The nurse reviews the records of clients scheduled for oxytocin induction of labor. Which findings should the nurse report to the provider because they contraindicate induction? Select all that apply.

options.text: Complete placenta previa
options.why: Correct. Placenta previa contraindicates vaginal birth and therefore labor induction.

options.text: Transverse fetal lie
options.why: Correct. A transverse lie cannot deliver vaginally, so inducing labor is contraindicated.

options.text: Previous classical (vertical) uterine incision
options.why: Correct. A classical incision carries a high risk of uterine rupture during labor, so induction is contraindicated.

options.text: 41 weeks' gestation with a reassuring fetal heart rate tracing
options.why: Incorrect. Late-term pregnancy is a common indication for induction, not a contraindication.

options.text: Active genital herpes lesion
options.why: Correct. Active genital herpes is an indication for cesarean birth, so vaginal labor should not be induced.

options.text: Prelabor rupture of membranes at 39 weeks
options.why: Incorrect. Term prelabor rupture of membranes is a common indication for oxytocin induction.

takeaway: Oxytocin induction is contraindicated whenever vaginal birth is: placenta previa, transverse lie, prior classical incision, active genital herpes.

stem: A client is bleeding heavily 30 minutes after birth from uterine atony. She has HIV infection controlled with darunavir and ritonavir, and her blood pressure is 118/72 mmHg. The provider prescribes methylergonovine 0.2 mg IM. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Give the dose because the client's blood pressure is normal.
options.why: A normal blood pressure removes one contraindication, but the drug interaction remains.

options.text: Give the dose IV push undiluted so it works faster.
options.why: Methylergonovine is not routinely given IV because of the risk of sudden hypertension and stroke, and the interaction remains.

options.text: Withhold the dose and contact the provider because ritonavir can dangerously increase methylergonovine levels.
options.why: Correct. Methylergonovine has a boxed warning against use with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors such as ritonavir, because raised levels can cause severe vasospasm and ischemia (ergotism). Another uterotonic should be used.

options.text: Give the dose and hold the client's antiretroviral medications for 24 hours.
options.why: Stopping antiretrovirals does not quickly remove the enzyme inhibition and risks HIV treatment failure.

takeaway: Methylergonovine is contraindicated with hypertension and with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (such as ritonavir) because of the risk of severe vasoconstriction.

stem: Fifteen minutes after receiving carboprost tromethamine 250 mcg IM for postpartum hemorrhage, a client has the following findings. Which finding requires the nurse's immediate action?

options.text: Wheezing with an oxygen saturation of 90%
options.why: Correct. Carboprost, a prostaglandin F2-alpha analog, can cause bronchospasm; wheezing with low oxygen saturation is a potentially life-threatening reaction.

options.text: Temperature of 100.2 °F (37.9 °C)
options.why: A mild temperature elevation is a common, expected effect of carboprost.

options.text: Two loose stools
options.why: Diarrhea is one of the most common adverse effects of carboprost.

options.text: Nausea without vomiting
options.why: Nausea and vomiting are common with carboprost and are managed with antiemetics.

takeaway: Carboprost commonly causes diarrhea, nausea and fever, but it can trigger bronchospasm; it is avoided in clients with asthma.

stem: A client at 40 weeks' gestation with one previous low transverse cesarean birth is admitted for induction of labor. The prescription is misoprostol 25 mcg vaginally for cervical ripening. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: Insert the misoprostol and monitor contractions and fetal heart rate for 4 hours.
options.why: This monitoring would be appropriate for a client without a uterine scar, but misoprostol should not be given here.

options.text: Start oxytocin first and insert the misoprostol 1 hour later.
options.why: Misoprostol and oxytocin are not used close together; oxytocin is generally started at least 4 hours after the last misoprostol dose, and misoprostol is not appropriate for this client.

options.text: Give the misoprostol orally instead of vaginally.
options.why: Changing the route does not remove the risk; any route of misoprostol for third-trimester ripening is avoided after cesarean birth.

options.text: Hold the dose and contact the provider because misoprostol raises the risk of uterine rupture after a cesarean birth.
options.why: Correct. Prostaglandins such as misoprostol are not used for cervical ripening in the third trimester in clients with a prior cesarean or major uterine surgery because of the increased risk of uterine rupture.

takeaway: Do not use misoprostol for third-trimester cervical ripening in a client with a uterine scar; the risk of uterine rupture is increased.

stem: A client at 31 weeks' gestation in preterm labor received terbutaline 0.25 mg subcutaneously. Before the next prescribed dose, her heart rate is 132/min and she reports palpitations and chest tightness. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Give the dose because tachycardia is an expected effect.
options.why: Some increase in heart rate is expected, but a rate above 120/min with chest tightness signals cardiotoxicity and is a reason to hold the drug.

options.text: Withhold the dose and notify the provider.
options.why: Correct. Terbutaline, a beta-2 agonist, can cause tachycardia, arrhythmias, myocardial ischemia and pulmonary edema. Maternal heart rate above 120/min or chest pain means the dose should be held and reported. The FDA also warns against injectable terbutaline beyond 48 to 72 hours.

options.text: Give the dose with a prescribed beta blocker.
options.why: Giving a beta blocker would defeat the drug's purpose and is not standard management; the dose should be held.

options.text: Increase the IV fluid rate and then give the dose.
options.why: Extra IV fluid can worsen the risk of pulmonary edema with beta agonists and does not address the cardiac symptoms.

takeaway: Hold terbutaline and notify the provider if maternal heart rate exceeds 120/min or chest pain, dyspnea or arrhythmia occurs.

stem: A client in preterm labor is prescribed oral nifedipine for tocolysis. Which assessment is most important before each dose?

options.text: Deep tendon reflexes
options.why: Reflexes are monitored with magnesium sulfate, not nifedipine.

options.text: Capillary blood glucose
options.why: Glucose is a concern with terbutaline and corticosteroids, not with nifedipine.

options.text: Maternal blood pressure
options.why: Correct. Nifedipine is a calcium channel blocker that causes vasodilation; hypotension (with headache, flushing and reflex tachycardia) is the main adverse effect, which can also reduce placental perfusion.

options.text: Hourly urine output
options.why: Urine output is critical with magnesium sulfate because of renal excretion; it is not the main concern with nifedipine.

takeaway: Check blood pressure before each dose of nifedipine for tocolysis; hypotension is its key adverse effect.

stem: A client at 32 weeks' gestation with gestational diabetes managed with insulin is admitted in preterm labor and receives betamethasone 12 mg IM. Which change in the plan of care should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: More frequent capillary glucose checks and possible insulin dose increases for several days
options.why: Correct. Corticosteroids raise maternal blood glucose for several days after dosing, so clients with diabetes need closer glucose monitoring and often more insulin.

options.text: Holding insulin for 24 hours because betamethasone lowers blood glucose
options.why: Betamethasone raises, not lowers, blood glucose; holding insulin could cause marked hyperglycemia.

options.text: Amniocentesis to confirm fetal lung maturity before the second dose
options.why: Lung maturity testing is not done before antenatal corticosteroids; the second dose is given 24 hours after the first.

options.text: Stopping betamethasone because it is contraindicated in diabetes
options.why: Diabetes is not a contraindication; the fetal lung benefit at 32 weeks outweighs the temporary hyperglycemia.

takeaway: Antenatal betamethasone causes transient maternal hyperglycemia; increase glucose monitoring and adjust insulin in clients with diabetes.

stem: The nurse teaches a client at 30 weeks' gestation in preterm labor about betamethasone. Which statement by the client indicates understanding?

options.text: "This shot will stop my contractions."
options.why: Betamethasone does not stop contractions; tocolytics are used for that.

options.text: "I will get one of these shots every day until the baby is born."
options.why: The standard course is two doses 24 hours apart, not daily injections until birth.

options.text: "This medicine treats an infection in my uterus."
options.why: Betamethasone is a corticosteroid, not an antibiotic.

options.text: "I will get a second shot in 24 hours, and it helps my baby's lungs mature."
options.why: Correct. Betamethasone 12 mg IM is given in two doses 24 hours apart to speed fetal lung maturity and reduce respiratory distress syndrome, intraventricular hemorrhage and death in preterm newborns.

takeaway: Betamethasone 12 mg IM × 2 doses, 24 hours apart, speeds fetal lung maturity; it does not stop labor.

stem: The nurse cares for clients who are Rh(D)-negative and have a negative antibody screen. In which situations should the nurse anticipate giving Rho(D) immune globulin? Select all that apply.

options.text: Amniocentesis at 16 weeks' gestation
options.why: Correct. Invasive procedures can allow fetal blood into the maternal circulation, so Rho(D) immune globulin is given.

options.text: External cephalic version at 37 weeks' gestation
options.why: Correct. Manipulating the fetus can cause fetal-maternal hemorrhage, so prophylaxis is indicated.

options.text: Abdominal trauma from a motor vehicle crash at 30 weeks' gestation
options.why: Correct. Abdominal trauma can cause fetal-maternal bleeding; Rho(D) immune globulin is given, with the dose guided by testing for fetal cells.

options.text: Birth of a newborn whose blood type is Rh(D)-negative
options.why: Incorrect. An Rh-negative newborn's blood cannot sensitize the mother, so it is not needed.

options.text: A client whose antibody screen now shows anti-D antibodies from a prior pregnancy
options.why: Incorrect. A client who is already sensitized will not benefit; the pregnancy is instead monitored for fetal anemia.

options.text: Birth of an Rh(D)-positive newborn 24 hours ago
options.why: Correct. Rho(D) immune globulin is given within 72 hours after birth of an Rh-positive newborn to an unsensitized mother.

takeaway: Give Rho(D) immune globulin to unsensitized Rh-negative clients after events that can mix fetal and maternal blood and within 72 hours after birth of an Rh-positive newborn.

stem: An Rh(D)-negative client gave birth 6 hours ago. Place the nurse's steps for giving postpartum Rho(D) immune globulin in the correct order.

options.text: Give Rho(D) immune globulin IM to the mother
options.why: The injection is given to the mother, not the newborn, after the earlier checks confirm it is indicated.

options.text: Confirm the newborn's cord blood is Rh(D)-positive
options.why: The newborn's Rh type is checked first, because the drug is needed only if the newborn is Rh-positive.

options.text: Confirm the mother's antibody screen (indirect Coombs) is negative
options.why: Next, the nurse confirms the mother is not already sensitized; if she is, the drug will not help.

options.text: Verify the prescription, product and the client's identity at the bedside
options.why: Once it is indicated, standard medication and blood-product checks are done right before giving it.

options.text: Document the dose and give the client a card noting she received it
options.why: Documentation and a record for the client come last; future providers will need this information.

takeaway: Postpartum Rho(D) immune globulin: newborn Rh-positive, mother unsensitized, verify, give IM to the mother within 72 hours, then document.

stem: A client who is positive for group B Streptococcus (GBS) is admitted at 39 weeks' gestation in active labor and receives IV penicillin G. The nurse tells the newborn care team that intrapartum prophylaxis was adequate. Which condition must be met for this to be accurate?

options.text: The first dose was given at least 1 hour before birth.
options.why: One hour is not enough time for adequate antibiotic levels in the fetus and amniotic fluid.

options.text: The first dose of penicillin was given at least 4 hours before birth.
options.why: Correct. GBS prophylaxis is considered adequate when penicillin, ampicillin or cefazolin is given at least 4 hours before birth.

options.text: At least two doses of penicillin were completed before birth.
options.why: Adequacy is defined by the time since the first dose (at least 4 hours), not by a set number of doses.

options.text: The membranes stayed intact until the antibiotic was started.
options.why: Membrane status does not define adequacy; the 4-hour interval does.

takeaway: GBS prophylaxis is adequate when penicillin, ampicillin or cefazolin is started at least 4 hours before birth.

stem: A client in labor is GBS-positive and has a documented history of anaphylaxis to penicillin. Her GBS isolate is susceptible to clindamycin. Which intrapartum prophylaxis should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Cefazolin IV
options.why: Cefazolin is used for penicillin allergy with a low risk of anaphylaxis; after anaphylaxis, a cephalosporin is avoided because of cross-reactivity concerns.

options.text: Ampicillin IV
options.why: Ampicillin is a penicillin and is contraindicated after anaphylaxis to penicillin.

options.text: Clindamycin IV
options.why: Correct. For clients at high risk of anaphylaxis, clindamycin is used if the isolate is susceptible; vancomycin is used if it is resistant or susceptibility is unknown.

options.text: No antibiotic, because the allergy prevents prophylaxis
options.why: GBS prophylaxis is still needed; alternative antibiotics are chosen based on allergy risk and susceptibility testing.

takeaway: GBS prophylaxis with high-risk penicillin allergy: clindamycin if the isolate is susceptible, otherwise vancomycin; cefazolin is for low-risk allergy.

stem: The nurse is giving routine medications to a healthy term newborn shortly after birth. Which actions are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Inject vitamin K (phytonadione) IM into the vastus lateralis.
options.why: Correct. The vastus lateralis is the recommended IM site for newborns, and IM vitamin K prevents vitamin K deficiency bleeding.

options.text: Apply erythromycin ointment in a ribbon along the lower conjunctival sac of each eye, from inner to outer canthus.
options.why: Correct. This is the correct technique for neonatal ocular prophylaxis.

options.text: Delay eye prophylaxis briefly so skin-to-skin contact and the first breastfeeding can happen during the first hour.
options.why: Correct. Eye ointment can be briefly delayed (generally within the first hour) to support bonding and early breastfeeding without losing effectiveness.

options.text: Rinse the eyes with sterile water after applying the ointment.
options.why: Incorrect. Flushing removes the medication; excess may be gently wiped away after about a minute.

options.text: Give vitamin K in the dorsogluteal muscle.
options.why: Incorrect. The dorsogluteal muscle is underdeveloped in newborns and close to the sciatic nerve.

options.text: Give vitamin K orally because it is the preferred route.
options.why: Incorrect. The AAP recommends a single IM dose; oral dosing is less effective at preventing late vitamin K deficiency bleeding.

takeaway: Newborn vitamin K is given IM in the vastus lateralis; erythromycin eye ointment goes in each lower conjunctival sac, inner to outer, and is not rinsed out.

stem: A parent asks why erythromycin ointment is being put in the newborn's eyes. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "It helps prevent a serious eye infection from gonorrhea that a baby can be exposed to during birth."
options.why: Correct. Erythromycin ophthalmic ointment is given to prevent gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum, which can cause blindness.

options.text: "It helps prevent newborn jaundice."
options.why: Eye ointment has no effect on bilirubin levels.

options.text: "It prevents chlamydia pneumonia in the baby."
options.why: Eye prophylaxis does not reliably prevent chlamydial eye infection or pneumonia; these are prevented by screening and treating the pregnant client.

options.text: "It keeps the baby's eyes moist during the first days of life."
options.why: The ointment is an antibiotic given to prevent infection, not a lubricant.

takeaway: Erythromycin eye ointment is given to newborns to prevent gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum.

stem: The nurse is giving vitamin K IM to a newborn who has not yet been bathed. Place the steps in the correct order.

options.text: Inject the medication at a 90-degree angle into the vastus lateralis
options.why: The injection is given after the site is prepared and dry.

options.text: Verify the prescription and identify the newborn by matching identification bands
options.why: Verifying the order and the newborn's identity comes first, as with any medication.

options.text: Perform hand hygiene and put on clean gloves
options.why: Gloves are needed because the unbathed newborn has blood and amniotic fluid on the skin.

options.text: Clean the anterolateral thigh with alcohol and let it dry
options.why: Site preparation comes right before the injection; letting the alcohol dry reduces stinging.

options.text: Apply gentle pressure to the site and document the dose
options.why: Pressure and documentation follow the injection.

takeaway: Newborn IM injection: identify, hand hygiene and gloves, clean the vastus lateralis site, inject at 90 degrees, then apply pressure and document.

stem: A term newborn weighing 3,300 g is born to a client who had no prenatal care. The mother's hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) result is pending. Which plan should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Wait for the mother's result before giving any hepatitis B products.
options.why: Waiting risks missing the 12-hour window for vaccine, which is critical if the mother turns out to be infected.

options.text: Give hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) now and hold the vaccine until the mother's result is known.
options.why: Vaccine is the key protection and should not be delayed; HBIG alone is not the plan for a newborn of 2,000 g or more with unknown maternal status.

options.text: Hold all hepatitis B products and advise the mother not to breastfeed.
options.why: Breastfeeding is not contraindicated with maternal hepatitis B, and withholding prophylaxis puts the newborn at risk.

options.text: Give hepatitis B vaccine within 12 hours of birth, and give HBIG by 7 days of age if the mother tests HBsAg-positive.
options.why: Correct. For newborns weighing 2,000 g or more whose mother's HBsAg status is unknown, CDC recommends hepatitis B vaccine within 12 hours of birth, prompt maternal testing, and HBIG no later than 7 days of age if the mother is positive.

takeaway: Newborn of 2,000 g or more with unknown maternal HBsAg: vaccine within 12 hours, test the mother, and give HBIG by day 7 if she is positive.

stem: A client who is breastfeeding has these prescriptions on postpartum day 2. Which prescription should the nurse question?

options.text: Ibuprofen 600 mg orally every 6 hours as needed for pain
options.why: Ibuprofen passes into breast milk in very small amounts and is considered compatible with breastfeeding.

options.text: Acetaminophen 300 mg with codeine 30 mg, 1 tablet orally every 4 hours as needed for pain
options.why: Correct. The FDA warns against codeine (and tramadol) during breastfeeding; mothers who are ultra-rapid metabolizers turn codeine into high levels of morphine, which can cause sedation and respiratory depression in the infant.

options.text: Docusate sodium 100 mg orally twice daily
options.why: Docusate is minimally absorbed and is compatible with breastfeeding.

options.text: Prenatal vitamin 1 tablet orally daily
options.why: Continuing a prenatal vitamin is commonly recommended during lactation.

takeaway: Avoid codeine and tramadol in breastfeeding clients because of infant respiratory depression; ibuprofen and acetaminophen are preferred.

stem: A client who is exclusively breastfeeding is 2 weeks postpartum and asks to start a combined estrogen-progestin pill. Which response by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: "Breastfeeding prevents pregnancy for a full year, so you do not need contraception yet."
options.why: Lactational amenorrhea is reliable only for up to 6 months, with exclusive breastfeeding and no return of periods; it is not protective for a year.

options.text: "Combined pills are the best choice right now because they do not affect your milk."
options.why: Estrogen can reduce milk supply, and early postpartum estrogen increases clot risk.

options.text: "Estrogen can lower your milk supply and increases clot risk soon after birth, so progestin-only methods or an IUD are usually recommended now."
options.why: Correct. Estrogen-containing methods are avoided in the first 3 weeks after birth because of venous thromboembolism risk and generally deferred during early breastfeeding; progestin-only methods and IUDs do not affect milk supply.

options.text: "You will not need birth control until your period returns."
options.why: Ovulation can occur before the first period, so pregnancy is possible before menstruation resumes.

takeaway: Early postpartum and during breastfeeding, choose progestin-only methods or IUDs; estrogen reduces milk supply and raises clot risk soon after birth.

stem: The nurse teaches a client with benign prostatic hyperplasia who is starting tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily. Which statement by the client indicates that teaching was effective?

options.text: "I will get up slowly, especially after the first few doses, and take it about 30 minutes after the same meal each day."
options.why: Correct. Tamsulosin, an alpha-1 blocker, can cause orthostatic hypotension and dizziness, mainly early in therapy, and it is taken about 30 minutes after the same meal daily.

options.text: "If the capsule is hard to swallow, I can open it and sprinkle it on food."
options.why: Tamsulosin capsules must be swallowed whole; they should not be crushed, chewed or opened.

options.text: "This medicine will shrink my prostate over the next 6 months."
options.why: Tamsulosin relaxes smooth muscle in the prostate and bladder neck; shrinking the gland is the action of 5-alpha reductase inhibitors such as finasteride.

options.text: "I do not need to mention this medicine before my cataract surgery."
options.why: Alpha-1 blockers can cause intraoperative floppy iris syndrome, so the eye surgeon must be told.

takeaway: Tamsulosin: rise slowly (orthostatic hypotension), take 30 minutes after the same meal, swallow whole, and tell the eye surgeon before cataract surgery.

stem: The nurse teaches a 66-year-old client with benign prostatic hyperplasia who is prescribed finasteride 5 mg daily. Which statements should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: "Anyone who is pregnant or may become pregnant should not handle crushed or broken tablets."
options.why: Correct. Finasteride can be absorbed through the skin and may cause abnormal genital development in a male fetus.

options.text: "It may take 6 months or longer before you notice improvement."
options.why: Correct. Finasteride shrinks the prostate slowly; benefit may take 6 to 12 months.

options.text: "This medicine lowers your PSA level, so tell any provider who orders a PSA test that you take it."
options.why: Correct. Finasteride lowers PSA by about 50%, which affects how results must be interpreted for prostate cancer screening.

options.text: "Stop taking it if your symptoms are not better in 1 week."
options.why: Incorrect. One week is far too soon to judge the effect of finasteride.

options.text: "Your urine will turn orange while you take this medicine."
options.why: Incorrect. Orange urine is an effect of phenazopyridine or rifampin, not finasteride.

options.text: "You may notice decreased sex drive or less ejaculate."
options.why: Correct. Sexual adverse effects such as decreased libido, erectile dysfunction and reduced ejaculate volume can occur.

takeaway: Finasteride: pregnant people should not handle broken tablets, effects take months, PSA is lowered by about half, and sexual adverse effects may occur.

stem: A client with stable angina who takes isosorbide mononitrate daily asks the nurse whether he can use sildenafil for erectile dysfunction. Which response is correct?

options.text: "You can take them safely if you space them 2 hours apart."
options.why: Spacing doses by a couple of hours does not prevent the interaction; both drugs remain active much longer than that.

options.text: "You can take half a tablet of sildenafil to avoid problems."
options.why: A lower dose does not make sildenafil safe with nitrates.

options.text: "Long-acting nitrates like yours do not interact with sildenafil."
options.why: All nitrates, including long-acting forms, interact with PDE5 inhibitors.

options.text: "Taking sildenafil with your nitrate can cause a dangerous drop in blood pressure, so they should not be used together; discuss other options with your provider."
options.why: Correct. PDE5 inhibitors and nitrates both increase nitric oxide-mediated vasodilation, and together they can cause severe, life-threatening hypotension; the combination is contraindicated.

takeaway: PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil) are contraindicated with any nitrate because of severe hypotension.

stem: A 61-year-old client arrives at the emergency department with chest pain. While the nurse prepares sublingual nitroglycerin per protocol, the client says he took tadalafil for erectile dysfunction 30 hours ago. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Give the nitroglycerin, because more than 24 hours have passed since the tadalafil dose.
options.why: The 24-hour interval applies to sildenafil and vardenafil; tadalafil lasts longer, so 30 hours is not enough.

options.text: Withhold the nitroglycerin and report the tadalafil use to the provider immediately.
options.why: Correct. Because tadalafil has a long half-life, nitrates should be avoided for at least 48 hours after a dose. The provider needs to know right away to choose other anti-ischemic treatment.

options.text: Give half the usual nitroglycerin dose and recheck the blood pressure in 5 minutes.
options.why: A reduced nitrate dose can still cause profound hypotension with tadalafil on board.

options.text: Give the nitroglycerin and place the client flat if the blood pressure drops.
options.why: Waiting to treat hypotension after giving a contraindicated drug is unsafe; the nitrate should not be given.

takeaway: Avoid nitrates within 24 hours of sildenafil or vardenafil and within 48 hours of tadalafil.

stem: A client who takes doxazosin for benign prostatic hyperplasia is starting sildenafil for erectile dysfunction. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: "Get emergency care if an erection lasts longer than 4 hours."
options.why: Correct. Priapism is an emergency; without prompt treatment it can permanently damage penile tissue.

options.text: "Rise slowly from sitting or lying, because doxazosin and sildenafil together can lower your blood pressure."
options.why: Correct. Alpha blockers and PDE5 inhibitors both lower blood pressure, so the combination can cause symptomatic orthostatic hypotension; therapy is started at a low sildenafil dose once the alpha-blocker dose is stable.

options.text: "Stop the medicine and seek care right away if you have sudden loss of vision or hearing."
options.why: Correct. Sudden vision loss (possible optic neuropathy) or sudden hearing loss are rare but serious adverse effects.

options.text: "If the first dose does not work within an hour, take a second dose."
options.why: Incorrect. Sildenafil should be taken no more than once a day.

options.text: "The medicine will cause an erection even without sexual stimulation."
options.why: Incorrect. PDE5 inhibitors enhance the response to sexual stimulation; they do not cause an erection on their own.

takeaway: Teach PDE5 inhibitor users: once daily maximum, seek care for an erection lasting more than 4 hours or sudden vision or hearing loss, and use caution with alpha blockers.

stem: A client has received testosterone cypionate injections for hypogonadism for 6 months. Which laboratory result should the nurse report to the provider?

options.text: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) 1.2 ng/mL
options.why: This PSA is in the normal range for the client's age and is not a concern by itself.

options.text: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 30 units/L
options.why: ALT of about 7 to 56 units/L is normal.

options.text: Hematocrit 56%
options.why: Correct. Testosterone stimulates red cell production; a hematocrit above 54% (normal adult male about 41% to 50%) increases the risk of clots and stroke and usually leads to holding or reducing therapy.

options.text: Total testosterone 550 ng/dL
options.why: This value is within the usual target range (about 300 to 1,000 ng/dL) and shows therapy is working.

takeaway: Monitor hematocrit in clients on testosterone; levels above 54% call for holding or adjusting therapy.

stem: The nurse teaches a client how to apply testosterone gel each morning. Place the steps in the correct order.

options.text: Cover the application site with a shirt
options.why: Clothing over the dried site prevents transfer of testosterone to other people.

options.text: Wash hands thoroughly with soap and water
options.why: Washing hands right after applying the gel removes drug that could be passed to others by touch.

options.text: Apply the prescribed dose to clean, dry, intact skin of the shoulders and upper arms
options.why: Application to clean, intact skin at the labeled site comes first.

options.text: Allow the gel to dry completely
options.why: The gel must dry before clothing is put on so it is absorbed and not rubbed off.

options.text: Before any expected skin-to-skin contact later, wash the application site with soap and water
options.why: Washing the site before close contact reduces secondary exposure of partners and children.

takeaway: Testosterone gel: apply to clean shoulders or upper arms, wash hands, let it dry, cover with clothing, and wash the site before skin-to-skin contact.

stem: A 3-year-old girl is brought to the clinic with new pubic hair, enlargement of the clitoris and rapid growth over the past 4 months. Which finding from the family history is most significant?

options.text: Her father applies testosterone gel daily and dresses her each morning.
options.why: Correct. Secondary exposure to topical testosterone through skin contact can cause virilization in children (FDA boxed warning). Children's symptoms usually improve once exposure stops.

options.text: She drinks two cups of soy milk each day.
options.why: Normal dietary soy intake has not been shown to cause virilization.

options.text: She uses a pea-sized amount of fluoride toothpaste twice daily.
options.why: Fluoride toothpaste in the recommended amount does not affect sexual development.

options.text: She completed a 10-day course of amoxicillin last month.
options.why: Amoxicillin does not cause signs of androgen excess.

takeaway: Children can be virilized by skin contact with a caregiver's testosterone gel; ask about topical hormone use in the home.

stem: A client with acute cystitis is prescribed an antibiotic and phenazopyridine 200 mg three times daily. Which statement by the client indicates that teaching was effective?

options.text: "Since this medicine treats the infection, I can skip the antibiotic once I feel better."
options.why: Phenazopyridine is only a urinary analgesic and has no antibacterial effect; the full antibiotic course is still needed.

options.text: "My contact lenses will not be affected by this medicine."
options.why: Phenazopyridine can permanently stain soft contact lenses.

options.text: "If my skin or eyes turn yellow, that is a normal effect."
options.why: Yellowing of the skin or sclera may mean the drug is accumulating or causing liver injury or hemolysis and should be reported.

options.text: "My urine will turn reddish-orange, and I will take this for only 2 days along with my antibiotic."
options.why: Correct. Phenazopyridine colors urine reddish-orange and is limited to 2 days when used with an antibiotic for a UTI.

takeaway: Phenazopyridine relieves urinary pain but does not treat infection; urine turns orange, it can stain contacts, and use is limited to 2 days with an antibiotic.

stem: The nurse teaches a 58-year-old client starting oxybutynin for overactive bladder. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Chew sugar-free gum or suck sugar-free candy for dry mouth.
options.why: Correct. Dry mouth is a common anticholinergic effect; sugar-free products ease it without promoting tooth decay.

options.text: Increase fluids and fiber to prevent constipation.
options.why: Correct. Anticholinergics slow intestinal movement and cause constipation.

options.text: Avoid strenuous activity in hot weather, because the medicine reduces sweating.
options.why: Correct. Decreased sweating raises the risk of overheating and heat stroke.

options.text: Report difficulty starting the urine stream or feeling unable to empty the bladder.
options.why: Correct. Anticholinergics can cause urinary retention, especially in older men with prostate enlargement.

options.text: New confusion or forgetfulness is harmless and does not need to be reported.
options.why: Incorrect. Confusion and memory impairment are central anticholinergic adverse effects, most common in older adults, and should be reported.

options.text: Take an extra dose if you have leakage during the day.
options.why: Incorrect. Extra doses increase anticholinergic toxicity; the drug is taken only as prescribed.

takeaway: Oxybutynin causes anticholinergic effects: dry mouth, constipation, heat intolerance, urinary retention and confusion in older adults.

stem: A client is prescribed oxybutynin for urge incontinence. Which finding in the client's history should the nurse report to the provider before the first dose?

options.text: Hypertension controlled with lisinopril
options.why: Well-controlled hypertension is not a contraindication to oxybutynin.

options.text: Uncontrolled narrow-angle (angle-closure) glaucoma
options.why: Correct. Anticholinergics dilate the pupil and can precipitate an acute rise in eye pressure in angle-closure glaucoma; uncontrolled narrow-angle glaucoma is a contraindication.

options.text: Osteoarthritis of both knees
options.why: Osteoarthritis does not interact with oxybutynin.

options.text: Hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine
options.why: Treated hypothyroidism is not a contraindication to oxybutynin.

takeaway: Anticholinergic bladder drugs are contraindicated in uncontrolled narrow-angle glaucoma, urinary retention and gastric retention.

stem: A client with nonobstructive urinary retention after surgery is prescribed bethanechol 25 mg orally three times daily. Which finding in the client's history should prompt the nurse to contact the provider?

options.text: Type 2 diabetes managed with metformin
options.why: Diabetes is not a contraindication to bethanechol.

options.text: Osteoarthritis of the hips
options.why: Osteoarthritis has no relevant interaction with bethanechol.

options.text: Asthma with use of an inhaler several times a week
options.why: Correct. Bethanechol is a cholinergic (muscarinic) agonist that can cause bronchoconstriction, so asthma is a contraindication. Atropine is the antidote for cholinergic toxicity.

options.text: Seasonal allergic rhinitis
options.why: Allergic rhinitis is not a contraindication to bethanechol.

takeaway: Bethanechol (cholinergic) is contraindicated in asthma, bradycardia, hypotension, peptic ulcer and mechanical GI or urinary obstruction; atropine is the antidote.

stem: A client with cystitis is prescribed nitrofurantoin. Which instruction by the nurse is correct?

options.text: "Take each dose with food or milk, expect your urine may turn brown, and report a new cough or shortness of breath."
options.why: Correct. Food improves absorption and reduces nausea, harmless brown discoloration of urine is common, and nitrofurantoin can cause acute or chronic pulmonary reactions that must be reported.

options.text: "Take it on an empty stomach with an antacid to prevent nausea."
options.why: Nitrofurantoin is taken with food; magnesium-containing antacids can reduce its absorption.

options.text: "Stop the medicine once your burning goes away after the first day."
options.why: The full prescribed course is needed to clear the infection and prevent relapse.

options.text: "If your urine turns brown, stop the medicine because it means kidney damage."
options.why: Brown urine is an expected, harmless effect of nitrofurantoin.

takeaway: Nitrofurantoin: take with food, brown urine is harmless, finish the course, and report pulmonary symptoms.

stem: A client receiving hemodialysis is prescribed sevelamer carbonate. Which instruction should the nurse give about when to take it?

options.text: Take it at bedtime.
options.why: At bedtime there is little dietary phosphate in the gut for the drug to bind.

options.text: Take it 2 hours after each meal.
options.why: By 2 hours after a meal, much of the dietary phosphate has already been absorbed.

options.text: Take it on an empty stomach first thing in the morning.
options.why: Taken without food, the binder has no dietary phosphate to bind.

options.text: Take it with each meal.
options.why: Correct. Phosphate binders work in the gut by binding phosphate in food, so they are taken with meals.

takeaway: Phosphate binders such as sevelamer and calcium acetate are taken with meals to bind dietary phosphate.

stem: A client with end-stage kidney disease on hemodialysis has been taking calcium acetate for 2 months. Which finding best indicates that the medication is effective?

options.text: Serum calcium increased from 9 to 11.2 mg/dL
options.why: A calcium of 11.2 mg/dL is above normal (about 8.5 to 10.5 mg/dL) and suggests hypercalcemia, an adverse effect of calcium-based binders.

options.text: Serum phosphorus decreased from 7.4 to 4.2 mg/dL
options.why: Correct. Calcium acetate binds dietary phosphate; a drop in phosphorus into the normal range (about 2.5 to 4.5 mg/dL) shows it is working.

options.text: Serum potassium decreased from 5.8 to 4.9 mEq/L
options.why: Potassium is controlled by diet and dialysis, not by phosphate binders.

options.text: Hemoglobin increased from 9 to 10.5 g/dL
options.why: Hemoglobin reflects anemia treatment such as epoetin and iron, not phosphate binding.

takeaway: Phosphate binder effectiveness is measured by falling serum phosphorus; watch calcium-based binders for hypercalcemia.

stem: The nurse is about to give epoetin alfa to a client with chronic kidney disease. Which finding should the nurse report to the provider before giving the dose?

options.text: Hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL
options.why: This hemoglobin is below 10 g/dL in CKD and is the kind of value for which epoetin is given.

options.text: Serum ferritin 300 ng/mL and transferrin saturation 30%
options.why: These values show adequate iron stores, which epoetin needs to work.

options.text: Blood pressure 188/106 mmHg
options.why: Correct. Epoetin can raise blood pressure, and uncontrolled hypertension is a contraindication; the provider should be notified before giving it.

options.text: Serum potassium 4.8 mEq/L
options.why: This potassium is within normal limits (about 3.5 to 5 mEq/L).

takeaway: Check blood pressure and hemoglobin before giving epoetin; uncontrolled hypertension is a contraindication.

stem: The nurse is developing a plan of care for a client with chronic kidney disease on hemodialysis who is starting epoetin alfa. Which interventions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Monitor blood pressure regularly.
options.why: Correct. Hypertension is a common adverse effect of erythropoiesis-stimulating agents.

options.text: Monitor hemoglobin and notify the provider if it rises above 11 g/dL.
options.why: Correct. For clients with CKD on dialysis, FDA labeling advises reducing or interrupting the dose when hemoglobin approaches or exceeds 11 g/dL (10 g/dL for clients not on dialysis), because higher levels increase the risk of death, myocardial infarction, stroke and thrombosis.

options.text: Assess iron studies and give iron supplements as prescribed.
options.why: Correct. Red cell production needs adequate iron, and most clients on epoetin need iron supplementation.

options.text: Expect hemoglobin to return to normal within 24 hours of the first dose.
options.why: Incorrect. Hemoglobin rises gradually, usually over 2 to 6 weeks.

options.text: Aim for a hemoglobin of 14 to 15 g/dL to relieve fatigue.
options.why: Incorrect. Targeting normal hemoglobin increases cardiovascular events and death in CKD.

options.text: Teach the client to report chest pain, leg swelling or new neurologic symptoms.
options.why: Correct. These may signal thrombosis, myocardial infarction or stroke, which are serious risks of epoetin.

takeaway: Epoetin in CKD: monitor BP, keep hemoglobin no higher than 11 g/dL, ensure adequate iron, and watch for thrombotic events.

stem: A 62-year-old client is receiving a phenytoin IV loading dose for recurrent seizures. Ten minutes into the infusion, the client's blood pressure falls from 128/76 to 86/50 mmHg and the heart rate drops from 84 to 50/min. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Stop the phenytoin infusion and notify the provider.
options.why: Hypotension and bradycardia during IV phenytoin are signs of cardiovascular toxicity, usually from infusing too fast; stopping the infusion is the immediate safety action before the provider decides how to resume at a slower rate.

options.text: Increase the infusion rate so the loading dose finishes sooner.
options.why: A faster rate is exactly what causes phenytoin-related hypotension and dysrhythmias; this would worsen the problem.

options.text: Flush the line with dextrose 5% in water.
options.why: Phenytoin precipitates in dextrose solutions and must only be flushed with 0.9% sodium chloride; flushing also does not address the hemodynamic change.

options.text: Recheck the blood pressure in 30 minutes.
options.why: Waiting while the drug continues to infuse delays treatment of a potentially fatal cardiac effect.

takeaway: IV phenytoin can cause hypotension, bradycardia and dysrhythmias when given too fast (adult maximum 50 mg/min); stop the infusion and notify the provider if they develop.

stem: A client with a seizure disorder has a serum phenytoin level of 26 mcg/mL and new horizontal nystagmus when looking to the side. The next scheduled dose is due now. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give the dose because nystagmus is an expected long-term effect.
options.why: Nystagmus is an early sign of phenytoin toxicity, not a benign effect, and the level is above the therapeutic range.

options.text: Withhold the dose and notify the provider of the level and the nystagmus.
options.why: The therapeutic range for total phenytoin is 10 to 20 mcg/mL; a level of 26 mcg/mL with nystagmus indicates toxicity, so the dose is held and the provider is notified.

options.text: Give half of the scheduled dose.
options.why: Nurses do not independently change the dose; the provider must decide on dose adjustment.

options.text: Give the dose with food to slow absorption.
options.why: Food does not meaningfully reduce the toxicity of a dose given to a client whose level is already high.

takeaway: Therapeutic phenytoin is 10 to 20 mcg/mL; nystagmus is the earliest sign of toxicity, followed by ataxia, slurred speech and confusion.

stem: A 34-year-old client with schizophrenia who has taken clozapine for 8 months says, "I've gained 20 pounds on this pill. I hate how I look, so I'm going to stop taking it." Which response by the nurse is most therapeutic?

options.text: "Clozapine is the only drug that has worked for you, so you have to keep taking it."
options.why: This dismisses the client's feelings and uses pressure rather than collaboration; it is likely to damage trust and adherence.

options.text: "Why are you more worried about your weight than about your symptoms coming back?"
options.why: "Why" questions put the client on the defensive and minimize a real concern.

options.text: "The weight gain has been really upsetting for you. Let's talk about it and about what options you could discuss with your prescriber."
options.why: This reflects the client's feelings, keeps communication open and supports shared decision making, including diet, activity and medication options, while avoiding an abrupt stop.

options.text: "Lots of people gain weight on clozapine. It's nothing to worry about."
options.why: False reassurance dismisses the concern; weight gain on clozapine is a real metabolic risk that needs attention.

takeaway: When a client wants to stop a psychiatric drug because of side effects, acknowledge the feeling, explore it and involve the prescriber; never argue, threaten or falsely reassure.

stem: The nurse is giving a phenytoin IV push dose to an adult client through a peripheral IV line in which dextrose 5% in water is infusing. Place the nurse's actions in the correct order.

options.text: Inject phenytoin slowly, no faster than 50 mg/min.
options.why: The drug is given only after the line is cleared of dextrose, and the rate limit prevents hypotension and dysrhythmias.

options.text: Attach a cardiac monitor, record a baseline blood pressure and confirm the IV is in a large vein, is patent and has a blood return.
options.why: Baseline rhythm and blood pressure let the nurse detect changes during the injection, and a patent, well-placed IV is needed because phenytoin is highly alkaline and can cause extravasation injury such as purple glove syndrome; both are done before the line is flushed.

options.text: Flush the line with 0.9% sodium chloride.
