stem: A client with cirrhosis and hepatic encephalopathy receives lactulose 30 mL orally every 6 hours, titrated to 2 to 3 soft stools daily. Over the past 24 hours, the client has had 8 large watery stools. The client is more confused than yesterday, and serum sodium is 151 mEq/L. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Give the next dose as scheduled because more stools will lower the ammonia faster.
options.why: Excessive diarrhea causes dehydration and hypernatremia, which can themselves worsen encephalopathy; more is not better.

options.text: Hold the next lactulose dose and notify the provider of the stool count and sodium level.
options.why: Correct. The goal is 2 to 3 soft stools a day. Eight watery stools with a sodium above normal (135–145 mEq/L) signal overtreatment and dehydration, which can worsen confusion; the dose needs adjustment and fluid replacement.

options.text: Give loperamide as needed to slow the stools while continuing the lactulose.
options.why: Combining an antidiarrheal with a laxative works against the treatment goal, and the provider must decide on dose changes.

options.text: Restrict oral fluids to reduce the volume of stool.
options.why: Restricting fluid would worsen the dehydration and hypernatremia.

takeaway: Lactulose is titrated to 2–3 soft stools a day; excessive diarrhea causes dehydration and high sodium that can worsen encephalopathy.

stem: A client with hepatic encephalopathy has a prescription for lactulose 20 g orally three times daily. The pharmacy supplies lactulose oral solution 10 g/15 mL. How many mL should the nurse give per dose?

options.text: 15 mL
options.why: 15 mL contains only 10 g, which is half the prescribed dose.

options.text: 20 mL
options.why: This treats the 20 g dose as if it were 20 mL; the concentration is 10 g per 15 mL, not 1 g per mL.

options.text: 30 mL
options.why: Correct. Desired ÷ have × volume = 20 g ÷ 10 g × 15 mL = 30 mL.

options.text: 45 mL
options.why: 45 mL contains 30 g, which is 1.5 times the prescribed dose.

takeaway: Always convert using the labeled concentration: lactulose 10 g/15 mL, so 20 g = 30 mL.

stem: A client being treated with oral vancomycin for Clostridioides difficile infection has 6 loose stools a day and asks for loperamide "to stop the diarrhea." What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "I'll give you loperamide now since you're on an antibiotic for the infection."
options.why: Loperamide is avoided in C. difficile infection because slowing the bowel keeps toxin in contact with the colon and can contribute to toxic megacolon.

options.text: "Loperamide can make this infection worse by trapping the toxin in your bowel. Let's focus on fluids, and I'll tell the provider how often you're going."
options.why: Correct. Antimotility drugs are generally avoided in C. difficile and other invasive or bloody diarrheas. The nurse supports hydration and reports stool frequency so the provider can evaluate response to treatment.

options.text: "You can take loperamide, but only if your stools become bloody."
options.why: Bloody diarrhea is a stronger reason to avoid antimotility drugs, not an indication for them.

options.text: "Diphenoxylate with atropine would be safer for you than loperamide."
options.why: Diphenoxylate is also an antimotility agent with the same risk in C. difficile infection.

takeaway: Avoid antimotility agents such as loperamide in C. difficile or bloody, febrile diarrhea; they can worsen toxin injury.

stem: Fatima Haddad, 32, has ulcerative colitis and is starting sulfasalazine. Which instructions should the nurse include in her teaching? Select all that apply.

options.text: Take each dose after a meal with a full glass of water.
options.why: Correct. Taking sulfasalazine after food reduces nausea and GI upset, and water helps prevent crystals forming in the urine.

options.text: Your urine or skin may turn orange-yellow; this is harmless.
options.why: Correct. Sulfasalazine commonly colors urine and skin orange-yellow and may stain soft contact lenses.

options.text: Report a sore throat, fever, unusual bruising or pallor.
options.why: Correct. Sulfasalazine can cause bone marrow suppression (agranulocytosis), so signs of infection or bleeding need prompt evaluation and CBCs are monitored.

options.text: Take the folic acid supplement your provider prescribed.
options.why: Correct. Sulfasalazine interferes with folate absorption, so folic acid supplementation is commonly prescribed.

options.text: Limit your fluid intake to reduce diarrhea.
options.why: Incorrect. Generous fluid intake is encouraged to prevent crystalluria and dehydration.

options.text: Stop the drug if your urine changes color.
options.why: Incorrect. Orange-yellow urine is an expected, harmless effect and is not a reason to stop therapy.

takeaway: Sulfasalazine: take after meals with water, expect orange-yellow urine, supplement folic acid, and report signs of infection or bleeding.

stem: Marcus Bell, 27, with Crohn disease is scheduled for his first infusion of infliximab. The nurse reviews his pre-treatment results. Which finding must the nurse report to the provider before the infusion begins?

options.text: Hemoglobin 12.9 g/dL
options.why: This is close to normal (about 13.5–17.5 g/dL for men), with mild anemia common in Crohn disease; it does not prevent infliximab therapy.

options.text: C-reactive protein elevated at 3.2 mg/dL
options.why: An elevated CRP reflects active inflammation, which is the reason for treatment, not a contraindication.

options.text: Positive interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) for tuberculosis
options.why: Correct. Tumor necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitors such as infliximab carry a boxed warning for reactivation of latent TB. A positive IGRA requires evaluation and usually latent TB treatment before the biologic starts.

options.text: Albumin 3.3 g/dL
options.why: Mildly low albumin (normal about 3.5–5 g/dL) is common with Crohn disease malnutrition and is not a reason to hold the infusion.

takeaway: Screen for latent TB (and hepatitis B) before any TNF inhibitor; a positive result must be addressed before the first dose.

stem: The nurse teaches the parent of a 9-year-old with cystic fibrosis about pancrelipase capsules. Which statement by the parent indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "If she can't swallow the capsule, I'll open it and sprinkle the beads on a spoonful of applesauce."
options.why: This is correct: the enteric-coated beads may be mixed with a small amount of acidic soft food and swallowed without chewing.

options.text: "I'll give the capsules at bedtime so they work while she sleeps."
options.why: This needs correction. Pancreatic enzymes must be taken at the start of every meal and snack so they mix with food; a bedtime dose without food does nothing for digestion.

options.text: "She should not crush or chew the beads."
options.why: This is correct: crushing or chewing destroys the enteric coating, inactivating the enzymes in stomach acid and irritating the mouth.

options.text: "Fewer greasy, foul-smelling stools will tell me the dose is working."
options.why: This is correct: less steatorrhea and better weight gain show that the enzymes are improving fat absorption.

takeaway: Pancrelipase is taken with the first bite of every meal and snack, swallowed whole or sprinkled on acidic soft food, never crushed.

stem: A client with cirrhosis is admitted with bleeding esophageal varices. Prescriptions include octreotide infusion, IV pantoprazole and IV ceftriaxone 1 g daily. The client has no fever and a normal white blood cell count. The client's spouse asks why an antibiotic is needed. Which explanation by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: "It treats an infection that caused the varices to rupture."
options.why: Varices rupture from portal hypertension, not from infection; the antibiotic is preventive.

options.text: "It is given to prevent serious infections, which are common after variceal bleeding in cirrhosis and increase the risk of rebleeding."
options.why: Correct. Short-term antibiotic prophylaxis is standard in cirrhosis with GI bleeding because it reduces bacterial infections (including spontaneous bacterial peritonitis), rebleeding and death, even without signs of infection.

options.text: "It lowers the pressure in the portal vein to slow the bleeding."
options.why: Octreotide, not ceftriaxone, reduces splanchnic blood flow and portal pressure.

options.text: "It reduces ammonia-producing bacteria to prevent confusion."
options.why: That is the role of rifaximin or lactulose in hepatic encephalopathy, not ceftriaxone in acute variceal bleeding.

takeaway: Cirrhosis with GI bleeding: give prophylactic antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone) plus vasoactive therapy such as octreotide; antibiotics reduce infection, rebleeding and death.

stem: Leon Fischer, 59, has cirrhosis with ascites and is being discharged on spironolactone and furosemide. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Weigh yourself every morning and report a gain of more than 2 lb (1 kg) in a day.
options.why: Correct. Daily weights track fluid balance and diuretic response; rapid gain suggests reaccumulating ascites or edema.

options.text: Limit sodium to about 2,000 mg a day.
options.why: Correct. Moderate sodium restriction (about 2 g/day) is a mainstay of ascites management along with diuretics.

options.text: Avoid ibuprofen and naproxen; use acetaminophen up to 2 g a day for pain.
options.why: Correct. NSAIDs can cause kidney injury, reduce the response to diuretics and raise GI bleeding risk in cirrhosis; acetaminophen at reduced doses (generally no more than 2 g/day) is the preferred analgesic.

options.text: Avoid all alcohol.
options.why: Correct. Abstinence from alcohol is essential to slow liver damage and can improve ascites.

options.text: Cut your protein intake sharply to prevent confusion.
options.why: Incorrect. Current guidance is to avoid protein restriction; clients with cirrhosis need adequate protein (about 1.2–1.5 g/kg/day) to prevent muscle loss. Encephalopathy is treated with lactulose and rifaximin.

options.text: Use a salt substitute to season food.
options.why: Incorrect. Most salt substitutes contain potassium chloride, which can cause dangerous hyperkalemia with spironolactone.

takeaway: Cirrhosis with ascites: daily weights, 2 g sodium, no alcohol or NSAIDs, no potassium salt substitutes with spironolactone, and do not restrict protein.

stem: The nurse is giving two medications through a client's gastrostomy tube while a continuous feeding is running. The medications are compatible with holding the feeding briefly. Place the steps in the correct order.

options.text: Give the first medication, prepared separately in water.
options.why: Each medication is prepared and given separately to avoid physical incompatibility and tube clogging.

options.text: Flush the tube with at least 15 mL of water.
options.why: This flush clears formula from the tube before any medication is given.

options.text: Pause the tube feeding.
options.why: The feeding is stopped first so medications are not mixed with formula, which can clog the tube or bind drugs.

options.text: Flush the tube with water.
options.why: A water flush between drugs (volume per facility policy) clears the first medication so it does not mix with the second.

options.text: Give the second medication.
options.why: The second drug is given after the between-dose flush.

options.text: Flush with at least 15 mL of water and restart the feeding.
options.why: A final flush clears the tube of medication before formula resumes, preventing clogging and interactions.

takeaway: Medications via feeding tube: stop feeding, flush with at least 15 mL water, give each drug separately with a water flush between, finish with at least 15 mL water, then resume.

stem: A client who has a nasogastric feeding tube and cannot swallow has these oral prescriptions. Which one should the nurse clarify with the provider before giving it through the tube?

options.text: Acetaminophen oral solution 650 mg every 6 hours as needed
options.why: A liquid preparation is appropriate for tube administration.

options.text: Metoprolol tartrate 25 mg tablet twice daily
options.why: Immediate-release metoprolol tartrate tablets may be crushed, dissolved in water and given through the tube.

options.text: Famotidine 20 mg tablet twice daily
options.why: Plain famotidine tablets may be crushed and given via tube, or an oral suspension can be used.

options.text: Metoprolol succinate extended-release 50 mg tablet daily
options.why: Correct. Extended-release products must not be crushed; crushing releases the whole daily dose at once and can cause bradycardia and hypotension. The nurse should ask for an immediate-release form or another option.

takeaway: Never crush extended-release, delayed-release or enteric-coated tablets for a feeding tube; ask for a liquid or immediate-release alternative.

stem: A client is prescribed 1,800 mL of a standard enteral formula to infuse by pump over 20 hours each day. At what rate in mL/hr should the nurse set the pump?

options.text: 75 mL/hr
options.why: 75 mL/hr is the rate for infusing 1,800 mL over 24 hours, not 20 hours.

options.text: 85 mL/hr
options.why: 85 mL/hr × 20 hours delivers only 1,700 mL, short of the prescribed volume.

options.text: 90 mL/hr
options.why: Correct. Volume ÷ time = 1,800 mL ÷ 20 hr = 90 mL/hr.

options.text: 100 mL/hr
options.why: 100 mL/hr × 20 hours delivers 2,000 mL, which exceeds the prescription.

takeaway: Pump rate (mL/hr) = total volume ÷ number of hours prescribed.

stem: The nurse is teaching a client to instill timolol eye drops, followed by a second prescribed eye drop. Place the steps in the correct order.

options.text: Gently close the eye and press on the inner corner of the eye near the nose for 1 to 3 minutes.
options.why: Punctal (nasolacrimal) occlusion after instillation keeps the drug in the eye and reduces absorption into the bloodstream, limiting systemic effects such as bradycardia.

options.text: Wash hands.
options.why: Hand hygiene comes first to prevent introducing microorganisms into the eye.

options.text: Wait at least 5 minutes, then instill the second eye medication.
options.why: Spacing different eye drops by at least 5 minutes prevents the second drop from washing out the first.

options.text: Tilt the head back and pull down the lower lid to form a pocket.
options.why: This creates the conjunctival sac that receives the drop.

options.text: Instill one drop into the lower lid pocket without letting the tip touch the eye or lashes.
options.why: Dropping into the conjunctival sac (not onto the cornea) and avoiding contact keeps the bottle tip sterile.

takeaway: Eye drops: clean hands, drop into lower lid pocket without touching, close eye and press the inner corner 1–3 minutes, and wait 5 minutes between drugs.

stem: A client newly diagnosed with open-angle glaucoma is prescribed timolol 0.5% ophthalmic solution, 1 drop in each eye twice daily. Which item in the client's history should the nurse report to the provider before the first dose?

options.text: Asthma treated with an inhaled corticosteroid
options.why: Correct. Timolol is a nonselective beta-blocker; enough is absorbed systemically through the nasolacrimal duct to cause bronchospasm. Asthma is a contraindication.

options.text: Osteoarthritis of both knees
options.why: Osteoarthritis has no interaction with ophthalmic beta-blockers.

options.text: Acid reflux treated with famotidine
options.why: Acid reflux and famotidine do not interact with timolol eye drops.

options.text: Hyperlipidemia treated with atorvastatin
options.why: Statin therapy and high cholesterol are not contraindications to timolol.

takeaway: Ophthalmic timolol acts systemically: avoid in asthma, severe COPD, bradycardia and heart block.

stem: An 81-year-old client who started timolol eye drops 3 weeks ago comes to the clinic. Which finding should the nurse report to the provider immediately?

options.text: Mild stinging in the eyes for a few seconds after each drop
options.why: Brief stinging is a common local effect and is not dangerous.

options.text: Apical pulse of 46/min and lightheadedness when standing
options.why: Correct. Systemically absorbed timolol can cause symptomatic bradycardia and hypotension, especially in older adults; this needs prompt evaluation.

options.text: Intraocular pressure lower than at the last visit
options.why: A lower eye pressure shows that the drug is working as intended.

options.text: Slightly blurred vision for a minute after instilling the drop
options.why: Brief blurring right after instillation is expected and resolves quickly.

takeaway: Report bradycardia, dizziness or wheezing in clients using timolol eye drops; teach punctal occlusion to limit absorption.

stem: The nurse is teaching Grace Mensah, 64, who has green-brown (hazel) eyes, about latanoprost 0.005% eye drops for open-angle glaucoma. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Instill one drop in each affected eye once daily in the evening.
options.why: Correct. Latanoprost is dosed once daily, usually in the evening.

options.text: The colored part of your eye may slowly turn browner, and this change may be permanent.
options.why: Correct. Latanoprost increases melanin in the iris; the change is gradual, most noticeable in mixed-color irises, and usually permanent.

options.text: Your eyelashes may grow longer and darker.
options.why: Correct. Eyelash growth and darkening, along with darkening of the eyelid skin, are known effects of prostaglandin analogs.

options.text: Use the drops twice a day if you want a stronger effect.
options.why: Incorrect. Dosing more often than once daily can actually reduce the pressure-lowering effect of latanoprost.

options.text: Any change in eye color will go away when the medication is stopped.
options.why: Incorrect. Iris pigment change is typically permanent, so it should be discussed before starting, particularly when only one eye is treated.

takeaway: Latanoprost: once daily in the evening; may permanently darken the iris and lengthen lashes; more often is not better.

stem: A client with glaucoma is starting pilocarpine eye drops. Which statement by the client indicates understanding of the teaching?

options.text: "My pupils will get bigger, so I'll wear sunglasses outdoors."
options.why: Pilocarpine is a miotic: it constricts the pupil. Pupil enlargement is the effect of mydriatics.

options.text: "I'll stop using the drops once my eye pressure is normal."
options.why: Glaucoma is a chronic condition; drops must be continued to keep pressure controlled and prevent vision loss.

options.text: "I may have headaches in the first few days, so I'll stop the drops if that happens."
options.why: Brow ache and headache are common early and usually lessen; the client should report them rather than stop the drug.

options.text: "I need to be careful driving at night because it will be harder to see in dim light."
options.why: Correct. Pilocarpine constricts the pupil, which reduces the light entering the eye and makes night and dim-light vision harder.

takeaway: Miotics such as pilocarpine shrink the pupil and impair dim-light vision; caution with night driving.

stem: A client is scheduled for a dilated eye examination, and the nurse is to instill cyclopentolate, an anticholinergic mydriatic. Which history should the nurse report before giving the drops?

options.text: Myopia (nearsightedness) treated with contact lenses
options.why: Nearsightedness is not a contraindication; contacts are simply removed before the drops.

options.text: A narrow anterior chamber angle noted at a prior exam
options.why: Correct. Pupil dilation can crowd the angle and block aqueous outflow, triggering acute angle-closure glaucoma in a client with narrow angles.

options.text: Type 2 diabetes without retinopathy
options.why: Diabetes is a reason for regular dilated exams, not a contraindication to them.

options.text: Seasonal allergic conjunctivitis
options.why: Allergic conjunctivitis does not contraindicate mydriatic drops.

takeaway: Mydriatics can precipitate acute angle-closure glaucoma in clients with narrow angles; report that history before dilating.

stem: The nurse is instilling antibiotic ear drops into the right ear of a 2-year-old with otitis externa. Which technique is correct?

options.text: Gently pull the pinna down and back, then instill the drops.
options.why: Correct. In children younger than about 3 years, the ear canal is short and angled upward, so pulling the pinna down and back straightens it.

options.text: Pull the pinna up and back, then instill the drops.
options.why: Up and back is the technique for adults and older children, whose ear canal curves differently.

options.text: Give the drops straight from the refrigerator to reduce discomfort.
options.why: Cold drops can cause dizziness, nausea and pain; drops should be warmed to body temperature by holding the bottle in the hands.

options.text: Insert the dropper tip into the canal so the drops reach the eardrum.
options.why: Inserting the tip can injure the canal and contaminate the dropper; drops are released into the canal without touching it.

takeaway: Ear drops: under about 3 years, pull the pinna down and back; adults, up and back; warm drops to body temperature first.

stem: A client with sepsis is receiving IV gentamicin every 24 hours and IV furosemide 40 mg twice daily. During morning care, the client says, "I've had a ringing in both ears since last night." What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Reassure the client that ringing is common in the hospital because of equipment noise.
options.why: Tinnitus in a client receiving two ototoxic drugs is a warning sign of possible permanent hearing loss and must not be dismissed.

options.text: Give the next gentamicin dose and request an audiology consult for after discharge.
options.why: Continuing the drug without evaluation risks irreversible damage; the provider needs to know now.

options.text: Hold the next gentamicin dose and report the tinnitus to the provider, along with the latest trough level and creatinine.
options.why: Correct. Aminoglycosides are ototoxic and nephrotoxic, and loop diuretics add to the ototoxic risk. Tinnitus requires prompt reporting so dosing can be reassessed using the trough level and kidney function.

options.text: Increase the client's IV fluid rate to dilute the drug.
options.why: The nurse cannot change the IV rate without a prescription, and this does not address the ototoxicity.

takeaway: Aminoglycosides plus loop diuretics raise ototoxicity risk; report tinnitus, vertigo or hearing changes before the next dose.

stem: A client with eczema on both forearms is prescribed triamcinolone 0.1% cream twice daily. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I'll rub in a thin layer only where the rash is."
options.why: This is correct: a thin layer on affected skin gives the effect while limiting absorption.

options.text: "I won't put this cream on my face unless my provider says I can."
options.why: This is correct: facial skin is thin and absorbs more steroid, increasing the risk of atrophy, so medium- to high-potency products are avoided there unless prescribed.

options.text: "I'll wrap my arms in plastic wrap overnight to help the cream work better."
options.why: This needs correction. Occlusion greatly increases absorption and the risk of skin thinning, striae and systemic effects; it should be used only if the provider specifically prescribes it.

options.text: "I'll let my provider know if my skin starts to look thin or shiny."
options.why: This is correct: skin atrophy, striae and easy bruising are local adverse effects that should be reported.

takeaway: Topical corticosteroids: thin layer, shortest effective time, no occlusion unless prescribed, and avoid thin skin areas.

stem: Sofia Delgado, 19, is starting isotretinoin for severe nodular acne and is enrolled in the iPLEDGE program. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Use two forms of effective birth control, starting before treatment and continuing until 1 month after the last dose, unless you commit to abstinence.
options.why: Correct. Isotretinoin causes severe birth defects; the REMS program requires two effective contraceptive methods (or committed abstinence) before, during and for 1 month after therapy.

options.text: You will need a negative pregnancy test before each monthly prescription.
options.why: Correct. Pregnancy testing is required before starting and every month during treatment for anyone who can become pregnant.

options.text: Do not donate blood during treatment or for 1 month after stopping.
options.why: Correct. Donated blood could be given to a pregnant person and harm the fetus.

options.text: Report sadness, mood changes or thoughts of self-harm right away.
options.why: Correct. Depression, psychosis and suicidal thoughts have been reported with isotretinoin.

options.text: Avoid vitamin A supplements while taking this medication.
options.why: Correct. Isotretinoin is a vitamin A derivative; added vitamin A increases the risk of toxicity.

options.text: You can share extra capsules with a family member who has acne.
options.why: Incorrect. Isotretinoin must never be shared; each person must be enrolled in the REMS program because of the risk of birth defects.

takeaway: Isotretinoin: strict pregnancy prevention and monthly testing, no blood donation, no vitamin A, no sharing, and report mood changes.

stem: A 17-year-old client has been taking isotretinoin for 2 months. Which finding requires the nurse's immediate follow-up?

options.text: Dry, cracked lips
options.why: Cheilitis is the most common, expected effect; lip balm is the usual treatment.

options.text: The client says, "I don't see the point of anything anymore, and I've been thinking about not waking up."
options.why: Correct. Isotretinoin has been associated with depression and suicidal thinking; expressed thoughts of death require immediate safety assessment and reporting.

options.text: Dry eyes that make contact lenses uncomfortable
options.why: Dry eyes are a common, expected effect managed with lubricating drops.

options.text: Occasional mild nosebleeds in dry weather
options.why: Mucosal dryness causing mild nosebleeds is common and usually managed with saline or humidification.

takeaway: Mucocutaneous dryness is expected with isotretinoin; mood changes or suicidal thoughts need immediate action.

stem: A client with deep partial- and full-thickness burns covering 30% of the body is treated with mafenide acetate cream twice daily. On day 4, the respiratory rate is 30/min. Arterial blood gases: pH 7.31, PaCO2 33 mm Hg, HCO3 17 mEq/L. Which interpretation by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: Respiratory acidosis from inadequate ventilation
options.why: PaCO2 is low, not high, so this is not respiratory acidosis.

options.text: Metabolic alkalosis from nasogastric suction
options.why: pH and bicarbonate are both low, which indicates acidosis, not alkalosis.

options.text: Respiratory alkalosis from pain-related hyperventilation
options.why: The pH is acidotic; the low PaCO2 here is the lungs compensating, not the primary problem.

options.text: Metabolic acidosis, possibly caused by mafenide
options.why: Correct. Low pH (normal 7.35–7.45) with low bicarbonate (normal 22–26 mEq/L) and a compensatory low PaCO2 (normal 35–45 mm Hg) is metabolic acidosis. Mafenide inhibits carbonic anhydrase and can cause this, especially over large areas; the nurse should report it.

takeaway: Mafenide penetrates eschar but is painful and can cause metabolic acidosis (carbonic anhydrase inhibition); watch ABGs and respiratory rate.

stem: Silver sulfadiazine 1% cream is prescribed for four clients with partial-thickness burns. Which prescription should the nurse question?

options.text: A 6-week-old infant with a scald burn on the forearm
options.why: Correct. Silver sulfadiazine is contraindicated in infants younger than 2 months (and in premature infants) because sulfonamides can displace bilirubin and cause kernicterus.

options.text: A 35-year-old with a grease burn on the hand and no drug allergies
options.why: There is no contraindication for this client.

options.text: A 70-year-old with type 2 diabetes and a flame burn on the leg
options.why: Diabetes is not a contraindication; the nurse will monitor wound healing and blood glucose.

options.text: A 12-year-old with a friction burn and a penicillin allergy
options.why: A penicillin allergy does not cross-react with sulfonamides; a sulfa allergy would be the concern.

takeaway: Silver sulfadiazine: avoid in sulfonamide allergy, in infants under 2 months, and in pregnancy near term; monitor for transient leukopenia.

stem: A 70-kg client with major burns is receiving lactated Ringer's solution titrated to urine output during the first 24 hours. Which hourly urine output best indicates that fluid resuscitation is adequate?

options.text: 15 mL/hr
options.why: This is well below 0.5 mL/kg/hr (35 mL/hr for 70 kg) and suggests under-resuscitation and risk of kidney injury.

options.text: 25 mL/hr
options.why: Still below the target of about 0.5 mL/kg/hr; fluids likely need to be increased.

options.text: 40 mL/hr
options.why: Correct. The adult target is about 0.5 mL/kg/hr, or roughly 30–50 mL/hr; 40 mL/hr is within range for a 70-kg adult.

options.text: 150 mL/hr
options.why: Output this high suggests over-resuscitation; excess fluid increases edema, compartment syndrome and pulmonary complications, so the rate is usually decreased.

takeaway: Burn resuscitation is titrated to urine output: about 0.5 mL/kg/hr (30–50 mL/hr) in adults; both too little and too much are harmful.

stem: The nurse is changing the dressing on a clean, red, granulating surgical wound healing by secondary intention. Which solution is best for cleansing the wound?

options.text: Full-strength hydrogen peroxide
options.why: Hydrogen peroxide is cytotoxic to new granulation tissue and fibroblasts and is not used on clean, healing wounds.

options.text: Povidone-iodine 10%
options.why: Povidone-iodine damages healthy healing cells and is generally avoided on clean granulating wounds.

options.text: Sterile normal saline
options.why: Correct. Normal saline is isotonic and nontoxic to healing tissue, making it the preferred cleanser for clean granulating wounds.

options.text: Diluted sodium hypochlorite (Dakin's) solution
options.why: Dakin's solution is reserved for infected or heavily contaminated wounds as prescribed; it can harm healthy granulation tissue.

takeaway: Clean granulating wounds: cleanse with normal saline and keep moist; avoid cytotoxic antiseptics.

stem: During a skin assessment, the nurse finds an area of intact skin over the right heel that is deep maroon and does not blanch. The area is boggy and painful, and the skin is unbroken. How should the nurse document this finding?

options.text: Stage 1 pressure injury
options.why: Stage 1 is intact skin with nonblanchable redness; deep maroon or purple discoloration suggests damage to deeper tissue.

options.text: Stage 2 pressure injury
options.why: Stage 2 involves partial-thickness loss with exposed dermis or an intact or ruptured serum-filled blister; this skin is intact.

options.text: Deep tissue pressure injury
options.why: Correct. Intact or nonintact skin with persistent, nonblanchable deep red, maroon or purple discoloration indicates a deep tissue pressure injury, which may evolve rapidly.

options.text: Unstageable pressure injury
options.why: Unstageable injuries have full-thickness loss with the base hidden by slough or eschar; this skin is intact.

takeaway: Persistent nonblanchable maroon or purple discoloration over a bony prominence is a deep tissue pressure injury, not stage 1.

stem: A client with peripheral arterial disease has a heel pressure injury covered with stable, dry, intact black eschar. There is no redness, drainage or fluctuance around it. A new assistive staff member asks whether the eschar should be scrubbed off. What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "Yes, the eschar must be removed so the wound can be staged."
options.why: Stable heel eschar is not removed, even though it makes the wound unstageable.

options.text: "Soak it in warm water daily to soften it before we remove it."
options.why: Softening and removing stable eschar on an ischemic heel can open a wound that may not heal.

options.text: "Apply a wet-to-dry dressing to loosen the eschar."
options.why: Wet-to-dry dressings are nonselective debridement and would disrupt the protective eschar.

options.text: "No. Stable, dry heel eschar acts as a natural cover; we keep it intact and float the heels off the bed."
options.why: Correct. Stable, dry, intact eschar on the heel or an ischemic limb serves as the body's natural biological cover and should not be softened or removed; the nurse offloads the heel and monitors for signs of infection.

takeaway: Leave stable, dry, intact heel eschar in place; offload the heel and report redness, drainage or softening.

stem: An adult client is diagnosed with scabies and prescribed permethrin 5% cream. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Massage the cream into the skin from the neck to the soles of the feet, including between fingers and toes and under the nails.
options.why: Correct. All skin from the neck down must be covered in adults, with attention to skin folds, finger webs and under the nails where mites hide.

options.text: Leave the cream on for 8 to 14 hours, then wash it off.
options.why: Correct. Permethrin 5% is left on for 8–14 hours (often overnight) and then removed by bathing.

options.text: Household members and close contacts should be treated at the same time, even without symptoms.
options.why: Correct. Treating contacts simultaneously prevents reinfestation.

options.text: Wash bedding and clothing used in the past 3 days in hot water, or seal them in a plastic bag for at least 72 hours.
options.why: Correct. Mites do not survive more than 2–3 days away from human skin.

options.text: If itching continues the next day, reapply the cream every day until it stops.
options.why: Incorrect. Itching often persists for 2–4 weeks after successful treatment because of the allergic reaction to mites; repeated daily application is not recommended and irritates the skin. A second application 1 to 2 weeks later may be prescribed.

options.text: Apply the cream only to the areas where the rash is visible.
options.why: Incorrect. Mites may be present on skin without a visible rash, so the whole body below the neck must be treated.

takeaway: Scabies: permethrin from neck to toes for 8–14 hours, treat contacts together, launder or bag items, and expect itching for weeks.

stem: The nurse teaches the parent of a 7-year-old with head lice how to use permethrin 1% lotion. Which statement by the parent indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I'll use a fine-toothed nit comb on her wet hair after the treatment."
options.why: This is correct: combing removes nits and dead lice and improves the cure rate.

options.text: "I'll wash her hair with shampoo and conditioner before putting on the lotion."
options.why: This needs correction. Conditioner coats the hair shaft and reduces how well permethrin binds; hair should be washed with a conditioner-free shampoo, rinsed and towel-dried.

options.text: "I'll leave the lotion on for 10 minutes and then rinse it off."
options.why: This is correct: permethrin 1% lotion is left on for 10 minutes and rinsed with warm water.

options.text: "If I still see live lice a week or more after this treatment, she may need a second one."
options.why: This is correct: a second treatment 7 to 9 days later kills lice that hatched from eggs that survived the first application.

takeaway: Permethrin 1% for lice: shampoo without conditioner, apply to towel-dried hair for 10 minutes, nit comb, retreat in 7–9 days if live lice are seen.

stem: A client received IV cyclophosphamide 6 hours ago. The nurse is planning care related to the client's urine and other body fluids. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Wear two pairs of chemotherapy-tested gloves and a protective gown when emptying the client's urinal.
options.why: Correct. Hazardous drugs and their metabolites are excreted in urine and stool for at least 48 hours after administration, so PPE is needed when handling excreta.

options.text: Wear a face shield if splashing is likely, such as when emptying a bedpan into a toilet.
options.why: Correct. Eye and face protection is added whenever splashes of contaminated body fluids could occur.

options.text: Discard contaminated incontinence pads in the designated hazardous drug waste container.
options.why: Correct. Linens and disposables soiled within 48 hours of hazardous drug administration are handled as contaminated per facility policy.

options.text: Handle the urine as regular waste because the drug was given intravenously, not orally.
options.why: Incorrect. The route does not matter; the drug and active metabolites are excreted in body fluids regardless of how they were given.

options.text: Allow a staff member who is pregnant to empty the commode if she wears one pair of exam gloves.
options.why: Incorrect. Staff who are pregnant or trying to conceive should be offered alternative duty to avoid hazardous drug exposure, and regular exam gloves are not adequate protection.

takeaway: Treat a client's body fluids as hazardous for at least 48 hours after chemotherapy: double chemotherapy gloves, gown, and face protection for splashes.

stem: A client with acute leukemia has an absolute neutrophil count (ANC) of 380/mm³ after chemotherapy. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Perform hand hygiene before entering the room and before any contact with the client.
options.why: Correct. Hand hygiene is the single most important measure to prevent infection in a neutropenic client.

options.text: Measure the temperature at least every 4 hours and report a fever right away.
options.why: Correct. Fever may be the only sign of infection when neutrophils are too low to produce pus, redness or swelling.

options.text: Take the temperature rectally for the most accurate reading.
options.why: Incorrect. Rectal temperatures, suppositories and enemas are avoided because they can injure the mucosa and introduce bacteria.

options.text: Remove the fresh flowers and potted plant a visitor brought.
options.why: Correct. Fresh flowers, standing water and soil can harbor bacteria and fungi; most protocols remove them for clients with severe neutropenia.

options.text: Allow the client's nephew, who has a cold, to visit if he wears a mask.
options.why: Incorrect. Visitors with active respiratory infections should not visit a severely neutropenic client.

options.text: Inspect the mouth, skin, perineal area and IV site for subtle signs of infection every shift.
options.why: Correct. Because inflammatory signs are blunted, careful daily inspection helps detect infection early.

takeaway: Severe neutropenia (ANC below 500/mm³): strict hand hygiene, frequent temperature checks, nothing rectal, no fresh flowers, no sick visitors.

stem: Ten days after chemotherapy for lymphoma, a client's ANC is 250/mm³. The client reports chills. Vital signs: temperature 101.3°F (38.5°C), heart rate 104/min, blood pressure 112/70 mm Hg, respiratory rate 20/min. What is the nurse's priority action?

options.text: Give acetaminophen and recheck the temperature in 1 hour.
options.why: Treating the fever without obtaining cultures and starting antibiotics delays care; neutropenic fever can progress to septic shock within hours.

options.text: Encourage oral fluids and apply a cooling blanket.
options.why: Comfort measures alone do not treat the likely infection.

options.text: Place the client on contact precautions and wait for the morning CBC.
options.why: Waiting is unsafe; neutropenic fever is a medical emergency.

options.text: Notify the provider, obtain blood cultures and start the prescribed empiric IV antibiotics within 1 hour.
options.why: Correct. Febrile neutropenia (a single temperature of 101°F [38.3°C] or higher, with an ANC below 500/mm³) requires blood cultures and broad-spectrum IV antibiotics as soon as possible, ideally within 60 minutes.

takeaway: Neutropenic fever is an emergency: cultures, then broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour.

stem: A client receiving chemotherapy for head and neck cancer has oral mucositis. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I'll keep using my regular mouthwash after every meal to kill germs."
options.why: This needs correction. Most commercial mouthwashes contain alcohol, which dries and irritates inflamed mucosa; a bland rinse of saline or saline with baking soda is used instead.

options.text: "I'll rinse with a salt and baking soda solution several times a day."
options.why: This is correct: bland rinses keep the mouth clean and moist without irritating it.

options.text: "I'll brush gently with a soft-bristled toothbrush."
options.why: This is correct: a soft brush cleans without injuring the mucosa (a foam swab may be used if brushing is too painful).

options.text: "I'll avoid spicy, acidic and very hot foods until my mouth heals."
options.why: This is correct: these foods increase pain and irritation of the mucosa.

takeaway: Mucositis: bland saline or baking soda rinses and a soft brush; avoid alcohol mouthwash and spicy, acidic or hot foods.

stem: During an IV infusion of doxorubicin through a peripheral IV, the client reports burning, and the nurse notes swelling at the site. Place the nurse's actions in the correct order.

options.text: Remove the IV catheter.
options.why: The catheter is removed after attempting to aspirate the residual drug through it.

options.text: Stop the infusion.
options.why: Stopping the infusion immediately limits the amount of vesicant entering the tissue.

options.text: Attempt to aspirate residual drug from the catheter with a syringe.
options.why: Aspirating through the still-placed catheter removes some of the drug before the catheter comes out.

options.text: Apply a cold compress as specified for the agent and elevate the extremity.
options.why: Cold is used for anthracyclines such as doxorubicin (heat is used for some other vesicants, such as vinca alkaloids); elevation reduces swelling. Any antidote (dexrazoxane) is given per protocol.

options.text: Disconnect the IV tubing from the catheter, leaving the catheter in place.
options.why: Leaving the catheter in place allows the nurse to try to aspirate the drug back out.

takeaway: Vesicant extravasation: stop, disconnect tubing (leave catheter), aspirate, remove catheter, then agent-specific compress, elevation, notification and documentation.

stem: Thirty-six hours after starting induction chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukemia with a very high white blood cell count, a client has these laboratory results. Which result should the nurse report first?

options.text: Potassium 6.4 mEq/L
options.why: Correct. Tumor lysis syndrome releases intracellular potassium; hyperkalemia (normal 3.5–5 mEq/L) can cause fatal dysrhythmias and is the most immediately life-threatening finding.

options.text: Uric acid 9.6 mg/dL
options.why: Hyperuricemia (normal about 3.5–7.2 mg/dL) threatens the kidneys, but it is less immediately lethal than severe hyperkalemia.

options.text: Phosphorus 5.2 mg/dL
options.why: Hyperphosphatemia (normal about 2.5–4.5 mg/dL) is expected in tumor lysis and must be treated, but it is not the first priority.

options.text: Calcium 8.1 mg/dL
options.why: Mild hypocalcemia (normal about 8.5–10.5 mg/dL) follows phosphate binding; it needs monitoring but is less urgent than potassium 6.4 mEq/L.

takeaway: Tumor lysis syndrome: high potassium, phosphate and uric acid with low calcium; hyperkalemia is the immediate threat to life.

stem: A client with Burkitt lymphoma is about to start chemotherapy and is at high risk for tumor lysis syndrome. Which interventions should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Begin IV hydration before chemotherapy starts, as prescribed.
options.why: Correct. Aggressive hydration increases kidney blood flow and urine output to flush out uric acid, potassium and phosphate.

options.text: Give the prescribed uric acid–lowering drug (such as rasburicase or allopurinol) before chemotherapy begins.
options.why: Correct. Uric acid control starts before chemotherapy. For clients at high risk, such as those with Burkitt lymphoma, rasburicase is usually preferred (after G6PD deficiency is ruled out); allopurinol is used for lower-risk clients and is started 1 to 3 days before treatment.

options.text: Measure intake and output closely and report a drop in urine output.
options.why: Correct. Falling urine output can signal acute kidney injury from uric acid or calcium phosphate deposits.

options.text: Give an oral potassium supplement to replace potassium lost through diuresis.
options.why: Incorrect. Tumor lysis releases large amounts of potassium; supplements could cause dangerous hyperkalemia.

options.text: Limit fluids at night so the client can sleep.
options.why: Incorrect. Fluid restriction works against the goal of a high urine output.

options.text: Encourage foods high in phosphorus, such as dairy products, to build strength.
options.why: Incorrect. Phosphorus is already released from dying cells; extra dietary phosphorus worsens hyperphosphatemia.

takeaway: Prevent tumor lysis syndrome with IV hydration, a uric acid–lowering drug started before chemotherapy (rasburicase for high risk if no G6PD deficiency) and close I&O and lab monitoring; avoid added potassium and phosphorus.

stem: The nurse reviews prescriptions for four clients on the oncology unit. Which prescription should the nurse question before giving it?

options.text: Allopurinol 300 mg orally daily for a client starting chemotherapy for leukemia
options.why: Allopurinol is standard prophylaxis for tumor lysis syndrome.

options.text: Ondansetron 8 mg IV before chemotherapy for a client with a normal QTc
options.why: This is appropriate antiemetic prophylaxis with a normal QTc.

options.text: IV normal saline at 150 mL/hr for a client at risk for tumor lysis who has normal heart function
options.why: Hydration is appropriate prophylaxis for tumor lysis syndrome.

options.text: Rasburicase IV for a client with hyperuricemia and a history of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency
options.why: Correct. Rasburicase is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency because the hydrogen peroxide produced as it breaks down uric acid can trigger severe hemolysis and methemoglobinemia.

takeaway: Rasburicase is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency; screen before giving it.

stem: The nurse teaches the parent of a 3-year-old about liquid ferrous sulfate drops for iron-deficiency anemia. Which statement by the parent indicates understanding?

options.text: "I'll give it between meals with a little orange juice and brush her teeth afterward."
options.why: Correct. Iron is best absorbed on an empty stomach with vitamin C; giving it toward the back of the mouth with a dropper and brushing afterward helps prevent tooth staining.

options.text: "I'll mix it into her bottle of milk so she doesn't taste it."
options.why: Calcium in milk decreases iron absorption, and large amounts of cow's milk contribute to iron deficiency in toddlers.

options.text: "If her stools turn dark green or black, I'll stop the iron and call you."
options.why: Dark stools are an expected effect of oral iron and are not a reason to stop it.

options.text: "I'll keep the bottle on the kitchen counter so I remember to give it."
options.why: Iron overdose is a leading cause of serious poisoning in young children; iron must be stored out of reach in a child-resistant container.

takeaway: Oral iron: give between meals with vitamin C, use a straw or dropper and brush teeth, expect dark stools, and store out of children's reach.

stem: A client with pernicious anemia is started on cyanocobalamin injections. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "My tongue should feel less sore as my blood count improves."
options.why: This is correct: glossitis improves with vitamin B12 replacement.

options.text: "I'll report any numbness or tingling that gets worse."
options.why: This is correct: worsening neurologic symptoms should be reported, because nerve damage can become permanent if B12 replacement is inadequate.

options.text: "I may feel more energy within the first few weeks."
options.why: This is correct: fatigue usually improves as red cell production recovers.

options.text: "Once my blood counts are normal, I can stop the injections."
options.why: This needs correction. Pernicious anemia is caused by a lack of intrinsic factor, so B12 must be replaced for life (by injection or, in some clients, high-dose oral therapy as prescribed).

takeaway: Pernicious anemia needs lifelong vitamin B12 replacement; stopping therapy allows anemia and nerve damage to return.

stem: A client with chronic kidney disease on hemodialysis receives epoetin alfa three times weekly. Before today's dose, the nurse reviews the client's data. Which finding should prompt the nurse to hold the dose and contact the provider?

options.text: Hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL
options.why: Correct. In CKD, FDA labeling directs reducing or interrupting the dose when hemoglobin approaches or exceeds 11 g/dL, because higher targets increase the risk of stroke, thrombosis, myocardial infarction and death.

options.text: Transferrin saturation 28%
options.why: A transferrin saturation above 20% shows adequate iron to support red cell production; it is not a reason to hold the drug.

options.text: Blood pressure 134/82 mm Hg
options.why: This blood pressure is acceptable; uncontrolled hypertension would be a reason to hold.

options.text: Hemoglobin was 9.6 g/dL last month
options.why: Last month's value of 9.6 g/dL was below 10 g/dL, which supported starting or continuing therapy; the current value is what guides today's dose.

takeaway: Epoetin in CKD: hold or reduce the dose as hemoglobin approaches or exceeds 11 g/dL, and hold for uncontrolled hypertension.

stem: A client receiving daily filgrastim injections after chemotherapy reports several symptoms. Which report requires the nurse's immediate follow-up?

options.text: Aching in the lower back, hips and sternum
options.why: Bone pain is the most common effect of filgrastim, caused by marrow expansion; it is usually managed with acetaminophen or other prescribed analgesics.

options.text: Pain in the upper left abdomen that spreads to the tip of the left shoulder
options.why: Correct. Filgrastim can cause splenic enlargement and, rarely, splenic rupture. Left upper quadrant pain with referred left shoulder pain needs immediate evaluation.

options.text: Mild redness at yesterday's injection site
options.why: Minor injection-site reactions are common and not dangerous; rotating sites helps.

options.text: A white blood cell count higher than last week
options.why: A rising WBC means the drug is working as intended; very high counts are reported per protocol, but this is the expected direction.

takeaway: Filgrastim: expect bone pain, but report left upper abdominal or left shoulder pain at once (possible splenic rupture).

stem: Twenty minutes into a transfusion of packed red blood cells, a client develops chills, a temperature increase of 2°F (1.1°C) and new itching. Place the nurse's actions in the correct order.

options.text: Notify the provider and the blood bank.
options.why: The provider directs treatment, and the blood bank must be told so the reaction can be investigated.

options.text: Stop the transfusion.
options.why: Stopping the blood first prevents more of the incompatible or reactive product from entering the client.

options.text: Send the blood bag and tubing to the blood bank and collect blood and urine samples as prescribed.
options.why: These items allow the blood bank to identify the type of reaction; this follows once the client is stabilized and the provider and blood bank have been notified.

options.text: Assess vital signs, breath sounds and level of distress.
options.why: Assessment identifies how severe the reaction is and whether emergency treatment is needed.

options.text: Disconnect the blood tubing and infuse normal saline through new tubing to keep the IV line open.
options.why: New tubing prevents more blood from the old line entering the client, and keeping the line open preserves access for emergency drugs.

takeaway: Suspected transfusion reaction: stop the blood, keep the line open with normal saline through new tubing, assess, notify provider and blood bank, then return the bag and send samples.

stem: An 83-year-old client with heart failure and an ejection fraction of 30% has a hemoglobin of 6.9 g/dL and is prescribed 2 units of packed red blood cells. Which plan best reduces the risk of a transfusion complication for this client?

options.text: Transfuse both units at the same time through two IV sites to shorten the procedure.
options.why: Giving two units at once delivers a large volume rapidly and greatly increases the risk of transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO).

options.text: Infuse each unit at a slower rate (completing each within 4 hours), assess lung sounds and oxygen saturation often, and give the prescribed furosemide.
options.why: Correct. Older adults with heart failure are at high risk for TACO. A slower rate, close monitoring for crackles, dyspnea and rising blood pressure, and a prescribed diuretic reduce this risk; each unit must still be finished within 4 hours.

options.text: Hang each unit to run over 6 hours to make sure it goes in slowly.
options.why: Blood must be completed within 4 hours of leaving controlled storage because of the risk of bacterial growth; the blood bank can split a unit if a slower rate is needed.

options.text: Premedicate with diphenhydramine to prevent fluid overload.
options.why: Antihistamines may reduce allergic reactions but do nothing to prevent circulatory overload.

takeaway: Older adults with heart failure are at risk for TACO: transfuse one unit at a time, slowly but within 4 hours, monitor lungs and give prescribed diuretics.

stem: Malik Johnson, 16, is admitted with a vaso-occlusive crisis from sickle cell disease. He rates his leg and back pain 9 out of 10. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Give the prescribed IV opioid promptly and reassess pain within 30 to 60 minutes.
options.why: Correct. Rapid, effective analgesia (ideally within 60 minutes of arrival) with frequent reassessment is the standard for vaso-occlusive pain.

options.text: Maintain the prescribed IV and oral fluids.
options.why: Correct. Hydration helps reduce blood viscosity and sickling, though fluids are given carefully to avoid overload.

options.text: Apply ice packs to the painful joints.
options.why: Incorrect. Cold causes vasoconstriction and can increase sickling; warm compresses are used instead.

options.text: Coach him to use the incentive spirometer every 1 to 2 hours while awake.
options.why: Correct. Incentive spirometry helps prevent atelectasis and acute chest syndrome, a leading cause of death in sickle cell disease.

options.text: Withhold opioids until laboratory results confirm a crisis.
options.why: Incorrect. No laboratory test confirms or rules out pain; the client's report guides treatment, and delays cause harm.

takeaway: Vaso-occlusive crisis: prompt opioids with frequent reassessment, hydration, warmth not cold, and incentive spirometry to prevent acute chest syndrome.

stem: On the second day of treatment for a vaso-occlusive crisis, a client with sickle cell disease reports new chest pain and a cough. Temperature is 101.5°F (38.6°C), respiratory rate 28/min and SpO2 88% on room air. What is the nurse's priority action?

options.text: Increase the PCA basal rate to relieve the chest pain.
options.why: The nurse cannot change PCA settings without a prescription, and more opioid could depress breathing in a client who is already hypoxemic.

options.text: Encourage the client to walk in the hallway to expand the lungs.
options.why: Activity increases oxygen demand in a hypoxemic client; the immediate need is oxygen and medical evaluation.

options.text: Apply oxygen to raise the SpO2 and notify the provider immediately.
options.why: Correct. New chest pain, fever, tachypnea and hypoxemia suggest acute chest syndrome, a life-threatening complication. Oxygen and urgent evaluation (chest x-ray, antibiotics, possible transfusion) are needed.

options.text: Give acetaminophen for the fever and recheck vital signs in 1 hour.
options.why: Treating the fever alone delays care for a potentially fatal pulmonary complication.

takeaway: New chest pain, fever, tachypnea or hypoxemia in sickle cell disease suggest acute chest syndrome: give oxygen and get help immediately.

stem: A client who received too much IV heparin has bleeding, and protamine sulfate is prescribed. The client has used NPH insulin for 10 years. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: Give the protamine by rapid IV push to stop the bleeding quickly.
options.why: Rapid administration can cause severe hypotension, bradycardia, pulmonary hypertension and anaphylactoid reactions.

options.text: Give the protamine slowly IV (no more than 50 mg over 10 minutes) and monitor blood pressure, heart rate and for signs of allergic reaction.
options.why: Correct. Protamine is given by slow IV injection with close monitoring. Prior exposure through protamine-containing insulin (NPH) increases the risk of hypersensitivity reactions, so emergency equipment should be ready.

options.text: Hold the protamine because NPH insulin use is an absolute contraindication.
options.why: NPH use increases risk but is not an absolute contraindication; the drug is given cautiously with monitoring.

options.text: Give phytonadione (vitamin K) instead because it works faster.
options.why: Vitamin K reverses warfarin, not heparin; protamine is the heparin antidote.

takeaway: Protamine reverses heparin: give slowly IV (no more than 50 mg over 10 minutes) and watch for hypotension and allergic reactions, especially after NPH insulin use.

stem: A client who takes dabigatran for atrial fibrillation arrives with a large, ongoing GI bleed and is hemodynamically unstable. Which medication should the nurse anticipate to reverse the anticoagulant?

options.text: Protamine sulfate
options.why: Protamine reverses heparin and, partially, enoxaparin; it does not reverse dabigatran.

options.text: Phytonadione (vitamin K)
options.why: Vitamin K restores vitamin K–dependent clotting factors and is used for warfarin; dabigatran is a direct thrombin inhibitor.

options.text: Desmopressin
options.why: Desmopressin increases von Willebrand factor and factor VIII; it is not an anticoagulant reversal agent for dabigatran.

options.text: Idarucizumab
options.why: Correct. Idarucizumab is a monoclonal antibody fragment that binds dabigatran and reverses its effect within minutes in life-threatening bleeding or before urgent surgery.

takeaway: Match the antidote: heparin, protamine; warfarin, vitamin K plus PCC; dabigatran, idarucizumab.

stem: A client who takes warfarin is admitted vomiting bright red blood. Blood pressure is 84/50 mm Hg, heart rate 124/min, and INR is 6.1. Which reversal plan should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Give vitamin K 10 mg by slow IV infusion along with 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC)
options.why: Correct. For major or life-threatening bleeding on warfarin, guidelines recommend holding warfarin and giving IV vitamin K (slowly, to reduce anaphylactoid risk) plus 4-factor PCC, which replaces clotting factors within minutes.

options.text: Hold tonight's warfarin dose and give oral vitamin K 2.5 mg
options.why: Holding a dose with low-dose oral vitamin K is used for an elevated INR without serious bleeding; it acts too slowly for life-threatening hemorrhage.

options.text: Give protamine sulfate 50 mg IV
options.why: Protamine reverses heparin, not warfarin.

options.text: Give idarucizumab 5 g IV
options.why: Idarucizumab reverses only dabigatran.

takeaway: Major bleeding on warfarin: hold warfarin, give IV vitamin K slowly plus 4-factor PCC; oral vitamin K is for high INR without serious bleeding.

stem: A client with breast cancer will receive an IV chemotherapy infusion this morning that will finish at 11:00. The nurse reviews the new prescriptions. Which one should the nurse clarify with the provider?

options.text: Acetaminophen 650 mg orally every 6 hours as needed for bone pain
options.why: This is appropriate for the bone pain that filgrastim commonly causes.

options.text: CBC with differential twice weekly
options.why: Regular blood counts are needed to monitor neutrophil recovery and response to filgrastim.

options.text: Filgrastim subcutaneously at 09:00 today, 2 hours before chemotherapy ends
options.why: Correct. Filgrastim should not be given in the 24 hours before or after cytotoxic chemotherapy, because rapidly dividing stimulated myeloid cells are more sensitive to the chemotherapy; it is usually started at least 24 hours after chemotherapy ends.

options.text: Ondansetron 8 mg orally every 8 hours as needed for nausea
options.why: This is an appropriate antiemetic prescription.

takeaway: Do not give filgrastim within 24 hours before or after chemotherapy; start it at least 24 hours after the chemotherapy ends.

stem: A client is prescribed metoprolol tartrate 37.5 mg orally twice daily. The pharmacy supplies 25-mg scored tablets. How many tablets should the nurse give for each dose? (The tablets may be split in half; round to the nearest half tablet if needed.)

options.text: 0.5 tablet
options.why: Half a 25-mg tablet is only 12.5 mg. This answer comes from inverting the ratio (25 ÷ 37.5 = 0.67) and rounding down.

options.text: 1.5 tablets
options.why: Desired ÷ have × quantity = 37.5 mg ÷ 25 mg × 1 tablet = 1.5 tablets. Because the tablets are scored, giving one and a half tablets delivers exactly 37.5 mg.

options.text: 2 tablets
options.why: Two tablets deliver 50 mg, which is 12.5 mg more than prescribed. Rounding up to whole tablets is not appropriate when a scored tablet can be split.

options.text: 1 tablet
options.why: One tablet delivers only 25 mg, which underdoses the client by 12.5 mg.

takeaway: Use desired ÷ have × quantity; split a tablet only if it is scored and the rounding rule allows it.

stem: A provider prescribes levothyroxine 0.15 mg orally daily. The available tablets are labeled levothyroxine 75 mcg. How many tablets should the nurse give?

options.text: 0.5 tablet
options.why: This inverts the ratio (75 ÷ 150). Half a 75-mcg tablet is only 37.5 mcg, a quarter of the prescribed dose.

options.text: 0.2 tablet
options.why: This results from converting 75 mcg incorrectly to 0.75 mg (0.15 ÷ 0.75). 75 mcg equals 0.075 mg, not 0.75 mg.

options.text: 2 tablets
options.why: Convert first: 0.15 mg × 1,000 = 150 mcg. Then 150 mcg ÷ 75 mcg × 1 tablet = 2 tablets.

options.text: 20 tablets
options.why: This results from converting 75 mcg incorrectly to 0.0075 mg (0.15 ÷ 0.0075). Any answer requiring 20 tablets signals a conversion error.

takeaway: Convert to the same unit before calculating: 1 mg = 1,000 mcg. An answer of many tablets or a tiny fraction of a tablet signals a conversion error.

stem: A client with a serum potassium of 3.3 mEq/L is prescribed potassium chloride 30 mEq orally once. The oral solution available is potassium chloride 20 mEq/15 mL. How many mL should the nurse prepare? (Round to the nearest tenth if needed.)

options.text: 40 mL
options.why: This multiplies by the wrong ratio (30 ÷ 15 × 20). 40 mL would deliver about 53 mEq, a dangerous overdose.

options.text: 10 mL
options.why: This inverts the ratio (20 ÷ 30 × 15). 10 mL delivers only about 13 mEq.

options.text: 15 mL
options.why: 15 mL is the volume that contains 20 mEq, not the prescribed 30 mEq.
Desired ÷ have × volume = 30 mEq ÷ 20 mEq × 15 mL = 22.5 mL. The liquid should then be diluted in water or juice as directed to reduce GI irritation.

takeaway: For oral liquids: desired ÷ have × volume. Dilute oral potassium solutions as directed and give with or after food.

stem: A client is prescribed ondansetron 6 mg orally every 8 hours as needed for nausea. The oral solution available is ondansetron 4 mg/5 mL. How many mL should the nurse give? (Round to the nearest tenth if needed.)

options.text: 1.5 mL
options.why: This divides 6 by 4 but forgets to multiply by the 5-mL volume that contains 4 mg.

options.text: 7.5 mL
options.why: Desired ÷ have × volume = 6 mg ÷ 4 mg × 5 mL = 7.5 mL.

options.text: 3.3 mL
options.why: This inverts the ratio (4 ÷ 6 × 5). 3.3 mL contains only about 2.7 mg.

options.text: 4.8 mL
options.why: This sets up the ratio incorrectly (6 ÷ 5 × 4), mixing the mg and mL values.

takeaway: Check that the unit in the answer matches the unit of the 'volume' term: mg cancel, mL remain.

stem: A child who weighs 44 lb has a fever. The provider prescribes ibuprofen 10 mg/kg orally every 6 to 8 hours as needed. The oral suspension available is ibuprofen 100 mg/5 mL. How many mL should the nurse give per dose?

options.text: 2 mL
options.why: This correctly finds 200 mg but divides by 100 without multiplying by the 5-mL volume, giving only 40 mg.

options.text: 22 mL
options.why: This uses the weight in pounds as if it were kilograms (44 × 10 = 440 mg), more than double the correct dose.

options.text: 10 mL
options.why: Weight: 44 lb ÷ 2.2 = 20 kg. Dose: 20 kg × 10 mg/kg = 200 mg. Volume: 200 mg ÷ 100 mg × 5 mL = 10 mL.
This multiplies the pounds by 2.2 instead of dividing (96.8 'kg'), producing a nearly fivefold overdose.

takeaway: Pediatric doses are ordered per kilogram: divide pounds by 2.2 first, then calculate the dose, then the volume.

stem: A child who weighs 24 kg is admitted with community-acquired pneumonia. The provider prescribes ceftriaxone 1,000 mg IV every 24 hours. The pediatric drug reference lists a dosage of 50 to 75 mg/kg/day for this indication. Which interpretation by the nurse is correct?

options.text: The dose is safe because the range is 545 to 818 mg/day.
options.why: This range comes from treating 24 kg as pounds and dividing by 2.2. The child's weight is already in kilograms.

options.text: The dose is safe because 1,000 mg is less than the 1,800-mg maximum.
options.why: Staying under the maximum is not enough; a dose below the minimum risks treatment failure and must also be questioned.

options.text: The dose exceeds the range of 50 to 75 mg and should be held.
options.why: This forgets to multiply by the child's weight; 50 to 75 mg is the per-kilogram amount, not the daily total.

options.text: The dose is below the safe range of 1,200 to 1,800 mg/day, so the nurse should clarify it with the provider.
options.why: Safe range = 24 kg × 50 mg/kg = 1,200 mg/day to 24 kg × 75 mg/kg = 1,800 mg/day. The prescribed 1,000 mg/day is below the minimum, so the nurse contacts the provider before giving it.

takeaway: A safe-dose check has two limits: question a dose above the maximum (toxicity) and one below the minimum (ineffective therapy).

stem: An infant who weighs 8 kg is prescribed ampicillin 500 mg IV every 6 hours. The drug reference lists a safe range of 100 to 200 mg/kg/day divided every 6 hours. What should the nurse conclude?

options.text: The dose is unsafe: 2,000 mg/day exceeds the maximum of 1,600 mg/day, so the nurse should hold it and contact the provider.
options.why: Safe range = 8 kg × 100 to 200 mg/kg/day = 800 to 1,600 mg/day (200 to 400 mg per dose every 6 hours). Ordered: 500 mg × 4 doses = 2,000 mg/day, which is above the maximum.

options.text: The dose is safe because 2,000 mg/day is below the maximum of 3,520 mg/day.
options.why: This converts 8 kg as if it were pounds and multiplies by 2.2 (17.6 × 200). The weight is already in kilograms.

options.text: The dose is safe because each 500-mg dose is below the maximum of 1,600 mg.
options.why: This compares a single dose with a daily maximum. The daily total (2,000 mg) must be compared with the daily range.

options.text: The dose is too low because the minimum is 800 mg per dose.
options.why: 800 mg is the minimum daily amount; divided every 6 hours, the minimum per dose is 200 mg.

takeaway: When a range is given per day, multiply the single dose by the number of doses per day (or divide the range by the dosing frequency) before comparing.

stem: A child who weighs 33 lb is prescribed morphine 1.5 mg IV every 4 hours as needed for postoperative pain. The pediatric reference lists 0.05 to 0.1 mg/kg/dose. What should the nurse conclude?

options.text: The dose is unsafe because it is below the range of 1.65 to 3.3 mg.
options.why: This uses 33 lb as if it were kilograms. Converting first gives 15 kg.

options.text: The dose is safe because it is within the range of 0.75 to 1.5 mg per dose.
options.why: 33 lb ÷ 2.2 = 15 kg. Range: 15 × 0.05 = 0.75 mg to 15 × 0.1 = 1.5 mg per dose. The prescribed 1.5 mg is at the top of the range, so it is safe to give with sedation and respiratory monitoring.

options.text: The dose is unsafe because it exceeds the 0.1-mg maximum.
options.why: This forgets to multiply the per-kilogram value by the child's weight.

options.text: The dose is unsafe because it exceeds the range of 0.34 to 0.68 mg.
options.why: This divides by 2.2 twice (15 ÷ 2.2 = 6.8 'kg'), producing a falsely low range.

takeaway: Convert pounds to kilograms once, calculate the per-dose range, and compare it with the single prescribed dose.

stem: A client is prescribed morphine 3 mg IV push every 3 hours as needed for pain. The vial is labeled morphine 4 mg/mL. How many mL should the nurse draw up? (Round to the nearest hundredth.)

options.text: 12 mL
options.why: This multiplies the dose by the concentration (3 × 4) instead of dividing.
This inverts the ratio (4 ÷ 3). 1.33 mL would deliver about 5.3 mg.

options.text: 7.5 mL
options.why: This is a decimal-place error; 7.5 mL of a 4 mg/mL solution would deliver 30 mg.
Desired ÷ have × volume = 3 mg ÷ 4 mg × 1 mL = 0.75 mL, drawn up in a 1-mL syringe for accuracy.

takeaway: For IV push volumes under 1 mL, use a 1-mL syringe and round to the hundredth only if the stem tells you to.

stem: A client who weighs 176 lb is prescribed enoxaparin 1 mg/kg subcutaneously every 12 hours. The prefilled syringe contains enoxaparin 100 mg/mL. How many mL should the nurse give? (Round to the nearest tenth.)

options.text: 0.8 mL
options.why: 176 lb ÷ 2.2 = 80 kg. Dose = 80 kg × 1 mg/kg = 80 mg. Volume = 80 mg ÷ 100 mg × 1 mL = 0.8 mL; expel the excess from the syringe before injecting.

options.text: 1.3 mL
options.why: This inverts the ratio (100 ÷ 80 = 1.25, rounded). It would deliver about 125 mg.

options.text: 1.8 mL
options.why: This uses the weight in pounds (176 mg), more than double the correct dose and a serious bleeding risk.

options.text: 8 mL
options.why: This is a decimal error; the subcutaneous route cannot hold 8 mL, which should prompt a recheck.

takeaway: Weight-based anticoagulants require converting pounds to kilograms first; an implausible injection volume signals a math error.

stem: A client is prescribed fentanyl 75 mcg IV push once before a procedure. The vial is labeled fentanyl 0.05 mg/mL. How many mL should the nurse give? (Round to the nearest tenth if needed.)

options.text: 0.7 mL
options.why: This inverts the ratio (50 ÷ 75 = 0.67, rounded to 0.7). At 50 mcg/mL, 0.7 mL delivers only 35 mcg.

options.text: 15 mL
options.why: This converts 0.05 mg incorrectly to 5 mcg. 0.05 mg × 1,000 = 50 mcg.

options.text: 1.5 mL
options.why: Convert: 0.05 mg/mL = 50 mcg/mL. Then 75 mcg ÷ 50 mcg × 1 mL = 1.5 mL.

options.text: 0.2 mL
options.why: This is a decimal-place error (0.15 rounded); it would deliver only about 10 mcg.

takeaway: When the order is in mcg and the label is in mg, convert the label to mcg (× 1,000) before setting up the ratio.

stem: A client is prescribed 1,000 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride IV over 6 hours by infusion pump. At what rate in mL/hr should the nurse set the pump? (Round to the nearest whole number.)

options.text: 167 mL/hr
options.why: Total volume ÷ total hours = 1,000 mL ÷ 6 hr = 166.7, rounded to 167 mL/hr.

options.text: 100 mL/hr
options.why: This rate would infuse the liter over 10 hours, not 6.

options.text: 28 mL/hr
options.why: This is the gravity drip rate in gtt/min using a 10 gtt/mL set (166.7 ÷ 6), not the pump rate in mL/hr.

options.text: 6 mL/hr
options.why: This divides hours by liters instead of volume by time.

takeaway: Pump rate (mL/hr) = total volume ÷ total time in hours.

stem: A client is prescribed cefazolin 2 g in 100 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride IV piggyback to infuse over 30 minutes. At what rate in mL/hr should the nurse program the pump?

options.text: 50 mL/hr
options.why: This rate would deliver 100 mL over 2 hours, not 30 minutes.

options.text: 100 mL/hr
options.why: This rate would deliver the bag over 60 minutes, twice as long as prescribed.

options.text: 3.3 mL/hr
options.why: 100 ÷ 30 = 3.3 is the rate in mL per minute; pumps are programmed in mL per hour.

options.text: 200 mL/hr
options.why: Convert minutes to hours: 30 min = 0.5 hr. Rate = 100 mL ÷ 0.5 hr = 200 mL/hr (or 100 mL ÷ 30 min × 60 min/hr = 200 mL/hr).

takeaway: For infusions shorter than an hour: mL ÷ minutes × 60 = mL/hr.

stem: A client is prescribed 1,000 mL of lactated Ringer's solution IV over 8 hours. No infusion pump is available, and the gravity tubing has a drop factor of 10 gtt/mL. At how many gtt/min should the nurse regulate the infusion? (Round to the nearest whole drop.)

options.text: 13 gtt/min
options.why: This divides the hourly rate by the drop factor (125 ÷ 10) instead of multiplying by it and dividing by 60.

options.text: 21 gtt/min
options.why: 125 mL/hr × 10 gtt/mL ÷ 60 min = 20.8, rounded to 21 gtt/min. (Volume × drop factor ÷ minutes = 1,000 × 10 ÷ 480 = 20.8.)

options.text: 31 gtt/min
options.why: This uses a drop factor of 15 gtt/mL instead of the 10 gtt/mL on this tubing.

options.text: 125 gtt/min
options.why: 125 is the rate in mL/hr; it has not been converted to drops per minute.

takeaway: gtt/min = total mL × drop factor ÷ total minutes. Always read the drop factor on the tubing package.

stem: A client is to receive 1,200 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride IV over 10 hours by gravity. The tubing drop factor is 15 gtt/mL. At how many gtt/min should the nurse set the infusion? (Round to the nearest whole drop.)

options.text: 120 gtt/min
options.why: 120 is the rate in mL/hr; it has not been converted using the drop factor.

options.text: 40 gtt/min
options.why: This uses a drop factor of 20 gtt/mL instead of 15.

options.text: 30 gtt/min
options.why: 1,200 mL ÷ 10 hr = 120 mL/hr. 120 mL × 15 gtt/mL ÷ 60 min = 30 gtt/min.

options.text: 20 gtt/min
options.why: This uses a drop factor of 10 gtt/mL instead of 15.

takeaway: With a 15 gtt/mL set, gtt/min = mL/hr ÷ 4; with 10 gtt/mL, ÷ 6; with 20 gtt/mL, ÷ 3; with 60 gtt/mL, gtt/min = mL/hr.

stem: A client is prescribed 100 mL of an IV antibiotic to infuse over 30 minutes by gravity. The secondary tubing has a drop factor of 20 gtt/mL. At how many gtt/min should the nurse regulate the infusion? (Round to the nearest whole drop.)

options.text: 67 gtt/min
options.why: 100 mL × 20 gtt/mL ÷ 30 min = 66.7, rounded to 67 gtt/min.

options.text: 33 gtt/min
options.why: This uses a drop factor of 10 gtt/mL instead of 20.

options.text: 50 gtt/min
options.why: This uses a drop factor of 15 gtt/mL instead of 20.

options.text: 200 gtt/min
options.why: 200 is the equivalent rate in mL/hr, not gtt/min.

takeaway: For short infusions, divide by the actual number of minutes (30), not by 60.

stem: A 2-year-old is prescribed D5 0.9% sodium chloride 600 mL IV over 24 hours. The nurse is using microdrip (60 gtt/mL) tubing with a volume-control chamber. At how many gtt/min should the infusion run? (Round to the nearest whole drop.)

options.text: 6 gtt/min
options.why: This uses a macrodrip factor of 15 gtt/mL instead of the 60 gtt/mL microdrip set.

options.text: 8 gtt/min
options.why: This uses a drop factor of 20 gtt/mL instead of 60.

options.text: 25 gtt/min
options.why: 600 mL ÷ 24 hr = 25 mL/hr. 25 mL × 60 gtt/mL ÷ 60 min = 25 gtt/min. With microdrip tubing, gtt/min always equals mL/hr.

options.text: 1,500 gtt/min
options.why: This multiplies by the drop factor but forgets to divide by 60 minutes.

takeaway: With 60 gtt/mL microdrip tubing, the drip rate in gtt/min equals the hourly rate in mL/hr.

stem: A mechanically ventilated client who weighs 198 lb is prescribed propofol 25 mcg/kg/min IV for sedation. The propofol emulsion is 10 mg/mL. At what rate in mL/hr should the nurse set the pump? (Round to the nearest tenth.)

options.text: 0.2 mL/hr
options.why: This finds the volume needed per minute (25 × 90 ÷ 10,000 = 0.225 mL/min) and forgets to multiply by 60 to get an hourly rate.

options.text: 13.5 mL/hr
options.why: Weight: 198 lb ÷ 2.2 = 90 kg. Dose: 25 mcg/kg/min × 90 kg = 2,250 mcg/min × 60 = 135,000 mcg/hr (135 mg/hr). Concentration: 10 mg/mL = 10,000 mcg/mL. Rate: 135,000 ÷ 10,000 = 13.5 mL/hr.

options.text: 29.7 mL/hr
options.why: This uses the weight in pounds (198) instead of kilograms (25 × 198 × 60 ÷ 10,000 = 29.7), more than doubling the sedative dose.

options.text: 135 mL/hr
options.why: This uses a concentration of 1,000 mcg/mL (1 mg/mL) instead of 10,000 mcg/mL, a tenfold overdose that could cause profound hypotension and apnea.

takeaway: mL/hr = mcg/kg/min × kg × 60 ÷ mcg/mL. Propofol is 10 mg/mL (10,000 mcg/mL); convert weight to kilograms and the concentration to mcg/mL before calculating.

stem: A client who weighs 154 lb has dobutamine 250 mg in 250 mL of D5W infusing at 21 mL/hr. The nurse calculates the dose the client is receiving to compare it with the prescription. What dose is infusing in mcg/kg/min? (Round to the nearest tenth.)

options.text: 2.3 mcg/kg/min
options.why: This divides by the weight in pounds (154) instead of kilograms (70).

options.text: 300 mcg/kg/min
options.why: This divides by the weight but forgets to divide by 60 minutes, giving a per-hour value.

options.text: 350 mcg/kg/min
options.why: 350 is the dose in mcg/min; it has not yet been divided by the client's weight.

options.text: 5 mcg/kg/min
options.why: Concentration: 250 mg ÷ 250 mL = 1 mg/mL = 1,000 mcg/mL. Hourly: 21 mL/hr × 1,000 = 21,000 mcg/hr ÷ 60 = 350 mcg/min. Weight: 154 ÷ 2.2 = 70 kg. 350 ÷ 70 = 5 mcg/kg/min.

takeaway: To check a running weight-based drip: mL/hr × mcg/mL ÷ 60 ÷ kg = mcg/kg/min.
