stem: A client with acute decompensated heart failure is prescribed nitroglycerin 10 mcg/min IV. The premixed bag contains nitroglycerin 50 mg in 250 mL of D5W. At what rate in mL/hr should the nurse set the pump?

options.text: 0.05 mL/hr
options.why: This finds the mL needed per minute (10 ÷ 200) and forgets to multiply by 60.

options.text: 3 mL/hr
options.why: Concentration: 50,000 mcg ÷ 250 mL = 200 mcg/mL. Dose per hour: 10 mcg/min × 60 = 600 mcg/hr. Rate: 600 ÷ 200 = 3 mL/hr.

options.text: 20 mL/hr
options.why: This inverts the ratio (200 ÷ 10).

options.text: 30 mL/hr
options.why: This miscalculates the concentration as 20 mcg/mL, a tenfold error that would deliver 100 mcg/min.

takeaway: For mcg/min drips (no weight): mL/hr = mcg/min × 60 ÷ mcg/mL.

stem: A client who weighs 92 kg is started on a weight-based heparin protocol at 18 units/kg/hr. The premixed bag contains heparin 25,000 units in 500 mL of D5W. At what rate in mL/hr should the nurse set the pump? (Round to the nearest tenth.)

options.text: 16.6 mL/hr
options.why: This uses a concentration of 100 units/mL (as in a 25,000 units/250 mL bag). This bag is 500 mL, so it contains 50 units/mL.

options.text: 27.6 mL/hr
options.why: This divides the hourly dose by 60 (1,656 ÷ 60 = 27.6) as if converting to a per-minute value. Heparin is ordered per hour, and the hourly dose must be divided by the concentration (50 units/mL), not by 60.

options.text: 33.1 mL/hr
options.why: Dose: 18 units/kg/hr × 92 kg = 1,656 units/hr. Concentration: 25,000 units ÷ 500 mL = 50 units/mL. Rate: 1,656 ÷ 50 = 33.12, rounded to 33.1 mL/hr. Heparin is a high-alert drug, so an independent double-check is required.

options.text: 66.2 mL/hr
options.why: This uses 25 units/mL, as if the bag were 1,000 mL, and would double the dose.

takeaway: Heparin infusions: units/hr ÷ units/mL = mL/hr. Recalculate the concentration from the bag label every time; it differs between 250-mL and 500-mL bags.

stem: A heparin protocol calls for an IV bolus of 80 units/kg before the infusion starts. The client weighs 154 lb. The vial available is heparin 5,000 units/mL. How many mL should the nurse give for the bolus? (Round to the nearest tenth.)

options.text: 0.9 mL
options.why: This inverts the ratio (5,000 ÷ 5,600).

options.text: 2.5 mL
options.why: This uses the weight in pounds (154 × 80 = 12,320 units), more than double the correct bolus.
This uses a concentration of 500 units/mL, a tenfold decimal error.

options.text: 1.1 mL
options.why: 154 lb ÷ 2.2 = 70 kg. Bolus: 70 × 80 = 5,600 units. Volume: 5,600 ÷ 5,000 × 1 mL = 1.12, rounded to 1.1 mL.

takeaway: Heparin comes in many vial strengths (for example 1,000, 5,000 and 10,000 units/mL); confirm the concentration and have a second nurse verify bolus volumes.

stem: A client who weighs 165 lb with diabetic ketoacidosis is prescribed regular insulin 0.1 units/kg/hr IV. The infusion contains regular insulin 100 units in 100 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride. At what rate in mL/hr should the nurse set the pump? (Round to the nearest tenth.)

options.text: 7.5 mL/hr
options.why: 165 lb ÷ 2.2 = 75 kg. Dose: 75 × 0.1 = 7.5 units/hr. Concentration: 100 units ÷ 100 mL = 1 unit/mL. Rate: 7.5 ÷ 1 = 7.5 mL/hr.

options.text: 0.8 mL/hr
options.why: This is a decimal-place error (0.75 rounded to 0.8). At 1 unit/mL, 0.8 mL/hr delivers only 0.8 unit/hr, about one-tenth of the prescribed dose.

options.text: 16.5 mL/hr
options.why: This uses the weight in pounds instead of kilograms, more than doubling the insulin dose.

options.text: 75 mL/hr
options.why: This multiplies by the weight but omits the 0.1 units/kg factor, a tenfold overdose.

takeaway: Insulin drips: kg × units/kg/hr = units/hr, then ÷ units/mL. A 1 unit/mL bag makes units/hr equal mL/hr.

stem: During handoff, the nurse checks a client's continuous heparin infusion. The bag is labeled heparin 25,000 units in 500 mL of D5W, and the pump is running at 18 mL/hr. How many units per hour is the client receiving?

options.text: 0.36 units/hr
options.why: This divides the rate by the concentration (18 ÷ 50) instead of multiplying the rate by the concentration.

options.text: 1,800 units/hr
options.why: This assumes 100 units/mL, the concentration of a 25,000 units/250 mL bag. This bag is 500 mL, so it contains 50 units/mL, and the client receives half this amount.

options.text: 450 units/hr
options.why: This assumes 25 units/mL, as if the 25,000 units were in 1,000 mL.

options.text: 900 units/hr
options.why: Concentration: 25,000 units ÷ 500 mL = 50 units/mL. Dose: 18 mL/hr × 50 units/mL = 900 units/hr. The nurse compares this with the current prescription and protocol.

takeaway: Units/hr = mL/hr × units/mL. Calculate the concentration from the bag actually hanging; heparin bags come in more than one volume.

stem: A client is prescribed ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once. The vial contains ceftriaxone 1 g powder. The label states that adding 2.1 mL of diluent yields 350 mg/mL. After reconstituting as directed, how many mL should the nurse withdraw? (Round to the nearest tenth.)

options.text: 0.7 mL
options.why: This inverts the ratio (350 ÷ 500).

options.text: 1.1 mL
options.why: This takes half of the 2.1 mL of diluent, ignoring that the powder adds volume. The label's final concentration (350 mg/mL) must be used.

options.text: 1.4 mL
options.why: Use the concentration after reconstitution: 500 mg ÷ 350 mg × 1 mL = 1.43, rounded to 1.4 mL.

options.text: 2.1 mL
options.why: 2.1 mL is the diluent volume, not the dose volume. At 350 mg/mL, 2.1 mL contains about 735 mg, far more than the prescribed 500 mg.

takeaway: After reconstitution, calculate with the final concentration printed on the label, not the diluent volume, because powders displace volume.

stem: A client is prescribed vancomycin 750 mg IV every 12 hours. The pharmacy sends a 1-g vial with directions to reconstitute with 20 mL of sterile water to yield 50 mg/mL, then further dilute the dose for infusion. How many mL of the reconstituted solution contain the prescribed dose?

options.text: 7.5 mL
options.why: This uses a concentration of 100 mg/mL; the label gives 50 mg/mL.

options.text: 15 mL
options.why: 750 mg ÷ 50 mg × 1 mL = 15 mL, which is then added to the prescribed diluent for infusion (vancomycin is never given IV push).

options.text: 20 mL
options.why: This is the entire vial (1 g), 250 mg more than prescribed.
This inverts the ratio (1,000 ÷ 750 × 20); it is more than the vial holds, which signals an error.

takeaway: Reconstituted dose volume = desired ÷ concentration per mL; an answer larger than the vial's total volume is always wrong.

stem: The nurse totals a client's intake for an 8-hour shift: 240 mL of coffee, 120 mL of apple juice, 180 mL of broth, and 300 mL of ice chips (facility policy: record ice chips as half their volume). An IV of 0.9% sodium chloride ran at 75 mL/hr for the entire shift, and two IV piggyback antibiotics of 50 mL each were given. What total intake should the nurse record?

options.why: This counts the ice chips at full volume (300 mL) instead of half.
This omits the 100 mL from the two IV piggybacks, which count as intake.

options.text: 690 mL
options.why: This counts only oral fluids and ice chips and leaves out all IV intake.

takeaway: Intake includes oral fluids, ice chips (per policy, often half volume), primary IV fluids, piggybacks, flushes and tube feedings.

stem: A postoperative client's intake over 12 hours was 1,800 mL. Output: urine 350 mL, 425 mL, and 275 mL; emesis 150 mL; and Jackson-Pratt drain 60 mL. What is the client's net fluid balance for the 12 hours?

options.why: This leaves out the 150 mL of emesis, which is part of output.
This leaves out the 60 mL of drain output, which must also be counted.
The sign is reversed. Intake exceeds output, so the balance is positive.
Output: 350 + 425 + 275 + 150 + 60 = 1,260 mL. Balance: 1,800 − 1,260 = +540 mL (intake exceeds output).

takeaway: Output includes urine, emesis, drains, NG suction and liquid stool; net balance = intake − output.

stem: A mother reports that her infant weighed 17 lb 6 oz at the last clinic visit. The nurse needs the weight in kilograms for a medication calculation. What is the infant's weight? (Round to the nearest tenth.)

options.text: 7.7 kg
options.why: This ignores the 6 oz (17 ÷ 2.2 = 7.7).

options.text: 8 kg
options.why: This treats 6 oz as 0.6 lb (17.6 ÷ 2.2). There are 16 oz in a pound, so 6 oz = 0.375 lb.
This multiplies by 2.2 instead of dividing. A kilogram value is always smaller than the pound value.

options.text: 7.9 kg
options.why: 6 oz ÷ 16 = 0.375 lb, so the weight is 17.375 lb. 17.375 ÷ 2.2 = 7.897, rounded to 7.9 kg.

takeaway: Convert ounces to pounds (÷ 16) before converting pounds to kilograms (÷ 2.2).

stem: A child who weighs 37.4 lb with an asthma exacerbation is prescribed prednisolone 1 mg/kg orally once daily. The oral solution available is prednisolone 15 mg/5 mL. How many mL should the nurse give? (Round to the nearest tenth.)

options.text: 4.4 mL
options.why: This inverts the ratio (15 ÷ 17 × 5) and would underdose the child.

options.text: 5.7 mL
options.why: 37.4 lb ÷ 2.2 = 17 kg. Dose: 17 kg × 1 mg/kg = 17 mg. Volume: 17 mg ÷ 15 mg × 5 mL = 5.67, rounded to 5.7 mL.
This uses the weight in pounds (37.4 mg) instead of kilograms, more than doubling the dose.

options.text: 1.1 mL
options.why: This divides 17 by 15 but forgets to multiply by the 5-mL volume.

takeaway: Three steps for pediatric liquids: lb → kg, kg × mg/kg = mg, then mg ÷ concentration × volume = mL.

stem: A client with chronic kidney disease who missed two hemodialysis sessions has a serum potassium of 6.9 mEq/L. Which ECG change should the nurse expect to see on the cardiac monitor?

options.text: Tall, narrow, peaked T waves
options.why: Hyperkalemia (normal potassium 3.5 to 5 mEq/L) first produces tall, peaked T waves; as it worsens, the PR interval lengthens, P waves flatten, the QRS widens, and a sine-wave pattern or ventricular fibrillation can follow.

options.text: A prominent U wave after the T wave
options.why: U waves are characteristic of hypokalemia, not hyperkalemia.

options.text: A prolonged QT interval
options.why: A prolonged QT interval is typical of hypocalcemia or hypomagnesemia.

options.text: ST-segment depression with flattened T waves
options.why: ST depression with flattened T waves is seen with hypokalemia (and with digoxin effect).

takeaway: Hyperkalemia: peaked T waves → wide QRS → sine wave. Hypokalemia: flat T waves, ST depression, U waves.

stem: A client who has been taking furosemide 40 mg twice daily reports leg cramps and generalized weakness. The serum potassium is 2.8 mEq/L. Which cardiac monitor finding is most consistent with this result?

options.text: Widening of the QRS complex with peaked T waves
options.why: A widened QRS with peaked T waves reflects hyperkalemia.

options.text: A shortened QT interval
options.why: A shortened QT interval is associated with hypercalcemia.

options.text: Absent P waves with a sine-wave pattern
options.why: A sine-wave pattern is a sign of severe hyperkalemia, the opposite imbalance.

options.text: Flattened T waves and a prominent U wave
options.why: Hypokalemia (normal 3.5 to 5 mEq/L) slows ventricular repolarization, producing flattened or inverted T waves, ST depression and a prominent U wave. It also raises the risk of dysrhythmias, especially in clients taking digoxin.

takeaway: Loop diuretics waste potassium; look for muscle cramps, weakness, flat T waves and U waves.

stem: A client with a serum potassium of 3.1 mEq/L is prescribed potassium chloride 10 mEq in 100 mL IV over 1 hour through a peripheral IV. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Administer the infusion with an electronic infusion pump.
options.why: Correct. IV potassium is a high-alert medication and must be given by pump so the rate cannot run in uncontrolled.

options.text: Confirm adequate urine output before starting the infusion.
options.why: Correct. Potassium is excreted by the kidneys; giving it to a client with oliguria (for example, less than 0.5 mL/kg/hr) can cause dangerous hyperkalemia.

options.text: Give the remaining volume as a slow IV push if the infusion falls behind schedule.
options.why: Incorrect. Potassium is never given by IV push or bolus; a rapid rise in serum potassium can cause cardiac arrest.

options.text: Assess the IV site frequently and ask the client to report burning.
options.why: Correct. Potassium chloride irritates peripheral veins and can cause pain and phlebitis; infiltration can injure tissue.

options.text: Increase the rate so that the dose infuses over 15 minutes.
options.why: Incorrect. That would deliver 40 mEq/hr, far above the usual peripheral limit of about 10 mEq/hr; higher rates require a central line and continuous cardiac monitoring per protocol.

options.text: Inject a vial of potassium chloride into a hanging bag of 0.9% sodium chloride if more potassium is ordered.
options.why: Incorrect. Additives are never injected into a hanging bag because the concentrated potassium can pool and be delivered as a bolus; use premixed bags from pharmacy.

takeaway: IV potassium: always diluted, always by pump, never IV push, usually no faster than 10 mEq/hr peripherally, and only with adequate urine output.

stem: The nurse teaches a client who has been prescribed extended-release potassium chloride tablets along with furosemide. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I'll take the tablet with a full glass of water right after a meal."
options.why: This is correct. Taking oral potassium with food and plenty of fluid reduces GI irritation.

options.text: "I'll swallow the tablet whole without crushing or chewing it."
options.why: This is correct. Crushing an extended-release tablet releases the full dose at once and can irritate or ulcerate the GI tract.

options.text: "I'll switch to a salt substitute so I can cut back on sodium."
options.why: This indicates a need for further teaching. Most salt substitutes contain potassium chloride, and using them with a potassium supplement can cause hyperkalemia.

options.text: "I'll call my provider if I have black stools or stomach pain."
options.why: This is correct. Black stools or abdominal pain can signal GI bleeding or ulceration from potassium tablets and must be reported.

takeaway: Clients taking potassium supplements should avoid salt substitutes unless the provider approves them, take tablets with food, and never crush extended-release forms.

stem: A client with a serum potassium of 6.8 mEq/L receives regular insulin 10 units IV with 50 mL of 50% dextrose. Which assessment is most important to detect a complication of this treatment over the next few hours?

options.text: Deep tendon reflexes
options.why: Reflex changes are monitored with magnesium imbalances, not insulin–dextrose therapy.

options.text: Urine specific gravity
options.why: Specific gravity reflects hydration status and does not detect the main complication of this treatment.

options.text: Point-of-care blood glucose
options.why: Insulin shifts potassium into cells but can also cause hypoglycemia, which may occur hours after the dose, especially in clients with kidney disease. Glucose is checked frequently per protocol (for example, hourly for several hours).

options.text: Serum sodium
options.why: Sodium is not significantly affected by this treatment.

takeaway: IV insulin for hyperkalemia lowers potassium temporarily; monitor glucose closely for hypoglycemia and recheck potassium because it shifts back.

stem: A client was admitted with a serum sodium of 114 mEq/L from chronic thiazide use. Twenty-four hours later, the sodium is 129 mEq/L. On day 3, the client develops slurred speech, difficulty swallowing and weakness in all four extremities. Which complication should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Cerebral edema from persistent hyponatremia
options.why: Cerebral edema occurs when sodium is low and water shifts into brain cells. This client's sodium has risen substantially, and the new symptoms followed the rise.

options.text: Osmotic demyelination syndrome
options.why: A 15-mEq/L rise in 24 hours exceeds the safe correction limit (generally no more than 8 to 12 mEq/L per 24 hours, at the lower end for high-risk clients). Rapid correction shrinks brain cells and damages myelin, especially in the pons; dysarthria, dysphagia and quadriparesis typically appear 2 to 6 days later. The provider must be notified immediately.

options.text: Hypercalcemia from thiazide therapy
options.why: Thiazides can raise calcium slightly, but hypercalcemia causes fatigue, constipation and confusion, not this pattern of bulbar signs and quadriparesis.

options.text: Water intoxication from excess free water
options.why: Water intoxication lowers sodium; this client's sodium has risen.

takeaway: Correct chronic hyponatremia slowly and recheck sodium often; overly rapid correction can cause osmotic demyelination (dysarthria, dysphagia, paralysis).

stem: An 84-year-old client from a long-term care facility has a serum sodium of 156 mEq/L, dry mucous membranes and restlessness. Blood pressure is 118/70 mmHg and heart rate is 92/min. Which prescription should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: 3% sodium chloride at 30 mL/hr
options.why: Hypertonic saline adds sodium and would worsen hypernatremia.

options.text: D5W IV at a controlled rate with serial serum sodium checks
options.why: Hypernatremia (normal sodium 135 to 145 mEq/L) in a hemodynamically stable client is treated by replacing free water gradually with a hypotonic fluid such as D5W, while sodium is checked frequently so it does not fall too quickly.

options.text: 0.45% sodium chloride infused rapidly to normalize sodium within 4 hours
options.why: A hypotonic fluid is appropriate, but lowering sodium rapidly lets water rush into brain cells and can cause cerebral edema and seizures.

options.text: Fluid restriction to 1,000 mL per day
options.why: Fluid restriction treats dilutional hyponatremia; it would worsen this client's water deficit.

takeaway: Hypernatremia is a water deficit: replace free water slowly with hypotonic fluid and monitor sodium closely to avoid cerebral edema.

stem: The day after a total thyroidectomy, a client reports tingling around the mouth and in the fingertips. When the nurse taps the facial nerve just in front of the ear, the client's upper lip twitches. Which imbalance does this finding indicate?

options.text: Hypermagnesemia
options.why: Hypermagnesemia depresses neuromuscular activity (weak reflexes, lethargy), the opposite of this finding.

options.text: Hypercalcemia
options.why: High calcium decreases neuromuscular excitability and causes weakness, not twitching.

options.text: Hyperkalemia
options.why: Hyperkalemia causes muscle weakness and ECG changes; it does not produce a positive facial nerve test.

options.text: Hypocalcemia
options.why: This is a positive Chvostek sign. Accidental injury to or removal of the parathyroid glands during thyroidectomy can lower calcium (normal total calcium about 9 to 10.5 mg/dL), causing perioral tingling, Chvostek and Trousseau signs, and possibly laryngospasm or seizures.

takeaway: After thyroid or parathyroid surgery, watch for hypocalcemia: perioral tingling, Chvostek sign (facial twitch) and Trousseau sign (carpal spasm with BP cuff).

stem: A client who takes digoxin 0.125 mg daily has symptomatic hypocalcemia, and the provider prescribes IV calcium gluconate. Which action is most important for the nurse to take during the infusion?

options.text: Maintain continuous cardiac monitoring
options.why: Calcium increases myocardial contractility and enhances the effect of digoxin, raising the risk of dysrhythmias and digoxin toxicity. The client needs continuous ECG monitoring and a controlled infusion rate.

options.text: Give the dose as a rapid IV push to correct the calcium quickly
options.why: Rapid IV calcium can cause bradycardia, dysrhythmias, hypotension and cardiac arrest; it is given slowly as prescribed.

options.text: Infuse it through the same line as a sodium bicarbonate infusion
options.why: Calcium and bicarbonate form a precipitate when mixed and must not share a line.

options.text: Apply ice to the IV site to reduce discomfort
options.why: Site assessment matters because calcium is irritating, but ice does not address the major risk for this client, which is cardiac.

takeaway: IV calcium in a client taking digoxin requires continuous ECG monitoring; never give calcium rapidly, and never mix it with bicarbonate or phosphate.

stem: A client with alcohol use disorder has received potassium replacement for 2 days, but the serum potassium remains 3 mEq/L. Today the serum magnesium is 1.1 mg/dL. What should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Increasing the peripheral potassium infusion to 40 mEq/hr
options.why: Faster peripheral potassium is unsafe and would not fix the underlying cause of the persistent loss.

options.text: Replacing magnesium, because low magnesium causes ongoing renal potassium loss
options.why: Magnesium (normal about 1.7 to 2.2 mg/dL; ranges vary by laboratory) is needed to retain potassium in the kidney. Hypokalemia often will not correct until magnesium is replaced, which is common in alcohol use disorder.

options.text: Restricting oral fluids to concentrate the serum potassium
options.why: Fluid restriction does not correct potassium depletion and may cause dehydration.

options.text: Holding potassium because the low level is likely a lab error
options.why: Two days of consistently low values with a low magnesium reflect a real deficit, not a lab error.

takeaway: Refractory hypokalemia: check and correct magnesium first; the kidneys keep wasting potassium until magnesium is replaced.

stem: A client with severe malnutrition (BMI 15) is started on parenteral nutrition. Which laboratory value is most important for the nurse to monitor closely during the first several days to detect refeeding syndrome?

options.text: Serum albumin
options.why: Albumin reflects long-term protein status and changes slowly; it does not detect the acute shifts of refeeding.

options.text: Serum amylase
options.why: Amylase is used to assess the pancreas and is not the main marker of refeeding syndrome.

options.text: Serum phosphorus
options.why: When feeding restarts, insulin drives phosphorus (along with potassium and magnesium) into cells. Hypophosphatemia (normal about 2.5 to 4.5 mg/dL) can cause muscle weakness, respiratory failure, heart failure and dysrhythmias.

options.text: Serum ammonia
options.why: Ammonia is monitored in liver failure, not refeeding syndrome.

takeaway: Refeeding syndrome: start nutrition slowly in malnourished clients and monitor phosphorus, potassium and magnesium closely in the first days.

stem: A postoperative client using a morphine PCA pump is difficult to arouse and has a respiratory rate of 8/min. ABGs: pH 7.29, PaCO2 56 mmHg, HCO3 25 mEq/L. How should the nurse interpret these results?

options.text: Uncompensated respiratory acidosis
options.why: The pH is low (normal 7.35 to 7.45), PaCO2 is high (normal 35 to 45 mmHg), and HCO3 is normal (22 to 26 mEq/L). Opioid-induced hypoventilation retains CO2, and the kidneys have not yet compensated.

options.text: Partially compensated metabolic acidosis
options.why: In metabolic acidosis, HCO3 would be low; here it is normal and the PaCO2 is the abnormal value matching the acidosis.

options.text: Uncompensated respiratory alkalosis
options.why: Respiratory alkalosis has a high pH and low PaCO2, the opposite of these values.

options.text: Fully compensated respiratory acidosis
options.why: Full compensation requires a pH back within 7.35 to 7.45 and an elevated HCO3; neither is present.

takeaway: Hypoventilation (opioids, sedation) retains CO2 and causes respiratory acidosis; HCO3 rises only after the kidneys compensate over days.

stem: A client with type 1 diabetes is admitted with Kussmaul respirations and a blood glucose of 512 mg/dL. ABGs: pH 7.24, PaCO2 28 mmHg, HCO3 12 mEq/L. How should the nurse interpret these results?

options.text: Uncompensated metabolic acidosis
options.why: The PaCO2 is already low, which shows the lungs are compensating, so this is not uncompensated.

options.text: Partially compensated respiratory alkalosis
options.why: The pH is acidic, so the primary problem cannot be an alkalosis.

options.text: Partially compensated metabolic acidosis
options.why: pH is low (acidosis); HCO3 is low (metabolic cause, matching the pH); PaCO2 is low as the lungs blow off CO2 (Kussmaul breathing), but the pH is still abnormal, so compensation is partial.

options.text: Fully compensated respiratory acidosis
options.why: Respiratory acidosis requires a high PaCO2; this PaCO2 is low.

takeaway: If both PaCO2 and HCO3 are abnormal in the same direction as each other and the pH is still abnormal, the imbalance is partially compensated.

stem: A client with long-standing COPD is seen in the clinic in stable condition. ABGs: pH 7.36, PaCO2 58 mmHg, HCO3 32 mEq/L. How should the nurse interpret these results?

options.text: Partially compensated respiratory acidosis
options.why: Partial compensation means the pH is still outside 7.35 to 7.45; here it is within normal limits.

options.text: Fully compensated metabolic alkalosis
options.why: If metabolic alkalosis were the primary problem, a normal pH would fall on the alkaline side (above 7.4). A pH of 7.36 points to an acid primary process.

options.text: Fully compensated respiratory acidosis
options.why: pH is normal but on the acid side of 7.4; PaCO2 is high (acid), matching that side, so the primary problem is respiratory acidosis. HCO3 is high from renal compensation, and because the pH is normal, compensation is full. This is typical of chronic CO2 retention in COPD.

options.text: Uncompensated metabolic alkalosis
options.why: An uncompensated alkalosis would have a pH above 7.45 and a normal PaCO2.

takeaway: With a normal pH, use 7.4 as the midpoint: the value (PaCO2 or HCO3) that matches the side the pH leans toward is the primary problem.

stem: The nurse uses a systematic approach to interpret an arterial blood gas. Place the steps in the order the nurse should perform them.

options.text: Evaluate the PaCO2 and decide whether it reflects respiratory acidosis, respiratory alkalosis or a normal value.
options.why: Second: after classifying the pH, look at the respiratory component (normal 35 to 45 mmHg).

options.text: Determine whether compensation is absent, partial or full by checking the opposite system and whether the pH is in normal range.
options.why: Fifth: compensation is judged last, once the primary problem is known.

options.text: Identify which value (PaCO2 or HCO3) matches the pH to name the primary disorder.
options.why: Fourth: the value that moves in the same direction as the pH is the primary cause.

options.text: Evaluate the pH and decide whether it indicates acidosis, alkalosis or a normal value.
options.why: First: the pH (normal 7.35 to 7.45) shows the overall acid–base direction.

options.text: Evaluate the HCO3 and decide whether it reflects metabolic acidosis, metabolic alkalosis or a normal value.
options.why: Third: then look at the metabolic component (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L).

takeaway: ABG steps: pH → PaCO2 → HCO3 → match the primary cause → assess compensation.

stem: The nurse reviews prescriptions for 0.45% sodium chloride IV. For which clients should the nurse question this fluid? Select all that apply.

options.text: A client with a head injury and signs of increased intracranial pressure
options.why: Correct. A hypotonic solution moves water into cells, including brain cells, and can worsen cerebral edema.

options.text: A client 6 hours after major burns with a blood pressure of 84/50 mmHg
options.why: Correct. Hypotonic fluid shifts out of the vascular space and does little to restore circulating volume; burn resuscitation uses isotonic fluid such as lactated Ringer's.

options.text: A hemodynamically stable client with hypernatremia from inadequate water intake
options.why: Incorrect. Hypotonic fluid is appropriate for replacing free water in hypernatremia when given at a controlled rate.

options.text: A client in hypovolemic shock from a GI bleed
options.why: Correct. Shock requires isotonic crystalloid and blood products to expand intravascular volume; hypotonic fluid leaves the vessels.

options.text: A client with DKA whose blood pressure has stabilized after initial 0.9% sodium chloride and whose corrected serum sodium is 147 mEq/L
options.why: Incorrect. Per ADA guidance, after initial isotonic resuscitation in DKA, 0.45% sodium chloride is appropriate when the corrected sodium is normal or high.

takeaway: Hypotonic fluids hydrate cells; avoid them when intravascular volume is needed (shock, burns) or when brain swelling is a risk (increased ICP).

stem: A client with heart failure and chronic kidney disease has received several liters of IV fluid over 2 days. Which findings indicate fluid volume excess? Select all that apply.

options.text: Bounding radial pulse
options.why: Correct. Increased circulating volume produces a full, bounding pulse.

options.text: Crackles in both lung bases
options.why: Correct. Excess fluid backs up into the pulmonary capillaries and leaks into the alveoli.

options.text: Neck veins distended with the head of the bed at 45 degrees
options.why: Correct. Jugular venous distention at 45 degrees reflects elevated venous pressure from excess volume.

options.text: Urine specific gravity of 1.035
options.why: Incorrect. A high specific gravity reflects concentrated urine, seen with fluid volume deficit; excess volume tends to lower it (normal about 1.005 to 1.030).

options.text: Hematocrit of 52%
options.why: Incorrect. Hemoconcentration (high hematocrit) suggests a deficit; fluid excess dilutes the blood and lowers hematocrit.

options.text: Weight gain of 1.5 kg (3.3 lb) since yesterday
options.why: Correct. A rapid gain of 1 kg (2.2 lb) corresponds to about 1 L of retained fluid.

takeaway: Fluid volume excess: bounding pulse, JVD, crackles, edema, rapid weight gain and dilutional labs (low hematocrit, low BUN, low specific gravity).

stem: An 88-year-old client has had diarrhea for 3 days. Which finding best supports fluid volume deficit in this client?

options.text: Blood pressure of 128/76 mmHg lying and 104/62 mmHg standing, with the heart rate rising from 88 to 112/min
options.why: A drop in systolic BP of 20 mmHg or more with a rise in heart rate on standing (orthostatic hypotension) reliably reflects reduced intravascular volume.

options.text: Skin on the back of the hand that stays tented after pinching
options.why: Older adults lose skin elasticity with age, so skin turgor on the hand is an unreliable indicator of hydration in this population.

options.text: Urine specific gravity of 1.010
options.why: This is within normal limits; a deficit would usually produce concentrated urine with a high specific gravity.

options.text: Hematocrit of 38%
options.why: This is within normal range; fluid volume deficit usually raises hematocrit through hemoconcentration.

takeaway: In older adults, rely on orthostatic vital signs, weight change, mucous membranes and labs rather than skin turgor to assess fluid deficit.

stem: A client's peripheral IV of 0.9% sodium chloride is infusing at 100 mL/hr. The client reports that the area around the site feels tight. Which assessment finding confirms infiltration?

options.text: The site is red and warm, with a firm, tender cord along the vein.
options.why: Redness, warmth and a palpable cord indicate phlebitis (inflammation of the vein), not infiltration.

options.text: The site is cool, pale and swollen, and the infusion has slowed.
options.why: Infiltration occurs when non-vesicant fluid leaks into surrounding tissue, producing coolness, pallor, edema and tautness, often with a slowed infusion.

options.text: There is purulent drainage at the insertion site and the client has a fever.
options.why: Purulent drainage and fever indicate a local or systemic infection.

options.text: There is blistering and skin breakdown at the site.
options.why: Blistering and tissue damage suggest extravasation of a vesicant drug; plain 0.9% sodium chloride is not a vesicant.

takeaway: Infiltration = cool, pale, swollen. Phlebitis = red, warm, tender cord. Stop the infusion and remove the catheter for either.

stem: On day 3 of a peripheral IV in the forearm, the nurse finds redness and warmth extending along the vein above the insertion site, a palpable cord and tenderness. The infusion is running well. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Flush the catheter with 10 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride to confirm patency
options.why: Patency is not the problem; flushing an inflamed vein can worsen injury.

options.text: Apply a cold compress and continue the infusion
options.why: The infusion should not continue through an inflamed vein; warm compresses are usually applied after the catheter is removed.

options.text: Stop the infusion and remove the catheter
options.why: These are signs of phlebitis. The first action is to stop the infusion and remove the catheter, then apply a warm compress, elevate the arm, start a new IV in the other extremity and document the phlebitis grade.

options.text: Slow the infusion rate and reassess in 1 hour
options.why: Slowing the rate does not stop the inflammation and delays the needed action.

takeaway: Phlebitis: stop the infusion, remove the catheter, restart in a different site (preferably the other arm), apply a warm compress and document.

stem: A client in shock is receiving norepinephrine through a peripheral IV while a central line is being arranged. The nurse notes that the skin around the site is blanched, cool and hard. What is the nurse's first action?

options.text: Notify the provider and ask for a prescription for phentolamine
options.why: Phentolamine is the antidote infiltrated into the area, and the provider must be notified, but first the drug must stop flowing into the tissue.

options.text: Apply a warm compress to the site
options.why: Compresses come later per protocol; they do not stop the vasoconstricting drug from entering the tissue.

options.text: Elevate the extremity on a pillow
options.why: Elevation may help later, but the drug is still infusing into the tissue.

options.text: Stop the infusion at that site
options.why: Norepinephrine is a vesicant vasoconstrictor; extravasation can cause tissue necrosis. Stopping the infusion at the site prevents further injury. Because the client depends on the drug, the nurse immediately arranges another access to resume it while the provider is notified for phentolamine.

takeaway: For any extravasation, stop the infusion first; for vasopressors, anticipate local phentolamine and urgently re-establish access because the client needs the drug.

stem: The nurse finds that a client's internal jugular central venous catheter has separated from the IV tubing. The client is suddenly short of breath, anxious and coughing. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Clamp the catheter
options.why: Air is still entering through the open catheter. Clamping (or occluding the hub) stops further air entry and is the first action; the nurse then places the client left side-lying with the head down (if not contraindicated), gives oxygen and calls for help.

options.text: Place the client on the left side in the Trendelenburg position
options.why: Positioning helps trap air in the right atrium, but air continues to enter until the catheter is closed.

options.text: Apply oxygen with a nonrebreather mask
options.why: Oxygen is important, but the air source must be stopped first.

options.text: Call the rapid response team
options.why: Help is needed, but the nurse can stop air entry immediately, which takes priority.

takeaway: Suspected air embolism from an open central line: close the line first, then left lateral Trendelenburg, oxygen, and emergency help.

stem: The nurse is changing the transparent dressing on a client's central venous catheter. Place the steps in the correct order.

options.text: Put on sterile gloves.
options.why: Third: sterile gloves are put on after the old dressing is removed and hands are cleaned.

options.text: Remove the old dressing with clean gloves, then remove the gloves and perform hand hygiene.
options.why: Second: the soiled dressing is removed with clean gloves, which are then discarded.

options.text: Scrub the site with chlorhexidine–alcohol using back-and-forth friction for 30 seconds and let it dry completely.
options.why: Fourth: friction cleansing reduces skin bacteria; the antiseptic must air-dry before the dressing goes on.

options.text: Perform hand hygiene and put on a mask; have the client turn the head away or wear a mask.
options.why: First: this reduces contamination of the insertion site.

options.text: Apply a sterile transparent semipermeable dressing and label it with the date.
options.why: Fifth: the new dressing covers the dry site and is dated so the next change is not missed.

takeaway: Central line dressing change: hand hygiene and masks → remove old dressing → sterile gloves → chlorhexidine scrub and dry → sterile dressing with date.

stem: A client has a nontunneled central venous catheter with a transparent semipermeable dressing that was changed 3 days ago. Which finding requires the nurse to change the dressing now?

options.text: The dressing is clear, dry and intact, and is dated 3 days ago.
options.why: A clean, intact transparent dressing is changed about every 7 days, so it is not yet due.

options.text: The client plans to shower later today.
options.why: The dressing is covered with a water-resistant barrier during showering; showering alone does not require a change.

options.text: One edge of the dressing has lifted away from the skin.
options.why: A loose, damp or soiled dressing no longer protects the site and must be changed right away, regardless of the date.

options.text: A chlorhexidine-impregnated sponge is visible at the insertion site.
options.why: Chlorhexidine sponges are part of CLABSI prevention and are expected under the dressing.

takeaway: Change transparent CVC dressings about every 7 days and gauze dressings about every 2 days, and immediately whenever the dressing is damp, loose or soiled.

stem: The nurse is teaching a client who will go home with a peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) for 6 weeks of IV antibiotics. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Do not let anyone take a blood pressure on the arm with the PICC.
options.why: Correct. Cuff pressure can damage or occlude the catheter and the vein.

options.text: Flush the catheter using a 10-mL or larger syringe.
options.why: Correct. Smaller syringes generate higher pressure that can rupture the catheter.

options.text: Cover the dressing with plastic wrap when showering and do not swim or soak the arm.
options.why: Correct. Keeping the dressing dry protects against infection; submerging the line is not allowed.

options.text: Lifting heavy objects with the PICC arm is fine once the site heals.
options.why: Incorrect. Heavy lifting (generally more than about 10 lb) and vigorous repetitive arm exercise can dislodge the catheter or cause thrombosis.

options.text: Report arm or neck swelling, redness at the site, or fever right away.
options.why: Correct. These can indicate deep vein thrombosis or infection.

options.text: If you feel resistance during a flush, push harder until it clears.
options.why: Incorrect. Forcing a flush can rupture the catheter or push a clot into the circulation; the client should stop and call the home infusion nurse.

takeaway: PICC home care: no BP or tight sleeves on that arm, 10-mL syringes, keep the dressing dry, avoid heavy lifting, never force a flush, and report swelling, redness or fever.

stem: A client's parenteral nutrition (PN) bag is almost empty at 85 mL/hr, and the pharmacy reports that the next bag will be 2 hours late. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Hang 10% dextrose in water at 85 mL/hr until the new bag arrives
options.why: PN contains concentrated dextrose, and the body responds with high insulin output. Stopping it abruptly can cause rebound hypoglycemia, so D10W is infused at the same rate (per facility protocol) and glucose is monitored.

options.text: Stop the infusion and flush the line with 0.9% sodium chloride
options.why: Abruptly stopping PN risks rebound hypoglycemia, and the line may occlude.

options.text: Hang 0.9% sodium chloride at 85 mL/hr
options.why: Saline provides no dextrose and does not prevent rebound hypoglycemia.

options.text: Double the rate of the new bag when it arrives to catch up
options.why: PN is never sped up to make up for lost time; a sudden glucose load can cause hyperglycemia and osmotic diuresis.

takeaway: Never stop PN abruptly or speed it up to catch up; if a bag is delayed, hang D10W at the same rate per protocol and check glucose.

stem: A client is receiving a 3-in-1 total nutrient admixture (dextrose, amino acids and lipids) through a central venous catheter. Which actions by the nurse are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Infuse the admixture through a dedicated lumen.
options.why: Correct. A dedicated lumen lowers the risk of infection and drug incompatibility; other medications are not added to or infused with PN.

options.text: Check capillary blood glucose every 4 to 6 hours as prescribed.
options.why: Correct. The high dextrose load can cause hyperglycemia, so glucose is checked regularly and insulin is given per protocol.

options.text: Increase the infusion rate if the infusion falls behind schedule.
options.why: Incorrect. Speeding up PN can cause hyperglycemia and fluid overload; the rate stays as prescribed.

options.text: Use a 1.2-micron in-line filter.
options.why: Correct. Lipid-containing admixtures require a 1.2-micron filter; the 0.22-micron filter used for dextrose–amino acid solutions would block lipid particles.

options.text: Weigh the client daily at the same time.
options.why: Correct. Daily weights track fluid balance and nutritional response.

options.text: Change the administration set every 96 hours.
options.why: Incorrect. Tubing for lipid-containing PN is changed within 24 hours of hanging because lipids support bacterial growth.

takeaway: PN with lipids: dedicated lumen, 1.2-micron filter, tubing changed every 24 hours, glucose and weight monitoring, and never catch up the rate.

stem: The nurse is preparing to give a unit of packed red blood cells to a client with an established 20-gauge IV. Place the steps in the correct order.

options.text: Obtain the unit of packed red blood cells from the blood bank.
options.why: Third: the unit is picked up only when the nurse is ready to start it, because the transfusion should begin promptly after release.

options.text: Confirm the provider's prescription and that signed transfusion consent is in the record.
options.why: First: the prescription and consent must be verified before any preparation.

options.text: Begin the infusion slowly and remain with the client for the first 15 minutes.
options.why: Fifth: most severe reactions occur early, so the nurse starts slowly and observes the client closely.

options.text: With a second qualified licensed person, verify the client's identifiers and the unit's information at the bedside.
options.why: Fourth: two-person bedside verification of the client and unit prevents ABO-incompatible transfusion.

options.text: Prime a blood administration set with an in-line filter using 0.9% sodium chloride.
options.why: Second: the tubing is prepared before the blood is obtained so there is no delay once the unit arrives.

takeaway: Blood administration: prescription and consent → prime set with 0.9% sodium chloride → obtain unit → two-person bedside check → start slowly and stay 15 minutes.

stem: A nurse is orienting a new graduate to blood transfusion safety. Which practices should the nurse reinforce? Select all that apply.

options.text: Use only 0.9% sodium chloride in the blood administration set.
options.why: Correct. Dextrose solutions can cause red cells to clump and hemolyze, and lactated Ringer's contains calcium, which can cause clotting in the line.

options.text: Complete each unit within 4 hours of spiking it.
options.why: Correct. Infusions longer than 4 hours increase the risk of bacterial growth.

options.text: Warm a cold unit briefly in the unit microwave.
options.why: Incorrect. Microwaving causes hemolysis; only an approved blood warmer is used when warming is indicated.

options.text: Inject a scheduled IV antibiotic into the blood bag to save time.
options.why: Incorrect. Nothing is added to blood products, and no medications are infused through the blood line.

options.text: Obtain vital signs before the transfusion and again 15 minutes after it starts.
options.why: Correct. Baseline and early vital signs allow detection of a transfusion reaction.

options.text: Use a blood administration set with an in-line filter.
options.why: Correct. The filter removes clots and debris from the blood product.

takeaway: Blood transfusion basics: 0.9% sodium chloride only, filter set, nothing added to the bag, vital signs before and at 15 minutes, finish within 4 hours.

stem: A child is prescribed a medication in mg/kg, and the child's weight is recorded in pounds. Place the nurse's calculation steps in the correct order before giving the dose.

options.text: Calculate the safe dose range using the mg/kg values in the drug reference.
options.why: Second: the safe range is calculated from the weight in kilograms.

options.text: Calculate the volume to give from the concentration available.
options.why: Fourth: once the dose is confirmed safe, the volume is calculated (desired ÷ have × volume).

options.text: Compare the prescribed dose with the safe dose range.
options.why: Third: the nurse confirms the dose falls within the range, or clarifies it with the provider if it does not.

options.text: Convert the child's weight from pounds to kilograms.
options.why: First: pediatric doses are weight-based in kilograms, so pounds are divided by 2.2 first.

takeaway: Pediatric dosing order: lb → kg, safe range, compare with prescribed dose, then calculate the volume.

stem: An 81-year-old client taking lisinopril and tamsulosin reported dizziness when standing this morning. At 0300 the client turns on the call light and says, "I need to get to the bathroom." Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: Have the client sit on the edge of the bed for a few minutes before standing, then assist the client to the bathroom.
options.why: Both drugs can cause orthostatic hypotension. Dangling before standing lets blood pressure adjust, and staying with the client prevents a fall if dizziness recurs.

options.text: Raise all four side rails and offer a bedpan instead.
options.why: Four raised side rails count as a restraint and increase injury risk because clients climb over them; it also does not address the need to toilet safely.

options.text: Encourage the client to walk quickly so the trip is short.
options.why: Hurrying increases the chance of losing balance; slow, deliberate position changes are safer for a client with orthostatic dizziness.

options.text: Ask the client to wait until the day shift, when more staff are available.
options.why: Delaying toileting is a common trigger for unassisted attempts to get up, which is a leading cause of inpatient falls.

takeaway: For orthostatic dizziness, change position slowly (lie, sit and dangle, then stand) and stay with the client; respond promptly to toileting requests.

stem: The nurse discovers smoke and flames coming from a client's room. The client is in bed. Place the nurse's actions in the correct order.

options.text: Close the door to the room and nearby doors to contain smoke and fire.
options.why: Containment is the third step (C in RACE); closing doors slows the spread of smoke and fire once the client is out and the alarm is raised.

options.text: Activate the fire alarm and report the fire's location.
options.why: Alarm is the second step (A in RACE); it brings help and starts the facility fire response after the client in immediate danger is moved.

options.text: Remove the client from the room to a safe area.
options.why: Rescue comes first (R in RACE) because the client in the room is in immediate danger.

options.text: Extinguish the fire if it is small, or evacuate as directed if it is not.
options.why: Extinguish/evacuate is the final step (E in RACE), using PASS with the extinguisher only if the fire is small and contained.

takeaway: Fire response follows RACE: Rescue, Alarm, Contain, Extinguish/Evacuate. Use PASS (Pull, Aim, Squeeze, Sweep) only for a small fire.

stem: A client in the emergency department becomes violent, strikes a staff member, and is placed in four-point restraints during the emergency before a prescription is obtained. Which action meets federal (CMS) requirements for this situation?

options.text: Obtain a PRN restraint prescription so restraints can be reapplied if the behavior recurs.
options.why: PRN (as-needed) restraint prescriptions are not permitted; each episode requires its own prescription.

options.text: Have the prescription renewed every 24 hours while the client remains restrained.
options.why: For violent or self-destructive behavior, an adult's prescription may be written for no more than 4 hours at a time (2 hours for ages 9 to 17, 1 hour under age 9).

options.text: Obtain a prescription promptly and ensure the client has a face-to-face evaluation within 1 hour of restraint application.
options.why: CMS requires a prescription from a licensed provider as soon as possible and an in-person evaluation by a physician, licensed independent practitioner, or trained RN/PA within 1 hour when restraint is used for violent behavior.

options.text: Check the client and document circulation every 4 hours.
options.why: A client restrained for violence needs continuous monitoring with frequent documented checks (commonly every 15 minutes per policy); every 4 hours is far too infrequent.

takeaway: Restraint for violent behavior: no PRN orders, prescription time-limited (4 hours for adults), face-to-face evaluation within 1 hour, and continuous monitoring.

stem: The nurse is about to give oral medications to a client who is hard of hearing. When the nurse asks, "Are you Mr. Okonkwo?" the client smiles and says, "Yes." What should the nurse do next?

options.text: Give the medications, because the client confirmed his name.
options.why: A yes/no answer is not reliable, especially for a client who may not have heard the question; this is how wrong-client errors happen.

options.text: Ask the client to state his full name and date of birth, and compare the answers with the identification band and the medication record.
options.why: Two client identifiers stated by the client and matched against the band and medication record is the standard for safe identification.

options.text: Confirm the room and bed number before giving the medications.
options.why: Room and bed numbers are never acceptable identifiers because clients move rooms and beds.

options.text: Ask the client's roommate to confirm the client's name.
options.why: A roommate is not a reliable source and this approach also breaches the client's privacy.

takeaway: Use at least two identifiers (such as name and date of birth), have the client state them, and match them to the ID band and record; never use room number.

stem: A charge nurse is working to reduce errors that occur during shift handoff. Which practice should the charge nurse promote?

options.text: Recording a report on a voice recorder so the oncoming nurse can listen later.
options.why: Recorded reports remove the chance to ask questions or clarify, which is a major source of handoff errors.

options.text: Giving report at the nurses' station to keep it brief.
options.why: Station report can be efficient but misses the chance to verify infusions, lines, and the client's condition together at the bedside.

options.text: Allowing each nurse to report in whatever order he or she prefers.
options.why: Unstructured reports lead to omitted information; standardized formats are recommended to reduce handoff errors.

options.text: Using a standardized handoff tool at the bedside, checking infusions and lines together, and allowing time for questions.
options.why: Structured handoff (for example, SBAR or I-PASS) at the bedside, with two-way questions and verification, is the best way to prevent communication-related errors.

takeaway: Safe handoff is standardized, done at the bedside when possible, includes verification of lines and infusions, and allows two-way questions.

stem: A client with a documented latex allergy asks which foods might cause a similar reaction. Which foods should the nurse include in the teaching? Select all that apply.

options.text: Bananas
options.why: Correct. Banana is one of the foods most often cross-reactive with latex (latex-fruit syndrome).

options.text: Avocados
options.why: Correct. Avocado proteins cross-react with latex and commonly cause reactions in latex-allergic clients.

options.text: Kiwi
options.why: Correct. Kiwi is a well-known latex cross-reactive fruit.

options.text: Chestnuts
options.why: Correct. Chestnut is one of the classic latex cross-reactive foods.

options.text: Eggs
options.why: Incorrect. Egg allergy is unrelated to latex allergy; eggs are not a latex cross-reactive food.

options.text: Cow's milk
options.why: Incorrect. Milk proteins do not cross-react with latex.

takeaway: Latex-fruit syndrome: teach clients with latex allergy to watch for reactions to banana, avocado, kiwi, and chestnut.

stem: A client has a sealed radioactive implant in place for cervical cancer. Which action by the nurse follows radiation safety principles?

options.text: Assign the same nurse to the client every day for continuity of care.
options.why: Staff should be rotated so no one nurse accumulates excessive exposure.

options.text: Plan care so tasks are done efficiently to limit time in the room, and wear a dosimeter badge.
options.why: Time, distance, and shielding are the core principles; minimizing time near the source and monitoring exposure with a badge protect the nurse.

options.text: Allow the client's 10-year-old grandchild to visit at the bedside for a short time.
options.why: Children under 18 and pregnant visitors should not visit a client with a radiation implant.

options.text: Encourage the client to walk in the hallway to prevent complications of immobility.
options.why: The client stays in a private room, usually on bedrest, to keep the implant in place and limit others' exposure.

takeaway: Radiation safety = time, distance, shielding: limit time, keep distance, rotate staff, wear a dosimeter, and restrict children and pregnant visitors.

stem: The home health nurse visits an 84-year-old client with advanced macular degeneration who lives alone. Which recommendations address the client's vision loss to improve home safety? Select all that apply.

options.text: Mark the edges of stair steps with brightly colored, high-contrast tape.
options.why: Correct. Central vision loss makes depth and edges hard to judge; high contrast at step edges reduces missteps and falls.

options.text: Use bright, even lighting and reduce glare with shades or matte surfaces.
options.why: Correct. Clients with macular degeneration need more light to see detail, and glare further reduces usable vision.

options.text: Use large-print or tactile labels and a magnifier for medicine bottles.
options.why: Correct. Reading small print on labels is difficult with central vision loss, which raises the risk of medication errors.

options.text: Keep furniture and frequently used items in the same places.
options.why: Correct. A predictable layout lets the client rely on memory and peripheral vision to move around safely.

options.text: Rearrange the furniture often so the client practices finding a new path.
options.why: Incorrect. Changing the layout removes familiar cues and increases the risk of tripping or bumping into objects.

options.text: Dim the lights at night so the client's eyes do not have to adjust.
options.why: Incorrect. Low lighting makes it harder to see obstacles; night-lights and good lighting along walkways are safer.

takeaway: For low vision: more light with less glare, high contrast at edges, large print or magnification, and a consistent layout.

stem: A client with carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE) cultured from a draining abdominal wound is admitted to a medical unit. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Place the client in a private room, or with a client who has the same organism if no private room is available.
options.why: Correct. Contact precautions call for a single room when possible; cohorting with a client colonized or infected with the same organism is the alternative per infection prevention guidance.

options.text: Put on a gown and gloves when entering the room, and remove them before leaving the room.
options.why: Correct. Gown and gloves are worn for all contact with the client and environment and are removed inside the room, followed by hand hygiene, so the organism is not carried out on clothing.

options.text: Wear a fit-tested N95 respirator for all care in the room.
options.why: Incorrect. CRE spreads by direct and indirect contact, not through the air. An N95 respirator is required for airborne precautions (for example, tuberculosis or measles), not contact precautions.

options.text: Keep a dedicated blood pressure cuff and stethoscope in the room for this client.
options.why: Correct. Dedicated or disposable equipment prevents transfer of the organism to other clients; shared equipment must be cleaned and disinfected before it leaves the room.

options.text: Wear the same gown to care for the client in the next room if no body fluids were visible on it.
options.why: Incorrect. Gowns and gloves are never worn from one client to another; contaminated PPE spreads multidrug-resistant organisms even when it looks clean.

options.text: Limit transport out of the room to medically necessary trips, and tell the receiving department about the precautions.
options.why: Correct. Limiting transport and notifying the receiving area (with the wound covered and contained) reduces environmental contamination elsewhere in the facility.

takeaway: Contact precautions for multidrug-resistant organisms: single room or cohort, gown and gloves on entry and off before exit, dedicated equipment, hand hygiene, and limited transport with notification.

stem: The nurse is leaving the room of a client with Clostridioides difficile infection after removing gown and gloves. Which action is most important next?

options.text: Use alcohol-based hand rub before leaving the room.
options.why: Alcohol does not kill C. difficile spores, so hand rub alone is not adequate after caring for this client.

options.text: Put on a new pair of gloves before touching the door handle.
options.why: Gloves are removed before leaving; wearing gloves in the hallway spreads contamination.

options.text: Wipe the stethoscope with an alcohol pad and take it to the next room.
options.why: Dedicated equipment should stay in the room, and alcohol does not kill spores; surfaces need a sporicidal (for example, bleach) product.

options.text: Wash hands with soap and water.
options.why: Soap, water, and friction physically remove C. difficile spores, which alcohol-based rubs do not destroy.

takeaway: For C. difficile, use contact precautions, dedicated equipment, sporicidal cleaning, and soap-and-water hand washing.

stem: The nurse checks a client who has soft wrist restraints prescribed to protect an arterial line. Which finding requires the nurse to intervene?

options.text: The restraint straps are tied to the movable side rails.
options.why: Restraints tied to side rails can tighten or injure the client when the rail is lowered; they must be secured to the bed frame.

options.text: Two fingers fit easily between each restraint and the client's wrist.
options.why: This is the correct fit; it prevents impaired circulation while still preventing removal.

options.text: The straps are secured with quick-release knots.
options.why: Quick-release ties are required so the restraint can be removed quickly in an emergency.

options.text: The flow sheet shows the client was offered fluids and toileting 1 hour ago.
options.why: Regular attention to fluids, toileting, and skin is a required part of restraint care.

takeaway: Secure restraints to the bed frame (never the side rail) with quick-release knots, allow two fingers under the strap, and meet basic needs regularly.

stem: The nurse finds a client lying on the floor beside the bed. The client is awake and says, "I slipped." Place the nurse's actions in the correct order.

options.text: Notify the health care provider and the client's family of the fall.
options.why: After the client is safe, the provider is notified so the client can be evaluated and any imaging or orders obtained; the family is informed.

options.text: Assess the client for injury, including head, neck, hips, and extremities, before moving the client.
options.why: After confirming the client is responsive and breathing, look for injury before moving to avoid worsening a fracture or spinal injury.

options.text: Stay with the client, call for help, and check responsiveness, breathing, and circulation.
options.why: The first step is to stay with the client, summon help, and confirm airway, breathing, and circulation.

options.text: Complete an incident (safety event) report.
options.why: The report is completed last, after client care, to support quality improvement; it is not placed in the health record.

options.text: Return the client to bed with enough staff or a mechanical lift.
options.why: Once serious injury is ruled out, the client is moved with adequate help or a lift to protect both client and staff.

takeaway: After a fall: stay and call for help, check ABCs, assess for injury before moving, move safely, notify the provider and family, then file a report.

stem: A client with a fractured left ankle is non-weight-bearing on the left leg and is learning to climb stairs with axillary crutches. Place the steps in the correct order.

options.text: Step up onto the stair with the right (unaffected) leg.
options.why: "Up with the good": the strong leg lifts the body onto the next step while the crutches support the weight.

options.text: Push down on the hand grips to shift body weight onto the crutches.
options.why: Weight moves to the hands on the crutches so the unaffected leg can step up.

options.text: Stand close to the bottom step with weight on the right (unaffected) leg and crutches.
options.why: The client starts close to the step in a stable position before moving.

options.text: Bring the crutches and the left (affected) leg up onto the same step.
options.why: The crutches and injured leg follow the strong leg up to the step.

options.text: Regain balance on the step before starting the next stair.
options.why: The client steadies before repeating the sequence to prevent a fall.

takeaway: Crutches on stairs: "up with the good, down with the bad" — the unaffected leg leads going up; the crutches and affected leg lead going down.

stem: A client who has used axillary crutches for 1 week reports tingling and numbness in both hands and forearms. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Tell the client this is expected and will go away as arm strength improves.
options.why: Tingling and numbness are not expected; they signal nerve compression and need to be corrected.

options.text: Advise the client to rest more of the body's weight on the crutch tops.
options.why: Leaning on the axillary pads is the cause of the problem, so this would make it worse.

options.text: Check crutch fit and teach the client to bear weight on the hand grips, not the underarms.
options.why: Pressure in the axillae can compress the brachial plexus ("crutch palsy"). Pads should sit about 2 to 3 finger widths below the axilla with weight borne on the hands.

options.text: Recommend that the client switch to a single-point cane.
options.why: A cane is not appropriate for a client who still needs crutch support, and switching does not fix the underlying technique problem.

takeaway: Crutch pads sit about 2 to 3 finger widths below the axilla; weight goes on the hands. Hand or arm numbness means axillary pressure on nerves.

stem: The nurse teaches a client with chronic insomnia about sleep hygiene. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I will get up at the same time every morning, even on weekends."
options.why: A consistent wake time strengthens the body's sleep-wake rhythm; this shows understanding.

options.text: "A glass of wine at bedtime will help me stay asleep through the night."
options.why: Alcohol may help a person fall asleep but it fragments sleep later in the night and worsens sleep quality, so this statement needs correction.

options.text: "I will stop drinking coffee by early afternoon."
options.why: Caffeine's effects last for hours; avoiding it later in the day is appropriate.

options.text: "If I can't fall asleep after about 20 minutes, I'll get up and do something quiet."
options.why: Leaving the bed when unable to sleep keeps the bed associated with sleep, which is a key sleep hygiene principle.

takeaway: Sleep hygiene: consistent wake time, limit caffeine and alcohol, keep the bed for sleep, and get up if unable to sleep after about 20 minutes.

stem: A client with heart failure is discharged with a 1,500-mL daily fluid restriction. Which statement by the client indicates understanding of the restriction?

options.text: "Soup, gelatin and ice cream don't count toward my fluid limit because they're foods."
options.why: Foods that are liquid at room temperature, such as soup, gelatin, ice cream and ice pops, count toward the fluid allowance; this statement needs correction.

options.text: "I'll save most of my fluid allowance for the evening so I'm not thirsty at night."
options.why: Saving fluids for one part of the day leaves the client very thirsty earlier and makes the restriction harder to follow; the allowance should be spread across waking hours.

options.text: "If my weight goes up, I'll just drink less the next day instead of calling anyone."
options.why: A gain of about 2 to 3 lb (1 to 1.4 kg) in a day or 5 lb (2.3 kg) in a week signals fluid retention and should be reported to the provider; self-adjusting fluids delays treatment.

options.text: "I'll spread my fluids through the day and use sugar-free hard candy or a mouth rinse when my mouth feels dry."
options.why: Spacing fluids over the day and relieving dry mouth without extra fluid (sugar-free candy, gum, mouth rinses or oral care) helps the client stay within the limit; this shows understanding.

takeaway: Fluid restriction teaching: count anything liquid at room temperature, spread fluids through the day, manage thirst with oral care or sugar-free candy, and report rapid weight gain.

stem: A client newly diagnosed with celiac disease is choosing meals. Which foods are appropriate for a gluten-free diet? Select all that apply.

options.text: Steamed white rice
options.why: Correct. Rice is naturally gluten free.

options.text: Corn tortillas
options.why: Correct. Corn does not contain gluten; plain corn tortillas are safe.

options.text: Quinoa
options.why: Correct. Quinoa is a gluten-free seed commonly used in place of wheat-based grains.

options.text: Beef and barley soup
options.why: Incorrect. Barley contains gluten.

options.text: Rye crackers
options.why: Incorrect. Rye contains gluten.

options.text: Whole-wheat pasta
options.why: Incorrect. Wheat is the main source of gluten.

takeaway: Gluten-free means no wheat, barley, or rye (remember "BRW"); rice, corn, and quinoa are safe choices.

stem: A 79-year-old client with severe hip arthritis feels the urge to void normally but often wets herself because she cannot reach the bathroom in time. Which intervention is most appropriate?

options.text: Set a toileting schedule every 2 hours and place a bedside commode within reach.
options.why: This is functional incontinence caused by mobility limits; scheduled toileting and closer access to a toilet address the actual cause.

options.text: Request a prescription for an indwelling urinary catheter.
options.why: An indwelling catheter is not indicated for incontinence alone and greatly raises the risk of catheter-associated urinary tract infection.

options.text: Limit fluids to 1,000 mL per day to reduce urine volume.
options.why: Fluid restriction causes concentrated urine, bladder irritation, dehydration, and constipation in older adults.

options.text: Have her wear adult briefs at all times instead of walking to the bathroom.
options.why: Relying on briefs alone does not promote continence and increases skin breakdown risk.

takeaway: Functional incontinence is a problem of getting to the toilet: use scheduled toileting, a commode, and easy-to-remove clothing — not catheters or fluid restriction.

stem: The nurse is providing oral care to an unconscious client. How should the nurse position the client?

options.text: Supine with the head of the bed flat
options.why: A flat supine position allows fluid to pool in the back of the throat and increases aspiration risk.

options.text: High Fowler's position with the head tilted back
options.why: Tilting the head back opens the airway to fluid and makes aspiration more likely.

options.text: Side-lying with the head turned toward the nurse, with suction ready
options.why: Side-lying lets fluid drain out of the mouth instead of into the airway, and suction removes any pooled secretions.

options.text: Prone with the face turned to one side
options.why: Prone positioning makes oral care difficult and unsafe and is not used for routine hygiene.

takeaway: For oral care in an unconscious client, use a side-lying position, minimal fluid, and have suction ready to prevent aspiration.

stem: A client receiving comfort care at the end of life no longer eats or drinks and breathes through the mouth. The client's daughter asks how she can help with her father's dry, cracked lips and mouth. Which action should the nurse recommend?

options.text: Give small sips of water from a syringe every hour.
options.why: A client who is no longer swallowing reliably can aspirate fluid given by syringe; mouth moistening is done without asking the client to swallow.

options.text: Moisten the mouth with a damp oral swab and apply a water-based lip moisturizer every 1 to 2 hours.
options.why: Frequent mouth care with a moist swab and a water-based moisturizer relieves dryness and discomfort safely and gives the family a meaningful way to help.

options.text: Clean the mouth with lemon-glycerin swabs several times a day.
options.why: Lemon-glycerin swabs dry and irritate the oral mucosa and can damage tooth enamel, so they worsen dryness.

options.text: Ask the provider to start IV fluids to correct the dry mouth.
options.why: Dry mouth at end of life is caused mainly by mouth breathing and is relieved by mouth care; IV fluids do not reliably relieve it and can increase secretions and edema.

takeaway: For dry mouth at end of life, provide frequent oral care with moist swabs and a water-based lip moisturizer; avoid lemon-glycerin swabs and fluids the client cannot swallow.

stem: A client in hospice care with end-stage lung cancer reports feeling short of breath while resting. The client's oxygen saturation is 95% on room air. Which nonpharmacologic measure should the nurse use first?

options.text: Lower the head of the bed so the client can rest comfortably.
options.why: Lying flat usually worsens breathlessness; an upright position eases breathing.

options.text: Apply a nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min.
options.why: Oxygen does not relieve dyspnea in a client who is not hypoxemic, and a tight mask can increase anxiety.

options.text: Close the windows and raise the room temperature.
options.why: A warm, still room tends to worsen the sensation of breathlessness.

options.text: Position the client upright and direct a fan to blow cool air toward the face.
options.why: Cool air moving across the face reduces the sensation of dyspnea, and an upright position improves lung expansion.

takeaway: For dyspnea at end of life, sit the client up and use a fan directed toward the face; oxygen helps mainly when the client is hypoxemic.

stem: A client is 2 days after a total hip replacement using a posterior approach. Which observation requires the nurse to intervene?

options.text: An abduction pillow is in place between the client's legs while in bed.
options.why: An abduction pillow keeps the leg from crossing midline and helps prevent dislocation; this is correct.

options.text: The client uses a raised toilet seat.
options.why: A raised seat keeps hip flexion under 90 degrees; this is correct.

options.text: The client is sitting in a low recliner and bending forward to put on shoes.
options.why: A low chair and bending forward both flex the hip past 90 degrees, which can dislocate a posterior-approach hip replacement.

options.text: The client uses a long-handled reacher to pick up items from the floor.
options.why: A reacher lets the client avoid bending at the hip; this is correct.

takeaway: After posterior hip replacement: no hip flexion past 90 degrees, no crossing the legs, no internal rotation; use raised seats, reachers, and abduction pillows.

stem: The nurse is reviewing findings from several 12-month well-child visits. Which finding should the nurse refer for further developmental evaluation?

options.text: A 12-month-old does not babble, point or wave and rarely responds when called by name.
options.why: No babbling, pointing or other gestures by 12 months, especially with poor response to name, is a red flag for a communication delay or autism spectrum disorder and needs prompt referral for evaluation and hearing testing.

options.text: A 12-month-old pulls to stand and walks while holding furniture but does not yet walk alone.
options.why: Cruising along furniture is expected at 12 months; many children walk independently between about 12 and 15 months, and failure to walk is a concern at about 18 months.

options.text: A 12-month-old says "mama" and "dada" to the right parent but has no other words.
options.why: Using "mama" and "dada" specifically is an expected 12-month language milestone; a larger vocabulary develops over the second year.

options.text: A 12-month-old repeatedly drops toys from the high chair and watches where they land.
options.why: Dropping objects and looking for them reflects developing object permanence and is normal play at this age.

takeaway: By 12 months, an infant should babble, use gestures such as pointing and waving, and respond to his or her name; absence of these needs referral.

stem: A 46-year-old client with no personal or family history of colorectal cancer or polyps asks when to begin colorectal cancer screening. Based on U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommendations, how should the nurse respond?

options.text: "Screening is recommended starting at age 50."
options.why: Age 50 was the former starting age; the USPSTF lowered it to 45 in 2021.

options.text: "Screening is recommended now, because it begins at age 45 for adults at average risk."
options.why: The USPSTF recommends colorectal cancer screening for adults 45 to 75 years at average risk.

options.text: "You can wait until age 55 because you have no family history."
options.why: Average-risk adults should begin at 45; having no family history does not delay screening.

options.text: "Screening is only needed if you notice blood in your stool."
options.why: Screening is done in people without symptoms; rectal bleeding needs diagnostic evaluation, not screening.

takeaway: USPSTF: screen average-risk adults for colorectal cancer from age 45 through 75.

stem: Based on USPSTF recommendations, which client should the nurse identify as needing a one-time abdominal ultrasound to screen for abdominal aortic aneurysm?

options.text: A 58-year-old man who currently smokes one pack per day
options.why: Routine AAA screening is not recommended before age 65, even for people who smoke.

options.text: A 70-year-old woman who has never smoked
options.why: The USPSTF recommends against routine AAA screening in women who have never smoked.

options.text: A 68-year-old man who quit smoking 10 years ago
options.why: Men aged 65 to 75 who have ever smoked should have a one-time ultrasound screening for AAA.

options.text: An 82-year-old man who smoked in his twenties
options.why: The recommendation applies to men aged 65 to 75; routine screening is not recommended at 82.

takeaway: USPSTF: one-time ultrasound AAA screening for men aged 65 to 75 who have ever smoked.

stem: The nurse teaches a client who is 10 weeks pregnant about food safety. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I will heat deli meats until they are steaming hot before eating them."
options.why: Heating deli meats until steaming kills Listeria; this is correct.

options.text: "I will avoid swordfish and king mackerel because of their mercury content."
options.why: These fish are high in mercury and should be avoided in pregnancy; this is correct.

options.text: "I will wash fresh fruits and vegetables before eating them."
options.why: Washing produce reduces exposure to Listeria and Toxoplasma; this is correct.

options.text: "The fresh queso fresco from the farmers' market is fine since it's made locally."
options.why: Soft cheeses such as queso fresco, especially when made from unpasteurized (raw) milk, can carry Listeria, which can cause miscarriage, stillbirth or newborn infection. Pregnant clients should avoid them unless the label states they are made with pasteurized milk.

takeaway: In pregnancy, avoid unpasteurized soft cheeses and cold deli meats (Listeria) and high-mercury fish; wash produce.

stem: A client who is exclusively breastfeeding her 6-day-old newborn asks whether the baby needs any vitamins. Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "Your baby should get 400 international units of liquid vitamin D every day, starting in the first few days of life."
options.why: The AAP recommends 400 international units of vitamin D daily, beginning soon after birth, for infants who are breastfed or partially breastfed, because human milk contains little vitamin D. This prevents rickets.

options.text: "Breast milk provides all the vitamins your baby needs, so no supplement is necessary."
options.why: Breast milk is the ideal food but is low in vitamin D, so breastfed infants need a daily supplement.

options.text: "Vitamin D drops can wait until your baby starts solid foods at about 6 months."
options.why: Supplementation should begin in the first days of life, not when solids are introduced.
