options.text: "Ten to fifteen minutes of direct sunlight each day will give your baby enough vitamin D."
options.why: Infants younger than 6 months should be kept out of direct sunlight to prevent sunburn; sun exposure is not a safe or reliable vitamin D source for newborns.

takeaway: Breastfed and partially breastfed infants need 400 international units of vitamin D daily starting in the first few days of life; keep infants under 6 months out of direct sun.

stem: The nurse teaches parents how to care for their newborn's penis after a circumcision done with a Gomco clamp. Which statement by a parent indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I will put petroleum jelly on the tip with each diaper change."
options.why: Petroleum jelly keeps the healing area from sticking to the diaper; this is correct after a clamp circumcision.

options.text: "I will gently wash off the yellow crust that forms on the tip."
options.why: The yellowish film is normal healing tissue that forms by about day 2 and should not be removed; scrubbing it can cause bleeding.

options.text: "I will fasten the diaper loosely for the next few days."
options.why: A loose diaper reduces pressure and friction on the healing area; this is correct.

options.text: "I will call the provider if there is bleeding that keeps oozing."
options.why: Persistent bleeding is a complication that should be reported; this is correct.

takeaway: After circumcision, the yellow exudate is normal healing tissue — leave it alone; use petroleum jelly (for clamp methods) and report bleeding or no urination.

stem: During an annual wellness visit, an 80-year-old client who lives independently describes several changes. Which changes are consistent with normal aging? Select all that apply.

options.text: Decreased sense of thirst
options.why: Correct. Thirst sensation declines with age, which is why older adults are at risk for dehydration.

options.text: Taking longer to recall a name, which usually comes back later
options.why: Correct. Slower recall and occasional word- or name-finding pauses are common with normal aging when they do not interfere with daily function.

options.text: Needing reading glasses or more light for close work
options.why: Correct. Presbyopia, loss of near focusing, develops with aging.

options.text: Waking once or twice at night to urinate
options.why: Correct. Bladder capacity decreases with age, so nocturia is common.

options.text: New confusion that developed over the past 2 days
options.why: Incorrect. Acute confusion is not normal aging; it suggests delirium and needs prompt evaluation for causes such as infection or medication effects.

options.text: Memory loss that prevents managing finances and medications
options.why: Incorrect. Memory loss that interferes with daily function is not normal aging and suggests a neurocognitive disorder.

takeaway: Normal aging includes reduced thirst, slower recall, presbyopia and nocturia; sudden confusion or memory loss that impairs daily function is never "just aging."

stem: The nurse plans to teach a client recovering from a myocardial infarction about a heart-healthy diet. Which observation best indicates the client is ready to learn?

options.text: The client nods while watching television when the nurse mentions diet.
options.why: Nodding while distracted does not show engagement or readiness.

options.text: The client says, "Go ahead," while rating chest wall pain 7 out of 10.
options.why: Significant pain interferes with attention and learning; pain should be controlled first.

options.text: The client asks, "Which foods should I stop eating now that I've had a heart attack?"
options.why: Asking a specific question shows motivation and readiness to learn, which is the best time to teach.

options.text: The client's spouse says the client is ready to hear about the diet.
options.why: Readiness must be assessed in the learner; the spouse's opinion does not confirm the client's readiness.

takeaway: Teach when the learner shows readiness — asking questions, comfortable, and not anxious or in pain.

stem: The nurse is teaching the parents of an 18-month-old about injury prevention. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep the child in a rear-facing car seat until reaching the seat's highest height or weight limit.
options.why: Correct. Current AAP guidance is to keep children rear-facing as long as possible, until they reach the seat's rear-facing limit.

options.text: Post the Poison Control number (1-800-222-1222) near the phone.
options.why: Correct. Poison Control should be called right away for any suspected ingestion.

options.text: Install safety latches on cabinets that hold cleaning products and medicines.
options.why: Correct. Toddlers explore by climbing and putting things in their mouths; locked storage prevents poisoning.

options.text: Set the water heater no higher than 120°F (49°C).
options.why: Correct. A lower water temperature reduces the risk of scald burns.

options.text: Keep syrup of ipecac at home to use after a poisoning.
options.why: Incorrect. Syrup of ipecac is no longer recommended; parents should call Poison Control.

options.text: Turn the car seat to face forward now that the child is older than 1 year.
options.why: Incorrect. Age 1 is no longer the cutoff; children stay rear-facing until they outgrow the seat's rear-facing limits.

takeaway: Toddler safety: rear-facing car seats as long as possible, locked storage, Poison Control number (no ipecac), and water heater at or below 120°F.

stem: The nurse teaches a client who is 24 weeks pregnant with her second child about the Tdap vaccine. Which statement by the client indicates understanding?

options.text: "I had Tdap during my first pregnancy 2 years ago, so I don't need it again."
options.why: Tdap is recommended during every pregnancy, regardless of when the last dose was given.

options.text: "It is safer to get Tdap after the baby is born."
options.why: Giving Tdap after birth does not provide the newborn with protective maternal antibodies; it should be given during pregnancy.

options.text: "Only my partner needs the Tdap vaccine, not me."
options.why: Vaccinating close contacts helps, but the pregnant client's vaccination is what passes antibodies to the baby.

options.text: "I should get Tdap during this pregnancy, between 27 and 36 weeks."
options.why: CDC/ACIP recommends Tdap during each pregnancy at 27 to 36 weeks so antibodies pass to the baby and protect against pertussis.

takeaway: Give Tdap in every pregnancy, at 27 to 36 weeks' gestation, to protect the newborn from pertussis.

stem: A client with advanced heart failure says, "I'm just a burden to my family now." Which response by the nurse is most therapeutic?

options.text: "You feel you've become a burden to your family. Tell me more about that."
options.why: Reflecting the feeling and inviting the client to say more is therapeutic and allows the nurse to assess further.

options.text: "I'm sure your family doesn't see you as a burden."
options.why: This is false reassurance; it dismisses the client's feelings and closes the conversation.

options.text: "Why do you feel that way?"
options.why: "Why" questions can sound judgmental and make the client feel defensive.

options.text: "Let's talk about something more positive, like your grandchildren."
options.why: Changing the subject blocks communication and suggests the nurse is uncomfortable with the client's feelings.

takeaway: Therapeutic responses reflect feelings and use open-ended invitations; avoid false reassurance, "why" questions, and changing the subject.

stem: A client hospitalized for major depressive disorder has been withdrawn for a week. Today the client is calm and smiling and has given a favorite guitar to another client. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Praise the client for the improvement in mood.
options.why: A sudden lift in mood with giving away possessions may mean the client has decided on a suicide plan; praising it misses the risk.

options.text: Document improved mood and request less frequent observation.
options.why: Reducing observation could leave a high-risk client unsupervised.

options.text: Ask the client directly, "Are you thinking about killing yourself?"
options.why: Sudden calm and giving away valued items are warning signs; asking directly about suicidal thoughts and plans is the priority and does not increase risk.

options.text: Call the family to share the good news about the client's progress.
options.why: This delays assessment of a possible suicide risk.

takeaway: Sudden calm or giving away possessions in a depressed client is a suicide warning sign — ask directly about suicidal thoughts and plans.

stem: The nurse is assessing an 86-year-old client with dementia who lives with an adult child. Which findings suggest possible abuse or neglect? Select all that apply.

options.text: Bruises in different stages of healing on both upper inner arms
options.why: Correct. Bruising on the inner arms in various stages of healing suggests repeated grabbing and is a red flag for physical abuse.

options.text: A stage 3 pressure injury and urine-soaked clothing
options.why: Correct. Poor hygiene and untreated pressure injuries suggest neglect by the caregiver.

options.text: The caregiver answers every question and refuses to leave the room
options.why: Correct. Controlling behavior and refusal to allow a private interview are warning signs of abuse.

options.text: Several prescriptions that were never filled
options.why: Correct. Withholding needed medications or care can be a form of neglect.

options.text: A single bruise on the shin that matches the client's report of bumping a table
options.why: Incorrect. A single injury consistent with the history in a common location does not by itself suggest abuse.

options.text: Thin, dry skin with age spots on the hands
options.why: Incorrect. These are expected age-related skin changes.

takeaway: Suspect elder abuse with patterned or multi-stage bruises, poor hygiene, untreated wounds, unfilled medications, and a caregiver who will not allow a private interview.

stem: A client comes to the clinic with bruises on her neck and arms. Her partner stays at her side and answers all of the nurse's questions. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Ask the client about the bruises in front of the partner to show transparency.
options.why: Asking about violence in front of a possible abuser can put the client in danger and prevents honest disclosure.

options.text: Arrange to interview the client alone in a private area.
options.why: Screening for intimate partner violence must be done privately, without the partner present, so the client can speak safely.

options.text: Tell the partner that the nurse suspects abuse.
options.why: Confronting the partner can escalate danger to the client.

options.text: Hand the client a domestic violence hotline card while the partner is watching.
options.why: Giving resources in front of the partner can provoke retaliation; resources should be offered privately and discreetly.

takeaway: Always screen for intimate partner violence in private, away from the partner; safety comes first.

stem: The nurse is talking with four clients who have experienced the death of a family member. Which client's experience most suggests prolonged (complicated) grief that needs referral?

options.text: A client whose husband died 2 weeks ago cries daily and has trouble sleeping.
options.why: Crying and sleep disturbance shortly after a loss are part of normal acute grief.

options.text: A client whose mother died 4 months ago feels sad on her mother's birthday.
options.why: Waves of sadness on anniversaries and special days are a normal part of grieving.

options.text: A client whose wife died 1 month ago says he sometimes briefly hears her voice.
options.why: Brief sensing or hearing of the deceased is common in normal grief and is not psychosis.

options.text: A client whose son died 14 months ago still feels intense longing every day, cannot work, and says life has no meaning.
options.why: Intense, persistent yearning with loss of function and meaning lasting longer than 12 months after the death fits prolonged grief disorder and needs referral.

takeaway: Normal grief comes in waves and gradually eases; intense daily yearning with impaired function more than 12 months after a loss suggests prolonged grief disorder.

stem: A client receiving chemotherapy says quietly, "God must be punishing me with this cancer." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "It sounds like you're wondering if your illness is a punishment. Would you like to talk about it, or would you like me to contact the chaplain or your own spiritual leader?"
options.why: This acknowledges the client's spiritual distress, invites further discussion, and offers spiritual care resources that fit the client's beliefs.

options.text: "God doesn't punish people with illness."
options.why: This imposes the nurse's beliefs and dismisses the client's concern.

options.text: "Cancer is caused by changes in your cells, not by God."
options.why: A scientific explanation does not address the client's spiritual distress and can feel dismissive.

options.text: "Let's focus on getting through your treatment today."
options.why: Changing the focus ignores the client's expressed feelings and blocks communication.

takeaway: For spiritual distress, acknowledge the concern without imposing your beliefs, explore it, and offer chaplain or faith-specific support.

stem: Two days after a confirmed myocardial infarction, a client refuses cardiac rehabilitation teaching and says, "I didn't have a heart attack. The doctors got it wrong." Which defense mechanism is the client using?

options.text: Projection
options.why: Projection is attributing one's own unacceptable feelings to someone else; the client is not doing that.

options.text: Denial
options.why: The client refuses to accept a confirmed, threatening reality, which is denial.

options.text: Displacement
options.why: Displacement is shifting emotions from their source to a safer target, such as yelling at staff when angry about illness.

options.text: Sublimation
options.why: Sublimation is channeling unacceptable impulses into socially acceptable activities.

takeaway: Denial is refusing to accept a painful reality; it can protect early on but becomes a problem when it blocks needed care.

stem: The nurse is screening a 38-year-old male client for unhealthy alcohol use during an annual visit. Which question is most appropriate?

options.text: "You don't drink too much, do you?"
options.why: This leading question invites a "no" and discourages honest reporting.

options.text: "Do you drink socially?"
options.why: "Socially" is vague and does not measure amount or frequency.

options.text: "How many times in the past year have you had 5 or more drinks in a day?"
options.why: This validated single-question screen (4 or more drinks for women) is specific and nonjudgmental; any such day is a positive screen.

options.text: "Why do you drink alcohol?"
options.why: "Why" questions can sound judgmental and do not measure use.

takeaway: Screen for alcohol use with specific, nonjudgmental, validated questions (single-question screen, AUDIT-C), not leading or "why" questions.

stem: A client with bulimia nervosa is admitted to an eating disorders unit. Which intervention should the nurse include in the plan of care?

options.text: Allow the client to eat meals alone in her room to reduce anxiety.
options.why: Eating alone gives the client a chance to hide food or purge; meals should be supervised.

options.text: Weigh the client at a different time each day so she cannot anticipate it.
options.why: Weights should be taken at the same time, in similar clothing, on the same scale for accurate comparison.

options.text: Focus conversations on calories and food choices.
options.why: Focusing on food reinforces preoccupation; conversations should address feelings and coping.

options.text: Supervise the client during meals and for a set period afterward, including bathroom use.
options.why: Observation during and after meals prevents purging behaviors such as self-induced vomiting.

takeaway: Bulimia care: supervise meals and the period after meals (including bathroom use), weigh consistently, and focus on feelings rather than food.

stem: A client who just learned of a new HIV diagnosis is tearful and has said only that she is afraid to tell her partner. Which statements by the nurse are therapeutic? Select all that apply.

options.text: "This is a lot to take in. I'll sit with you for a while."
options.why: Correct. Offering self and presence supports the client without forcing conversation.

options.text: "What concerns you most right now?"
options.why: Correct. An open-ended question invites the client to share priorities in their own words.

options.text: "You mentioned you're afraid of telling your partner. Can you say more about that?"
options.why: Correct. Reflecting and exploring a stated concern encourages the client to express feelings.

options.text: "Don't worry, HIV treatment is so good now that you'll be fine."
options.why: Incorrect. Although treatment is effective, this is false reassurance that dismisses the client's feelings.

options.text: "Why didn't you get tested sooner?"
options.why: Incorrect. This "why" question sounds blaming and makes the client defensive.

takeaway: Therapeutic techniques include offering self, open-ended questions, and reflection; avoid false reassurance and "why" questions.

stem: After receiving report, the nurse must see four clients. Place the clients in the order the nurse should see them, from first to last.

options.text: A client 1 day after appendectomy who rates incision pain 6 out of 10 and last had an analgesic 4 hours ago
options.why: Pain needs timely treatment, but the client is stable, so this client comes after the two unstable clients.

options.text: A client with an upper GI bleed whose blood pressure is now 86/52 mm Hg with a heart rate of 118/min
options.why: Hypotension with tachycardia suggests hypovolemic shock — an unstable circulation problem — so this client is second.

options.text: A client scheduled for discharge today who has questions about follow-up appointments
options.why: This client is stable and the need is not urgent, so this client is seen last.

options.text: A client 6 hours after a thyroidectomy who has new noisy, high-pitched breathing
options.why: Stridor after thyroidectomy signals airway obstruction (from swelling, hematoma, or laryngeal spasm); airway is always first.

takeaway: Prioritize airway, then breathing, then circulation; unstable clients before stable ones, and routine needs last.

stem: A nurse is using START (Simple Triage and Rapid Treatment) at a mass casualty scene. Place the steps of the START assessment in the correct order.

options.text: Check perfusion with a radial pulse or capillary refill.
options.why: Perfusion is assessed third; an absent radial pulse or capillary refill over 2 seconds means the victim is tagged immediate (red).

options.text: Assess mental status by asking the victim to follow a simple command.
options.why: Mental status is checked last; inability to follow simple commands means immediate (red), otherwise delayed (yellow).

options.text: Direct everyone who can walk to move to a designated area.
options.why: The first step separates walking wounded (minor, green) from those who need further assessment.

options.text: Check respirations, repositioning the airway if the victim is not breathing.
options.why: Breathing is assessed second; no breathing after airway repositioning is expectant (black), and a rate over 30/min is immediate (red).

takeaway: START: walking? → respirations (reposition airway; >30/min = red) → perfusion (radial pulse/capillary refill) → mental status (follows commands).

stem: The RN asks an unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP) to measure vital signs for a client who had a colon resection yesterday. Which instruction is most appropriate?

options.text: "Please take Mr. Delgado's vital signs at 1000 and tell me right away if his systolic pressure is below 100 or his heart rate is above 110."
options.why: This instruction gives a specific client, time, and clear reporting parameters, meeting the right direction and communication part of delegation.

options.text: "Check on Mr. Delgado's vitals sometime this morning and let me know if anything looks off."
options.why: This is vague; it gives no time or reporting criteria, so abnormal findings may not be reported.

options.text: "Take Mr. Delgado's vital signs and decide whether he needs pain medication."
options.why: Deciding on medication requires nursing judgment and cannot be delegated to a UAP.

options.text: "Take Mr. Delgado's vital signs and chart them; I'll look later."
options.why: Without parameters for immediate reporting, a dangerous change could go unnoticed for hours.

takeaway: Effective delegation gives specific instructions: which client, what task, when, and exactly what findings to report right away.

stem: A client named her close friend as health care agent in a durable power of attorney for health care. The client is now unconscious after a stroke. The friend says the client clearly stated she would not want long-term mechanical ventilation, but the client's adult children demand "everything be done." Which statement reflects the nurse's understanding of this situation?

options.text: "The children's wishes take priority because they are the legal next of kin."
options.why: A legally appointed health care agent takes precedence over next of kin when the client cannot decide.

options.text: "The health care agent makes decisions based on the client's known wishes, and the care team should follow them."
options.why: The agent named in a durable power of attorney for health care speaks for the client; the team can involve the ethics committee if conflict continues, but the agent's decisions guide care.

options.text: "Treatment must continue until a court decides between the family and the agent."
options.why: Court involvement is not routinely needed; a valid health care agent already has decision-making authority.

options.text: "The nurse should follow whichever choice keeps the client alive longest."
options.why: Care follows the client's known values and wishes as expressed through the agent, not the nurse's preference.

takeaway: When a client cannot decide, the appointed health care agent speaks for the client's known wishes and outranks other family members.

stem: In an urgent care clinic, the nurse notices loop-shaped bruises in different stages of healing on the back of a 4-year-old. The parent says the child "bruises easily from playing." What is the nurse's legal responsibility?

options.text: Wait until the provider confirms that abuse occurred before making a report.
options.why: Mandated reporters must report a reasonable suspicion of abuse; proof or confirmation is not required, and waiting can leave the child in danger.

options.text: Ask the parent's permission before contacting child protective services.
options.why: Parental permission is not needed to report suspected abuse, and asking may alert a possible abuser and endanger the child.

options.text: Report the suspected abuse to child protective services (or as state law directs) and document the findings objectively.
options.why: Nurses are mandated reporters in every U.S. state. Patterned bruises in different stages of healing that do not match the history create a reasonable suspicion that must be reported promptly; good-faith reports are legally protected. Findings are documented objectively, with measurements and the parent's exact words.

options.text: Confront the parent about the bruises to find out what really happened.
options.why: Confronting the parent can escalate risk to the child and is not the nurse's role; investigation belongs to child protective services.

takeaway: Nurses must report a reasonable suspicion of child abuse; proof and parental permission are not required, and good-faith reports are protected.

stem: The nurse manager is reviewing privacy practices on the unit. Which actions violate client confidentiality under HIPAA? Select all that apply.

options.text: Two nurses discuss a client's new cancer diagnosis while standing in line in the cafeteria.
options.why: Correct. Discussing protected health information in a public area where others can overhear is a breach.

options.text: A nurse opens the health record of a neighbor who is admitted to another unit, out of concern.
options.why: Correct. Accessing a record without a work-related need is a violation, even with good intentions.

options.text: A nurse posts a photo on social media of the unit whiteboard showing client names.
options.why: Correct. Posting identifiable information online is a serious privacy breach.

options.text: A nurse leaves a workstation logged in with a client's chart open while going to lunch.
options.why: Correct. An unattended open record allows unauthorized viewing.

options.text: A nurse shares a client's current status with the oncoming nurse during handoff.
options.why: Incorrect. Sharing information with members of the care team for treatment purposes is permitted.

options.text: A nurse discusses a client's lab results with the provider who is treating the client.
options.why: Incorrect. Communication between treating clinicians is permitted for treatment.

takeaway: Share health information only with those who need it for care; avoid public conversations, curiosity look-ups, social media posts, and unattended screens.

stem: A client receives a dose of medication intended for another client and has no adverse effects. The nurse completes an incident (safety event) report. Which action by the nurse is correct?

options.text: Write "incident report completed" in the client's progress note.
options.why: The incident report is a confidential quality-improvement document and should not be mentioned in the health record.

options.text: Place a copy of the incident report in the client's chart.
options.why: Incident reports are not part of the client's health record.

options.text: Include in the report which coworker the nurse believes caused the error.
options.why: Reports should state objective facts, not opinions or blame.

options.text: Document in the health record the medication given, the client's assessment, and notification of the provider.
options.why: The health record should contain the objective facts of what happened to the client and the care given, without reference to the incident report.

takeaway: Document the facts and the client's care in the chart; complete the incident report separately and never reference it in the health record.

stem: An off-duty nurse stops at the scene of a car crash and offers help before emergency medical services (EMS) arrive. Which action is consistent with the protection provided by Good Samaritan laws?

options.text: Give care within the nurse's level of training, accept no payment, and stay until someone with equal or greater training takes over.
options.why: Good Samaritan laws generally protect people who give emergency care in good faith, within their training, without compensation and without gross negligence. Once care begins, the nurse stays until care is handed off to avoid abandonment.

options.text: Perform any procedure that might help, because all actions taken in an emergency are protected.
options.why: Protection does not extend to gross negligence or to care beyond the nurse's training; the nurse should not perform procedures, such as invasive airway techniques, that are outside nursing practice at the scene.

options.text: Leave the victim once bleeding is controlled, because an off-duty nurse has no duty to remain.
options.why: After care has begun, leaving before EMS or another qualified person takes over can be considered abandonment.

options.text: Accept a gift of money from the victim's family the next day as thanks for the care.
options.why: Accepting compensation for emergency care can remove Good Samaritan protection in many states; the care should be given without expectation of payment.

takeaway: Good Samaritan protection covers good-faith emergency care within your training, without payment and without gross negligence; once you start care, stay until a qualified person takes over.

stem: An RN holds a multistate license under the Nurse Licensure Compact (NLC) in her home state. She begins providing telehealth follow-up to a client who lives in another compact state. Whose nurse practice act must she follow when caring for this client?

options.text: Only the nurse practice act of her home state, because that is where she is licensed
options.why: Under the NLC, the license is issued by the home state, but practice is governed by the law of the state where the client is located.

options.text: The nurse practice act of the state where the client is located
options.why: Nurses practicing under a multistate license must follow the nurse practice act of the state where the client is located at the time of care.

options.text: Whichever state's nurse practice act is less restrictive
options.why: Nurses cannot choose the more convenient law; the client's location determines which law applies.

options.text: No nurse practice act, because telehealth is regulated only by federal law
options.why: Telehealth nursing is regulated by state boards of nursing; there is no exemption from the nurse practice act.

takeaway: Under the Nurse Licensure Compact, a nurse follows the nurse practice act of the state where the client is located.

stem: A charge nurse is reviewing which situations should be entered in the facility's safety event (incident) reporting system. Which situations require a report? Select all that apply.

options.text: A nurse notices that a dose of enoxaparin was drawn up for the wrong client and stops before giving it.
options.why: Correct. A near miss, an error caught before it reached the client, is reported so the system weaknesses that allowed it can be fixed.

options.text: A client is found sitting on the floor beside the bed with no apparent injury.
options.why: Correct. Falls are reported whether or not an injury occurs; the client still needs assessment and provider notification.

options.text: An alert client refuses a scheduled dose of furosemide, and the nurse documents the refusal and notifies the provider.
options.why: Incorrect. A competent client has the right to refuse medication; documenting the refusal and notifying the provider is the appropriate response, and the refusal is not a safety event.

options.text: An infusion pump allows a free flow of IV fluid when the tubing is removed from the pump.
options.why: Correct. Equipment malfunctions are reported, and the device is removed from service and kept for inspection; serious device problems may also be reported to the FDA.

options.text: A nurse gives an as-needed analgesic within the prescribed interval and documents the client's pain rating 1 hour later.
options.why: Incorrect. This is routine care given as prescribed and documented; no event occurred.

takeaway: Report errors, near misses, falls (with or without injury) and equipment malfunctions through the safety event system; routine care and a competent client's informed refusal are documented in the record, not reported as events.

stem: A 4-year-old arrives at the emergency department with a temperature of 104°F (40°C), drooling, a muffled voice, and sitting upright leaning forward. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Use a tongue depressor to look at the child's throat.
options.why: Examining the throat can trigger complete airway obstruction in suspected epiglottitis and should be done only where emergency airway support is ready.

options.text: Lay the child flat to get an accurate respiratory rate.
options.why: Lying flat can worsen airway obstruction; the child should stay in the position of comfort.

options.text: Keep the child upright on the parent's lap and have emergency airway equipment ready.
options.why: Drooling, muffled voice, high fever, and tripod positioning suggest epiglottitis; keeping the child calm and upright while preparing for airway management is the priority.

options.text: Give the child sips of cold water to soothe the throat.
options.why: A child who is drooling cannot swallow safely and may need an airway procedure; keep the child NPO.

takeaway: Suspected epiglottitis: keep the child calm and upright, do not examine the throat, keep NPO, and have emergency airway equipment ready.

stem: A 10-month-old has viral gastroenteritis with mild dehydration and is being managed at home. Which instruction should the nurse give the parent?

options.text: Give apple juice or a sports drink to replace lost fluids.
options.why: Juices and sports drinks have too much sugar and too little sodium, which can worsen diarrhea.

options.text: Stop all fluids and feeding for 4 hours to rest the stomach.
options.why: Withholding fluids worsens dehydration; rehydration should begin right away.

options.text: Feed only bananas, rice, applesauce, and toast until the diarrhea stops.
options.why: The BRAT diet is no longer recommended because it lacks enough protein, fat, and calories.

options.text: Give small amounts of oral rehydration solution often, such as 5 mL every few minutes, and continue breastfeeding.
options.why: Small, frequent amounts of oral rehydration solution are tolerated even with vomiting, and continuing breast milk supports recovery.

takeaway: For mild to moderate dehydration in children, use oral rehydration solution in small, frequent amounts and continue breastfeeding or a normal diet.

stem: An adult client has partial-thickness burns over the entire anterior trunk and the entire right arm. The client also has superficial (first-degree) sunburn on the face. Using the rule of nines, what is the total body surface area (TBSA) burned?

options.why: Anterior trunk 18% + entire right arm 9% = 27%. Superficial (first-degree) burns are not included in TBSA calculations.
This counts only the anterior trunk and leaves out the right arm (9%).
This adds the face (4.5%), but superficial burns are not counted when calculating TBSA for fluid resuscitation.
This counts the front and back of the trunk (18% + 18%) and leaves out the arm. Only the anterior trunk (18%) and the right arm (9%) have partial-thickness burns.

takeaway: Adult rule of nines: head 9%, each arm 9%, anterior trunk 18%, posterior trunk 18%, each leg 18%, perineum 1%. Count only partial- and full-thickness burns.

stem: A 3-year-old has had vomiting and diarrhea for 2 days. Vital signs: heart rate 168/min, respiratory rate 34/min, blood pressure 94/58 mm Hg. Capillary refill is 4 seconds and the hands and feet are cool. How should the nurse interpret these findings?

options.text: The child is stable, because the blood pressure is normal for age.
options.why: Children maintain blood pressure until late in shock; a normal reading does not rule out shock.

options.text: The child is in compensated shock and needs immediate intervention.
options.why: Tachycardia, delayed capillary refill (over 2 seconds), and cool extremities with a maintained blood pressure indicate compensated hypovolemic shock; hypotension is a late sign in children.

options.text: The child has mild dehydration that can be managed with oral fluids at home.
options.why: Delayed capillary refill, cool extremities, and marked tachycardia indicate more than mild dehydration.

options.text: The child is in decompensated shock because of the high respiratory rate.
options.why: Decompensation is marked by hypotension and altered consciousness; this child's blood pressure is still maintained.

takeaway: In children, tachycardia and poor perfusion signal shock before blood pressure falls; hypotension is a late, ominous sign.

stem: A 77-year-old client is admitted with a urinary tract infection. Which findings should alert the nurse to possible early sepsis? Select all that apply.

options.text: Respiratory rate 24/min
options.why: Correct. A respiratory rate of 22/min or more is an early warning sign of sepsis (qSOFA criterion).

options.text: New confusion about the date and place
options.why: Correct. Altered mental status is an early sign of sepsis, especially in older adults.

options.text: Systolic blood pressure 96 mm Hg (baseline 134 mm Hg)
options.why: Correct. Systolic pressure of 100 mm Hg or less is a qSOFA criterion and suggests poor perfusion.

options.text: Temperature 95.9°F (35.5°C)
options.why: Correct. Hypothermia (below 96.8°F [36°C]) can occur in sepsis, particularly in older adults.

options.text: Heart rate 78/min
options.why: Incorrect. A heart rate of 78/min is within normal limits; tachycardia over 90/min would be concerning.

options.text: Urine output 50 mL/hour
options.why: Incorrect. Urine output of at least 0.5 mL/kg/hour (about 30 mL/hour or more in most adults) shows adequate kidney perfusion.

takeaway: Early sepsis: rising respiratory rate, new confusion, falling blood pressure, and abnormal temperature (high or low); older adults may not have a fever.

stem: Four hours after abdominal surgery, the nurse reviews findings for four clients. Which client shows early (compensated) hypovolemic shock?

options.text: Heart rate 64/min, blood pressure 148/72 mm Hg, warm dry skin, alert
options.why: These findings are within normal limits and show no sign of shock.

options.text: Heart rate 128/min, blood pressure 76/48 mm Hg, lethargic, urine output 10 mL/hour
options.why: Hypotension, lethargy, and very low urine output indicate progressive (decompensated) shock, not early shock.

options.text: Heart rate 112/min, blood pressure 116/96 mm Hg, restless, cool skin
options.why: Tachycardia, narrowed pulse pressure (20 mm Hg) from vasoconstriction, restlessness, and cool skin with a maintained systolic pressure are classic early compensated shock.

options.text: Heart rate 52/min, blood pressure 182/68 mm Hg, irregular respirations
options.why: Bradycardia, widened pulse pressure, and irregular breathing (Cushing triad) indicate increased intracranial pressure, not hypovolemia.

takeaway: Early hypovolemic shock: tachycardia, narrowing pulse pressure, restlessness, and cool skin before the systolic pressure falls.

stem: A 20-kg child is receiving IV fluid resuscitation for burns covering 25% of total body surface area. The nurse records the hourly urine output. Which hourly urine output shows fluid resuscitation is adequate?

options.text: 8 mL/hour
options.why: This is 0.4 mL/kg/hour, below the pediatric target, and suggests under-resuscitation.

options.text: 12 mL/hour
options.why: This is 0.6 mL/kg/hour, below the target for a child under 30 kg.

options.text: 16 mL/hour
options.why: This is 0.8 mL/kg/hour, still below the target of 1 mL/kg/hour.

options.text: 22 mL/hour
options.why: The target for children under 30 kg is about 1 mL/kg/hour: 1 mL × 20 kg = 20 mL/hour, so 22 mL/hour indicates adequate resuscitation.

takeaway: Urine output guides burn resuscitation: about 1 mL/kg/hour for children under 30 kg and 0.5 mL/kg/hour (30 to 50 mL/hour) for adults.

stem: The nurse is caring for a 2-year-old admitted with croup (laryngotracheobronchitis). Which finding indicates worsening airway obstruction that requires immediate intervention?

options.text: Stridor while resting quietly, suprasternal retractions, and new restlessness
options.why: Stridor at rest with retractions and agitation signals significant upper airway obstruction and hypoxia; the nurse stays with the child, keeps the child calm and upright, and anticipates nebulized epinephrine, oxygen and provider evaluation.

options.text: A harsh, barking cough that is worse at night
options.why: A barking (seal-like) cough that worsens at night is the classic expected finding in croup.

options.text: Stridor that occurs only when the child cries or is upset
options.why: Stridor only with agitation suggests mild croup; stridor at rest is the more serious finding.

options.text: A temperature of 100.6°F (38.1°C) and a runny nose
options.why: Low-grade fever and coryza from the viral illness are common in croup and are not signs of airway compromise.

takeaway: In croup, stridor at rest, retractions, and restlessness (or a child who becomes suddenly quiet and tired) signal worsening obstruction; a barky cough alone is expected.
